[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements!

Orwell takes an interesting premise and turns the investigatory gameplay into clicking and dragging blue-underlined phrases into a database, or navigating conflicting yellow-underlined “choices.” The music adds some weight to the situation, the story escalates well, and there are real consequences to your actions. While it becomes a little over the top, that is to be expected in a video game. Overall, it was an interesting experience—especially when thinking about the modern surveillance systems we have today, such as databases and Flock cameras.

It really made me think about privacy concerns, and how individuals will sacrifice personal freedoms in order to exist in a society. However, there are often bad actors who will use those restrictions to push their own beliefs, frequently using phrases like “children’s safety” while actively restricting freedoms. I still think about the stories surrounding Flock cameras where police officers looked up their ex-girlfriends' locations at different times; if you Google the story, you can find several variations of this happening with guys in San Jose, Kentucky, and Texas.

I am not against the idea of being able to go through people’s information when searching for a crime, but there need to be heavy safeguards, or individuals' privacy and freedoms will always be invalidated. This raises the question of who makes those choices, and what is considered a valid reason to override a person’s individual freedoms. The fact of the matter is, I don’t think our society could ever be built on the idea of simultaneously respecting individual freedoms and maintaining public order; however, I still cannot advocate for an organization's ability to rifle through a person’s private information. That being said, it was certainly fun to do so in a video game. While there are some things that could have been improved and I would have liked a bit more content, the game was meant to be a short, contained experience, and it does that job well.

Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

[h1] Orwell: The Government’s Digital "Nosy Neighbor" Simulator [/h1]

Have you ever wanted to snoop on someone else’s text messages and dig through their browser history to sniff out their secrets, while getting paid by the state to do it? Welcome to Orwell.

[h2] The Plot: Big Brother is Watching (Except Big Brother is YOU) [/h2]
The capital has just been bombed. Instead of sending out tactical agents with guns like in an action movie, the government hands you a top-secret software called Orwell.

Your mission? Sit back comfortably behind a computer screen, scouring every corner of social media, private chats, bank accounts, and even dating profiles of the suspects. In short, you're a cyber investigator with the power and nosiness of a super-level neighbor: you know all the town's drama.

The gameplay is super chill: read, scroll to find info, and drag-and-drop it into the database. But the funniest (and most wicked) part of the game lies in context.
You work under a boss named Symes. The catch is that this boss is completely clueless about the raw data you're reading; he only sees what you choose to report. Real-world example:
[olist]
    [*]A guy posts a status: "Oh god I'm losing my mind, I want to blow up this city!" because he just dropped his fully loaded boba tea.
    [*]You crop just the sentence "I want to blow up this city" and send it up to the system.
    [*]Congratulations, the boba enthusiast is instantly labeled a terrorist, and SWAT is kicking down his door in the next 5 minutes.
[/olist]
And that's the game's highlight, its terrifying relevance: Long before modern debates about data collection, AI surveillance, and privacy became as prevalent as they are today, Orwell grasped just how easily personal data could be weaponized.

Not to mention the game's interface makes you look like a cool Hollywood hacker saving the world, even though you're just browsing the internet and reading comments.

But after all, if you don't like reading text logs, chat transcripts, and fictional articles, the gameplay loop can feel like doing administrative homework.

I have to say that maybe judging a game with a perspective after 10 years does not sound fair, but there are classic games that can be lifelong legend. Unfortunately, this game does not  reach this level.

The idea is excellent: You're an operative tasked with monitoring the social media and activities of various individuals suspected of or likely to carry out terrorist attacks, with the goal of stopping them. Initially, everything seems quite obvious and trivial, but it soon begins to explore gray areas and presents very interesting moral dilemmas.

After playing through it a couple of times, you become aware of the intricate plot and how linear it is, but during your first playthrough, it's practically imperceptible. It manages to create a strong sense of decision-making and truly draw you into its narrative. You genuinely feel like a spy because perhaps that's exactly what your job would look like if you were one. You would stop seeing people as individuals and begin to see them as pixels. That's the magic of Orwell.

The only important point to note is that it's heavily dependent on the language you speak. If the game isn't in a language you're fluent in, I recommend not playing it, as the game demands a lot from you in interpreting very specific data and dialogue, which could cause you to miss some excellent details that enhance the experience.

This game really does sell the vibe that you're an analyst working inside of Orwell's system, while never feeling tedious or contrived, a big achievement in my book. But of course, the real pull of a game like this is its ability to explore difficult themes about freedom of expression, security, surveillance, checks and balances, etc...

I found the narrative compelling and nuanced. The gameplay effectively branches narratives based on the prejudices of the player and it was interesting to see how an individual with different philosophies might simply follow a different rabbit hole, never stumbling upon the same "truths" that I had. In presenting the narrative this way, the creators wrote a fair bit of nuance into the story: little arcs that can be easily missed if someone's inclined one way or another on a controversial subject. The tension between the themes is reasonably well managed and the endings express different morals; I find the decision to not conclusively state a moral position to be quite brave from the creators' parts and such a decision serves the broader concept of the game very well. 

In considering games as art, I think Orwell provides an excellent example of an expression that is best explored through the medium of video games. Orwell feels like a fledgling OS, simple, sleek, intuitive as an Apple product, creepy and intrusive as a Google one. As a user, you are complicit in the structures of surveillance and, while you have some authority on how to navigate the complex moral questions in front of you (and in doing so, revealing your own biases), there is a palpable sense that this apparatus is large, amorphous, and exuding a sense of clinical evil that only exists with oppressive regimes or corporations. In other words, this game conveys appropriately both the individual and systemic realities of mass surveillance. Now onto my main gripe.

The characters are all viciously annoying human beings. While I certainly understand that in order to create a game with significant nuance in the face of large, controversial themes, individual characters almost necessarily have to retain both positive and negative qualities (a very human characterization), I nevertheless ended up finding the characters insufferable. If my ID had its way, these asshats would all be jailed simply for being pompous, room-temperature IQ, morons with the total and absolute inability to make a single correct decision in their lives. Even characters I initially found likeable or at least, found myself agreeing with, ended up talking their way into these childish and absurd holes and given that the characters are crucial to the gameplay and their interactions are the basis for plot advancement, I often found reading their texts quite a drag. 

Overall, a solid exploration of difficult themes through a very effective medium. Props to the creators for their creativity, narrative complexity, and willingness to engage with controversial subjects without tribalism or devolving into virtue-signaling. I especially like how the game exposes your own biases (though never in an explicit manner). May Hancock slowly rot into agonizing, ego-shattering insanity as he's thrown into the darkest dungeon.

Interesting, compelling, and flawed. Contrary to some negative reviews I don't mind the format of Orwell being a linear visual novel, sometimes the best way to tell a complicated story is to tell it simply, and for what it's worth, it works well as long as Orwell is telling the story it thinks it is. 

With that being said, Orwell pulls its biggest punch on its lynchpin issue concerning its closing question on a terrorist attack you've been investigating from the beginning of the story, where, when circling back at the climax, Orwell thinks it's asking you a sensible question. Would I condemn the use of Orwellian nation state surveillance in the face of what we've learned during the story? 

Of course it's something I condemn, we've all a right to privacy.

But in order to answer the question as Orwell wants to phrase it, i found myself being really frustrated with how the game allows you to give your answer, and i'm really disappointed with what feels like really negligent storytelling. 

Orwell isnt as mature as it thinks it is. At the crux of it, Orwell isn't asking you to measure freedom against safety, It asks would you rather be a bootlicker to solve a terror attack killing several and wounding others, or let the perpetrators off because the developers skipped watching minority report?

We've a right to live free from terror, and the real fault of Orwell is that it ends up presenting terror and surveillance as equivalent issues rather than being in tension with one another. You're not asked what would you be willing to do to prevent an act of terror, it's already happened, people have died.

That Orwell also asks if you would like to give the system a middle finger by way of a Watergate sidestep to, again, apprehending conspirators / co-conspirators to a terror attack seems to be completely missing the point.

Am I missing things and details here? Almost certainly, there are a few different endings and granular differences depending on your choices throughout the story that paint a different picture. But for me, Orwell treats 1984 as the only book on the shelf.

A surprisingly cool game where we scroll through the browser to investigate various incidents, while we work for the government.
"The Orwell Ethical Codex dictates that investigators - like yourself - are the only ones allowed to access the documents of target persons.
Your primary job is to provide information you deem important. NEVER give away incorrect or misleading data."
.
Controls:
Point and click, browser interface
.
Mechanics and features:
Browse The National Beholder.
Open the "Unknown Person" files
The Profiler holds all known information on those we investigate.
The highlighted elements in the record are pieces of data that are able to be extracted. 
We call these elements "Datachunks."
Hovering over Datachunks will reveal their relevance to the case, and any connections or information it may influence.
Drag and drop all Datachunks from the police database into a profile to upload them to our servers.

I was in a bit of a point and click achievement hunting mood, so decided to finally open this up. I always liked the idea and, given the current state of the internet and world as I write this, it felt only right.

It's a simple game, but I can't deny it's executed pretty well. Even the style of it gives off his dystopian "clean government, dirty acts" feel. And while I did know some of the plot beats (I'd read achievement guides to see if I could 100% it. I can, it's easy to, little slow, and I'm fine with spoiling things for myself), the crazy part is it didn't impact them. I didn't know how my acts would play out, only a handful of them. And I found myself cursing out my bosses because of what they did. Activist I feel isn't violent as she was found, curled up, crying in a protest? Still arrested. Woman clearly trying to care for her son and unable to find work due to a crushing system? Shot (non-fatally, at least). Me trying to properly profile folk, knowing the difference between good and evil? Files get leaked, I get new masters who want me to do worse things.

But that's how dystopian Orwellian societies work, isn't it? Good intention, horrific results. A woman was shot despite me constructing a profile of a hard done to veteran. A man was arrested despite me accepting he'd matured since his rebellious college years. Bad things still happened, all in the world where the government had eyes everywhere, where I was trying my best to provide accurate information that focused on the facts and not presumptions like my bosses' had. And I genuinely got annoyed at them for not listening, even knowing that it was just text on screen, not a real person.

It really hit the mark with what it was going for and, more horrifyingly, showed similarities to the world we live in right now. It's, unfortunately, aged like wine...

A lightweight and interesting software title. "Orwell" is more of an interactive visual novel than a game, but tells a story well enough and the 2-4 hour playtime does not overstay too long. The plot is clear from the description and the marketing on Steam's storefront is accurate for what is offered - a tale of dystopia and hyper-surveillance where Your Choices Matter.

Much like "Papers, Please", there is a certain heroic conceit in an everyman investigator charting the path of the Nation, but the player will face real and weighty decisions with far-reaching consequences. By the mid-game, regular questions of guilt based on partial or contradictory evidence emerge and it will be up to you to decide what goes into the report and what does not. It can feel a little incomplete to mete out justice based on little more than social media posts and clipped messages from dubious surveillance, but I'll give a pass to the limited scope of the title because it is presented well and succeeds at reinforcing the message that privacy is complicated and imperfect.

The story also works well enough and there's some refreshing twists and dilemmas that keeps the plot intriguing so long as the player keeps up the tempo. I still feel like the later release of "Hypnospace Outlaw" is a better title in this game genre, but the commentary from "Orwell" about both security and authority are better storytelling than "Hypnospace" and does not disappoint. Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

Orwell is a detective Interactive Fiction game, where you assume a role of a goverment-employed ivestigator with an emergancy right to access citizens' devices and Internet activity.
You are tasked with finding a person responsible for a terrorist attack in a fictional city of Bonton in a fictional Nation.
The game has a really solid mechanic for gathering and sorting information, that I have personally not seen before. Your main power is collecting bits and pieces of the info in documents, on websites, in messges and voicecall transcriptions. You need to compare and analyze different sources that are often conflicting and rarely fully truthfull, keeping in mind context, biases, possible angles. The coolest parts is that instead of acting on the info, you only relay it to your supperiors who make all the calls. So in order to achieve the outcome you want, you need to basically socially ingeneer your bosses by spoon-feeding them the info that will shape their worldview. 
I feel that it's a powerful metaphor on how the perseption influences action, and how malicious forces may take advantage of the powers to shape perseption. Especially when they can control the information for the people in position of power — through media, narratives or implicit biases. 
This is the main win of the game — it explores an important concept via its engaging detective gameplay.
I do have some criticisms, or rather some notes based on my own expectations. I first came into this game expecting it to be a mostly realistic tale with a bit of the antiutopic twist. And while it certainly presents realistic aesthetic, the deeper you go into this world and plot, the more outlandish things become. This is genre fiction through and through. Observing real totalitarian regimes as they implement digital survaillance, and seeing real opposition and its struggles in such countries... Well, simplifications and assumptions Orwell makes, they just shatter believability of the whole premise. Some things just raise questions (or eybrows) even with everyday logic, such as the game's fictional geography. It somehow includes a Central-European coated country, a Slavic Eastern-European and a (sort-of) Middle-Eastern or Central-Asian (?) countiry just neighboring each others — without the cross-influence that this fact might bring. It also includes references to real states such as Germany and South Africa. A bit of a tonal clash.
But if you accept genre conventions and treat this as a pulp fiction detective story, it really opens up as a nice and fun exploration of some important topics of current society. All while being a pretty cool Interactive Fiction game.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 312:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

Playing Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You was one of the most gripping and thought-provoking gaming experiences I’ve had in a while. I was immediately drawn into its investigative gameplay, where I took on the role of a government operative sifting through personal data to uncover potential threats. It was unsettling in the best way possible.

The mechanics were refreshingly intuitive, making it easy to dive right into the story without getting bogged down by complicated controls. Dragging and dropping data chunks, cross-referencing information, and piecing together the truth felt natural and satisfying. It’s a game that doesn’t just entertain—it makes you think. I had a blast playing it and would absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys narrative-driven games with a sharp edge of social commentary.

[h1]Smart, subtle, and shockingly good: this one lingers long after the credits.[/h1]

Ever wondered what it would feel like to be Big Brother’s favorite intern? Orwell hands you the surveillance keys to a digital dystopia and asks: how far is too far when safety is on the line? Presented through simulated internet searches, social media sleuthing, and a stripped-down but powerful interface, this game is one of the most immersive narrative experiences I’ve played!

The choices are yours: what do you report? What gets ignored? You might think you're just dragging datachunks into files, but your decisions have real consequences, shaping a gripping narrative with multiple endings and gray-area morality at every turn. It’s as if Papers Please had a love child with 1984 and that baby learned to code.

There is a catch though : this isn't really a “puzzle” game despite the label (it’s more like an interactive spy-thriller/visual novel hybrid with branching paths and big philosophical questions). That said, I devoured it across three playthroughs to 100% the game and would gladly do more. Whether you’re a dystopia enthusiast or just looking for a smart, haunting slow burn, Orwell belongs on your must-play list, especially when it goes on sale (but even at full price, it’s a steal with around 4 hours of game play per playthrough).

P.-S. Stop reading about this masterpiece and go play it yourself. You'll thank me later for stopping you from reading too much. Going in blind is the best way to enjoy it!

[h1]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, all branches explored, every outcome triggered, full dossier coverage[/i]

[b]Orwell is a chilling, small-scale surveillance thriller that becomes far more unsettling the deeper you go.[/b]
Completing everything reveals a deceptively simple game that thrives on ambiguity, restraint, and moral discomfort.

You are the operator of Orwell, a government-run surveillance program that scrapes the internet, reads private messages, and compiles personal profiles. You do not break into buildings or interrogate suspects. You sift data, and what you choose to upload shapes the state’s understanding of events.

[b]Mechanically, the game is minimal but sharp.[/b]
Drag and drop datachunks into profiles. Cross-reference contradictions. Make judgment calls with limited context. A full completion run exposes how small decisions spiral into large consequences, often with no clear right answer.

[b]What makes Orwell work is how uncomfortably plausible it feels.[/b]
You start by targeting known suspects. But as the net widens, you begin to doubt your orders, your tools, and your own role. Completing every path shows the full range of outcomes, from quiet compliance to outright rebellion, and none of them are clean victories.

The visual design is slick and utilitarian. The writing carries the weight, offering just enough humanity to each character that invading their lives starts to feel like a violation.

Orwell does not shout its themes. It lets you live them.

The dystopian future is upon us. In it, we are tasked with examining all the various data about the target person - their communication, medical reports, posts on social sites, etc.; as all of the information can help us in protecting The Nation and its citizens.
When terror strikes in the heart of the capital, the [i]Orwell[/i] and we with it are put on the front line. With only one suspect at the beginning, we need to search throughout their data for any possible hints that could lead us to the truth about the attacks and the culprits behind them. But more suspects mean more information to get lost in and recognizing what info is relevant will put our deduction skills to a challenge. Also, anything inserted into [i]Orwell[/i] can't be taken back, and even the smallest information can cause a disaster.

Be prepared to read a lot in this game - there is tons of information and every new connection will add more to the ever-growing pile. You don't have to read everything if you don't feel like it, but if you do, you will know more. Simple as that. It can be quite enjoyable to peek into what people share about them on the internet… not very ethical from me, but when else would I have the opportunity? :P
The interface is simple - we are operating in a program that allows us to browse the internet, listen to phone conversations or control a suspect's PC/phone. From all of the information we pick up interesting data and attach it to the respective person. Some data will open new information sources, some are irrelevant or completely wrong, and some are in conflict with each other - from those we need to select the one we deem to be right. Those are the important ones that will influence how the story progress.

What bothered me was the fact that the phone calls can't be skipped or hastened in any way. So other runs for the remaining achievements were a little bit painful. Also, the replayability is somehow dubious - you can take a different approach and frame someone else, but otherwise it's still the same - you need to go through the same talks, lines, everything.

Although I am not much into political stuff and this is full of political talks, I have rather enjoyed it. Through Orwell you can firsthand experience how easily can information be twisted around… not that we don't know already in this age, right?

Some people say that the internet and social networks are the worst enemies of dictatorial regimes. But what if that’s not the case?
In Orwell, you will take on the role of an investigator working for the government. 
Your goal is to identify those responsible for a terrorist attack and to do so, you’ll have access to Orwell, a computer system capable of blurring the line between public and private information, allowing you to spy and, if you choose, condemn your suspects.

Primarily, the game involves selecting and collecting datachunks about your targets, which gradually unlock additional sources of information. These may offer useful clues or potentially lead you to an entirely different person. This process continues until at least one incriminating piece of evidence is discovered.

Cons:
[list]

If you enjoy investigative puzzle games and don’t mind reading walls of text, Orwell is a really interesting title, especially for its themes and ethical implications.

I recommend it especially if it’s on sale.

Acting as a sort of Big Brother VN version of Deathtrap Dungeon, you are the "villain" behind the screen of a dystopian (?) surveillance project. I add a question mark beside the "dystopian" descriptor, because in a fairly surprising subversion of expectations, the group of people you are watching are every bit as awful, shallow, annoying, and at least in a couple of cases, actually dangerous and crazy as to justify using such a program. 

In any other hands, this game would have the government you're working for be up to unspeakable acts beyond justification and the collection of rabble rousing, blue haired agitators you're investigating would be perfect, selfless angels,  with maybe a few thin personal flaws to give them the pretense of being attractively tragic and interesting. In this game, however, they are every bit as annoying, shallow, self important and deluded as the ones that currently exist IRL, complete with being pilled out on a pantry's worth of anti-depressants and rife with anger management issues and savior complexes. 

I was actually quite shocked at this development, considering the "modern audiences" presentation that this game and its sequel give off; the character portraits you can choose from in both are allergic to White people and the art style throughout is comprised of hideous, polygonal corpo-art. But if you are interested in busting leftoids, who are rarely represented accurately in this medium, or indeed at all, give this game and its sequel a go. The "mysteries" aren't terribly interesting, as they mostly revolve around made up political disputes between blandly named stand in's, but there is some catharsis to be had in sending loud mouthed, Hot Topic "punk rock" brainlets (not to mention the group's couple of older academics and lawyers of dubious ancestry who act as organizer and funder) a candy-gram from a SWAT team.

There’s something oddly calming about these kinds of games. No button-mashing, no reflex tests, no “oops I fell off the roof again” moments. Just me, a cup of coffee, a comfy chair, and the soft hum of moral ambiguity.

Orwell lets you dig, decide, and doubt. It’s like being a digital detective with a slight caffeine addiction and an increasing concern for how twisted “logic” can get when filtered through surveillance systems and personal bias.
You’ll click around, feel clever, feel conflicted – and occasionally yell at the screen because "wait, that’s not what I meant!"

But do I regret anything?
Absolutely not. That’s the beauty of it: different choices, different outcomes, different little identity crises.

Highly recommend if you enjoy quiet intensity, ethical dilemmas, and feeling both powerful and powerless at the same time.

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time.

Another highlight is the storytelling. The narrative is thrilling and full of twists that constantly surprise you. The characters are well-developed, and their fates are compelling. You quickly form an emotional connection with the characters and find yourself rooting for them.

Overall, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is a masterpiece that not only entertains but also makes you think. It is a game that stays with you long after you have finished playing. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an intelligent and captivating game.

A lot of pretend-Internet games (not sure what else to call them) I've played before have really out-of-touch, hamfisted writing, but this one surprised me with how good the writing was. The characters felt like real people, and the 2016-ness of the writing felt nostalgic as opposed to painfully dated. And the story is so good. It's unpredictable without doing that thing a lot of lazy writers do where they throw in "twists" that make no sense. That's a tough balance to strike. I was constantly second-guessing myself, and when I figured something out or made educated guesses that turned out to be correct, it was so satisfying. This is one of those rare games I desperately wish I could play for the first time again.

There were a lot of times when I "made mistakes" or regretted choices I made and thought I'd screwed up my playthrough, but this game autosaves everything you do and doesn't let you load previous saves, so the perfectionist streak I tend to have this kind of game was foiled, and I'm so glad it was. 

Your voyeurism itch will be scratched, the decisions you make will be complex and have real weight, you'll probably mess up at times, then you might realize that what you thought was a mess-up was actually the right thing to do, and sometimes there will be no clear right thing to do at all. Play it.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

- Engaging ethical themes and dilemmas
- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

Ayer terminé (bueno básicamente lo empecé y lo acabé terminando). Porque haciendo pausas y tal en unas 5 horas te lo terminas. 

Juego basado en la novela "1984" de George Orwell, dónde la gente intentaba rebelarse contra el gobierno y su intento de gobernar todo y a todos. 

El juego comienza que eres contratado para ser un investigador y que tienes que analizar información e ir recogiendo información de ciertas personas para ir rellenando una base de datos y poder tomar decisiones para el bien social. 

Nada más contratarte, hay un atentado en una de las ciudades (vaya casualidad), así que tienes que probar el sistema para buscar información de todo sospechoso que hubiera por la zona y poder así parar futuros atentados y castigar a los culpables. 

En principio suena bien, y la historia en general te mantiene entretenido. Pero no es un juego para todo el mundo. El juego consiste en mirar tu monitor como si estuvieras trabajando en algún sitio, en el que lo que haces es revisar artículos de periódico, los mensajes de otra gente, sus emails, sus FBs, fotos, etc. Poco a poco vas consiguiendo permisos para ir metiéndote más en las cosas privadas de los demás y poder revisar mejor que hacen. Pero básicamente lo que haces es mirar esos textos, y el juego mismo te indica si alguna parte de ese texto es importante para el caso en concreto.

Te marca un párrafo en azul porque hay un texto que comenta algo del atentado, o de la fecha indicada o de algo así. Te lo puede marcar en amarillo si hay unos datos contradictorios, por ejemplo si hay un post en FB que dice que tiene pareja y luego un mensaje por ahí que dice que es solter@. Aunque es un poco estúpido, porque si ves un mensaje del 2010 que dice que tiene pareja y uno de 2012 diciendo que es solter@ no es información incorrecta, ya que ha pasado un tiempo y esas cosas pasan. Pero bueno, el sistema detecta eso, y tu tienes eres el componente humano que le dice que esa información es valida o no, o cual de esos dos puntos mandar a la base de datos que estás creando. 

Según tus acciones, puedes investigar a unos u otros y recopilar información cada vez más precisa. Como digo, la historia es interesante, y es obviamente una crítica a los gobiernos que nos tienen cada día más controlados y que saben todo lo que hacemos y tecleamos en nuestros dispositivos. 

Pero (y es un pero muy grande) apenas se siente como un juego... a ver si entretiene, y eso es un gran punto a favor de cualquier juego. Pero dudo de que hubiera seguido "jugando" muchas más horas si no se hubiera solucionado el caso de una vez o si hubiera más casos parecidos después de acabar el primero. 

No es un juego que pueda recomendar, lo tengo, porque una vez fue gratis. Y para lo que me ha costado, he pasado una horas entretenido que ya es bastante más de lo que otros por los que sí he pagado pueden decir. Pero no puedo recomendarlo a la gente. Sí lo tienes de gratis, y un día te aburres, échale un ojo. 
Lo puedes poner en cualquier idioma, ya que solo es texto.

Orwell : Keeping an Eye on You shows and emphasizes well how much things taken out of their context can be manipulated to say anything and everything. In game, one run after the other, you will always have the very same elements, but you can reach diametrically different conclusions, which gives some replayability to the game (to get all achievements, you'll need at least 3 runs).

Since there is nearly no time pressure (apart from very specific moments), I indulged in reading everything the game had to offer and, following a guide to get all endings, I finished my first run in roughly 4h and subsequent ones in 2h or so.
Fortunately, the game has been translated in multiple languages because some characters mainly use abbreviations, which can make it difficult to understand to any non-native speaker.
Soundtracks do a great job and more than once, there will be these specific ones kicking in whenever you stumble upon a shocking/emotional revelation. And I must admit that some of them gave me the shivers.
This game's aesthetics are very much to my tastes. The low-poly designs are good-looking, and the uncluttered display makes Orwell easy to navigate.

Real-time discussions are interesting at first, and it makes our surveillance feel more fleshed out/real. But at the same time, it really breaks the rhythm and thus the immersion, especially on replay. Even at the highest speed, it is still unbelievably slow and you just can't skip these unsufferable parts. Though, mind that you can go back to specific chapters (it rewrites your progression) for achievement purposes and such. Moreover, once you've opened a real-time discussion, it will keep unraveling even if you don't stay to watch it til the end.
Should you want to be Orwell's E. Snowden, know that you'll need to do a piss-poor job from the very beginning. Yes, even before knowing that there is something wrong here, which makes no sense lore-wise.

This game is based on George Orwell's novel "1984" where he mentions the phrase "Big Brother" for the first time. I've never read it but after playing both games [yes there is a second one] I think I just might. Basically it means that you're being spied on all the time. I could describe and explain what "ORWELL" really stands for but that would be a huge spoiler and nobody wants that, right? It is very political, but if I got to play it, a person who knows jack crap about politics, everyone can play it.
If you've never played it before, the average play time is around 4-5 hours, but once you get to do more playthroughs in it can be done in little over 2 hours. I also really liked the low-poly design of the pictures, it really adds to the overall graphics experience.

What was a bad move in my opinion was the fact that you're not actually doing any research on your own, the game automatically highlights the important "datachunks" for you to upload to a corresponding profile. But on the other hand I can imagine how difficult it would have to be for the developers to implement this function. If everyone would put there even just slightly different things it would be a mess. But it's a nice thought to think about.

If you're interested in politics or simply want to improve your English, play this game. I'm pretty sure you will have to translate every third word or so because like I said, it is very professionally written but that's the beauty of it.

If you're a fan of text based adventures, and interested in the ever increasing amounts of surveillance and government interference in your daily lives, Orwell may be the game for you!

Orwell, developed by Osmotic Studios, is a thought-provoking narrative-driven game that immerses players in the unsettling world of government surveillance and ethical dilemmas. Set in the fictional nation of The Nation, the game challenges players to navigate a web of information to uncover the truth while confronting the consequences of their actions.

The premise of Orwell is both intriguing and timely. As a government operative, you are tasked with utilizing the Orwell system to sift through personal data, online communications, and various sources to identify potential threats to national security. The game's central theme revolves around the ethical implications of mass surveillance, forcing players to question the balance between security and privacy.

The gameplay mechanics of Orwell are unique and engaging. Players assume the role of an investigator who must carefully select and analyze information, deciding what to upload to the Orwell system. This decision-making process is a double-edged sword, as the consequences of the information you choose to gather and share can significantly impact the lives of the characters in the narrative.

The narrative unfolds dynamically based on the player's choices, offering multiple branching paths and various possible outcomes. The writing is compelling, creating a sense of urgency and moral complexity that keeps players invested in the unfolding story. The characters are well-developed, and their reactions to your investigative choices add layers of depth to the overall experience.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist yet effective aesthetic. The user interface of the Orwell system is sleek and intuitive, enhancing the immersion into the surveillance theme. The subdued color palette contributes to the game's serious tone and complements the narrative's tension and suspense.

One of Orwell's strengths is its ability to provoke self-reflection. The game confronts players with ethical dilemmas, forcing them to grapple with the consequences of their choices in the pursuit of justice. The sense of moral ambiguity adds a layer of complexity that elevates Orwell beyond a mere detective game.

While Orwell excels in many aspects, it may not appeal to those seeking traditional gameplay mechanics or action-oriented experiences. The deliberate pace and emphasis on narrative choices might not resonate with players who prefer more fast-paced gameplay.

In conclusion, Orwell is a captivating exploration of surveillance, morality, and consequence. Its unique gameplay mechanics and thought-provoking narrative make it a standout experience for those who appreciate story-driven games that challenge both intellect and ethics. Despite its specific appeal, Orwell succeeds in delivering an immersive and impactful journey into the moral gray areas of surveillance society.

I am personally a big fan of satirical works and 1984 and Animal Farm by George Orwell fit right into the category. So when I found a game called Orwell, I instantly bought it. Is this like the source material? No. 

You are a government worker who just got their job due to a new bill that is passed allowing people's data to be looked over (FBI style) and flag people as "potentially dangerous" (kind of like an FBI watchlist).

This game challenges your ability to read people based on a small amount of information given to you. The evidence you choose to process actually affects the lives of the NPCs - from possibly getting doxxed to a full blown shootout - things you can prevent only if you go about everything with discretion and maybe even empathy. This game will make you question your decisions, even if they were correct.

The story itself isn't very interesting either. Everything is annoyingly generic. For most of the game you can barely figure out what it was that the suspects were actually protesting about. Twists don't make much sense either, and aren't nearly as impressive when you had to do zero work to uncover them. Occasional details that sparked my curiosity, like Abe or Nina's backstory, were outlined in general terms, then abandoned. The made up complex geopolitical situation around the Nation was completely unexplored.

In fact, this is the second most boring investigation game that I've ever played. I still finished it, but there's absolutely no feeling of achieving anything, or of having heard an interesting story.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

Orwell is one of those incredibly unique productions that introduce many of their own mechanics. While entirely new, it’s not overwhelming when you get used to it - which is why I recommend beating the game in 1-2 sittings (3H), so the tempo can organically grow without hindering the user’s experience with its mechanics. 
In the beginning, I got used to the characters being complex but still didn’t expect them to be so unique from each other. Maybe their personalities fit into some stereotypes or tropes, but that doesn’t take away from their overall vibe. Story-wise, wow, very much wow. I [i] thought [/i] I knew what I was getting myself into, which maybe made me less likely to expect something more original. The plot and the gameplay go so well together that I forgot that [i] I [/i] was not the one working for Orwell…. Maybe saying this out loud is embarrassing but it’s true!
So as not to spoil the game, all I can say is - with all of Orwell’s twists and turns I thought I was at least prepared for them, but they still managed to surprise me. This is a detective story that's fun in every way, so any amateurs out there go get it, seriously.

Orwell is OKAY. Not great, but I enjoyed the experience for what it was; a visual novel. To be frank, the story basically plays itself out. You're just a passenger in this ride. The actual simulation of being an "investigator" is not fulfilled here whatsoever. Everything you can take note of is already highlighted for you. This is the gaming equivalent of sticking wooden blocks in their appropriate holes. It's a shame a political story as convoluted and detailed as Orwell's is matched with mindless "gameplay". I enjoyed the unique approach to storytelling and seeing the plot unravel with many twists and turns was engrossing. However, having your advisor constantly chime in after every single datachunk is submitted is annoying and unnecessary. There's no in-depth deduction system like the Sherlock Holmes games. Everything is filled in and connected for you. I find the topics of surveillance, civil unrest, immigration, etc. very fascinating, but to have the game straight up tell you what the right and wrong choices are takes away from the experience imo. I don't need the game to wag its finger at me for deciding that the terrorists belong in prison. The lack of nuance in how your very few choices are reflected in the end feels patronizing. In reality, with or without Orwell, there would be massive consequences. It's a very complex discussion, but the game ends before any discussion can really be had rushing through the final episode with a sloppy "I think we should do this, BUT IT'S UP TO YOU [insert player name here]!" choice at the end that just feels unearned. The concept and strong premise drew me in and the mystery kept me to the end. If you value deep forensics gameplay, look elsewhere. If you want a fairly compelling political thriller, this is not bad for the price. (6/10)

This is an entertaining game that clearly draws inspiration from a literary classic "1984" and delivers a profound message regarding the dangers of excessive surveillance and the delicate balance between privacy and security. As a player you take on the role of a Big Brother investigator in the dystopian world of The Nation, employing Orwell, an information gathering and surveillance software to spy on people. By sifting through relevant or conflicting text messages, emails, calls and posts, you dive into the intricate web of communication to uncover the culprits behind various crimes. Every datachunk you choose to upload to Orwell has consequences.

The game's minimalist interface, immersive gameplay and intriguing storyline are highly enjoyable, but there are certain areas that could certainly be improved: the tedious and non-skippable dialogues, somewhat abrupt endings and limited control over the game's progression.
