[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]

Just to blow of some steam about how disappointed I am in this game, I'll address a couple reviews:

“Grabs the problem of how we balance our own liberty and our safety and turns it into a thrilling adventure.” 9/10 – Polygon
It does make a feeble attempt at tackling the problem of balancing safety and liberty, but fails miserably. Not only does it not represent what you could call Orwellian infrastructure, it doesn't even try. Access to information is limited and the information itself misinterpreted. Your "superior" is clearly opinionated, easily influenced and not of very high deductive capacity. Hardly a "thrilling adventure", the pace of the game is dictated by the game, not by the player. You can't move fast, despite the game making constant remarks about how you should. Nothing about this is thrilling, it's a very slow burner, except it isn't good. It's attempting to show flaws in Orwellian policies but fails to represent them, only showing flaws in its own design.

“A harrowing look into a reality where Big Brother is always watching” Rock Paper Shotgun
The only "harrowing" thing about this game is how it managed to get out of indev. The UI of this game is atrocious in both mechanical as well as logical sense. Mechanically navigating anywhere in this game is a pain in the bum, and the game punishes you every time you try to make more than 1 action per 10 seconds. The whole bit about conflicting data chunks is just stupid. First of all it should have a dating mechanism in the data collection software, which would prevent 90% of the data chunk conflicts in the first place. Secondly, why bother trying to pick one out of the 2 conflicting data points when all you're doing is presenting to someone who can clearly barely tie their own shoe-laces, much less decide outcomes for other people. I wouldn't let this "Adviser" choose the color of desktop background, much less my or anyone else's legal standing. Oh and did I mention: You can't go back on whatever the "Adviser" was saying either, so tough luck if you wanted to submit 2 pieces of information and started navigating before you can notice the Adviser popping up on screen, immediately skipping possibly vital dialog.

“In an age where so much personal information is willingly released by so many, Orwell brilliantly explores the implications of this data being misinterpreted.” 8/10 – GameSpot
This. That's the exact problem with the game, there isn't supposed to be an interpretation to be done in the first place. At the start of the game, you're presented with the job of a data-gatherer. It's not up to you to interpret this data and neither should it be up to the "Adviser". Not just because his brain activity matches that of a fork, but because he simply does not have all the data. Neither does the player, nobody does. Once the information is conclusive all on it's own and only then should there be an attempt at interpretation. It's a simple rational analysis up until then. Or at least it should've been. Instead the game constantly pedals it's own point with forced story-telling.

About the game Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You, I can say that this game is one of the most thought provoking and immersive experiences I have had in a long time. The game takes place in a dystopian world where the government has implemented a surveillance system to monitor every aspect of its citizens' lives.

As a player, YOU are tasked with being the "investigator" who must review and analyze the information gathered by the Orwell System to uncover potential threats to society. However, it is up to you to determine what information is relevant and what is not, and every decision you make has consequences.

The game makes you feel like you have actual power over people's lives, and the experience of constantly analyzing data and making decisions about what information to act on or ignore makes the whole experience feel very intense and immersive .

The game's graphics and sound design are also excellent, bringing the world of Orwell to life in vivid detail. The characters are well developed, the dialogues captivating and thought-provoking.

Overall, Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is an excellent game that offers players a unique and immersive experience. It challenges us to think about the consequences of our actions and the ethics of surveillance in a society that values freedom and privacy. If you like narrative games that make you think, then this is definitely worth checking out.

I came here having tried Orwell a few years ago and didn't take to it... Then I played "Return of the Obra Dinn" and was so entranced by it I searched for "Game like..." and this came up, so I went back and started over.

I'll just say that this game is NOTHING like "Return of the Obra Dinn".    It feels like the "Walking Simulator" of detective games. You don't 'detect' so to speak, more than you just walk through scads and scads of documents and photographs, and picking out important pieces that are pre-highlighted for you.  Occasionally you get to make a moral / ambiguous choice between two things with far too little / ambiguous information.   This is kind of the point of the game... To show how easily we can be led down a path of conclusion based on scant evidence... Is the player 'aware' enough of the situation to select the correct interpretation.  Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not.

Where Orwell falls down is that the consequence of what you pull out of the documentation isn't always clear.   You can be pulling out loads of stuff, with the occasional snide / snippy remark from your 'advisor', with no noticeable progress in the game.  Then all of a sudden, you pick something and *BOOM*  the whole world spins on its axis, and you suddenly get more context, albeit too late.

Now, as I said, the 'late information binding' thang is the whole Orwell shtick, but it's really s****g annoying when you're playing.  It's only in the end game, that the whole POINT of the game becomes clear and you realise that the annoyance you're feeling has a purpose.

Then the game offers you a moral choice...   Carry on, or rebel.  For me, the decision was pretty clear cut, but it didn't look like it had much effect, tbh.     And that's the other big issue, is that you're never sure if you chose correctly, wrongly, or your choice made no major difference.  Some might say this adds 'replayability', but to be honest, I don't think I can be bothered clicking through dozens of semi-meaningless PDFs for another 10 hours to choose different outcomes to test the theory....

This is a visual novel along the same lines as A Lost Phone. Everything you might want to click is almost always highlighted with a red box, star, or a red/blue/grey page icon by the resource's entry in your listing, so getting lost and missing things is tricky. The main challenge is deciding what to submit as evidence and what not to. In my first playthrough, I submitted everything I found, just to see what it did, but in later playthroughs I was more discerning, shaping the narrative to my own ends.

The story is a fairly good one about omnipresent surveillance, though unlikely to give chills to anyone who knows the NSA exists. The system in the game is *ridiculously* hobbled compared to real-world ones: they can only spy on people they have permission to; they can only view documents and devices that have been revealed through the investigation; they can't communicate; they can't correct any ambiguities with better information; they can't... etc etc. It's a deliberately-hobbled system, for reasons made clear during the game, but it does have the advantage that, technologically at least, they have access to *everything, immediately*.

All possible endings are morally ambivalent, so there's arguably no "good" or "bad" ending.

While there's an option to speed up phone calls and messaging, it only works a little bit, speeding it up from "interminable crawl" to "this is bearable, but still painful to replay". There are some minor bugs about the highlighting of things, particularly where mouseovering things doesn't always show the tooltip describing its effects. But the tooltips aren't critical, you can guess from context.

100%-ing the achievements it is a bit of a pain for completionists, since you have to play through it 2.5 times, but it's entirely possible, and the game repays another playthrough or two because there are multiple endings and outcomes for most of the characters, depending whether you play pro-government, pro-activist, or somewhere between.

[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

Orwell is really good.

It starts as a simple "first day on the job" where you're discovering the world the game takes place in, and the people you're going to learn everything about.

But then the morality of what is in front of you hits. You are gathering a staggeringly terrifying amount of data, literally everything you find about people, through their phones, computers, emails, you even hack into their accounts.
At that point, you either decide to play along the system's rules, follow orders and send people in prison, regardless of the fact they're actually guilty or not, because [b]you made them guilty anyways[/b], or you start to use the scary amount of information collected to actively work against the machine, to right the wrongs of a government that doesn't shy away from considering [b]any[/b] of it's citizens as a threat if that's what it takes to keep the machine going.
A fabricated justification to secretly introduce mass surveillance, a system in which everyone and anyone is a target and where constructed truths that profit the top of the food chain are invaluable in the eyes of the people that operate that very system.


That aside, the group that the game centers around, Thought, is fascinating, and there are many twists and turn in their interactions that will keep you wondering how each piece of the puzzle can fit with the others. Some of these characters are incredibly well written and others are complete mysteries.

The gameplay is mostly browsing documents and sliding data into a box. From which set of data you collect (and which you either by mistake or on purpose, don't collect), different things will happen and you will be able to affect the direction of the story over the course of 5 days.

Visually, it is very clean and neat, almost cold, and it's probably on purpose. Your character is using a software that is "the most powerful mass surveillance tool ever made". It's not here to be pretty, it's here to be efficient.
 The interface is simple and easy to grasp. The "geometrical" style of the pictures in various documents is a nice touch.

The music is mostly just ambience, you don't even notice it until you do, which in my opinion, is just how it should be for this type of game.

At first I wasn't sure if i would like the game, as some story driven games I like, but others I don't. However, I very quickly found out that I was going to like the game, and I enjoyed it the whole way through. Orwell pushes you to use processes of investigation to try and prevent tragedy using a sophisticated surveillance system. The game mechanics are actually very fun, as you have to do some detective work to find connections by eavesdropping on what people say on the phone, over text, through their bank account purchases, social media accounts, etc. You even get to the point where you have to help provide information to a SWAT team during a raid, for example. Your actions have consequences. I got a few things wrong, and some people died...

This game is... strange in a wonderful way. You basically spend the entire game crawling through phone records, text messages, and webpages, putting together profiles of people. You get to decide what's "important" and what isn't, and see what happens based on those choices.

The plot is excellent and relevant, and despite having horrifically bad graphics (which is intended), it doesn't actually detract from the experience.

I keep coming back to this game.

There is not much branching narrative or deeper exploration to be had past the first play, but there is something immersive about feeling like a cog in a much larger dystopian machine. It speaks of the information we offer freely on the internet, and how a uncaring but well-intentioned governmental implement can mismanage things even when they are being careful and methodical.

Each story beat is another day, so I take measured day-by-day experiences, logging out at the end of my shift and logging in the next day to continue my work. There's some meditation to the practice, but it is paired with the stress that every choice you make could have irreparable consequences.

A terrorist bomb kills a number of people, and it's your job to investigate the suspects - with the help of a handy new government surveillance program that gives you access to their email, their phonecalls, their text messages, their credit card statements, and even data on their personal computers. Add any data that you believe is relevant to their dossiers, while ignoring anything that's not relevant. Another investigator looks at what you've added to their dossiers and gives you tips for what to investigate deeper; he can also draw conclusions from what he sees and call in police action.

The entire game takes place within the Orwell desktop interface. It's beautifully simple and yet gives easy access to all the information you'll need. 'Orwell' is a clever game of finding connections between people, discovering motives, and summarily deciding who's guilty of what ... and, ultimately, passing judgment on whether or not a system like this is a benefit to humanity.

Huckleberry pancakes.

1 3/4 cups all purpose white flour
4 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 1/2 cups of buttermilk
5 tablespoon butter, melted
2 large eggs
1/2 cup Huckleberries
In medium bowl combine flour, sugar, baking powder and salt, set aside. In small bowl combine buttermilk, butter and eggs. Add buttermilk mixture to the flour mixture, combine until mixed do not over mix (I prefer to use a whisk it does the best job). Fry at 400 degrees. Pour about 1/4 cup of batter on the griddle and sprinkle with the huckleberries.

Cook on first side about 3 minutes until bubbles appear along the edge of the pancake. Flip and cook for 2 minutes more and golden brown. Serve with a big pat of butter, and some pure maple syrup ( get the real stuff it is worth it).

I wrote this review on a whim after re-reading 1984, but to be sure I was assessing the game fairly I replayed the first couple of "days" (levels). I think my impressions are still accurate, and the game is still not worth playing. So on the one hand, at least the game is memorable. On the other:

In a word (one of George Orwell's own, suitably enough) the game is 'doubleplusungood'. It has very little to do with the author except for the state-surveillance meme - which was, in the first place, only "the tutorial" of 1984 - so that the game seems reluctant to explore or understand its own namesake. This is more noticeable in the sequel, which is less interested in recreating the horrifying Newspeak of 1984 ("we shall make thoughtcrime [ideological dissension] literally impossible, because there will be no words in which to express it") so much as awkwardly recreating the contemporary and vapid phenomena of 'fake news narratives'. It's cheaply political, far from the surgical satire with which George condemned his contemporary socialists, or the Isaianic fury with which he condemned the whole politically progressive enterprise. All told, the devs would have been better off writing an essay on 1984 than making two (soon to be three, I hear) shoddy video game adaptations; but should they direct their talents to original systems and concepts, I strongly believe they can make a playable game.

I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. 

-There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need.

-This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright.

-Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

Orwell is a short but very well executed mystery detective.

The game starts off with the player working as an investigator in a security program called Orwell which allows tracking of every step of every person in The Nation. What starts as a detective case of a terrorist attack with a single suspect quickly turns into series of endless leads and plot twists.

Although most of the game consists of reading text it wasn’t boring for a second. Player has all the information at the palm of their hands and yet not everything is relevant or even true which forces fact checking and making decisions about the information they use and provide to the case. It’s even possible to leave out crucial information if a player thinks it’s a right thing to do.  It’s hard to describe the experience without spoiling anything but the story, consequential choices, dilemmas, connections you make during your investigation and twists around every corner are impeccable and had me on the edge of my seat for the entire playthrough. 

This game is definitely not for everyone, hell, I didn’t even think I myself would like it, but if you’re into mysteries and detectives it’s a must play. I’m usually not a big fan of these type of games or indie games in general, but Orwell blew me away, it was a brilliant experience.

This game saved my life.

I am 35.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Instead of playing the game as someone living under the system, you are a part of the system. You are the one spying on these people and handing over their personal and/or private information to the government. You choose what information to include or exclude. Whether these people live free, die, or spend life in prison is entirely dependent on what information YOU give to your superiors. And your opinion can be swayed. I didn’t know what to expect going into Orwell, but was delighted by its engaging storytelling and effective worldbuilding. In this game, you play as an employee of a fictional government tasked with investigating a terrorist attack. To this end, you utilise the “Orwell” system to monitor the online activity, history, and live chats of persons of interest. This plays like a hybrid of visual novels and point-and-click adventure games, as you scroll in-game websites and remote desktops to find information relevant to the case.

The game’s real achievement is that despite its ambitious concept, Orwell offers a great balance of freedom and guidance. There is just enough secondary or irrelevant information available to you that discovering a new clue feels groundbreaking and rewarding. At the same time, pages containing unread details are marked on your menu and guiding commentary from your handler keeps the game moving at a decent pace. I never felt lost or stuck about what to read or add to a suspect’s profile, apart from the intended moments of contradiction or misinterpretation which I won’t spoil here.

I highly recommend this to people who enjoy detective games like “Her Story” or even sci-fi noir like “Deus Ex”. I’ll definitely play this again to try for another ending!

Clearly one of the most controversial and contemporary games you'll ever find, Orwell surely in one finest example of a masterpiece.
First and foremost, although this game is set in a fictional nation, ( called The Nation, which I believe is quite intentional to max the immersivity factor) this game keeps things ''real'', in  a most disturbing matter, I might add.
Gameplay and story wise, you'll spy on some citizens of this nation connected to a terrorist act.
You'll do so by going through articles, reports, their electronic devices, ect.. like in a real investigation.
But, as you can clearly imagine, the gameplay and story is just there to highlight the idea behind the game:  how easily privacy can be broken with the right tools and how easily one can use the fear for safety to limit freedom to a nation ( I mean, it's right there on the Title, so it's not like the developers intentions were so obscure).
The astonishing fact is how the game manages to convey this idea: fluidly and graciously creepy.
As one interested in such topics and as a reader of Orwell's novels myself ( Which, I believe, all should read at least one in their lifetime ) it is refreshing to see a game about media manipulation and secret police done quite right ( I was gonna add ''cyberpunk'' to the list of things that this game is... but since we have reached a certain point in technological evolution, it's  safe to say that is really a frightening and possible reality).
Also, the game never guides too much the player and never gives multiple solutions to a particular problem.
So, Is it worth buying? Yes, absolutely. Actually, I would say it should be MANDATORY ( the irony isn't lost on me) for gamers of any age to play this game.
And if don't agree... just remember, big brother is always watching 0-0

How do you keep privacy in the age of information?
Orwell is a game about freedom of thoughts, in a world where that very same freedom gives way to danger. What could the criminals be hiding in those text convos and phone calls? That's for you to find out. Are they planning to strike x or y? That's for you to find out. Are they criminals in the first place, or are they just tokens in someone else's game?
Orwell makes you constantly think and question about how you judge people, who naturally keep secrets and lie in everyday life. How can you know a person, and yet know nothing at all at the same time? How do you know this line of data risks that same person's life?
It's a constant battle of what are you willing to upload, and what to keep hidden. First time in forever has a single line of uploaded text changed the course of the game so radically to the point where I didn't want to go on. What a brilliant consept, and what a brilliant execution. [i]Die Gedanken sind frei - Thoughts are free.[/i]

[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. It takes a little bit more than one hour per episode, maybe faster if you just drag and drop without reading.
Even if having a [i]know it all[/i] tool, there are plenty of mysteries to uncover and discovering bit by bit the personalities and relationships of the people you [strike]spy on[/strike] is pretty addictive.

The presentation is pretty nice with its stylish interface. Graphics isn't the most important part of the game but it's good that it's pleasing to the eyes. The music does also its job, it changes when there's a [b]gasp[/b] moment. 

In summary, I recommend this game if you like simple but well told story in a different way than just watching Netflix. It has a nice conspiracy/detective vibe and getting to the finish is an entertaining (and bumpy) ride.

GENERAL OVERVIEW
Awesome game and "out-of-the-box" genre. Gameplay is very interesting since you analyze the suspects from a digital device, without physically following them. You get to know every small aspects of their lives, but this is a factor that greatly complicates the developer's work. For the ones who love the detective genre, this one is a very good choice. But I can't give a fully positive opinion on this: let's start with the upsides.
PROS
1)Rich and deep story. Keeps the gamer interested.
2)Orwell system is very well structured, its display is simple and not effort-requiring.
3)Plot-twists excluded, the game is actually chill. It keeps you concentrated, but not nervous or stressed. The fact that you can sit down and think of your next move, gives the game the right pace.
CONS
1)Low graphic and audio impact. Although the story keeps the gamer focused, that is probably the only one factor. I dare to say the game has a poor multimedial content. Characters don't "say" a single word for all the story.. You just hear music and other minor sound effects.
2)Too often it remains unclear where "the game finishes and the gamer starts". Has it ever happened to you that you can't understand how heavy will your decision be on your remaining gameplay? It happens too many times in Orwell. It's not clear when your action will bring to irreversible consequences, and this is annoying. Sometimes it feels like the game is playing you, and this is boring because the plot does not prompt the player to take important actions.
3)Insufficiently exhaustive tutorial. Although Orwell is pretty much a game with a "simple dynamic", basically gathering relevant information, I think that the small tutorial in the beginning does not clarify enough what the Orwell system is about. Even though in the tutorial-phase of the game is explained how you should deal with Orwell, the gamer fully grasps the concept after some time, and this is not acceptable in a game where choices matter (especially in one where it's not clear where choices are supposed to be made!). I came from hundreds of detective-genre games but this one is different, the developer knows, so maybe they should have stressed the basic principle more.
4)Lack of languages. This is a text-adventure. There should be plenty of available languages! I understand that this would be an incredibly long job... But this is a noticeable downside. This is quite a problem for non-natives english speakers, and a barrier for non english speakers.
5) You gather information on this system called Orwell, but as you go on with the game, you may find out more precise details, or that the information you considered relevant are just circumstancial. This is a normal day in the life of an investigator. So, why can't the player modify the datachunks relating to characters' pages? this is a forcing. A super complex system like Orwell doesn't allow the investigator to cancel what he wrote?
OVERALL OPINION
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a very nice game, that will be appreciated by most of the detective-games community. It's passionating, you would never desire it to end, it makes you feel a real investigator. Nevertheless, it has noteworthy downsides and there's a wide improvement margin under some aspects. Recommended.

[h1] Internet voyeurism in the name of public safety [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is an unconventional, surprisingly open-ended game about performing surveillance work on the Internet in the name of safety and anti-terrorism measures. 

As a newly appointed surveillance worker, you are to investigate a newly committed terror bombing. Who did it? Why? Does the culprit belong to a larger cluster of terrorists? Will it happen again? As you investigate, various suspects will emerge. You find out about their existence through good old-fashioned online stalking: social media, email accounts, and private chats are all fair play. Their past, their personalities, and their interconnections become increasingly clear, and the online posts gradually deepen into surprisingly convincing pictures of real human beings, with real lives, who are subject to real integrity violations. They may be guilty, or they may not. You, however, most certainly are; rummaging through every embarassing forum post, every private email, and every delicious piece of browser history for your superiors to harvest. After all: your employers are morally perfect people, who can be trusted with this information. Right? 

Game mechanically, [i]Orwell[/i] plays like a text-based point-and-click puzzler featuring source criticism. You will often simply drag and drop information highlighted to you. In these cases, the game feels like story-based pixel hunting. Occasionally, there is misleading information: quotes out of context should not be taken as gospel, nor should outright lies. Every now and then, sources contradict one another. It is then up to you to decide who to trust.  This game flow continues unimpeded for most of the game, eventually growing slightly stale and mindless before some lategame twists shake things up. Progression went smoothly most of the time. The only bottlenecks were the few times a single, specific piece of information was needed to move on, sending me backtracking for details I had missed.

There are various [i]1984[/i] references, and the entire game is essentially Orwellian themes translated to a 21st Century surveillance society. The idea of reluctantly serving a tyrannical regime is here, although lighter. So is the fear of punishment for having the wrong sympathies. Again, this paranoia is more impactful in the novel, but not without merit here either. Although [i]Orwell[/i] never reaches the same psychological detail as the novel (understandable, given its 5-hour runtime), it works as a re-tread of these themes. The difference is the packaging: the surveillance is no longer camera-based, but has moved to the Internet accounts and hardware of the modern era... like my Steam account, and the PC used for this review.

The game makes a point about our own responsibilities; about how the cog in the surveillance machine has a will of its own. The difference is that here, the point is made interactively. In doing so, [i]Orwell[/i] becomes reminiscent not only of [i]1984[/i], but of [i] Paper's Please[/i] as well. That game, too, raises the question of whether "just having followed orders" is sufficient to escape moral responsibility. Indeed, [i] Paper's Please[/i], and [i]Orwell [/i] are both graphically simple games, with simple puzzle gameplay and complicated social issues side by side.  

Posting this review makes me slightly uncomfortable. I am wary of the data I upload to the Internet. This review is part of my digital fingerprint. A piece of me, my tastes, my way of expression, and my experiences are now up there for anyone to see. I hope you enjoyed the access.

A dire and very timely warning, the game takes places in a fictional country where the government is adopting more and more authoritarian and - well, Orwellian - methods of surveillance and control. You're recruited by the eponymous government agency that is in charge of combating crime, and your handling of emerging evidence determines if you contribute to the country's descent into a police state or not.  

I liked the premise, but I found it all a bit too caricatured, although the game switches things up by presenting an alternate contemporary reality where the authoritarian push comes from the other side. 

Most of all, I was disappointed that the game puts a prominent highlight on every relevant piece of information you come across. Not only that, you even get direct notifications for cross-referenced sources, so basically you don't even have to read and remember anything. Sure, you make some interesting (but as I said, also pretty obvious) decisions about what to do with the tidbits, but it would be so much more fun and engaging if you actually had to identify the relevant puzzle pieces on your own. 

Maybe these mechanics are just there for the sake of convenience, but ultimately they make the sleuthing trivial, and that's a problem when combing through news/websites/chats *is* the gameplay.

Orwell does present a good criticism of government security and crime-fighting total surveillance programs that have been popping up around the world for at least the last decade. The story highlights many of the fundamental issues with such programs. It's just a pity that the story experience is ruined by the restrictive gameplay system, that forces you to do things in a silly way and backtrack to earlier data sources to use data blocks only later unlocked..

A key plot device element that got totally overlooked in the game design is that an attentive player could turn the use of the Orwell system on its head quite early on significantly affecting the story outcome to fit the canon narrative, but this is simply not possible in the game.

Oh dear, oh dear - what a disappointment. I had high hopes for this, but it essentially proved to be a pretty linear story in to which you fit, with some variations. Steam says I've played for four hours, which is enough for 1.5 play through and to see that my actions have, by and large, very little effect on the outcome of the game.

Now, some people like this sort of game - the sort of people who thought Telltale games were amazing. I don't. I guess I wouldn't mind if it was a big story, but tbh it's over pretty quick. 

So, gameplay - pretty weak. Longevity, dreadful - I won't bother coming back to this. Sure, I know I can tweak the outcomes a little, but ultimately it doesn't really matter.

Now for the concept - some people reviewing this have described as some kind of clever, deep warning about the state and it's Orwellian nature. Ok, this isn't a new concept and there are other games that do it better - more to the point - there are other films that do it better (some based on Orwell's own work). I found this a blunt effort to make a point that is pretty obvious to most of us. Maybe that's what people like, I don't. I prefer a little subtlety - not being slapped in the face by the concept every few seconds. 

So, in short. This could have been a great game, if either the library of stories was bigger or the player could have more impact on the outcome. The positives? Well the user interface works fairly well, although there is a lot of repeat clicking and the bookmark system doesn't seem to work desperately well - those are minor complaints though. Graphically, it looks ok - there just isn't much substance to back it up. I'm glad I waited for it to be on sale.

This game is... Well, it's different.
I understand that some people have their objections against it but it's interesting. At first you start it as any "adventure" game and focus on simply picking up information (and think this game is silly because it all boils down to simply pulling highlited items from one window to another; ok, it's got a story but that's as much "interactive" as it gets).
Then you notice that you get to chose not only which of conflicting parts of data you pass on to the system, but also how many of them you decide to omit.
Then you notice that your choices do have an impact on the story and how it unfolds.
Of course, you may treat this as a manifesto against surveilance but can also treat it as an interesting experiment in balancing the needs of the many with the needs of ones. This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

The opportunities to spy on everyone and everything quickly become unnervingly attractive.

One catch: Orwell has multiple endings and the story can go a number of different ways, but progression can feel frustratingly limited at times. While the player does have the freedom to decide which evidence to submit/ignore, they are often required to stick to a specific list in order to move forward. However, the upside to this is that progression is nearly always intuitive. 

While not perfect, Orwell allows players to become an omniscient government agent who can truly see all, using formidable tools to influence a nation. I highly recommend this game with a solid 8/10 rating.

My one main complaint about the game is that occasionally, you will get "stuck" and get frustrated (don't worry, you can't actually get stuck). I was trying really hard to only put relevant data in the Orwell database and sometimes I would have put everything in that I wanted to use, and the game would not progress. I would now be randomly putting info into the database to progress the story, resulting in me regretting some of my uploads. This could have been solved by giving the player more background information about the game and the game world so that it was more obvious what is relevant at times. There are also a few classic video game annoyances where you upload something and your boss completely twists that information into something it didn't mean, but at least in this game that is the point.

MAJOR SPOILERS:

By the mid to late game, I successfully felt "icky" about my actions, so the game is really good. The game is basically rigged so that on your first play through, you will probably provide too much information about a murderer and cause the cops to kill said person when they are arrested, which makes you reflect on your indirect involvement in their death. Again, providing more info at the start of the game would have probably helped people not accidentally kill this person, but I think this was the best part of the game in terms of how it sticks with you after you finish it. It definitely showed how your "well-meaning" efforts to catch the "bad guys" can become a slippery slope.

The problem I have with this game is that it tries to hold you accountable for choices you did not make. Your task in Orwell is simply to retrieve information, someone will make a decision based on the information you collect. However, you are not in control of when this person makes a decision, so at times your attempt to gather all information to get the full picture are halted midway.  In addition, you are forced to choose between information chunks at crucial moments in the game even though there is no reason why you should. By doing so, the game forces you to not consider the entire context. And what does the game do to you at end? Blame you for not considering the entire context.

Another problem I have with this game is the more philosophical debate of an Orwellian surveillance system. By pretending that there is no separation of power or strict legislation on how evidence may be gathered, the creators abuse the fictive setting to criticize such a system. Yes, such a system would be horrible in certain dictatorship countries that currently exist, but we already know that don't we? It's an interesting concept that can be used for good as well. This nuance is missing in the story and as a result the writers and this game discredit themselves as a worthy piece of fiction.

It was an enjoyable and unique game. It definitely makes you consider our current surveillance in the world and how it's all headed to exactly what George Orwell predicted in 1984. The puzzles are fun, the gameplay is fun, and the UI is good. But every time I see this game in my library it almost feels like I wish I never got the game. There was a specific choice in the game that had some current day political bias in it, and although it definitely wasn't over-bearing, it did make me think less of the game.

Now as my memory of the story has faded all I am left remembering of this game was the excellent sound and UI design, and the one foolish story decision which I disagreed with. Despite this, I'd still rate the game 7/10. But in a market with more 9/10 and 10/10 games than you could ever play, why would you ever spend money playing a *good* game when you can buy a *great* game?

I clocked in 6 hours total to complete the game. Alright not a lot of game play, but honestly, I’m okay with this because Orwell is a really high-quality game. The music wasn’t grating as some games tend to be, and the UI was very simple, polished, and intuitive. The filters used on the photos of people to give us our character avatars were a bit odd I will admit. (The fishing picture, bruh Josef, wtf are those teeth man?) It made me chuckle a few times, but it really didn’t take away from the quality of the game. As far as game play goes, think of this similar to Papers Please with the addition of choices and story impact. You play as an investigator of the surveillance program called Orwell. You listen to phone calls, read chats, and search the internet for relevant information. This information is then forwarded to your adviser who analyzes your data and acts accordingly. This is where the fun comes in. You can pick and choose what you send to be considered relevant, leaving out certain parts of information, or choosing to mislead the investigation with out of context statements etc. It’s interesting that your choice in data basically drives the story. There’s 5 chapters, so it’s not a lengthy game if you’re not reading through all of the material. The game is very throughout with providing all sorts of tidbits and lore to make it seem like a real program. This isn’t a high-impact gaming experience, more-so an enjoyable romp through the hypotheticals of excessive surveillance and its possible consequences.  This was an interesting as well as thought provoking game, and I appreciate all the thought and effort that was clearly put into it. I would surely recommend this to casual gamers. I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

"Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You" has a novel approach to the adventure/mystery game format, where the gameplay of highlighting the Internet history of People of Interest feels natural and the themes of modern surveillance fits like a glove. I recommend it to fans of story rich adventure/mystery games and people interested in media discussing state surveillance.

In Orwell, just as you can find the "right" perpetrator with the extreme access to personal information, the gameplay also showcases how that power to secretly surveil is just as capable of destroying lives. AAA games like the "Watch_Dogs" series have attempted to grapple with the same subject matter, but invariably it is portrayed as a superpower for a modern action hero. This feels like a much more grounded and mature take on epistemic injustice.

An interesting game that has you in control of a “Big Brother” surveillance system named Orwell. You must find out who or what is behind several violent attacks on a city. As you go through the story you must upload information you deem important (or fake info to throw Orwell off). Emails, texts, phone calls, computers, websites, etc. it’s all available to search through and piece the puzzle together. There is a lot of reading, but the info you can upload will get highlighted automatically. Sometimes there are conflicting pieces of information and you’ll need to decide what to upload.

The story is good with some twists and turns. It does have several endings and outcomes depending on your choices throughout each day. The gameplay is very straightforward and you can dumb it down to dragging things from one side of the screen to another until things happen. If you get into the game, it feels more than simply drag and drop. I found myself pausing and thinking things through, second guessing, regretting some uploads, etc. 

I did come across a rather annoying bug which seems to be common when looking at the discussions. Seemingly at random, when you hover over a highlighted piece of information it will not show you the summary of what gets uploaded to Orwell. This is a huge bummer because then you are uploading information that you may think one thing but the game thinks another. Sometimes logging out and going to the main menu fixes it, but not always. 


[b]Conclusion[/b]
I went back and played through it a second time to see different outcomes and to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed my time with the game and would recommend it on sale.

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

After that, I can't say much without spoiling something, so either buy it or give the demo a try.

Essentially presents the counter-argument to "I have nothing to hide" in game form, and it does so brilliantly.

The game is set up so that you look through documents and conversations and can present evidence to your adviser who can't see what you see. In this way you can include bits and pieces of information to shape the narrative however you want by taking things out of context or choosing not to send pertinent information. In doing, so an innocuous statement can be construed as proof of wrongdoing, and lies can be presented as evidence without sending the actual facts. In other words, you can choose to send innocent people to jail and let criminals go free if you so wish merely by the power of suggestion.

The only negative in the presentation is that in multiple playthroughs you can't fast forward or skip conversations. The game is short enough that I was willing to sit through them, and you can multi-task by starting conversations then looking at other things, but it would have been nice to save a few minutes here and there.
NSA Prism Simulator!

The technology displayed in Orwell is already out there, though it's not called Orwell. And it's much more sophisticated. Whether you're a government agency, an intelligence agency or just someone powerful who has the ability to tap into the right resources, the data are out there. Government records, bank records, phone tracking, social media, internet activity, etc. It's already here and it's not that hard to piece together. Obviously, this is just a game, so it's perfectly understandable why Orwell isn't as sophisticated.

So, we live in a very terrifying world, it seems... but this game actually made me realise it's not as grim as it looks like. The concepts and warnings of this game, given the state of our society and the in-game characters, actually fall flat and, like I said, make you realise it's not that bad. Was that the intention, I wonder.

Why? Well, the majority of the monitored characters are either massive jerks (Cassandra and Harrison) or dangerous and certainly deserving investigation (I've already spoiled too much). And investigation isn't necessarily a bad thing. Even before the information age, there were detectives and police officers investigating crimes and stuff. The thing is about finding the right balance, I guess, but that's out of the scope if this game and its message.

Before this game, these things always worried me and I always thought about the impact on us all. Innocents caught and crushed between the merciless cogs of surveillance and false illusion of freedom. However, I failed to take into account that it's not just those behind those tools that are jerks. It's also those who end up between those cogs. So hey, maybe it's not so grim after all.

Like that line in the 1984 book about imagining the future -- a boot stamping on a human face, forever. If that face belongs to a jerk, then it's actually kinda good. True, innocent people will still get caught between the cogs, but at least it's not 100% just innocents. It probably is more like just 10% of the time. Cool. Thank you, Orwell, I guess I can sleep better at night today. :)

+ the story has some pretty great twists and turns that are really unique.
+ the ending I got was incredibly satisfying, and I appreciate being allowed to side with either Thought or The Nation (I don't think that's a spoiler, this wouldn't be a very good story-driven, "choices matter" game if it didn't have multiple endings). for those who have played the game, I sided with Thought because not only do I agree with them, but also because I found them to be written in a nuanced way, that they were in the right as far as the narrative framing is concerned, and I thought that it was more interesting to try and cover for them, rather than obeying the fascists calling the shots. if you sided with The Nation for whatever reason, it's definitely worth trying Thought's ending, because it's morbidly hilarious what the final nail in the coffin you use is.
- without spoiling the ending, I have a few narrative problems which are just... not great to see? for starters, two members of Thought are giving their options for what they think you should do, but then they refer to the wrong one as their plan (ex. you can do my plan of going to the store, or the other one of staying home--but they're mixed up). they also seem to immediately learn complex concepts you had to be taught in the tutorial, like, immediately. one of them is tech savvy enough for me to buy it, but the other one isn't and they're the one who name-drops this hyper-specific jargon they shouldn't know. while this does not ruin my enjoyment of this story (hence my recommendation), it feels like there was a bit of a rush, where the ending goes.

overall, pretty damn intriguing, and it's not like a lot of media as of late which invokes George Orwell's legacy without truly understanding who he was as a person. that's enough for me to give it some level of praise.

Overall: I liked this game. I found this to be a thought-provoking experience, one that I really was dedicated to the characters and interested in the story.

The story revolves around an attack on a local landmark, to which you only have one lead: a woman who was arrested in connection to a riot in the same place. You dig around as a member of ORWELL, which is a very invasive project designed to gather any and all information on whoever their higher-ups authorize them to. As you gather more information, you get authorization to investigate more people tied to the first. It becomes interesting, and twists and turns along the way manage to catch you off guard.

The style of game-play is similar to how one would read a book to fill out a homework assignment, made easier by highlighting the important bits. I fell into that sort of thought process, and then the game became interesting. Usually, things are marked in blue, but a second marking, a yellow highlight, means there is conflicting information.

It went from a read and extract to a branching story - one that you could influence based on what you chose. In my first play-through, I tried to get the truth, or what I thought could be the truth, but what I had selected painted a bleak view of the suspects. I realize now that what I had chosen influenced how characters were perceived, which was a very nice touch. 

I recommend this game, especially for people who are into mystery and observation sims (is that a genre? This game is about government spying, so if you're into that, that's what I mean).
