I've never actually made a review for a game before, but as I got the last achievement(which I did in only - I think - three games I own) and finished the game for like the fourth time, I think a positive review is mandatory. 

God, I love this game.

I'm a fan of these "political simulators" as I've seen these kinds of games adressed as, those where the player works for the government/media or some other important institution and makes decisions that later change the lives of the characters around them in various ways.

In this game, you play as an investigator for a nation-wide surveillance program, in which you have to collect information on potentially dangerous(according to your superiors at least) people and put them into a system, based on which the people above you then act(I suppose it's kind of a bad description, but whatever), and it's probably the best game of it's kind for me, though people might be inclined to disagree.

Orwell required some logical thinking, but not to a degree it was difficult, which I liked - I had to think about it, but I wouldn't get lost in it. I liked the characters, they were fun, none of them was obnoxious to me(some find the advisor - the character of your coworker, that at first guides you through the game and to who you forward your chosen information you find - very obnoxious, but for me, he was the best character, honestly), and I liked seeing the details, or bigger things change based on the choices I made in various routes.

I'd say the game has some replay value - if just to see the three more endings you didn't get on the first try, or to change  the fates of some characters who's lives you directly influenced through your actions.

It's a text based game, so I wouldn't recommend it to people who don't like to read much while playing games, but I think that's obvious from the pictures, videos, maybe even premise...

There's one thing I could think of critiquing right now, which is that when you're listening to people's phone calls or reading their texts in the game, at least to me it's lengthy even if you have the speed of those things set to the highest, mainly during replays.

I'm not sure if I'd buy it for ten euros though - I bought this game on sale, but then again, I bought almost all the games I own on Steam during a sale. If I think about it... I'd probably buy it for the full price now, knowing just how much I liked it, but if you aren't completely sure you're going to love it, I would probably wait for a sale. But maybe I just don't like spending too much money on Steam, since the price isn't even THAT high if I look at it transcribed to my country's currency.

Overall, I can say that I enjoyed Orwell very much, it's one of my most favorite games of all time, even if it might not be one of the objectively best games I played, it is one of the best for me, and I'd recommend it to anyone who would ask.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.

You probably heard the term 'Orwellian', 'Big Brother' or 'NewSpeak'. These terms come from the book Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984), a dystopian social science fiction novel by George Orwell, written in 1949 shortly after Word War II.

In this game you are monitoring citizens by listening in on their calls, watching their social media and pulling information from web sites, and by doing so gathering information. Your supervisors will then determine if they are a security risk and take action. The data you supply can be conflicting and it is left up to you to decide which data is true and thus steer your supervisors in the right (or wrong) directions. I have not finished the game, but I suspect that you will discover facts along the way that will sway you to work against your employers and have you try to help overthrow the government.

Were you truly doing your job or were you groomed and manipulated?

It's a rather interesting ride that gathers speed and doesn't let up at the end. It makes you think that if you can incriminate someone with just a few uttered words taken out of context and twisted to another's agenda... what's preventing that from happening today?

The game has choice-based gameplay ala Telltale and Quantic Dream but is much more nuanced in its approach, allowing mostly complete freedom over what information the player decides to upload and share to this program. The story is very interesting and has a few plot twists to keep things interesting, and these are perfectly timed as well, occurring almost exactly when you think you've figured it out. Despite the game being entirely text and image based, it succeeds in being significantly more interesting than some higher budget titles which put a lot more time into their narratives. The soundtrack is also surprisingly good, and is even dynamic to an extent, changing when you read certain bits of texts that have reveals in them. It's a great time, doesn't overstay its welcome and is the perfect price, so I'd highly recommend it. 9/10.

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive dystopian mystery clicker with one of the most obvious titles on this planet. Seriously, tell me you don't have an inkling of what this game is about just by reading it. No? 
Well - Orwell touches on government surveillance, privacy in the age of send/receive, newsfeeds and - on the philosophical level - shockingly personal themes such as morality, autonomy and group culture. It also teeters on the sociological side of things with themes of the looking-glass self, or how we present ourselves to the world/others. Let's talk about the narrative. I'll try not to spoil too much.

------------------------------------

You are, well, yourself. You live in a non-disclosed location as an investigator who has just been contracted to work on a secret government project by The Nation; A country that is, simply put, not doing so great from the leadership aspect. The Nation is undergoing political turmoil, both inner and outer, and is seeing a concerning increase in violence, extremism and terrorist attacks. This has led the country to establish increasingly dystopian methods of surveillance. 

The beginning scene sets the tone with you looking through multiple sets of cameras on an otherwise normal day in a city square. The cameras scan the citizens, seemingly referencing police files to determine if they're a threat. So far, so good! A blue haired girl quietly walks past and the camera begins to buzz, showing that - !!! - she has had an encounter with the law in the past. We tensely follow her as she gets on a bus and it drives away. Hm. Well, surely that's not THAT out of the ordinary, right? We all know someone who has a blot on their record. Surely, we shouldn't judge unless they've done something terrible? I'll reserve my judgement. 

And then a statue a short distance away is engulfed in dust, shrapnel and the sounds of an otherwise normal day being eviscerated as a bomb explodes. Well, damn.

This is where you come in, Investigator. You have been hired to test the efficacy of the brand new "Orwell" project. Orwell is a hot-off-the-assembly-line database tool that allows you to search nearly anything there is to know about a person. It creates links between people for referencing and logs any interesting findings you catch - referred to as 'datachunks' within each person's "file". Your job is to prevent any other terrorist attacks from occurring as well as finding out who could've been behind such a horrible event.

-------------------------------------

The success of Orwell is predicated on it's atmosphere - and it is indeed the game's biggest asset. However...

If I can be quite honest - the writing itself isn't anything revolutionary here when it comes to it's subject matter. Some of the dialogue is great, engrossing even. Some of it is extraordinarily cringey, for lack of a better word. A certain aforementioned blue-haired character comes to mind, especially near the end game. Some laughably unbelievable behavior occurs that can really mess with your vibe once you understand exactly how the plot is shaping itself.

Writing quibbles aside, immersion is ultimately what reigns supreme here. The developers have created such an oppressively paranoid atmosphere with the simple interface and nerve-wracking audio cues that it's incredibly easy to be charmed and overlook it's relatively short length. This is a game that benefits from not overstepping it's own ambition. 

I've seen a few other reviews being slightly critical of the fact that more characters weren't involved in the overall game - but I think that this actually works in Orwell's favor. The gameplay is the *absolute* definition of repetitive. You shift between tabs, you drag and you drop. That's it. If the gameplay wasn't so story centric and was more sim-based (with more options within the Orwell interface), I would agree with those criticisms and want to be Big Brother until the end of time. However, this is an actual story game. Consider this to be a dystopian choose your own adventure.

To end this ramble, let's talk length and price. I spent 3.4 hours on this game and completed it. It's currently $9.99 on Steam. I myself, being transparent, did not pay $9.99 for this. I received it in a bundle along with it's sequel. So you ultimately will have to make your own call here - but I will say that YES - Orwell is indeed worth $10 just for the first playthrough alone. 

Not very many games touch upon these themes, and I do consider these to be important themes considering the time/political climate we live in right now. Regardless of how successful the game is at making a statement on these themes, I appreciate the effort. And a lot of effort has gone into this game. 

I very much recommend you give it the chance, it may very well cause you to look over both digital shoulders.

Having both elements of seriousness in maintaining the peace and order of the nation, coupled with a few occasionally humorous moments helped to offset the tiresome feeling of focusing too hard on the 'job' and rather reminds us to realise that the system is in fact still inept at reading human communications. This draws into my next point in that initially, I thought that the game would be a lot more general with more cases, similar to quantity over quality. However, I soon realised that having the player focus on one specific case was much better, in fact, as there was a lot more pressure on you to suffer the consequences of having ingrained human qualities pertaining morality and such. Overall, it's a brilliant game, albeit a rather short one, that allows for a few more playthroughs after the initial run.

Orwell to my comprehension is a game set in Britain, being in a timeline where camera's and invasive technology are being ushered in by the government, under the guise of safety. The game's premise, location and the name itself draw distinct premise to a book, written by an individual who fought the Spaniards in the 20th century. The man had other notable accomplishments, such as wrestling adult elephants in front of rural Indian villagers, as a gesture of the might of Great Britian. A really interesting mystery game where you act as a Big Brother-esque government surveillance agent thrown into an attempt to stop a series of terrorist bombings. Comb through people's computers, text messages, and phone calls, make connections, fill out their profiles, and try to discover who is responsible. 

The mystery element is really well handled. The game is challenging without feeling unfair, and I definitely liked the opportunity to have some (small) influence on the story and its conclusion. It was a lot of fun combing through the various resources to try and identify which bits and pieces of information were most important. Something unique to this game is the fact that you also have to determine how to deal with directly conflicting information and determine which information should be trusted and which shouldn't. 

Controls were all simple and intuitive. Be aware that the entire game is primarily played via interacting with text transcripts. I would almost call it something closer to interactive fiction than a more "traditional" video game, or even a visual novel. Which I love, but can understand where it may not be to some people's tastes. It's a beautifully executed idea and I had a lot of fun playing it. It is a fairly short game--maybe 7-8 hours to play through, some of which is taken up by unskippable audio conversations--but it didn't feel like it was too short or rushed.

On a more critical note, I will say that the overall "message" of the game isn't necessarily executed as well as it could be. Obviously a highly restrictive Big-Brother-esque surveillance state with, apparently, very little in the way of due process is not a good thing. But (some of) the people you are investigating have absolutely killed people and are planning to do so again. I understand that the game wants there to be tension between these ideas, but I don't know that it necessarily succeeds, especially given the fact that through careful choices on your part as an "agent" you can generally avoid any truly upsetting outcomes. It suggests more that this technology is acceptable in the "right" hands, which I'm pretty sure was not the goal of the creators. The sequel, Orwell 2, does a much better job of highlighting the ways that these types of abuses of power and surveillance can badly hurt the populace they're being used to monitor.

Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

This is a tricky one.

On one hand, the execution is solid. It's essentially a slightly-more-complex visual novel about parsing data from presented sources. The interface, etc, all work well for that.
(Though I do wish that linking image would be marked in some form. I spent 15 minutes trying to find a 'New Entry' on a page only to realize that a picture was actually a clickable link, in which the new entry was to be found...)

Positive shout-out to the music, too. If all you do is watch text scroll by, it's hard to build tensions... but the occasional suspense-heavy tunes that play whenever a big twist shows up on your screen, is perfectly executed.

But... then there's the actual gameplay. Which is, as said, essentially just a slightly more complex Visual Novel with some choice elements and branching paths. Which might simply not be a thing for me.

The topic portrayed in the game is very interesting, and I feel like it's handled in a perfect way. It's clear that the devs of this game want to explain the issues with an all-encompassing surveillance network to potential users, but they do so in a relatively fair and unbiased way, that (alongside countless instances of meta-commentary), essentially underline how difficult ethical use of such a system is, by inserting the player AS that ethical control mechanism. 

Lastly, I do however have to point out the longlivety and replayability of the game: 4 hours to finish, and given the core of the game is the motivation to figure out what is going on, I can't see myself playing through a second time. It's like watching a movie you already know. Nothing will surprise you, and given the only format is text, I don't think there'll be much in the ways of discovering subtle nuances and foreshadowing. There's achievements and all that for trying out different paths and endings... but I'm not going to click through a visual novel just for that.

The game comes at a low price point of 10€ though, which somewhat compensates for the point mentioned above.


In summary, I'll therefore give the 'game' a nondescript passing grade. It does not, to me, qualify as a good purchase 'for a game', but I do give it merit for being an interesting and thought-inducing piece of contemporary art.

Do not buy this if you want a lengthy, complicated mystery novel, or expect actual gameplay.

But do consider getting this if the topic of ever-increasing surveillance, and digital privacy interest you, and/or you wish to engage in an interesting 'what if' scenario.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

Orwell is one of those games I played several years ago, that still elicits a groan of disgust everytime I see it in my games library. 

The game concept itself sounds extremely interesting and intriguing, but the game itself doesn't care as much about the game mechanics as it does the uninteresting writing about its unlikeable cast. All of the characters I quickly grew to dislike as I felt they were caricatures of what an amateur creative writer thought 'interesting' people would act like. I dislike the geometric art style and feel it feels particularly dated (though I've never liked it), but that's more of a personal taste.

The first act was the strongest as I hadn't grown tired of the writing yet, and the plot hadn't started indulging in it's pointless conspiracy drivel that dominates the later acts. The writing wears its politics on its sleeves with the implicit assumption that the player shares the authors values which even if you do will feel grating. 

The ending and climax are the worst offenders because what should feel like a reward for finishing the game just felt unrewarding and absurd. It eschews all world-building and you have to accept the conceit that there's only like 20 people in its world. Consequences are divorced from logic and it feels terrible. Granted I know there are multiple endings, however to reach another one I would have to play through this terrible game again, and it's simply, completely not worth it. 

I recommend avoid.

I don't play much games.

 But I was just browsing my library with the thought "maybe I'll try something" and the title caught my eye, so I read the description. 
And installed it.
And then spent 5 continuous hours playing it, finished it at 2am. 

That (and the fact that I decided to write a review, which I don't ever do) says something about Orwell.

The controls are easy, it's just a clicker with drag-and-drop. 
But the story and how our info affects it is amazing. Deep characters, entangled information which you need to filter, and what you learn about all the people despite not interacting with them directly... it's impressive.

During the course of gameplay you'll regret making some decisions. You'll learn how much power you hold and how information can be manipulated and wrongly interpreted, just to fulfil someone's agenda. 
And you'll probably learn to get better care of your data as it shows reality of doxxing (gathering seemingly small info on an individual from many different places on the web and making a full profile out of it).

If you are a security geek, you probably knew all that already - but you might still enjoy it like I did.
I'd recommend sharing the game with all your friends who think gov surveillance is "not a problem" because they "have nothing to hide" and who don't get explanations why it's bad. - This game will [i]show[/i] them why it is.

It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

A narrative-driven game, Orwell puts you in the role of a government agent spying on unuspecting citizens' private life in order to maintain peace, law & order. Although, contrary to the inspiration of its namesake, the dystopian world of the videogame doesn't reach the extreme attitudes of "1984" of banned art, love and emotions, but is focused mostly on addressing the issue of abuse of privacy in the name of stability and fighting crime.

In all honesty I hadn't really paid attention in the description and the details of the game and I thought I would have control over a much larger variety of random citizens and decide their fate in unrelated cases, but instead I got involved into a much more story-focused game, sort of a political thriller, where you , the player, much investigate the online presence and phone calls of a group of suspects to decide who is responsible for a series of bombings, with the suspects soon becoming more of a "main/supporting cast" entagled in this one single case . However, my false expecattions didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game as it proved equally fun and interesting.

As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of you reading articles, browsing sites or hacked computers and recorded discussions, uncovering clues that open new places and suspects to investigate but it can feel a little hand-holding especially in the early parts of the game where there is really little to do other than adding all the automatically selected useful information to each suspect's profile and only towards the second half and the end of the game does it provide a little bit more challenge and interesting tougher choices. The outcome can slightly change depending on your actions and the information you provide, although sometimes the game does not exactly make its intentions clear - does it expects you to be good at your job (and the game itself)? Or are you supposed to be a buffoon and ignore vital information about a person's physical and mental health? 
in the second part and especially towards the end of the game where the mechanics shine, it becomes much more interesting and it does a much better job presenting theses questions where the stakes are higher and giving you choices that matter much more and i wish I could see more of this intense decision-making more in the early part.

In terms of graphics i think it's pretty clear that this game will appeal to those who do not need fancy graphics but are fans of endless text boxes. The presenattion is quite good with presenting a dystopian version of the internet and social media,
the artstyle is quite appealing with stylized polygonal semi-realistic pictures and thanks to the story-driven nature of the game, a moody soundtrack that ramps up the intensity when major twists and revelations happen.

So overall, perhaps not as deep of a political/"FBI" simulation as it could have been, focusing more on telling a story, Orwell at least succesfully achieves its goal, to present a thought provoking discussion about government surveillance and the grey area surrounding it - a world that isn't always easy to separate into "good" and "bad" guys and where the ends don't always justify the means. Or do they?

What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.

No, not the visuals, not a screaming animatronic bear, the SOUNDTRACK. Buy this game. Play it. Think about free will and death. Then buy the sequel.

This game feels like a visual novel. You are in charge of gathering information on different suspects of a terrorist attack with the help of Orwell a software that gather information from social media, phone calls, emails...

Pros:
Good story and concept.
Great Design
Shows how easy it is to make a profile of someone from what you can gather on the internet

Cons:
Lack of real choices or intelligent ones. The software preselects whatever information you want to add to the suspects profiles and forces you to choose between "conflicting" information, but an individual thoughts are not black or white. Most people tweet stuff that they regret later or that do not represent there views...
Bugs. The software sends you notification to read new information and add it or not to the profiles, but sometimes it doesn't work. Either doesn't show a notification or notifies you of something you already read or already added to the profile. Which leads, sometimes to reread every piece of information to find the one entry you missed in order to continue to the next chapter.

After a couple of hours I felt it was not very enjoyable to hunt for new information or get blocked on a chapter for a while even though the game tells you that you can omit to upload information to the suspect profiles...
I still think it is a great idea but they should leave more decisions to the player and don't block the player from continuing through the story. If the player didn't find enough evidence than he will not find the culprit --> Game over rather than be stopped from advancing.

[b]Good grief, this game is awful for all the right reasons![/b]
I originally bought this game because of the artstyle and the "UI-based gameplay" rather than another FPS or platformer. I did not expect to get roped into an hour long, complicated, dangerous and honestly mindboggeling conflict between The Nation and it's citizens. But I can't say that I regret it...

Honestly, the game is absolutely amazing. The many characters feel full and alive, with unique personalities and even their own way of typing, which is an incredible level of attention to detail. The game had me so immersed I was actually feeling dread for these characters, and felt so responsible (read: guity) for what happened to them. The story twists and turns many times in a chapter, to the point where it can at times be difficult to follow along, but luckily it always ends up making sense.
The game tackles a very relevant topic in a way that never tells you what to think, but forces you to truly think about it anyways. I found myself halfways through the game suddenly realising that I had started on the side of the citizens, but became more and more interested in preserving myself, and more importantly the Governments interests, which kinda made me [i] super uncomfortable with myself [/i]. But sometimes that's really what you need with topics like these. And getting it with fun gameplay, intense plottwists, characters you quickly bond with and soundtrack and soundcues exactly on point was an experience for sure.
It's not the longest game, but also not the biggest price so it adds up.

As for the ending tho, and this is where the game visibly lacks...
[spoiler] The ending kinda hit me out of left field, and all the loose ends kinda just unraveled even more. Uncovering the fact that Abraham was dead was a shocker for sure, but it got messy when trying to figure out when he immigrated, why the obituary was in his old name, when he died. I barely got time to figure it all out before the ending came crashing. Juliet being the bomber felt... Very out of the blue. Maybe I just missed something sure, but there didn't seem to be a lot of clues that she was the type of person to do such a thing, and she still doesn't. The limit on data-uploads really added stress to the game, but also made it feel very tight, and so made the rest of the ending feel haphazard and like it was just trying to get out of the way as quick as possible...[/spoiler]

All in all: [i] god this game is good[/i]

A unique take on Orwellian philosophical ideals presented through interactive means, with the Player through gameplay mechanics being forced to utilize a totalitarian and invasive computer program. While having a clear political stance regarding the advantages/disadvantages of such program, the game through amazing writing (and no voice-acting!) creates some of the most memorable characters and dilemmas in recent years. With a humane yet intelligent insight on why thought and freedom of thinking are abandoned concepts in our modern social media era, Orwell creates intense emotional moments through mere text messages and news articles. By simple choices made by the Player, the success and failures of both the program and the revolutionary ideals are affected, and through interactivity the dilemmas of privacy invasion takes its own unique turn. Definitely a game for anyone wanting both a harrowing story and an artistic experience that can't be told in another medium.

Right off the bat, anyone who actually made it through their reading list in highshool English class would most likely predict any new game titled ‘Orwell’ might be about to try and thematically explore both technological authoritarianism and very grey morality. In this case, you’d be right, and this new Orwell sees to ape the mechanisms of power in its namesake’s classic ‘Nineteen Eighty-Four’, but now with a slick Twenty-First Century look, a whole new lexicon of doubleplusgood compound word gibberish, and by placing you – the player – behind the controls of the surveillance state’s nightmare machine. 

The premise of Orwell is that you are the most recent new recruit at the security department of a ruthless, modern, one-party dictatorship’s unfeeling government office and are being assigned to the task of monitoring a national database’s worth of information through little more than mouse control click-and-scroll from your work-issue laptop. The slightly dubious nature of having an inexperienced new hire involved in top-level security quickly proves useful when your “impartiality” sees you assigned to the task of using your new toolset to find the culprit(s) behind a recent bombing at a public park political demonstration.            

The gameplay itself is initially interesting, and certainly unique among what games I’ve seen, however, when you’re several hours in and starting to wind up the story, it might start to feel a bit samey and unchallenging. Essentially the central puzzle at hand at any given time is navigating one of your open browser pages to read or listen to the right excerpt of information, then follow a hyperlink on that page until the story eventually runs through all its possible strands and you get some new pile of expy social media pages to comb through. I can’t say I found the story itself to be anything hugely impressive, and despite the game’s store page and other Reviews implying an ability to sway a branching plot, that isn’t really the case in any major sense.

I’ll go ahead and officially Recommend Orwell on the basis of its high level of polish, full Steam community integration (Trading Cards, Achievements, Chat Emotes, and all the rest) and an extensive effort by the devs to continue patching in further international language support. But apart from that, I can’t strictly say you should pick this game up unless it’s on sale, and/or, or just really want to try this specific sort of art-project-come-‘game’.

Modern-day 1984 (as if the name wasn't hint enough). Search people's emails, texts, phone calls for evidence. Search newspapers, blogs, and so on for evidence. Use this evidence to slowly uncover what the government has been up to as well spying on some citizens to see how they're connected and if they're involved in some recent terrorist attacks.

Don't go into this expecting this to be a mystery where you use your brain to solve crimes by spying on people. It's not. It's more like a visual novel, and like a visual novel there's a lot of railroading. All the data you need (and some you don't; you get to decide which to upload, though some data is needed to progress the story) is highlighted for you in the documents you read. Not only that, but the documents where said data is are marked so you can find them easily. 

That being said, I found this game surprisingly enjoyable! I actually felt bad spying on people, and I'll admit there were several "oops" moments where I felt even worse, not realizing what the consequences of revealing certain information would be until after the fact. The story had me engaged, I liked the characters who all had their own unique voices and stories to tell as you spied on their lives. 

Only minor quibble I can think of is the writing: this needed a few more rounds of editing. Grammatical mistakes, spelling errors, and punctuation errors were frequent enough to be noticed, but not enough to detract or distract from the story. A lot of the writing was unpolished, which is fine in text messages between friends, but not when you're reading a supposedly top-of-the-line news article from the government.

Some of the reveals in conversations felt a bit forced for the sake of moving the story along, too, but again, extreme nitpicking. This is a great game and I'd recommend it to everyone and anyone.

Pros:

+ Engaging story with plot twists
+ Spying on people during their messages/phone calls felt realistic and almost makes you feel like you're dealing with a real person
+ Gave me some laughs when I was nitpicking with irrelevant data chunks
+ Story has different directions
+ The tense music felt great
+ Dialogues and texts were very well-written

Cons:
- Very short game

Only get it on sale though. Game hour/dollar ratio is bad.

TLDR: This is a very different and morally challenging game. The game play itself is easy but the story is really in depth and there are many choices that have severe consequences. It is short, but it has great replayability to explore how different choices affect the world. Definitely pick it up!

Orwell has a compelling story set in a dystopian maybe-not-so-future where the government has begun a program to monitor any and everything in real time.

The story was very good, however, to experience all of the options you have to replay the full game. There are several 7+ minute conversations paced out painfully slowly. I get that the pacing is set to make it feel like you're monitoring this real time (and that's important in a few cases!) but the majority of the time, pretty much any time there isn't tense music going on, the game needs an option to skip through the snoozefest that is the communications system. I legitimately got up, made myself a meal, and came back to find one segment still running. What was an engaging and interesting storyline the first time around became a complete drag by the end.

I got this game on sale, and I'm glad I did because it's only really good for one play through. I was strongly compelled by the storyline, but my decisions in-game didn't heavily factor in to vast majority of the narrative, which made it more of a novel. Pros: The art is great, the sound atmosphere is good, the story is strong, and the dialogue around security vs. privacy is handled masterfully, but, Cons: it only takes a few hours to get through and the majority of the storyline is set in stone before the player weighs in. Something I would have liked to see the game creators lean into more is the security footage access, which is only featured at the very beginning of the game. The fact that it's left out for the remainder seems like a plot hole in a story where Orwell is tapped in to everything. I strongly agree with other players that the highlighting of relevant information babies the player through the document-sifting, and would have liked more of a challenge there. But, they did a good job world building with those documents, you just have to have the patience to ignore the highlights and read all of them to get a full grasp of the characters and their society. It was such a compelling narrative I only left the computer once while playing, and I'll definitely be playing the sequel.

Orwell is an excellent puzzle/detective-type game which has you working for a national surveillance test, poring over news articles, social media, phone calls, emails, text messages, you know it!

The setup is very straightforward, who is the terrorist responsible?  Finding out will require a lot of reading of materials, sometimes many times, as you select "data chunks" to give to the Orwell program for analysis (and potentially new materials to look over!)  In that way the play is quite simple, just drag and drop highlighted data, but be careful!  Not all data is current, and some data conflicts!  You also need to take into account the personalities of the people you are investigating, are they hiding something? Are they boastful?  Be aware that in many ways, you will reap what you sow.

The game is pretty simple to play, in my opinion, and you are basically being hand-held over the first in-game day.  The challenge comes from the narrative you want to put into Orwell, will you seek out the truth or serve the state?  Something that was very unexpected for me was the emotional response to events in the game.  At one point I actually cried: I prevented a catastrophe, saving lives, which felt very good, but it laid bare the potential effectiveness of a system that seeks to remove all privacy and could have went wrong very easily.

I also want to say something to the more pessimistic or paranoid about games where you serve something 'evil' and close to reality: this is a story-puzzle game, and has a very defined message.  A CIA AI tutor it is not.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good mystery and most especially likes to read.  I wish there were more games where you teeter on the edge of being a web junkie and a librarian, ha!

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a truly immerse adventure experience. The mechanics are intuitive and organic, as such, there is a bit of a learning curve in the beginning. The game still has new tricks to teach you even in later stages, as you realize exactly how much you can do, and how it mimics real life. The "interface" for the game is itself a computer screen. You shift through various types and sources of information, trying to differentiate what is real from what isn't, and resolving inherent contradictions. Any mistakes you make could impact the course of the game and the outcomes of the "case" you are working and the characters, who are complex, "real" feeling characters whose fates you can easily begin to care about as the plot progresses. The story is engrossing, and excellently written, with lots of potential twists and turns. The gameplay gets very meta near the end, and the choices you make matter - as have the ones who have made throughout the earlier game. I got the sense that there were many different variables that could result in many different outcomes at the end. 

I played through the game in almost 5 hours and I'm excited to do another run through in the future. It's definately something you want to experience in a single sitting for best results, and the length and depth of the game is perfect for this. I normally am not eager to replay a game, but with this one I can't hardly wait.

It's really hard for me to determine whether I do or don't recommend this, as I'm right on the line. I think overall, though, I have to lean into not recommending it.

The game starts off really well, with a really balanced juxtaposition of people being concerned about privacy versus the very real result of what you're able to accomplish through spying, really highlighting the blurred line between privacy and security. Further, the fact that there are rules in place - such as you can't hack someone without what is essentially a warrant from higher up in the system - makes it feel more grounded, and honestly like a more fair system. 

However, as you reach the end of the game, this completely falls apart. In the closing act, you get beaten around the head with the game designers' opinion, which is a very black-and-white "spying bad, privacy good", which entirely undermines the nuance the entire game up until that point had executed so well. I'll save the spoiler-filled rant for the end.

In addition to this, the gameplay has some glaring flaws. There are certain pieces of information that you absolutely [i]must[/i] collect to move forward, which is sometimes information that seems completely irrelevant (and you're outright told not to submit irrelevant information), forcing you to comb through every possible source with a fine-toothed comb, and sometimes just guess what they want you to submit.

Also, you can only extract verbatim phrases to submit, devoid of any context or clarification. Often, this leads to bizarre interpretations from the game. Like, apparently the game makers think [spoiler]that Depression or PTSD are things that make someone dangerous, rather than being a potentially debilitating disability[/spoiler]. Or perhaps you want to flag one piece of information because of it's context, but because that context isn't part of the auto-selected snippet, the game completely misinterprets it. For example, [spoiler]one girl is in a relationship with a guy, and helps herself to his wallet to make a couple purchases. Any reasonable person would have enough context to say, "Oh, she's borrowing his wallet, and he's only mildly annoyed that she's spending a lot? Clearly they are in a very serious relationship." How about the game? "She took his wallet? She has a history of theft! She's clearly a criminal!"[/spoiler] Like, wtf?

So that's why I just can't recommend this game. Despite the promise it shows, it really undermines itself, especially in the final stretch.

Now, about that endgame rant... Endgame spoilers follow: [spoiler]You reach the end of the game, and basically get lectured at by someone who (1) organized multiple bombings that killed dozens of people, (2) lied to and manipulated multiple friends to do her dirty work, ruining their lives, and (3) is completely unrepentant (going with the "can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs" excuse). What's worse, is that she did all this to protest the whole mass-spying thing, but the only reason you're even spying on anyone in that community is because of the bombings! Literally, she created the problem that she's complaining about.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Meanwhile, you (potentially) used [i]your[/i] minor sin of spying to save dozens or even hundreds of lives at the mall [i]she[/i] tried to bomb - targeting civilians to make people care more about her message. She also blames you for sending police in who end up killing her friend, just because, you know, they actually [i]were[/i] guilty of setting bombs to kill people, and opened fire on the police. How dare those cops return fire on a known bomber who is armed and dangerous just because she shot first![/spoiler]

[spoiler]And what's worse, is that all the other people involved in the plot-device-conference-call at the end [i]take her side![/i] Like, [i]really?[/i] In the end, you're basically pushed to take down the entire system you've been a part of, despite the fact that the game shows it doing an objectively good job of keeping people safe and bringing conspiracies to justice, because spying is bad, just, end of story, just take our word for that.[/spoiler]

The main issue I had with the game was how limited I felt throughout it. Basically - you play as an investigator and loads up information to a network made to, well, spy on people. However, what information you can load up is already pre-decided by the game, which at times left the player with knowledge that couldn't be used in game. In addition, you couldn't take any data back or update it - unless the game wanted you to. The Orwell-system in the game didn't feel fully developed.

In conclusion, I feel as if the game was released before it was fully finished. I often felt frustrated, wondering why I wasn't able to upload information I found interesting, and that it felt unrealistic that such a complex system wouldn't be able to handle conflicting data. But I did find the concept interesting.

I wish there was a "Maybe" rating. This was so solidly middle of the road. A Perfect 2.5/5. This game is a narrative uncovered through a government surveillance system, and we're really taking the good with the bad here. 

The good: The mechanics of the game are interesting, and pay off in a very satisfying way. The visuals are nice and the interface is inoffensive. 

The bad: The character writing is mealymouthed, badly-paced and lacking a fresh core message. The narrative is hung on characters that are one-dimensional. The message is nothing new, but the 1984 But It's Got Facebook appeal could sell it's rhetorical points a lot easier if these characters felt rounder or even spoke in a slightly modern voice. A game where you follow people's daily communications should lead to these characters feeling richer and more developed. But it managed to avoid that altogether in favor of long, trite conversations, and worldbuilding with zero payoff. There were also a few shaky attempts at social commentary? For a game about investigating people for voicing their Alternative Ideologies, it all felt flimsy, like it didn't have enough confidence to have a real point of view. To it's credit, the story itself had some really interesting and surprising turns! But it was all at the end, AND all at once in a truly maddening choice of pacing.

All this is... fine, I suppose, considering these characters' actions and moral codas don't feel meaningfully attached to the larger ethical decision you're ultimately faced with. Instead, I felt like I was reading a 90's screenplay about Post-college Anarchist Mallrats and their One Cool Professor trying to make their mark on the world. Mostly because Orwell takes itself really, painfully seriously.

Overall, worth playing for the moments where the story and gameplay align nicely, but DEFINITELY get it on sale. Full price? Idk. Torrent Hackers instead. It has the same self-important tone and fakey computer-whiz stuff, but at least that had Angelina Jolie in it.

This is one of the more unique games I've played.  If the themes of George Orwell's 1984 resonate with you (and they might, regardless of whether you know that famous work or not--the concept of "Big Brother" is pretty much in the cultural lexicon, regardless of familiarity with its origin), then this will definitely interest you.  If you like detective games, it scratches that itch as well.  There's a good amount of interactivity, even though the game is primarily story-driven.  The act of what is essentially data-mining is nicely streamlined so that it isn't really too tedious.  When new "datachunks" are revealed, it really feels like relevant discovery, slowly building a picture from tiny puzzle pieces of data.  There's some choice in the game, as well, though not so much that repeated playthroughs would result in a lot of variation.  However, at 4 hours, I've played through the game once, so it isn't a vast time investment.  At $2.49, due to the Steam summer sale, the price was such that even a disappointment wouldn't have bothered me much.  But I was pleasantly surprised.  I'm going to play the second one as well.  Snatch this up when on sale.  I don't think you'll be too disappointed either.
