[h1]NSA Simulator[/h1]

Did you ever want to be Snowden? Now you can! 

The main differences between Orwell and NSA are probably: 1 - NSA agents have unrestricted access to a lot of private pornography, whereas Orwell didn't bring that to the table; and 2 - NSA spies private communications worldwide, while the action in Orwell is limited to a single country ("The Nation").


Orwell is a game of the mind. Your rewards for playing it won't be adrenaline rushes, glorious murderings or highscores, but  intriguing revelations, plot twists, meaningful consequences to your choices and, specially, a troubling insight into the mess this kind of global-spying system can easily become.

While playing, you'll probably find yourself thinking, "Sh*t. I probably shouldn't have uploaded that information", many times. And you can't take it back.

Judgment can be rushed, claimings issued in a moment of candor can be taken too seriously, harmless comments might be taken off context. And innocent people will pay for it.

It's not always easy to datamine accurate evidence. Even though you have access to a lot of confidential information, you don't have access to [i]all[/i] information. Mistakens and misjudgments [i]will[/i] happen.

And Orwell does a great job showing that. It's an important lesson, if you ask me.


It's hard to talk about these things without wedging in a personal opinion on the matter, so here's mine:

If we really want the security such invasive systems could bring, I'd rather have an AI in charge. Having humans running something like NSA is a catastrophe.

If an "investigator" is in a bad mood, seeking personal vendetta, doesn't have a perfect memory, loses focus, generally lacks attention, is anxious, enraged, didn't get a good night's sleep, is inherently evil or simply stupid, bad sh*t is bound to happen. And at least one of these things is true for literally every single human being, 100% of the time.

So, global cyber-spying should often lead to undesired results, while fundamental rights are guaranteed to be violated. Deliberately using such tools for unethical purposes, on the other hand, is very, [i]very[/i] easy.

It's a dangerous thing. In the best case scenario, an agent who screws up is going to lose his job. Meanwhile, some innocent person will have had their lives ruined forever. Those who cause harm are left unharmed, so they can (and will) keep doing it without fear or concern. It's a human thing -- either something can make you suffer, or you don't care about it. And that's another reason why you can't have [i]people[/i] with this kind of power.

Also, I don't want some random nerd hidden in some underground government facility watching me banging my girlfriend. I'd probably be OK with an AI doing it.


So...

[b]In short:[/b]
If you want to get a good insight on what kind of crap can happen when you can freely spy on people, even while having the best intentions at heart, using a smaller-scale system than the ones we currently have implemented in the real world, Orwell is likely your best choice.

I am conflicted about Orwell. On one hand, it's a good game, with a lot of qualities and good storytelling. On the other hand, its message fails to be as impactful as it could be and there are some flaws that occasionally pulled me out of the experience. I did enjoy the game, thus I do recommend it, but there was an undeniable voice in the back of my head that grumbled throughout. As a result, this review might read as more negative than not, which doesn't necessarily reflect in the game. Take that into account.

Let's start with an annoyance that is present throughout the whole game: the Advisor. In Orwell, you're the Investigator, and what you do is find information and uploading it for review in order to get access to more information. The Advisor is the person on the other end, the one getting the information you're uploading. The main problem is that the Advisor never shuts up. 95% of the time that you upload something, a pop-up window with the Advisor's comment will show up. As anyone that has experienced pop-up advertisements online could tell you, this is really annoying over time. The only reason why this doesn't break the game is because the dialogue is good, but it doesn't change the fact that a lot of it should have been cut.

My second issue is the lack of connectivity between gameplay and story. The narrative, as the name suggests, deals with issues of privacy, power structures and individual responsibility. The problem is that there is a lack of logic between choices and consequences, meaning that even if you're being thoughtful about your choices, they can still lead to consequences that seem... unfair. There is an argument that this shows the unfairness of the system, but the thing I feel is sacrificed is emotional investment. What is the point of caring if you can't affect the outcome? It discourages critical thinking, despite that being a vital part of the story. On top of this, we're not shown enough examples of the system working that poorly, meaning that the ending (which gameplay-wise is really good) lacks impact.

Furthermore, a smaller gripe I have with the game is sound direction. I don't know whose idea it was to have dramatic music playing when you scroll onto an important clue, but it was a bad idea and feels patronising. "Oh look, this is really important!" says the game, not letting the player actually be invested and figure it out for themself. Hell, most of the time I didn't even have a chance to read the clue before the game told me that it was important through the music! Based on this, I would actually recommend playing on mute, with your own music or something.

Despite all of this, Orwell is a fine game. It has good dialogue, good investigatory gameplay that it does some clever things with and a pretty great cast of characters with a lot of quality interactions. While some of the promise of the game remains unfulfilled, an equal part is actualised, meaning that the game is worth picking up and playing. With some tempered expectations, at least.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is pretty much police state simulator 2016. You play as an investigator spying on citizens of The Nation to maintain peace and order for the state.

The gameplay consists of reading articles, profiles, text messages, emails etc and clicking on highlighted text. Sounds pretty lame but who knew clicking on highlighted text could be so addictive? By reading various bits of info you piece together the overarching story and you ruin careers, make arrests and generally be an authoritarian douchebag. Or you can flout the rules and share incorrect information and be a bit of a rebel.

Said story is where the game really shines. As you're prying in to peoples private lives you begin to actually care about them and their troubles, and finding out what happens to to them is one of the things driving you on to the end. While spying on the various characters in the game you'll also read articles about current events, fleshing out the world and The Nation's history. The games central mystery unfolds in a satisfying way with plenty of (sometimes predictable) twists and turns along the way.

I finished my first playthrough by being a good little government lackey, taking pride in the fact that everyone hated my devotion to the state and making sure I crushed my enemies. I suppose next time I'll be a terrori- uh, political activist. I particularly enjoyed getting moaned at by my superiors for collecting pointless information such as favourite colours and foods.

I enjoyed the games soundtrack too, although to be fair its mainly all just ambience.

My only real criticisms of the game are it's quite short (7ish hours - although there's things you can do differently allowing multiple playthroughs), and I would've have liked more opportunities to be a sinister government agent, though as it's a story based game I can't knock the devs too harshly for that. 

In summary: If you want a short, simple game with a good story and multiple endings you can't go wrong with Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You.

Orwell resembles Hypnospace Outlaw with a lens of ripped-from-the-headlines political thrills rather than the bittersweet memories of a technology that has since gone disastrously wrong. 

It enables you to indulge your voyeuristic urges and piece together a mystery through evidence gathering, inductive reasoning, and plain ol' guessing at what the authors intended. The sleek UI, maybe-too-obvious musical stings, and actually-pretty-well-constructed material surrounding the central mystery, all help spark the player's curiosity. That, combined with a ongoing series of unfolding conspiracies, creates a whodunit that is, at minimum, passable. 

The two major strikes against this game are its UI and its actual writing. 

You need to juggle a web browser, a list of wiretapped communications, and a list of hacked computers, and the conversations progress at a quasi-real-time (read: agonizingly slow) pace. It doesn't ruin the game, but it does make certain points a slog. 

The writing is...meh. The dialogue feels rather stilted in places, particularly during more emotionally-charged moments. Moreover, the handful of red herrings that the game throws at you are really damn obvious if you've ever seen a social media feed. I didn't predict every single plot development that the game threw at me, but the attempts at misdirection felt more like they were thrown in by obligation more than anything else. 

These don't ruin the game; however, I wouldn't play the game again anytime soon. 

I paid about 3 bucks for about 4 hours of a decent game and an opportunity to explore a nice little plot, wrapped in mediocre dialogue and menu navigation. It was definitely worth the price of entry. I wouldn't necessarily regret paying full price for the experience, but at that point its value becomes far more subjective.

To complete the game is about 5-6 hours. You serve the role as "investigator" and find information on suspects involved in crimes.  Another government official makes arrest decisions based on the information that you choose to (or not to) give him.  You cannot directly communicate with this official, only send him certain pieces of information.

This creates an interesting dynamic. You can present misleading evidence to get people arrested, or you can try to protect those who you think are not troublemakers. You feel like you have a lot of power, but at the same time, you'll often have information misinterpreted. A complaint that I have is that sometimes, certain pieces of information seem completely irrelevant, but are needed to be sent to progress the story. At some points I just found myself essentially uploading everything to make the plot advance.

At certain points in the game you'll be given a choice between 2 conflicting pieces of evidence, where you can only upload one. Sometimes, it was completely unclear which evidence was the "truth". However, other times, I was able to take a logical guess as to what was correct based on other information I had found.

Supposedly, there are multiple endings based on the decisions you make (I have not replayed the game yet). I elected to NOT savescum to get the most desirable outcome (though I think my run was mostly clean), and I highly suggest you don't either. Believe me, it's more !!!FUN!!! that way.

As a whole, it's a very good game with a couple of flaws. Worth buying on a sale. Probably not worth full price unless this type of game interests you.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

An interesting title. It's essentially a simulation of what it would be like to work as an impartial agent for a foreign government, spying for them, gathering data and sharing it with your adviser so that they can make decisions about who is a suspect and attempt to stop them. This basically all takes place from your character's computer screen.

In essence, the plot revolves around you, the "investigator", being tasked with finding out who is responsible for a recent bombing in a public place within "The Nation" (the country that runs this Orwellian nightmare). The first chapter is basically the tutorial, but don't let that fool you into believing your choices don't matter.

EVERY piece of data you choose to share can be used by the "adviser" (a partner who can speak to and advise you but you can never speak to yourself) to make decisions about what to do next. If you, say, take words out of context, you can get someone arrested for nothing at all. Then again, maybe that's worth it (do the ends justify the means?) to stop a terrorist bombing. This game is basically a series of choices. You won't always have much time to act. Most of the time you're given free reign and only after tossing in specific information are you able to advance, but it works together pretty well. Once you beat the game, you're likely to want to replay chapters to fix details you messed up, causing an unexpected result. I often find I mess up more than once (I've played more than 6 hours, but I haven't seen every result) and, somewhat frustratingly, have to do the whole chapter over again just to get back to that point and fix it, but it's not so bad. If you approach the game as an "I'll try my best and live with the consequences" sort of thing, the end result could be pretty amazing. I highly recommend that at least for your first playthrough.

Don't fret over mistakes. Try your best.

And if you like the idea of being what basically amounts to a spy in the IT department, you'll probably enjoy this game. The sequel isn't quite as incredible, but that's mostly because it isn't really a sequel. I think it takes part along the same story which doesn't make much sense because I always got the impression you were the only team using Orwell. I think the developers just wanted to make another game and couldn't justify it properly. It's alright. I would still suggest playing the sequel after just because it's a fun concept and the developers deserve the support. They worked hard on this and it very clearly shows. Good concept, good aesthetic design, interesting story. It's a mystery you can unravel for yourself and it's a damn enjoyable one at that. Please, sincerely, give it a try if this sounds at all enticing.

It's not an immensely long game (probably about 6 hours for your first time through), but that by no means makes it less worthwhile.

It doesn't overstay its welcome and delivers a satisfying experience.

The game starts very simply:
There was a terror attack, and it’s up to you to investigate all available sources to discover who is responsible.
Basically detective work in the 21st century.
But as the game progresses, you discover there is much more than meets the eye.
Not only the suspects you track, their actions and relationships, but also your actions, and those of your superiors, all become important.
You start off as a mere spectator, but even by witnessing the events, you are already impacting them.
And once you realize your impact on the world you were meant to observe, you’re now faced with difficult choices.
Choices that are not right or wrong - only choices you need live with for the rest of your life…

This is a really good game, that dives deep into questions of terror, accountability, privacy, and more.

The only issue I had with this game, is that even though you don’t have to submit every single piece of evidence you find.
And can be even reprimanded for submitting irrelevant evidence,
The game simply refuses to progress until you submit almost every piece.
For example:
Let’s say you discover a person likes strawberry ice cream. But that has nothing to do with determining if he’s a terrorist or not, so you ignore this piece of info (mark it as ignored).
Then nothing happens. The game simply refuses to progress any further.
So you submit the only remaining piece of info, that the suspect likes strawberry ice cream, and like clockwork, you’re immediately reprimanded by your superior that this piece of data has nothing to do with the case at hand (daaa….).
But then suddenly the suspect receives an incriminating phone call - and the game suddenly starts progressing.

So instead of submitting useless data being a trigger to game progression, simply marking the data as “ignored” should serve the same purpose.

Other than that - it’s a really good game.
Much better than it’s sequel (Ignorance is Strength)

I usually don't like games with lots of reading. The exception to that rule is this game. The narrative being told from the view of the spy software Orwell with the player being the investigator using the tool, playing middleman between the AI and what actually gets processed, is a great twist to how visual novels usually work.

The game's interface, while relatively simple, but maybe a bit cluttered, is very easy to use while still giving the player tools to not get lost between sources of information, marking sources with new information, sources with unsubmitted "data chunks" and sources with disabled (marked by the player as not important or false information) "data chunks" with icons.

The artstyle is is unique and definitely detailed enough to get a good picture of the people involved in the story. The OST does its job very well and never got boring to me, even after multiple playthroughs, rare sound effects help convey the impact of situations very well.

Something I find interesting about the players' comments on this game is: 
Almost all comments in English are positive, while players from other countries are more likely to find the story disputable. The question is that should we forgive a terrorist that murdered innocents in the name of "privacy" or "freedom"?  Is our privacy a price too high to take for national security? While these questions are arguable enough, the game has its own tendency of siding with Juliet and overthrow the ORWELL. But making the opposite decision doesn't necessarily mean "2+2=5". Unlike 1984, we don't torture people for holding different opinions; we don't spy on people wherever they go;   All we concern is to make sure that the criminal doesn't leave unpunished by the law.

Downloaded this game purely as a time burner between bigger games, but did not see me enjoying this as much as i did. Great game with attention based around the narrative. Heavy Information collecting and decision-making make the story very engaging.

The game advertises itself as a Big Brother simulator, but it doesn't [i]quite[/i] reach that level of depth and intrigue that kind of premise could reach.

However, I don't think Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You isn't a bad game at all. I think it's definitely a concept that is executed well. You play as an investigator who's collecting information on a variety of people through public channels, such as social media outlets, and private channels such as one's email. These pieces of information are used as evidence to solve the crime you're assigned to.

There is some decision-making in the game and it was interesting to see how the conversation changes between characters after performing certain actions. There are a couple of routes to take, but ultimately, the resolution is relatively the same. I don't mind this that much, and I honestly think true choice games are difficult to make, unless you have the resources as a studio.

However, the main element I found to be lacking was the story; it was rather light. There are a few tense moments in the story, but overall, it seemed like the writers decided on a safer route. I was expecting somewhat darker and more philosophical themes to be used in the game. They are touched upon lightly, but not expanded to play any significant role. Given the premise, there's a whole world of deep possibilities that could be played out, but the writing just scratches the surface of this. In the end, I found myself wanting a little more out of the game.

All in all, the game was less than satisfactory for me and I'd give it a neutral rating, if I could. If you're new to the whole 'mass surveillance' idea and want to see a taste of what a game could do with that idea, then sure, go play this. But if you want something deeper, this isn't quite it.

Side note: I also bought and played the DLC and it's just more of the same, in my opinion.

Compelling psychological deduction game, piece together information found in newspapers, social media, personal data and prevent a terrorist attack, aka cyber stalking - the game.

You will not always know what the "correct" answer is and it is up to you to decide which often contradictory data chunks are relevant to the case. If you mindlessly upload everything without question and without considering the context, you will probably not have such a good time. 
I would have prefered if the develeopers didn't differetate between blue and yellow data chunks. They aren't that different anyway and I would recommend ignoring the color coding as much as you can.

I can also see this working great in an educational setting or for people who usually don't play video games.

Each bit of information can lead to access to more documents and I really enjoyed how that exploration helped flesh out the story universe. It raises interesting questions about modern-day or even future surveillance, the fragmented parts of ourselves that we put out onto the internet, and how the things we put online, without context, can end up creating a narrative that might not be entirely true. This game honestly fucked me up a bit by the end of it.

At first it kinda comes off as a Death and Taxes kind of game, but no. It is one long single story arch that is honestly wonderfully crafted. My investment and intrigue in the game honestly just grew more and more as the game went on and went in turns I didn't expect. I often found myself expecting one culprit only to move on to another and another and another as I found and submitted more evidence.

I played the whole game in 5 hours, but honestly I will go back for more. I have more achievements to get and I want to see what else I can find. I still have a bunch of questions and I want to find the answers!

Game play wise the choice mechanics here are really interesting. Rather than just swipping information away like you do in most games like this, you are given loads of info and can pick and chose information that you submit based on what the system deems relevant for you to possibly submit. Then there are some bits of info that are game changing. You also can't go back and take back previously submitted information, previous info you have supplied can only be updated.

All the info is presented to you in a way that you can just select the highlighted sentences and submit the info. You can submit evidence without actually reading the whole articles or chats or what ever it is that highlighted sentence is in. However, that is because the system only selects what it finds relevant. Sometimes the context surrounding that sentence can drastically change it's implications. Which is an amazing way of proving one of many points in this game. If you look at the small picture and just submit the evidence based on what the system shows you, you will get a lot more things wrong. I know because at first I didn't read statements completely. Then I realized a few times I messed up, I wished I could take something back but I couldn't and slowly I became more cautious of what I submitted. This also applied to times that I submitted fishy or questionable evidence only to realize a few web pages or convos later that the info was inaccurate.

If you like thought provoking story lines. The kind of game that afterwards you question of you did the right things, this is a great game for you. It's slightly slow pacing at first, but if you can get passed that the game will have you hooked. Another good comparison would be that if you are into Black Mirrors on Netflix, this is a game you are sure to enjoy.

Everything Edward Snowden Warned Us About: The Game. There are two dimensions about Orwell's political commentary that are particularly powerful. One, that in this age of mass surveillance, drone warfare, informatics, etc., surveillance produces certain forms of intimacy. When the people you learn to profile and study can be led to arrest or even death, it's devastating; it demonstrates how surveillance demolishes those on both sides of the snooping relationship. Second, Orwell has done a phenomenal job in its lore and worldbuilding--websites have the character, look, and rhetoric of the kind of online media ecology that we see in the real internet. The quotidian dimension of this setting demonstrates how this mass surveillance of the control society has become so regularized and normalized within a historical moment most of us consider "normal" and safe. Orwell denaturalizes this to great effect.

All of that said, Orwell ends far too abruptly, with a climax that doesn't quite feel earned. This game could've easily gone on for twice as long, and the payoff probably would have been more rewarding. Nevertheless the accomplishments of the game put it squarely in the "positive" category for me. Quite an achievement.

This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs.  As the game went on, I found myself getting glitched to certain websites, mostly the [spoiler]work profile of the concerned one woman after she died in a shootout with law enforcement, and occasionally it would glitch to her dating profile.  This would normally happen when I was in either the listener or insider tools, seemingly never when I was on the reader tool already.  It would just switch me over as I tried to open a file on the insider, or load up into a machine, or even when I'd try opening a new conversation in the listener.[/spoiler]
One more slight drawback about the game is that sometimes you get told a bit too much by the game.  Game not letting you progress?  Something you thought was a lie was probably true.  Yellow highlight instead of blue?  You're going to get some information that conflicts with that.  I realise it would be a lot more work but a way to mark information as lies rather than just disabling it might help.  People don't always tell the truth and if you come to the conclusion that something true is a lie, it would be nice if the game didn't give away that you're wrong by just stopping time for you.  As for the other issue, it might be nice getting a window saying "Hey, this piece of information you're trying to add conflicts with this other information you've already added...which one do you think is true?", instead of just "Hey, at some point probably in the next 10 minutes you'll get another piece of information that will conflict with this here, we know that even though in-universe we haven't made the connection that that page with the conflicting information even exists!"

All in all a really great game with a simple premise, easy to learn with some fairly minor flaws that can honestly be overlooked most of the time.

Other than some slight annoyances in the mechanics: delay when uploading files, max type speed or speed speed not fast enough for skipping through 2nd playthrough, uploading onto wrong profile or an unsuccessful upload has the same color so therefore looks exactly like the successful upload, and some confusing prompts/options at times. Orwell tells a compelling story from a interesting perspective.

Every once in a while, a game will come along that you simply won’t put down and will try to finish in one sitting. For me, Orwell fits that category, for it was thoroughly engrossing.

As the name suggests, Orwell deals with privacy and government surveillance. You are an ‘investigator’ of the new Orwell application, an app which, with the right authorisation, allows you to snoop on people’s phone calls, e-mails and all their online histories at will.

It is a disturbing look into a surveillance state, and yet, by putting you in charge it opens the door (and your mind) to justifying the system.

In the introduction, there is a terrorist bombing that kills some people. That’s where you come in, you’re in to investigate the prime suspect and ultimately to bring down the terror cell. You pick datachunks, which is vital (and non-vital/misleading) information and assign it to a person of interest in order to shape a narrative about them.

For example, you can use it properly in order to keep the authorities informed about a person’s whereabouts or connections with other people. Likewise, you can misuse it, say you might see a Twitter conversation where someone says “oh that’s torture!” (in reference to being taken out nightclubbing to dance) and the system will update to suggest that the person in question is, actually, a genuine torturer.

It is pretty obvious that Orwell intends for you to use your best judgement in the situation, take it seriously as a proper investigative tool and suddenly the arguments for invasive surveillance look quite appealing, especially if you succeed in foiling terror actions. Use it inappropriately on the other hand and suddenly things look a bit bleak.

For me, Orwell’s story was enticing and gripping. I was captivated trying to deny the terror actions, but also by the investigation into the terror cell. I don’t want to spoil anything, but basically, I swept through this in one sitting, without breaks, in just over four hours.

Why not a higher score? Well, I did encounter some bugs. At one point in a new chapter it would keep defaulting back to the previous chapter’s screens. I had to reboot the game in order to cut this nonsense out and continue. Without these, I may very well have given a 9, but I think that perhaps, would be too generous given the nature of the game. Still, this is a very good game.

Interesting little game. To describe it best I might as well lead you through my experience as I played through it. 

After the start and a bit further in I started worrying whether it could really give one that special something that we are all looking for in games. Is it to linear? Do I really need to investigate? Is it a no-brainer drag and drop? Do my decisions even matter in the end? And certainly it took a bit but as the story opened up I caught myself questioning my previous thoughts and decisions more often. Was it a coincidence? Is it the truth or an attempt to mislead? What am I missing? This struggle continued for a while, clicking and reading through pages of information, until the story picked up the pace and gave me the opening for the final push. The positive jump in mood and anticipation of finally unraveling it all made the last stretch a very entertaining experience. One might ask: Is it just the ending then that is good? No, everything together, the conclusion just as much as the road leading up to it made it all worth it.

It wasn't perfect. I had some rare situations where I felt forced to make a questionable decision just to progress. And personally I might have wanted to see more irrelevant pieces of information that are better hidden and more indistinguishable from important ones. Maybe even a complete overhaul of the presentation of parse-able information which would make it harder to find them. Could have been a harder difficulty option? 

With that said. I can only recommend it. Give it a try.

[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

I think Orwell as a game is a great concept, but could have been executed far better. The game highlights important information, and railroads you into making choices that aren't backed by evidence. It doesn't provide enough detail for you to make judgement calls, but leaves you between two equally plausible answers, and forces you to make a choice. A better way of doing this would have been to present more information than necessary, and let players sort out what's important, and take their own notes. I would have preferred the game to involve less bias - letting players make their own choices, and come to their own conclusion on the benefits - or invasions - of government surveillance. I also feel the ending was robbed from me. I simply couldn't figure out how to support the cause of Thought, and wanted to have to face the ethical dilemma of doing so. OK - to start with the bad; the way progression works is, to say the least, not exactly flawless. At multiple times I felt I had no choice but to do the exact opposite of what my intuition really led me towards, because if the story hasn't moved forward in a while, and you've already done everything that seems sensible, you've no real choice but to just take random stabs. You never know what will push the game to move the story forward, and unfortunately it can really weaken the immersion when you're going back to accept data points you had previously ruled out just on the off chance one of them will finally trigger the script to move forward.

Also, it sometimes feels a little restrictive that you are never freely choosing what information to select for processing - rather, you are selecting which of the automatically flagged information to process. So, sometimes it simply doesn't highlight something which might seem important to you, and sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information flagged isn't quite what you expected. To some extent, these can be forgiven as contributing to the theme that you are not entirely in control of the "Orwell" program, but nonetheless, this can also pull you out of the game if something really catches your attention but the lack of a flag is effectively the game telling you to ignore it.

Those minor irks aside, though - I actually thought this game was very good.

The story is interesting, and generally does an excellent job of avoiding lazy narrative tropes or character stereotypes. The combination of inferring information from investigating documents and reading call or chat transcripts as a means of piecing together events is used to excellent effect. Overall, the story is easily engaging enough to keep you invested in the game throughout, wanting to untangle all the details. 

The mechanics, despite the little irks I mentioned at the beginning of the review, also work really nicely on the whole. They feel genuinely fresh and original, and effectively encourage you to keep paying attention while working through a fairly hefty pile of documents.

I also appreciate that your choices make some meaningful differences, and the story is a manageable enough length that upon finishing my first run I immediately started another to try to reach the other outcomes. However, the repeat playthroughs to see the other possibilities play out weren't remotely enjoyable... The amount of identical information you have to grind through easily outweighs any enjoyment form seeing the alternative paths.

So, only worth playing through once, and not particularly long - but for the duration of that first playthrough, it's an interesting game with original mechanics and the story holds your attention.

I wouldn't pay full price, but if there's a decent discount I'd certainly recommend checking it out.

There is a character, Harrison O'Donnell, who leaves a vivid and unforgettable impression on me. [spoiler] He is just a veil and hypocritical creep, writing columns for the official media while secretly scheming actions toward the government. However, I would still like to regard the behavior of being two-faced as hypocrisy and it should be condemned, but in a less aggressive way. As for the existence of the system, I have to admit its important function and efficiency to prevent certain people from doing harm to the public. I want to briefly discuss branching paths in this game. There are plenty of them, but unlike other games they are not straightforward choices like with typical dialog options. Instead it's a sequence of choices that you make that add up to a result branching in either direction. But for many of the choices you're not given any indication that they are in fact involved in a branching path. This makes it more realistic, but you'll need to keep in mind that although the game let's you process all digital information and out of curiosity you might (like me) want to postpone your decisions until you've processed them all, you will miss out on several branching paths, not realising that processing some innocuous looking data shards you actually forced yourself down a certain path. Once you figure out how rich this game is in its branching paths, you'll be looking at possibly replaying it several times. This game's replay-ability isn't great. Not knowing what comes next is really the driving power behind this game, so replaying it isn't nearly as exciting.

I enjoy several game genres, but for a slow, relaxing experience, this type of game suits me best. In the same vein as titles such as Papers, Please and Not Tonight, Orwell does it with a twist. It essentially turns your desktop into the computer of the intelligence gather used in the game.

Orwell, however, is a step up. It's fun, but it's also quite creepy and invites an examination of the risks of our "share everything on the Internet" culture. Is your Facebook account linked to your Instagram account? Is your name on either one the same as the one on your LinkdIn? In Orwell, connections like these allow you, the investigator, to track people across a virtual Internet, constantly digging for more information.

Ethical and moral choices arise. An early one (during the tutorial section, but still a possible spoiler) is the decision between [spoiler] reporting the "friendly" theft of a credit card. Report it and have the card canceled, or don't report it so further card activity can be tracked? [/spoiler]

This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.

A fun little document reading simulator.

Seriously, that is the gameplay. It's like a season of 24, where you have to find out where the bomb is going to go off, and it's all up to you, but instead of an elite anti-terrorist agent, you're some rando sitting in front of a PC, hired to sift through documents. That is literally who you are, in the universe of the game. You submit portions of documents to the system, and this unlocks more documents. That may sound a little silly, but the game explains itself pretty well.

No need to worry about 'pixel hunting' or broken logic - all problems are solved and the plot is progressed in all cases by finding the right entry in the right document. If anything, the game holds your hand. 

You can only submit portions of any document that the system deems potentially relevant. You cannot get a game over - you could play this game through by blindly submitting every bit of highlighted text you found, without paying attention to the plot.

But the plot itself is worth paying attention to - a slow-burn story of a parallel world with technology from five minutes into the future. That lawyer guy on youtube who rates the legal accuracy of various pieces of pop culture would probably not rate this thing too highly. But it is fun, and the rationale for everything that happens is internally consistent.

There are branching paths and different outcomes to minor plot points, as well as alternate endings, depending on how you play  - which boils down to which pieces of information you choose to submit or not submit. It is worth the second and even third play-throughs needed to explore every possible outcome.

Which brings me to my two main complaints:

- There is a checkpoint system, limited to the five main chapters/days of the campaign. You can replay a previous day/chapter, but as soon as you start say, chapter two, your progress in the remaining 3 chapters is lost.

- There is no fast-track buttons for voice or text conversations - they play out in real time, complete with 'realistic' pauses, whether you like it or not.

Neither of these are game-breaking, and are more just quality of life features that I found to be conspicuously absent. Their absence mean that secondary playthroughs for achievements/branch discovery take a little longer than they otherwise would.

I bought Orwell on sale, and went in to it without doing much homework, but I got the impression that this would be several distinct yet related cases. It's more like one big ongoing case. Also in contrast to the Ace Attorney games, which Orwell reminds me of just a little, the plot is a little more serious, and the characters a little less colorful. But if you like that series, or sifting through documents to find a terrorist in a dystopian alternate world sounds like fun to you, and if none of what I have written sounds like a deal-breaker, and you find this game at a price that you think is worth ten or so hours of gameplay, go for it.

One final thought - this game is about a surveillance state, but it doesn't take the easy way out. It poses the dilemma of government overreach/corruption for 'safety' vs. privacy/freedom concerns in an interesting way. I would not say that Orwell is quite as brilliant or profound as some of the glowing reviews suggest, but I do like the way that the plot, the gameplay, and the endings you are able to choose all come together to get you thinking about this issue, even if just a little.

It is very biased towards why all this is a bad idea and pretty much gives no indication why and how it could actually work. And you know, that all would have been fine if done right, but everything in the story hinges on a lot of coincidences and it takes away from how an actual Orwell system could maybe properly work.

It still wouldn't, but this case does not show the actual flaws of such a system. And that is the problem of this game. It starts off by you following ONE suspect. In a true case you would have had information on everyone at the crime scene, and this is only the first big flaw why this is a bad representation of a system like this. [spoiler]And then that suspect ends up not being involved at all, but by coincidence she does happen to be in contact with the true criminal. Oh, sure, the writers eventually tried to make a link and explain it was the criminal who was responsible for the first suspect to be a the crime scene. Which ends up with the story making even less sense as there is absolutely no indication why the criminal would even want this suspect to be at the first crime scene.[/spoiler] And it just goes downhill from there, with more random stuff happening that just happens to be convenient for this poor mirror or a true spying system.

Conclusion: Good concept, but the writing keeps it from being a good game.

Orwell puts you in the position of a security agent digging through public and private information to uncover the truth. Or to pull everything out of context to fabricate a lie. Or to be honestly mistaken, and be responsible for the prosecution of innocent people. Your actions have consequences, so you are presented a constant ethical dilemma, and are second-guessing yourself on every plot-twist and turn as events unfold.

Its very well put together, multi-faceted story is extremely engaging, though told only through text and simple graphics. The replay value is however badly hurt by chats and phone calls going on in real-time, making you wait minutes on end through a conversation you already know before you finally have the possibility to explore another outcome.

All in all this game has made me feel like a creepy stalker, government disobeying rebel and unethical secret agent, It has made me laugh, shout in anger, feel defeated, and cheer in victory-- as well as making me more aware of the power of information and social media. Wholeheartedly recommended to anyone interested in story-driven dystopian games, investigation, manipulation, and Facebook conspiracists.

This game is a punch in the gut.

It gives you a slow lead in to a game and very quickly spirals into an uncontrollable tailspin of compounding decisions.

There are genuine heart-wrenching consequences to the actions you take if you choose wrong.

The game is a warning on the dangers that come with complete surveillance, how people can become collateral damage to someone thinking they have all the information to make an informed decision.

Regardless of what you do, in your quest to find "that guilty person" you will accidentally impact and potentially destroy the lives of so many other people.

It's such a simple game.  It's not difficult.  It's a game that makes you think about real life, about how our decisions can affect others.  It's a game that teaches you that there is always a "next step" when it comes to trying to attain complete safety for a society, and that trying for it can ultimately destroy the society and everything it stands for.

Alright, I'll keep this as basic as I can so you know what you're getting yourself into.


[h1] The Story [/h1] 

First off, this is a spoiler free re-view, If you are looking for spoilers, please don't this game is depending on 
[b] ENTIRELY [/b]  on the story. That being said the story itself is brilliant. The characters are like-able (and quite the opposite as well), the plot unravels so well that you never know what happens next or what awaits you and the atmosphere of it all gets more and more intense as you progress. 

[h1] Game-play [/h1] 

There is not much to be said about game-play, it is fairly basic, but works incredibly well. Basic web-coordination and a little bit of memory/logical thinking will save you a lot of time. However, depending on [b] YOUR [/b] choices, some key parts of the story will change (There is no real ''answer'', most of the time going with your gut is the best you can do). In the end, your choices will impact the outcome, and the ending of the game itself.

[h1] Soundtrack [/h1] 

It started off very simple, generic investigation theme and yaddi yadda, you get the point. However, I soon found out that the music itself is very dynamic and will change depending on the situation you will find yourself in. Thanks to that little touch it kept me on the edge of my seat, and dropped my jaw when it was supposed to, great work, loved it.

[h1] Re-play ability [/h1] 

The game has multiple endings and some key factors change the story, so the way you play can be completely different from how another person would play. Other than that, once you complete the game, you know the story as well as the ''plot-twists'' that will appear, so you have the upper-hand, so to speak. 

[h1] Worth it ? [/h1] 

Absolutely ! The game is very short and as of the day of this re-view, it has one sequel. You can complete it in under 5 hours, for all achievements about 8-9 I wager. Although I recommend buying it while it is on sale and preferably in a bundle with the sequel. I would rate this game an 8/10, it is a really good game, but a bit too short for my liking.

The government is spying on its citizens. Don't worry, I'm not about to launch into a rant about the Investigatory Powers Act. Rather, this is the set up to Orwell, a five-part episodic adventure about the tension between privacy and national security. Set in The Nation, Orwell is a visual novel in which you voyeuristically watch over a group of activists—trying to determine who is responsible for a series of bombings.

The titular Orwell is a program for surveilling The Nation's citizens. You play as an investigator, and your job is to analyse the digital footprint of any citizens that The Party has marked as a potential threat. At first you're scouring public and state records—newspapers, websites and police databases. But soon, the intrusion goes deeper. You read emails and chat logs, listen to phone calls, and, in extreme cases, dig through your target's computer.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player.

Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.

ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

8/10: A great immersive 'clicking sim' story game, with a couple of rough edges.

The good: I was completely engaged with the game from start to finish (binged it in 1 session). I felt that the difficulty, pacing and depth was just right for most of the game. The fact that the most minor of decisions are final and cannot be undone even though their consequences might not be realized until an hour or two later really kept me on my toes. While most of the game plays like a relaxing interactive story w/o difficulty there was just enough setpiece 'puzzles' (where a key decision required rereading every piece of information thoroughly and thinking hard) to create a good cycle of tension without feeling exhausting. And just when my brain was out of juice, the game ended. Beautiful

The bad: 1) the fact that the 'important information' to your investigation is hard-coded rather than free to deduce by yourself rears its ugly head occasionally. The developer, understandably, didn't account for every permutation that information might be read from. So, for example, when I'm asked to provide a portrait of a target and the game doesn't let me submit that one picture because the dev missed it it was a a little frustrating. It frustrates because, while minor, the immersion drops and the plot's rails become visible for just a second. 

*2 INVOLVES MINOR PLOT SPOILERS* TLDR: meh ending

[spoiler]2) The obligatory *twist ending* was not well executed. I imagine I'm not the first one to pick up on that given how glaringly it stands out from the quality of the rest of the game (can be read as a plus.). Arthur Conan Doyle's (Sherlock Holmes) rules of a good detective story require that the answer be obvious 'had you known X', ie there must be a underlying logic to it that the reader/player was only unable to uncover until the end due to not having all the pieces. The secret villain showed no indication that [hidden] was capable of performing the act even after everything was revealed, which makes the reveal feel like plain shock value. In fact I was absolutely caught off guard by the reveal when it was done through NPC dialog. 

To the devs: Objective fact reveals like "surprise he/she was actually secretly there" or "he/she is acting mysteriously" alone does not convince me that they are secretly the culprit. You gotta show motive, character, drives. Not what they did but why they did it.[/spoiler]

Overall, would absolutely say that the game nailed what it set out to do, i.e. letting you roleplay as a Big Brother spying and tearing through everyone's personal info on a quest to stop terrorism. And the moral of the story was made pretty well: guessing who someone is through their personal info alone without context is inaccurate. That the plot that came attached to that experience, and the human limitations of the dev, is a little underwhelming does not discount the fact that I was completely immersed into it. Which is a rare thing
