A fascinating examination of a surveillance state in the modern age of connectedness and social networking. You play as an criminal investigator by trawling through personal conversations, private social media posts and transcribed phone calls looking for relevant information and, later, incriminating evidence. The onus is on the player to identify what is relevant; exposing ethical dilemmas around privacy, selective reporting of information and being intentionally mislead. 

Comparisons with novels like [b]1984[/b] are all bit invited by the game's title. While the novel had the benefit of originality, this game forces the player out of passive observation into an active role. While the game's events are fixed and the set of possible outcomes predetermined, the narrative the player weaves as they learn more about the actors is their own, leaving room for regret and introspection not possible through a novel. While we often construct narratives that we would always be "good people", games like [b]Orwell[/b] or [b]Papers Please[/b] challenge us to both be that person in difficult scenarios and to understand what "good" actually is.

A bit short with around seven hours of game play but worth it. However, there is a lot of reading and comprehension, which may put off those looking for something more cathartic than cerebral.

I found the story is engaging enough, and the game explores some interesting concepts and questions. Many of the themes have already been thoroughly explored in a variety of philosophical sci-fi / dystopian plots, but the gameplay made me feel involved, and the not-too-distant, not-so-different-future setting instilled a teensy bit of discomforting familiarity with the game world.

Obviously if you're not into decision-focused, plot- and character-centered games or not a fan of story-telling primarily through pictures and text, this game might not be your dig.

Disclaimer, i got this game for free from some giveaway, though even if I didnt i doubt my opinion would change much because my concept of price-to-quality probably needs some work. Basically you can more or less take this as a review without worrying about if i got it for free.

TL;DR at bottom if you want that.

Orwell is... well an Orwellian game (I think i'm using that right). You are more or less the disembodied investigator (with a face and directly spoken to though) that is responsible for keeping tabs on several people, and uncover the story of a recent bombing in a (probably) realistic surveillance state (or whatever its called exactly). It's not a blatant dystopia where the government is paranoid of everyone, its a much more gray area, where everyone lives generally normal lives, but should the need arise the government can quickly go through everything they have online. 

Day 1: investigate connection of one citizen to a bombing. Is it coincidence they have a police record and happen to be leaving the area barely a minute before the bomb goes off?  

Day 2: things go from bad to worse. I'm not going to go farther, but it goes from "uncover truth of a recent tragedy" to "[i]make sure any tragedies are prevented, [b]at all costs[/b][/i]"

The game's art style is really good, though there is the awkward/uncanny face photos every once in a while, but generally are pretty good.

The main music loop is good. Its not amazing, but it doesn't get annoying. Some of the musical stingers are a bit on the nose, but at the same time i often get chills from them, even the relieving ones. Not many scores do that so regularly. they can sometimes sorta spoil some of the twists, but usually just by a few seconds, at most. Even then, its basically saying "[i]read carefully motherf***er, there are lives on the line with this one, [b]dont f*ck this up[/b] [/i]"

The game overall is sorta short (single digit hours, but more than one sitting, unless you plan to speed through it in a day, which i do NOT recommend, this is a game you take your time on, see last line of above paragraph) with not much replay value by itself, but I came back to it after a few months, mostly fresh after forgetting many of the exact details (with all the info you collect, some of the bits are bound to be"unloaded" by your brain)

TL;DR, a slow and well paced thinking game, unique art, good main theme and heavy hitting moments. 9/10. Worth a few dollars, imo (though again not the best judgement for that).

Just remember, your actions have consequences. [i][b]Don't screw it up

This is a beautiful game engine and fantastic and engaging story, ruined by a shitty ending that artificial constraints force you into. Yes, there are alternate endings but you have to play through the whole game again to find them, and also explicitly ignore the things that the game itself expects you to do; you're now gaming the game design, not playing the game.

It's a shame. I had a great experience and now it's utterly ruined because they couldn't close it off.

The mystery itself is interesting and entertaining, but the real value here is thinking about surveillance and information - I found it very difficult to maintain appropriate boundaries for what was "relevant" to the investigation or not. Mental states? Blog posts? Divorces? It certainly makes it difficult to want to endorse human judgment as the right way to make these decisions, except that also that also your own judgment is what makes things turn out better (and it's not obvious that strict rules would do a better job). So it gives you a lot to think about.

In one of the classes I'm taking at the university I'm attending we were required to study the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, Edward Snowden, and a few other things relating to that. And the more I see the more I begin to realize that this game is scary accurate to the real thing. From everything I can tell this is almost exactly what it's like to be a part of the real thing from how information is collected, to how everyone you know becomes a target, to even how [spoiler] it's revealed that even you are being monitored [/spoiler]. At the same time though it asks all these brilliant questions that make you question even whether it's better to possibly give up your privacy, your own thoughts for a bit of extra security, as you go around monitoring people's knowing what you're doing is wrong you can't help but feel like you've done the right thing when you actually save the lives of more people, and prevent additional terror attacks.

This game is scary accurate to the real thing, and if you care even remotely for your privacy you need to give this game a chance.

*TL;DR AT BOTTOM* 
Firstly I'd just like to say I'm not one to review games often, but I'll give it a shot. I'll give a little overview of my view, a summary of how the game works, some of the pros, the cons, who I'd recommend the game for, and then a final rating.

So I've just finished playing through one run of the game, well doing one run through of it and I have to say I've really enjoyed it. It's incredibly well designed, with a brilliant branching storyline which you have a direct effect on. Admittedly it only has a few hours of playing if you only want to do the one run through, but if you're even more of a completionist than I am there is some replayablity, as the different choices you make influence the development of the situation, who gets arrested, who is charged with what, through to the political outcomes.

Basically the game focuses on a network of people who are implicated after a bomb goes off, and you play the role of an investigator, who has the job of going through various news sources, private files, phone calls, social media communications etc, and choosing what datachunks to process, in order to solve the various tasks you are presented with. Sometimes you might face conflicting bits of data, and it's down to you to choose what to process, this can be based on ignorant sources, or particular context of the sources. 

As mentioned, the storyline that you can influence is particularly interesting, and the general depth to the characters and plot is quite phenomenal. The game itself runs very easily, and though overall you are a little guided with what to look at, this fits with the overall design of the surveillance system you are a part of. I particularly like the flexibility you have, in that if you want you can be like me and just read through loads of different material which might not even help you, but can immerse you in the setting. Further, there were one or two moments where I was wondering what should I do next, but as it all turned out I had overlooked or forgot about particular things, so it's not too complex, but does require a little thought.

In terms of negatives, there's not too much to complain about. In terms of the game, maybe the ability to load up the game on the different days or after each task is done, particularly towards the end of the story, would be good, in order to just look at the different endings without a full replay. I loved the story, and look forward to playing the next game, but I still would have loved if the game had been longer. Which brings me to the price, at £7.19, for only 4 hours content (well for me anyway with only one run through), the game might be a little steep, but I really enjoyed it to be honest, and if you see it in a sale, go for it.

Overall I'm going to say the game itself is a 9/10, very well designed, but the experience as a whole is more a 7/10 due to the limited playtime for the price. Long review for sure, but hope it helped. Enjoy your day!

TL;DR: Well designed game with branching/influenceable story, deep setting, drawing on relevant themes with surveillance, government, and freedom vs security, unique game type, quite a price for relatively short amount of playtime, deffo worth on sale, 9/10 game itself, 7/10 factoring in price and content.

To start this review, I would like to mention that I am a massive fan of Orwell, both author and game. I found this game shortly after reading the novel this game is based on, Nineteen Eighty-Four. And let me tell you, it sure does scratch the Orwell itch. Playing the game I truly felt put in the role of a member of the Party, demanding subservience over the serfs of the Nation and ensuring it's complete control. The story is a very interesting and engaging detective drama with, while not very deep, enjoyable characters as well as unique moments. The gameplay has you scour through newspapers, dating profiles, texts, dms, websites, having you discern useful information for your investigation, including having you choose between conflicting information. What's really interesting about this game, however, is it's branching paths you can take based on what information you choose to add and omit, leading to different outcomes for the people whose lives you essentially control. There are multiple distinct endings and several different ways you can get to them that makes this game worth replaying (unless you're like me, who chooses to replay the game and get the same ending [spoiler] Long live Oceania! 2+2=5! So I'd say, if you're a fan of George Orwell, detective stories, dystopia, or some healthy social and political commentary, I'd say this is the game for you. This a pretty clever little narrative game. 

You essentially play the role of an investigator using a survelliance software system called Orwell, and investigate people that are citizens of a country referred to as "The Nation", that seems to be modeled off of present day Western nations like the US, UK, Canada etc. You don't have total access to everything, as your adviser often needs to 'get clearance' to add someone to the target list, but you still wield a chilling amount of investigative power eventually. 

This is not set in an extreme totalitarian world like the state of Oceania in [i]1984[/i], but a mostly present day world. It's a bit ambiguous though, as a couple real countries are referred to eventually, and 'The Nation' has some ominous things about it that suggest a veiled totalitarianism, especially with references to 'The Party'.  

There isn't alot of 'gameplay' to it, as you basically just use the mouse to collect bits of information on people from your various electronic sources. It's UI is basically the same ideas as using a computer and web browser.  

While all selectable information is highlighted for you, you do have to make decisions about what information to upload to a person's Orwell profile, and that can have major consequences for events in the story.  Some info is obviously useful, some is just mundane, some bits of info conflict with others. With the conflicting info though, i wish there were sometimes more avaliable info to make a better judgement, but I guess that's the point. 

There are at least a few different endings, but you may have to do a full playthrough again to get them, i'm not sure. 

Without giving away any spoilers to the story, there is a persistent (and i'm sure intentional) irony about the people you are tasked to investigate.  The in-game stated purpose of Orwell and your position is to protect the nation from terrorist threats.  The story starts off when a small bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza.  From that point, the network of people you investigate are all tied to the ideology of wanting privacy. Basically, you are doing the exact things that are fueling this ideology. 

This is excellent social and political commentary in the form of a simple game, and I would definitetly recommend it!

An amazing piece of commentary on encroaching surveillance tech and how woefully susceptible it is to misuse, misinterpretation and bad faith justification using poor or skewed implementation. 

Some say you have nothing to fear if you have nothing to hide, but the game asks, what if you should be afraid of those looking?

[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. 

I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up.

I just finished the 1st episode (?... Season?... ?...) and I wanted to write a review since I have seen a negative review boil the game down to reading through a bunch of things and dragging pieces of text to a window. Yes. That's true; you do do that. However. In Orwell, you play the role of an investigator and as the story (yes there is a story, and, imho, a pretty well written one) unfolds into later chapters and becomes more complex, you as the investigator need to not only decide what information is important but also make judgement calls as to what piece of information is more correct (yes there are many times where information you come across is in conflict with another piece of information) when there is a discrepancy. There in lies the -real- beauty and, what I believe, to be the point of the game. I won't say more so as not to spoil it, but once you get to the end I think you'll see what I mean.

In any case, correctly unraveling the story requires you to learn about and know the characters involved as you need to also build a mental picture of who these people are and their social network (how they relate to one another). I would say it's definitely -not- a traditional game as the medium is click-drag and let go, but that's really more the medium than anything and a different experience is many times why people play a game by an indie studio; they are looking for a different experience.  And lets face it, people play visual novels (are they really even a game?). This game at least requires you to problem solve and critically think; there's even a deeper message behind it (again, no spoilers :) ).

The tl;dr is, yes it's click-drag, but it's real entertainment is in the story, the message behind it, the problem solving, the critical thinking, and making connections that don't immediately jump right out at you.

In [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] you play as an investigator hired by [i]The Nation[/i], a country led by an authoritarian government named [i]The Party[/i], to work at [i]Orwell[/i], a covert surveillance system commissioned by the Ministry of Security through the Safety Bill. In the beginning you need to investigate a young woman with criminal history after a bomb goes off at the Freedom Plaza. Then, the story escalates. The main question this game presents is whether you'd sacrifice your freedom and privacy for "safety".
This game will run on any modern computer and I recommend it to any mature person who has 10€ to spare, specially if they have read and liked 1984. It is obviously not as intricate as the book, but it's very interesting nevertheless.
I have a negative remark to make about this game, though: [u]it is very slow[/u]. I personally read faster than the maximum text speed of this game and, specially when replaying to explore different options and get achievements, it put me off a little. Otherwise, I had a very pleasant experience.

If you liked [i]Orwell[/i], I would also recommend that you play [i]Headliner: Novinews[/i].

You play as an investigator for a government project called Orwell, which has been kicked into action after a bombing at a national monument. Your job is to use what's effectively GoogleGovernment to investigate suspects, finding how they're related to each other, and know as much about them as possible. The game has 3 endings I know of, and probably many more. The ending you get depends upon what information you place into Orwell. 

The game features a very unique and simple look, with low poly art for things such as images and the background, and what's effectively Internet Explorer and files displaying the information you have on suspects. The game's 'Internet Explorer' is used to discover information about people while on the other hand, the 'files section' shows all the information you placed into Orwell on a specific person, classed into categories, and people's relationships to one another.

Unfortunately, the game's does nothing when it comes to replaying, a concept I've only ever seen played off in Oxenfree, but 100% should be implemented in more games. After your first run, you know how the story twists and turns and can already account for it ahead of time.

I did not enjoy this experience, i did not find it fun, and here are my main complaints:

1) You spend all of your  time sifting through emails and texts looking for important information or data chunks. This is not a challenge because the information is highlighted for you. To make matters  even dumber, the specific emails, texts, etc are marked with an icon to show you which ones have the important information you need to act on.

2) The important decision points in the game are also highlighted in bright yellow as conflicting data chunks. You have to choose which one Orwell (the computer) will consider as fact. Often times you have to do this without any way of knowing the actual truth, but the implications of the choices are always glaringly obvious. 

3) There are data chunks that have to be given to Orwell for the story to progress, even if you don't  want to provide it. This is the one thing the ruined the experience for me, and made it obvious that the program is leading you by the nose and you have no real control. I get it. You can't read a book from the middle out, and in a "game" that is basically just a click-through-story you have to proceed in the order the author intends. All the important information has to be in place for the story to make sense. 

Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but I also take issue with the name of this "game". Orwell is a stupidly ironic name. George Orwell was an opponent of totalitarianism, not it's champion. Perhaps a better literary subject to steal would have been Colossus (Dennis Feltham Jones). At least that Colossus was a computer.

This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

Orwell is- as the name implies- a government surveillance simulator.  You are an operator of the new titular system Orwell, and you are told to help the government of The Nation to catch a terrorist.  As the plot unfolds, you find yourself having to increasingly question what you're doing, and whether the ends- catching actual murderers- justify the means, the lies, and the rights you've violated to get there.

As you process information on your targets, you find related documents to the info you're processing.  Now and then this proves finnicky, with some documents unlocked in a manner very reminiscent of a Point-and-click adventure game's "How does THAT make sense?!" moments.  In addition, while the story has a great deal of branching going on (with choices being made based on what data you choose to process and which of pairs of conflicting data you choose to work with), many of the points it tries to bring up fall hollow as some of the very, very evil people you deal with try to decry the bad you've done to catch them.  Imagine if Hitler had been captured by the Allies, and on the stand in Nuremberg said "Okay, so yeah, I genocided a LOT of people and that was probably wrong, but I HAD to; the Treaty of Versailles was inexcusable!"  Much like one is not inclined to listen to Hitler's points about the morality of excessive punitive measures in war treaties, the end of Orwell leaves you less than immersed and willing to concern the finer points of the game's questions on the morality of government surveillance, largely due to the person presenting the final decision.

All of that aside, however, this game gets a very firm recommendation.  It was a deep and interesting game, and despite being shot in the foot by some despicable characters (in among some very good and well-written ones) it still managed to raise thought-provoking questions on how far is too far for a government to go to catch criminals.

A decent narrative experience about mass surveillance.

Your task is seemingly simple: uncover the truth behind the Freedom Plaza bombing. In order to achieve this, you will traverse blogs, read social media and eavesdrop on people's calls. Every bit of information (here called "chunk") may be helpful to determine who was the perpetrator all along.

Well, of course it would not be [i]that[/i] easy. More and more people appear to be involved, more and more information is conflicting, meaning you have to decide which data you will input into the eponymous Orwell system (and *when* will you input them) for the government to act on.

While your actions will have consequences, this is still a linear experience.

If you are a fan of such games, why not giving it a try?

Note: I [b]DO NOT[/b] recommend the sequel, which is a far shorter game and does not provide enough novelties to be worth your attention. Stick to this one.

[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

Gameplay wise Orwell is an episodic, point and click, interactive visual novel, in a dystopian future, with interesting questions regarding freedom, privacy, security and the pros and cons of the digital era. As a researcher you have to use Orwell (a complex governmental surveillance system) to investigate the lives of multiple citizens of the fictional country "The Nation", and find out those responsible for a series of terror attacks. You can do this by listening to phone calls, reading blog posts, and personal e-mails, hacking laptops, phones and going through medical files, bank records etc. As you make your connections and draw your conclusions you can tailor the story here and there, and you can decide who to incriminate or who to help, but overall your choices do not define the final outcome of the game that much. I liked the atmoshpere and the story has some interesting twists, plus there are multiple endings so it has some replay value as well. Good job Osmotic Studios, this was a very enjoyable experience.

I was happy to find out that there is a sequel to Orwell, I'll definitely buy it in the upcoming months!

Orwell is a unique concept that keeps you digging for the entire time.

You play as a government investigator of The Nation, using the Orwell system to collect information about people who pose potential threats to The Party.

It pulls heavy inspiration from George Orwell's 1984, and you'll notice it right off the bat, with your advisor going by the name "Symes".

It's a short game, and to 100% it, you won't need more than 7-8 hours, but I really feel like it's worth your time. It gives a scary, realistic insight about a path down to an Orwellean future, where everything you say and do is on display for the government.

It felt especially bad because the game is fake-real-time, meaning things happen "as time goes by", but really only the game progresses as you take actions. So what would almost always happen was that (literally) immediately after submitted your hypothesis - your guess - as a FACT, the game goes "oh, this just in! Here's the information you could have used to make a sound judgement, if you'd just waited to click send for 5 seconds!". You continuously felt like an absolute impatient amateur switching between doing monkey work gathering information and then posting your guesses as facts to a board. And why can't I then write them and say "Hey, I just got this information! You know that thing I said earlier? Yeah, something has come up, and that is now completely wrong!" Absolutely destroyed my immersion.
All in all, the game just made me more and more annoyed, as the focus was more on "gut-feeling" than "deduction" (and maybe there's some social commentary on that. I never got it). In the end, the game feels more like a visual novel with tacked on interactive elements - more than it feels like an immersive story where you feel like an Orwellian observer and manipulator.

Thanks to the recent sale on narrative games and my watching Oreimo for the first time (Do not ask about the correlation) I decided to pick up this game as there is little more fascinating to me than dystopian scenarios and a good mystery story - which is of course what we have right here otherwise I wouldn't be talking about it.

While I am not one to preach about privacy issues in real society this game offers a powerful insight into where things go wrong, even when it seems all the necessary precautions are being made to keep privacy invasion to a minimum. The core concept sees you working for the government of a fictitious foreign nation which has introduced numerous security systems and laws in order to reduce crime levels. While this is all well and good in theory it fails to stop a terrorist attack taking place in plain view of the entire nation. Your task - and there is no choice but to accept it - is to investigate the suspicious individuals linked with these attacks by searching through their social media, medical documents, online dating accounts - literally any source of digital information in which small chunks of information can be uploaded to the government in order to draw conclusions.

What those conclusions are however is often up to you, while the game does a very good job of using all its various information sources to lead you to the right chunks of data conflicts do arise. When a chunk of data contradicts with another it is up to you to decide which side of the argument you wish to submit. You can draw a conclusion quickly, or use all the information at your disposal to logically determine which is correct - simple though it sounds there are instances where no amount of logic will lead to the answer, the choice is then left to your conscience, and which choice you believe is the right one to make. Take note that the game makes no attempt to hide the fact that you are affecting real (fictional) lives and the implications of your actions will very quickly become apparent - People will almost certainly die because of things that you have done, or that you did not do.

Before I continue rambling about the core concept of this game and how powerful it is and how exciting it is to slowly unravel the mystery at the heart of things though, I do have to comment on probably the one thing that really stood out to me  - [b]Sound[/b]
Yes it is weird to comment about how powerful sound is when you play a 6 hour game that for almost its entirety is the same slow jingle of ambient generic "We are a megacorporation" music, there was never a point in the game where i wasn't drastically unsettled by the sudden, VERY powerful changes in this music that occurred the few times where a huge piece of key information is displayed on the screen for the first time. Your eyes might not even be there yet, you might still be reading the paragraph above and just preemptively scrolled the page down already but BOOM, the music plays, something big is right there in front of you, highlighted in blue and in plain view. Your eyes aren't there yet but you know it is there. You want to finish reading the paragraph above for full context, but it's right there. You know it is there. You must look. You must.

TL;DR: Powerful game, intriguing mystery afoot, definitely recommend, please play with sound

[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.

I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter. Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

I mean, we're basically living in a world where we're being tracked and viewed as corporate commodities, so this game isn't much of a stretch. Still, I found myself really enjoying Orwell - so much so that I purchased the next game in the series (Ignorance is Strength) shortly after completing it. The basic premise behind Orwell is that you're an investigator snooping on your fellow citizens in order to connect the dots behind a larger conspiracy. Your choices, of course, will have an impact on the game's ending; they'll also decide the fate of individual characters - whether they escape, get arrested, or even die. The storyline is interesting and presents you with a lot of ethical dilemmas; things are never black and white, although you can certainly make some intriguing choices trying to adhere to such a worldview.

Overall, I don't have many complaints about the game itself. The UI is pretty slick and easy to navigate. Music is nice. However, I wish there was a way to easily skip/speed through phone calls and such. If you want to unlock every achievement, then you'll need to play through the game 3 or 4 times; having the ability to skip or speed through certain dialogues/events would make that feel less cumbersome. I mean, it's worthwhile to replay the game just to see what happens when you make different choices or approach situations from another perspective; it can just feel a bit tedious when you're looking for a specific achievement.

As an added bonus, the second game in the series (Orwell: Ignorance is Strength) takes the events of the first game into consideration. You can even import your investigator's decisions, allowing you to relive the events of the first game while playing through the second. I won't spoil anything, but I like that the developer made that decision; it ties the games together nicely. I'd recommend this game for fans of the cyberpunk/dystopian genres, especially - you'll definitely appreciate the themes and overall feel of the game.

Good things:

- Loved the game mechanics. Yes, it's a simple drag and drop game, but the beauty is in this simplicity.
- Loved the realism. Characters seemed like real people who can make mistakes, make jokes, panic, and lie.

Bad things:
- Calls and text conversations tend to be slow and are not able to be skipped.
- I had to play the whole game three times to get all achievements. Although, there was a bit more to learn each time, it was still very boring.

I loved the game mechanic, which was utterly innovative. I loved the headline feature as it helped with worldbuilding and let you know about storyline events. The plot was solid and I loved the way the plot twists slowly unfolded. The characters were well fleshed-out as well.

 I will say there's limited replay value and because of that the game felt a little short. Additionally, unless it was simply the way I played, everyone suspected WAS guilty in some form. You were technically right in getting the police involved each time. I would have liked to see a point where you got someone who was tangentially involved (like one of the people running the cybercafe) be arrested/interrogated etc. Since the idea is that suspicion is enough to assume guilt, having an innocent person be suspected would have helped prove the point of the system's wrongness. That's mostly nitpicking though, and not a huge issue. 

Additionally, since you generally had to choose specific data chunks to advance the story it limited your ability to alter the plot. Which, it's an authoritarian regime so if you didn't give the required information that would likely turn out badly for you- but that also adds to the lack of replay value. If there was more alternative routes I would definitely play through each, so I'm just a little disappointed that I can't do so.

I don't think replay value is the only thing that determines whether a game is good, and this one certainly left an impression. I highly recommend it and I'll definitely be getting the sequel somewhere down the line.

So, where to get started ... Orwell was one of  the many games in my steam library collecting dust because I got it at some point but never got around to actually playing it. I picked it first over other games as I just started reading a book called '1984' by George Orwell. For anyone who enjoyed the book it's worth checking out the game. Although the book has a much better story in my opinion and if you enjoyed the game you really should check it out.

It took me about 5 hours for my first run. For me it was quite  an immersive experience and the game does a really good job at making you feel at the center of the plot. The story is not linear and the choices you make do feel like they actually matter unlike the old fallout games.  It was an interesting experience, but at some points the gameplay did hinder you with an obtrusive dialogue of your 'advisor', but not to the point if it becoming annoying.

To summarize without spoiling, it's about the future and ethics of our civilization and how we'll deal with privacy. Just as the book did, but in a simply numbed down version. The game is therefor not perfect, it lacked some depth in certain parts of the story. But the fact that you can go and play the game again will make the second time playing a complete different experience as you can now advance with knowledge of your previous playthrough which makes up for it.

~~==~~ 🐺 *Verdict* 🐺 ~~==~~
Should you get and play this game? Maybe, it's not for everyone. If you're interested in a more reading based game where choices matter that explores the future of privacy, than yes. In case you're not hyped about something like that I would still give the game a go if you can get it on sale

I found this game to be very interesting in concept, but a little lacking in execution.  The two main criticisms I have are related to the design of Orwell System itself I suppose.  Without spoiling anything, there are times where two 'conflicting' pieces of information need to be picked between in order to advance the story line down any given path.  However, in most cases this conflicting information isn't actually conflicting.  ie: A person did this one thing at time A, versus something completely else at time B.  Both of these statements could be inherently true, but must only one can be chosen as a fact.  I certainly understand why these choices are being presented to the player, and what they represent, but by accepting one as the truth, the Orwell System automatically eliminates the other as even a possibility.  A good investigator would accept both possible truths and investigate them for veracity and relevance, which is another flaw in the Orwell System; there is no verification and I suppose that's the point of the whole thing, but AS an IRL investigator, it bothers me to no end.  

The second issue I have with Orwell is that it can cherry pick information out of text which is likely relevant to a person I'm investigating, and it can tell me which person it's relevant to and even what the information represents, but the system isn't sophisticated enough to automatically assign that information to the relevant person??!  I have to manually choose that person from the suspect 'web' and then add the information.  If I don't the system tells me it's the wrong person.  If you know it's the wrong person, why not just put the information where it belongs??

Neither of these issues are game-breaking, and overall I enjoyed the 4 hours I spent figuring things out.  

A 'meta' issue I have with the Orwell System is how laughably unnecessary it is.  While the real-time information and telephone call intercepts were all incredibly helpful, a team of investigators using today's investigative techniques, with search warrants and without violating anybody's constitutional rights, likely could have come to the same conclusions.  A large amount of obtained information was all accessible on public webpages, and a check of a suspect's name, social media profiles, and close friend's social media would be the first stop in an investigation of this magnitude.

I did not expect this game to be as good as it was. None of the screenshots let me understand the limits and ramifications that the game system has in place, nor did I expect real-time sequences of information gathering and dissemination.

A+ will play again.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a game where you play as an investigator hired outside the Nation. Your task is to discover a crime detail by searching from suspects' background information which you can gather around the web, to be later uploaded into Orwell security program. You will be accompanied by a single adviser in your every work session, their task will revolve around information that you put into Orwell, for them to act based on your input.

The game sets you into the day at the time a bombing is occurred at a public place. Your first day would revolve around investigating who's behind this bombing. You could work all-day long if you want and maybe put all the datachunks - highlighted information - available into Orwell [spoiler]since you are not "timed" until Episode 5[/spoiler], easy as is. But of course, the common ground is to double-check whether a datachunk is valid to your investigation, or they were there only as mere decorations of information scattered freely on web. Your understanding of validity will be tested, well, more or less.

The music managed to keep me into focus, with not too over-exaggerated tunes (listened to them on Spotify and looped them for some time). There are some tense moments - indicated by shock-therapy tune - where you have to choose which info is MORE valid among the other. You will be the judge of things revolving around the web information, but you know what to do. You have been trusted by the Nation to work with them, but are they trusted enough? Theoretically, they should be, giving the ability to build this seemingly-flawless program where you could uncover the truth of these people you're given task to keep an eye on.

Finishing the game, I'm telling you, they indeed work like a charm. Too well.

Oh, also low poly art-style. New term and style to adore in general.

Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value. 

I've seen a few comparisons made to Papers, Please, which is less slick to play but rather more profound to actually experience because of the huge number of variations in how it can go. Orwell comparatively lacks depth, but because you spend more time with all the characters and get to know them better (since you're snooping through their gadgets and availing yourself of some very personal details of their lives), what happens to them matters a lot more to you. At least, it mattered more to me. In Papers Please I was more concerned with getting myself and my family out of dodge. 

Think of Orwell as an interactive dystopian techno-thriller and you've got a pretty good idea what you're in for.

There's several overarching themes in Orwell - technology, totalitarianism, propaganda, identity - and Orwell blends them quite well. It's akin to a visual novel, with the story unfolding as you choose what to upload to the Orwell  program and seeing how your choices affect the story. Though that is also its weakness.

Orwell's systems are displayed as "datachunks", uploadable bits of information to fill out a person's profile. However, those datachunks are pre-highlighted, bringing the only gameplay decision to be "Do I upload info 1 or info 2?". Finding new information feels less like being a detective and more like rote drag-and-drop to progress the story. Important datachunks are highlighted, the media it's in is also highlighted and you have your handler telling you which media to check. There's no skill involved.

Overall the story is interesting and well-presented, but gameplay lets it down. Other games present similar themes and gameplay better. If you want more totalitarianism, Papers Please is a better example of it. If you want to feel like a detective, Her Story or Return of the Obra Dinn do those aspects far better. If you want a quick, good story then buy Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You.

The game sounded really interesting but after 2 hours of playtime I refunded it. The idea that you hunt for information and decide what to pass on and what to keep private is a nice way of turning a game into a subtle reference to personal bias. A clever idea that could have been great. The problem is that, certainly for the 2 hours I played, that simply wasn't the case. There is no hunting for information. It is handed to you on a plate. The basic routine is this:

A page of information is loaded and appears on the right of the screen. Important parts of the text are highlighted. Click the highlighted text and drag it to the Orwell upload facility on the left of the screen. Drag enough pieces of text and a new page of information is presented to you with highlighted parts. Drag and drop. New page. Drag and drop. New page.

You will discover social media handles. Great, now you can hunt the person down and..oh wait, no their feed just gets presented to you with highlighted text. Drag and drop.

You manage to get the telephone number of a suspect. Now you can tap their line and listen in on their conversations. Oh wait, it just gets presented to you, no action required. Never mind, look, there's the symbol to say they are about to have a conversation. QUICK, check in and listen to them before they...oh wait, no. You can simply ignore the symbol for half an hour and then check it, because the messages only start when you open up the screen. If these really are terrorists, they are the most considerate ones on the planet as they refuse to start their conversation until you are listening in. Try to keep up? No need, go make a drink, come back and find the page of text. Ignore the drivel, the important bits are highlighted.  Drag and drop.

Still, your decisions about what to upload is really what the game is about. Except that even in those first 2 hours there were a few occasions where I decided not to upload something because it appeared to be out of context. A message displaying agressiveness or hatred of the state, but in the context of the document it seemed to be just social media waffle and not really genuine terrorist. So I didn't upload it. Result? Nothing. The game simply wouldn't progress until I uploaded it. The choice was removed. So after a while of hunting and finding no new clues I reluctantly uploaded the info and lo and behold a new page of information was presented to me. Drag and drop. Rinse and repeat.

Clearly a lot of people have found something great in this game and I truly love the concept but I cannot recommend it for what it claims to be.  If you are looking for the perfect Drag and Drop Simulator to spend your evenings on though, you can't go wrong here.

This game comes from the same niche genre as Papers, Please, in which you operate as a government official tasked with keeping your country "safe" in a dystopian, high-surveillance world. It's a breath of fresh air in what I hope to be a more well-explored type of gameplay and setup. Instead of being the person to dismantle The System with guns a-blazing, you are a body warming your seat at a desk and following through with what your superiors ask of you--namely, monitoring and surveillance of certain individuals suspected of being involved in recent terrorist attacks in your country's capital. While many might find this to be a boring game, for us info-hunters and online archive fiends, this is exactly up our alley (and regardless, many people found themselves plenty surprised with how engaging Papers, Please was despite it being literal desk duty). The process of determining the relevant information from the chaff is an exercise in your detective work; conflicting bits of information challenges your ability to intuit context and intent, the results of your choices ultimately influencing the file you are compiling for your superiors, who can only draw conclusions based on it. Since they are depending on you to be diligent and honest, you are responsible for their ultimate decision on how to proceed at the end of the day. The interface is smooth, streamlined, and well-organized; your overseer Symes and his commentary on your findings is a tiny light in what would otherwise be a soul-sucking experience (at the end of the day, you are cutting your Persons of Interest into tiny bits of info); the music is an understated, mechanical heartbeat similar to Massive Attack's "Teardrop on Fire", famously used as the theme for the show House, M.D.. And at the end of the day, your choices matter. Only complaint is that sometimes your brain is thinking farther ahead than the game. There are several times when I thought "Wait, I remember who this is. I might as well jump on it upload a profile pic and the info from that file I found on them" but discovered I had to wait until the game found them relevant enough to devote any attention to them. I love this game and what it has to offer, and if anything I've said has piqued your interest, I pretty much guarantee you won't be disappointed.

Orwell does one thing very well: it accurately simulates the tedium inherent in most government jobs. If you ever wanted to know what it's like to work at the DMV or IRS, Orwell is your game. The simplistic click-and-drag gameplay might have been mitigated by an interesting story or characters, but Orwell's plot is boilerplate paranoia fiction delivered in screen after screen of dull exposition. The puzzle design vacillates between the extremes of baffingly obtuse and blaringly obvious. At several points, I found myself simply clicking through every single screen and selecting every random bit of data I could simply to progress the story.

On the plus side, the ambient soundtrack is pleasant and includes the occasional dramatic sting to highlight twists in the storyline. The Orwell UI is clean and easy to navigate. I also think that the developers had the best of intentions to create a game that grapples with the rise of the surveillance state in modern societies.

Unfortunately, good intentions don't trump bad game design. Stay away from Borewell.

So, here's a detailed rundown so far:

Story:
The game starts out with a cinematic that introduces the world and how it advanced it is in terms of technology. You will play as a rookie investigator of sorts who will undergo a basic test of performance. Here, it lays out your role and responsibilities clearly without being overly confusing. After all the introductions, the actual story starts. The story is INTENSE. It tries to confuse you but you want more of it. And the urge just doesn't stop until you get clearance. Especially where your choices matter.

Characters:
The characters feel alive. You can tell that a lot of work has been put into these characters as you get to know their backgrounds, way of thinking, motives, goals, etc. Heck, I even relate and sympathize with some of these characters.

Sound:
Sometimes so relaxing like you had a good day at work. Sometimes so intense that you want to scream "Damn this scroll bar!!!!11" as you race against time scrolling down frantically looking the datachunk (piece of information) in hopes that it may change the potential outcome. Sometimes grim when you find out secrets that the characters themselves never mentions.

UI:
I love the simplistic yet futuristic UI design and world setting. It helps keep you immersed in the game which revolves around you, the player, acting as an investigator from when you start the game and through your whole playthrough.

Overall:
Still on the edge of my seat while writing this review. This game is very well-made. The world is solidly built, the characters feel alive, the soundtrack enhances the gameplay, and the UI fits into the setting extremely well. If you have played hacknet, emily is away, or similar games, then this game shares a resemblance to those. It's a very personal experience and a very pleasant one at that.

Orwell is a really cool idea. You take the role as a investigator tasked with combing thru internet records and conversations of members of an activist group to find out if any of them are the culprit in a terrorist bombing. It's a slow game, but engageing. Also shouldn't surpise anyone that's it is a really political game, a scathing comment on totalitarian survailence.  

The gameplay concists of finding importatnt information and uploading them to your supervisor. The clever part with the mechanics is that you can choose to upload or not upload various data and while it at first seems like you really have no control over how the information will be used, that's kind of the point of the game. Depending on what you choose to upload pretty much everyone can be made look guilty, be it from off hand comments, things taken out of context or carefully selected data while ignoring other information. Yeah, did I mention that it's kind of obvious what the devs think of the concept of Big Brother... The dialogues and plot are very well writen and is belivable for the most part. The ending is kind of brilliant. 

The only thing I think they could have done better with was that they made the nation and political party in power in the game kind of fascist to begin with, it would have been a lot more clever to have it take place in a country that was much less a police state and still have the orwell system in place. But overall a really good and unique game.

In Conclusion, 

Orwell is a reasonably thrilling game about being a cog in a surveillance state. It requires a substantial amount of reading, with many insignificant choices, and only a few consequential decisions. It makes reasonable use of a unique visual aesthetic, and good musical cues, but is hampered by only average dialogue between the characters. The story moves along swiftly enough, as long as one isn't too picky about what they pass along to Symes, especially because progressing requires submitting most of the data available. Orwell doesn't have much unique that hasn't already been said about surveillance, but the ending is reasonably powerful and compelling.

I enjoyed Orwell a bit , but it's not as much a superior offspring from 1984, as a subordinate clause.

[h1]Orwell - Parts 1 and 2[/h1]

[b]Orwell[/b] was a fairly unique experience, with perhaps some similarities to visual novels and point-and-click puzzle games. It is well made and combines narrative and gameplay to keep the player intrigued and eager to find out more. It also seems to have plenty of replay value with a number of different paths and outcomes available depending on the choices you make. Whilst the same can be said of Orwell: Ignorance is Strength it doesn’t quite pack the same punch. The second instalment is shorter, has less variety in terms of proceedings and outcomes and the narrative is not as well written or constructed.

In short, if you’re looking for a slow-paced, thought-provoking game with a political theme (and don’t mind 4-6 hours of reading) I’d definitely recommend Orwell but maybe give Orwell: Ignorance is Strength a miss, or approach it with lower expectations.

[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.
