I don't review games very often, but I felt that I needed to throw out my two cents on this game. I haven't read any other reviews, so I'm not influenced by what other people think of it.

I went into this game almost entirely blind. I got it a long while ago, and just got around to installing and playing it today. I sat down to give it a quick try, see if I would enjoy it, and ... 3 hours later, I finished the story. It's not a sprawling 100 hour experience, but those 3 hours were intense, and I was locked into the events the entire time.

A brief summary: you play an Investigator using a program called Orwell, which sifts through social media profiles and newspaper articles (and maybe listens in on a few phone calls) to try to track down criminals. Specifically, a bomb has gone off in a public plaza, and you need to find out who did it.

There are some great twists and turns along the way, and I enjoyed myself the entire time. One moment in particular had me literally on the edge of my seat, biting my lip while I listened to a conversation unfold, unable to do anything but wait to see what would happen. This was a conversation that only occurred because of choices that I had made, and in the end, I had to live with the consequences of those choices. It was rough, and it was emotional, but it was amazing.

Anyway, I love this game. I give it a 4/5 on my "arbitrary 5 point rating scale". The writing felt a little clunky at times, which is really the only complaint that I have, and it's not bad enough to really detract from the experience. Please give this game a try!

Graphics: 5/5
 - It's VERY stylized, so it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but I really loved the way everything looked. The UI was clean and easy to maneuver, and the portraits and pictrues were very compelling for me.

Sound: 4.5/5
 - Very immersive music, and the sound effects felt right at home. Since there's no audible dialogue in this game (when you're "listening" to a phone conversation, you're reading the text transcription of that conversation), the music rising and falling gave some amazing feels. There are also times that the music will suddenly move from calm and serene the intense and pounding when you're reading articles or some such, indication that you've found a piece of information that drastically changes things. I give it 4.5 instead of 5 because the different tracks don't flow into each other - when one starts, the previous one stops instantly, giving a weird stutter.

Gameplay: 4.5/5
 - The gameplay is very simple: click, drag, scroll, read. There's no much to it, and for the most part, everything is very responsive. The .5 points left off was for the fact that, occasionally, dragging data into place was a pain in the ass. Sometimes my pointer just wouldn't grab ahold of something.

Writing: 4/5
 - The story itself is awesome and very compelling. Often times, the dialogue was fine, but there were some times that the dialogue felt stilted and clunky, and unnatural, sounding like someone writing lines for a game, rather than natural conversation. Again, it didn't affect my enjoyment, but it was something I noticed.

Replayability: 3/5
 - Here's the thing. I haven't played the game a second time yet, but it's definitely possible to do so. There are events within the game that would have gone differently if I'd chosen different options (I won't forgive myself for failing to prevent an attack). The reason I say 3/5 is because there would still be a LOT of repetition to sit through. Many conversations that you will already know the outcome of, that move along at the same pace as before. That pace is AWESOME when you're reading everything for the first time, but on a second playthrough, it will probably get tedious. Once I play through a second time, I will readdress this score, but for now, the 3/5 represents the fact that I don't really want to play through a second time for a while.

Aside from some issues where relevant information wasn't "flagged" for selection, and the occasional goofy conversation, Orwell is a pretty solid game about the pitfalls of the surveillance state. You witness the story unfolding through articles, conversations, and eventually some more intrusive searching, and have the opportunity to decide what is and is not worthy of consideration. In doing so you change the course of the investigation itself, casting suspicion based on your reporting to your advisor.

It's executed pretty well, with a good style and simple interface. It starts off fairly straightforward, and you're left to discover for yourself just how subjective the process can be. You'll be railroaded a bit into reporting certain information for the story to proceed, but there's plenty of wiggle room for you to be the by-the-book investigator or the secret resistance hero with what you do and do not upload.

Not sure if I want to go back through and try to influence the story more heavily than my first play through, but it's made me very interested in the second season.

I think the game first of all deserves plaudits for style and storytelling, interwoven into gameplay. This kind of indie game really shows what's capable in interactive media, including making the player a participant in the activities. No two ways about it, you don't walk away with clean hands from this narritive. And god, that's just unbelievably cool. I can't think of any other medium that works as well. By uncovering the stories that these characters contain, the player gets pulled into the drama and hell, I'd say I believe these characters more than I would in a traditional triple-A game narritive. This is partially due to the strength of the writing but also due to the computer interface framing device which allows for a completely seamless experience.

But what this game really does well is play with its themes. It's a power trip, to dig through people's lives and find the bits and pieces that fit into a story that you can tell someone else. It's also remarkably disturbing how plausible it all is, and how effectively the player can go about their business. As I played, I started wondering to myself how much art might imitate life. How far away are we from the very horror portrayed here? How do we defeat such a tool? Is there anywhere else to go after that?

The game also does a great job of leaving a very plausible trail of breadcrumbs to follow, with a good amount of leeway into what needs to be found and in what order. The actual layout of the story isn't entirely known to me (what exactly is cleverly scripted) but I'd say the rails are actually fairly wide at parts, and usually coming to a head with each chapter. The space to move around here is necessary both to keep the player engaged and addicted, but also to make the simulation seem plausible. If the story was too narrow it would feel a bit too pre-arranged, but there's some actual detective work to do here and that's quite marvelous, if not novel.

For those on the fence, play this game. Completely worth your 5 hours. With a chaser of Citizenfour while you're at it. Crazy that I'm playing with the notion of a game properly adding to the political discourse, yet here we are. I suspect this game will linger with me for a long while.

In a dystopian but not far-fetched future that is dominated by public AND private surveillance, you're an investigator tasked with digging through the personal information of citizens of "The Nation", in the name of national safety above all else. While this is for the most part a linear game, you alone decide what information you upload to the Orwell Database, your employer. This means you alone have the power to decide what the public and the government knows about specific people.

So when you're assigned to an incident that shakes The Nation to its very core, you are the one who decides what happens next. And you're going to feel pretty strongly about it, one way or another.



This is a game that made me feel things I haven't before. Good things, bad things, and to be honest things about [i]me[/i] I weren't that aware of myself. Like I said, it was a strange experience.

Citizen science is the idea of having research conducted in organised form by non-professionals under the direction of scientific institutions. Some well-known examples of citizen science are found in astronomy and ornithology. In The Nation this philosophy has recently been extended into the realm of national security. Following the the Safety Bill that was initiated by The Party in 2012 the government of The Nation has received extended ability to observe the communication between its citizens in the name of national security. This has enabled the Orwell programme of surveillance, where Investigators have access to the communications of target persons and Advisors make recommendations for further actions. The similarities with citizen science is that the Investigators are just ordinary people from outside The Nation who look at the vast amounts of information and mark which data chunks that may be of interest. The Advisors, on the other hand, are professionals with experience and good contact with the legal authorities and they work with the provided data chunks. This system certainly ensures that not one single person gets too much power over the course of the investigations.

In Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You the player takes the role as a recently recruited Investigator. As a first case the player will have to look at a bomb that exploded at Freedom Plaza in central Bonton killing several citizens. A woman known to the police was seen at the scene and the player has to figure out whether she was involved in the terrorist attack.

The gameplay is straight-forward. It is just about using the Orwell interface to look at the data that are available and to decide what is relevant for the case at hand and what is not. It is fascinating to see how much of the interpretation of the available information depends on the context, meaning that the ordering of information has a big impact on the conclusions that are made. I liked the general idea of working with limited knowledge to understand a plot that is not straight-forward. The story itself makes sense, but it is only towards the end that I could see it so playing the game is like reading a good detective story with a possibility to make bad decisions which have effects on the outcome. Surprisingly for a detective story, Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also had a good replayability value, at least for me. I really had to see if it was possible to choose the bits of information I transferred in such way to make the best possible outcome, for the people involved, and for the citizens of The Nation as whole…

This is a truly amazing game. It really gets you thinking about mass surveillance. It's hardly impartial, but you get to see both the good and the bad aspects. You're a government operative of sorts investigating ongoing acts of terrorism in a fictional country only ever referred to as The Nation. This takes the form of mining people's websites, phone calls, text messages, etc looking for connections between various people of interests trying to build a case against the guilty and rule out the innocent. 

The actual gameplay boils down to reading through the various sources presented to you and pulling out highlighted text for presentation to the system so there's not a lot to it mechanically, but the story's well drawn and the characters are generally believable so you get pulled in pretty quickly. The subtleties generally come when you're presented with conflicting evidence and you need to decide what to mark as ignored and what to upload, as that will directly impact exactly how the people involved will get treated. 

I assumed it would go in hard on the 'surveillance is bad' angle but it as your character potentially instrumental in stopping people get murdered its position isn't as cut and dried as that. Ultimately you're playing a story with a few chances to influence it so if that's not your bag you won't enjoy it. If you're into that kind of thing though it's certainly a unique and interesting way of presenting a narrative (though it's entirely reading and clicking shit so your level of tolerance may vary).

There's a demo that already tells quite a lot about this game. I'll just assume now that you've already played the demo and I will only go into details.

Episode 1 (the demo) is great: You have a target, you dig into her personal information, discover her personality, her social media accounts, her relations. You feel like digging into information you're not supposed to know, you're spying a stranger and soon feel like you know everything about him.

Sadly, Orwell can't keep quality this up. You're still wiretapping calls, crawling through social media accounts, gathering information and finding connections. However, the people aren't really the focus anymore - after episode 1, the story becomes more linear, you'll try to find out information about possible terrorist groups, but the game will just throw all the personal information at you while you're doing that. You don't really have to piece clues together, crawl through articles by yourself or solve riddles.

To summarize, Orwell simply feels like a visual novel that gives you a decision once in a while. Decisions, that - at least that's how they felt to me - barely have any impact. Few datachunks might lead to a different result, most don't, and some have to be uploaded so that the story progresses, even though they might seem misleading to you. However, the game doesn't give you the chance to dig deeper into those datachunks.

In the end, you'll be scrolling through new articles which the game throws at you, extracting 90% of the datachunks you find there to piece together the story while some guy comments every single of your actions. You'll do that for about 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you read the texts, and then the credits will roll.

Don't get me wrong - the story was exciting from beginning to the end, I enjoyed Orwell a lot, but it's way behind its potential. It gives the player almost 0 freedom and one might argue, whether or not this is intentional because of its setting.

If you regret one of your decisions, i.e. you accidentally uploaded a piece of information that you didn't want (which happened to me few times), bad luck. There's only autosave (it saves after every single decision) and you can't replay single chapters - even after finishing the game and can only start from scratch. There's not a lot replayability to it and the achievements are basically "don't upload a specific piece of optional information" which is kind of... meh. But it's the only thing this game offers and I can't imagine it being exciting anymore after you know the story.

If you like the setting, get it for a low price, enjoy it once, never touch it again. Then maybe look at the sequel (Ignorance is Strength) which improves on a few things (it actually gives you some freedom and you have to piece together some clues by yourself), but on the other hand tells a boring cliché story with uninteresting characters that ends after less than 3 hours.

It's so shame because episode 1 was so intriguing, but at least the demo shows you exactly what to expect from this game. If you enjoyed the demo and want more - go for it. If you didn't, skip the game - it won't become better after episode 1.

The endings of the game illustrate a profound philosophical statement that is revealed through allegory.

Of the three endings, both condemning Delacroix or condemning Thought, ultimately, is short-sighted and misses the point. By condemning Delacroix, an individual is removed, however, the system remains largely intact and unchanged, which falls short of the motivation for condemning Delacroix in the first place. By condemning Thought, you've done your job, however, completely overlooked Orwell's dire short-comings.

In life, [b]the average person scarcely once considers themselves as the prime suspect[/b]. Why incriminate yourself when you can incriminate everyone and anyone else? This is the question that the third ending addresses. The answer is this: By incriminating everyone else, you have deluded yourself into believing that you were somehow left out of the picture. 8/10 loved digging into people's private lives for hours.

So, you're nobody important. And a nearby country is looking for people like you (not-important foreigners with an Internet access) to offer them a job. So you take it.

Your first task is to make a background check on this girl. She's a suspect, possibly connected to a minor terrorist attack.  So you start digging, but the longer you dig, the messier her story gets. Turns out that the government has some unique tools that will help you find more data - a limited access to the girl's social media. And she is typing with her friend - right now.

You are not making one moral decision after another, you don't try to protect your family and keeps yourself safe. You truly are just an employee. Terrorists killed people. And they want to strike again. And you can stop them... But to do so, you need to completely invade civilians' privacy. Break into the most intimate parts of their lives. And even if you decide it's justifiable, you are more than aware of how abusive the same tools can be. How mishandling them may ruin careers.

But on the other hand... If you quit, people will die. You could have save them, and you won't, it's pretty much you fault. And the deeper you go, the more barriers you have to breach. Even to the point when finding yet another cellphone that you can hack into makes you smile. 

So... What are you going to do?

In a time where the internet and smartphones carry all our information, we are all too easy to spy on. What would happen if the government invaded your privacy to fight terrorism? How far would you let them go? Where's the line?

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You does a fantastic job at showing you the dangers of, well, an orwellian society in modern times. All you do in this game is read webpages, eavesdrop conversations, and hack people's devices, and however simple that sounds, it still feels thrilling to upload someone's dirtiest secrests to Big Brother for the government to act upon.

This game integrates gameplay and narrative brilliantly in a way I haven't seen anywhere else. Please do yourself a favor and give this gem a chance.

It's not an issue, but it points to the story being "smaller" than it could have been, and that there would have been room for more elaboration and maybe even several intertwining stories. That would of course be a completely diferent game, story-wise, but I can see a possibility for greatness here. 

Don't get me wrong, I LOVED the game and I'll be playing the next one as soon as I have time.

Game took me 4 hours to complete 1 playthrough, although you can do multiple playthroughs, depending on what information you find and what connections you make. This game is reading intensive, as you will be sifting through web pages, call logs, chat logs, browser histories, etc. There's also quite a bit of filler information, which is to be expected in this kind of job where you are aggregating huge amounts of data and your job is to sift through that information and find the relevant information.

Not every piece of date is true. There are dead ends and outright lies. Your job will be to try to paint an accurate portrait for your agency to do its job correctly. This game does a great job of putting you in the center of the action as you feel as though you are a real investigator. As the story progresses, you become an even bigger part of the action.

This game isn't for everyone. The gameplay mechanic itself can get tedious at varying times. You really don't stray from what you're doing from the start of Chapter 1 all the way to the conclusion in Chapter 5. So if you don't like parsing information, you will be bored. However, the story keeps it all together and gives purpose to your actions. 

[b]Rate 7/10. Really solid game, interesting story, great ending(s), but the gameplay could have used more variety.[/b]

So, the criticisms of this game have been well-aired by now, and I agree with many of them. Nevertheless, I found playing it pretty compelling, if just for the idea of putting myself in the shoes of an investigator given access to private surveillance data, and the fact that there is no way to keep your ethics pure here.

The game features you, an analyst for an Orwellian society where surveillance and spying on citizens has become the counter-measure of terrorism and crime. To fully understand the Orwell experience, I recommend you read 1984 by George Orwell or try and make pro-Trump comments on Facebook and be arrested by the thought-police.

Anyway, in here you read people's personal information, social network activity, blogs, personal messaging and calls. While you're at it, you will extract "datachunks", parts of highlighted data, to profile the people you're investigating, and to decide the best course of action. The catch in all of this is that your assistant, the one giving the orders to security teams, will only know the data your forward to him, and will act accordingly to that. Feeling like stopping that Tumblrina from getting wine? Forward the credit card info to your assistant, and you will prevent it. Feeling like killing a mother and leaving his child orphan? Go ahead!

Your choices have an impact on the nation.

Orwell was an interesting experience, with a lot of potential and promise. I will say that I did enjoy the game for the most part, however, there are some glaring details which ruined it for me. 

The game relies on you (the investigator) uploading particular parsed sections of text to the server (Orwell), which means that whenever you come across a piece of information which is a "trigger" for want of a better term, it is highlighted - regardless of its relivence (and some information is totally surplus to requirement, a lot in one case). This means that most of the information which you read through, including important plot points, or interesting backstory, is largely irrelivent and the player (or at least I did) found myself just slowly scrolling to the bottom of every document to highlight all the options before I read anything at all. This is especially clear when investigating information which contradicts other information which has not been disclosed yet (marked by yellow highlighting instead of blue), as it will always be yellow, even if you have access to but haven't discovered the other piece of information yet - which unless the investigator is psychic, makes zero sense. A shame, since this dulls enthusiasm for what could otherwise be an engaging plot.

While processing this information you are presented with multiple occasions where information would be important to the case, but you cannot add it to your current file or create a new file because the game is not ready for you to do so. You will then later come back to re-read and submit this data after the game tells you the information you already noticed is important. This is irritating and makes the player feel like mommy is holding their hand through the entire experience, rather than allowing them to work on their own initiative. Although on reflection, this is most likely because the order in which the data is presented to you is not well organised from a storytelling perspective.

Attention to detail is somewhat lacking for a detective game also, as on multiple occasions you are directed to a forum which is occasionally updated with new articles to peruse. Unfortunately, when these articles are "published" the game does not update the "last logged in" sections of the user's profiles, which creates confusion over the timeline [spoiler]especially since this becomes important later in the story[/spoiler].

However, the largest problem is that there are several key events which the game does not provide you enough information to correctly answer (and there is a correct answer), which leads to the player essentially taking a wild guess as to which of the options is the correct one. If you are fortunate, you will get the result which you were looking for - if not... well you'll have to go through the entire game again from the beginning, as the game auto-saves after every piece of information you upload.

Overall, Orwell is a thought-provoking and mostly enjoyable game, but it does have it's flaws. If you can overlook them however, you will appreciate the intention of the developer. At this point I have to decide if I recommend Orwell or not, and it is difficult...

I'm divided about Orwell.

It's also a point and click game, which is my least favourite genre. Orwell requires the player to read lots of information and click everything, often randomly, to discover the facts and evidence to allow events to proceed. What that translates to in real terms is long stretches of tedious, patience-testing reading and clicking. Not really my thing. 

For those reasons, I was very tempted to quit early in the game; however, as time went on I found the experience more and more engaging. I found plenty to enjoy and applaud and played it through to the end (admittedly, through gritted teeth at times). The ambition, the storyline, the interesting mechanics, the excellent cast and the consequential nature of the choices to be made are all worthy of note, and any game that tries to do something new and interesting should be applauded.

[h1][url=store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/]Orwell[/url] presents a decent diminutive mystery with pertinent social commentary through a very unique, novel yet straightforward approach to interactive storytelling.[/h1]

The game first asks you to create an investigator profile through its polished interface, effectively recruiting you in the ranks of Orwell, followed by a stylish low-poly security footage opening that sets the stage for the ongoing investigation. Your role is essentially to play the human element in what would otherwise be an extremely complex data mining algorithm in a surveillance system.

Gameplay in many ways feels like browsing through restrained web pages obtained through a very limited portion of the internet. You select which datachunks to upload to Orwell's server, which in turn unlock more related headlines, websites, restricted documents, private emails, bank accounts, and eventually tap into phone and text conversations between suspects.

New bookmarks just appear by themselves as revealed by your adviser. You don't have any actual research to do, all important clues are automatically highlighted, and as such the game first appears to be completely linear and rather easy. There is initially no clear reason not to upload data other than rare instances with conflictual information, where only one of two bits can be sent.

Then it gets a bit more complex and the story evolves into a satisfyingly more sophisticated mystery with multiple threads to investigate. You can decide to withhold information that you judge inadequate or untrue, and your choices can have pretty severe consequences in some cases. While there are few or no time sensitive actions, tension builds up a lot in the final chapter where you have a limited number of uploads available before a major event triggers.

There is no undo and your decisions clearly define paths that lead to multiple endings. One-way conversations with your adviser also create a pretty unique relationship.

Be prepared for lots and lots of reading. The game features sparse audio and pleasant low-poly aesthetics, but too few rendered footage and no voice overs.

The game's world also feels relatively small scale with only about a dozen significant characters in the story, despite a background of terrorism and international tension. Another odd thing is when you gain access to a suspect's PC or smartphone, only a handful of files are shown. This limited scope nevertheless keeps things manageable.

The mechanics are buggy. There are several instances where if you fail to make a specific decision or if you do so in an unintended order, the game will not let you go any further and you get no clues that there's a bug until you realized that you've exhausted all possible resources and see that the game just won't move forward.

Orwell has definitely made it onto my list of indie favorites. One of the most interesting and engaging games I've played in a long time.

[b]Story[/b]
The story and characters are well written, realistic, and relatable. The pacing is perfect and each chapter will leave you anxious to get into the next one. The world has depth and lives and breathes. Your actions feel as though they carry real weight with consequences that follow you. This is the sort of story that you'll think about and speculate about even when you're not playing. It's obvious a lot of thought was put into Orwell.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
I think it's fair to say Orwell is more of an interactive novel than a game. But that by no means is a mark against it.

Gameplay is simple but effective. You play as an investigator trying to solve a recent bombing using whatever online information, public or private, is made available to you. When you come across information that your system (named Orwell) recognizes as relevant to one of your target persons, it becomes highlighted and you can choose to upload it to Orwell's database where your superiors can then see it and act on it.

But this surveillance system isn't perfect. Sometimes conflicting or irrelevant information will be highlighted and you'll have to use your best judgement when choosing what to upload. I won't explain more in depth than that - I think the rest of the gameplay is best experienced when you discover it yourself. But I promise the gameplay isn't the mindless drag and drop that it might seem.

And what I thought was neat is that while some aspects of the gameplay might seem arbitrary or slightly confusing at first, these mechanics have a real canon, in-world explanation that is revealed as you progress. The gameplay really feels like part of the story here.

[b]Performance[/b]
It'll probably run on just about anything.

[b]Length[/b]
There are five chapters, each of which took me 45-60 minutes or so. Some people might complete it faster since I'm the methodical, read-everything-before-moving-on sort (which is rewarding with Orwell). Very little (if any) replay value though. Some people might recommend playing it all in one sitting, but I would say taking day or two long breaks like I did is the way to go.

[b]Price[/b]
Full price at the time of this review is $10. I was able to grab Orwell while it was temporarily free. $10 seems a little bit steep at first, but considering the ~5 hours I got out of it and the impression it left on me, I would say Orwell is easily worth that much. You can probably also count on Orwell going on sale or getting it cheap in a bundle if you're still on the fence.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Get it. If you enjoy indie games, get it. If you like a good detective story, get it. If surveillance or digital privacy even remotely interest you (which they should), get it.

The Story:
You operate a special hacking suite provided by the government to pry into someone's life and essentially build a report about the person and their activities. There is person receiving your report and they act on what you provide. It was interesting to follow and felt real enough to hit home a lot of times. 

The Visuals:
The art choice was interesting for the characters giving them a somewhat pixelated look. The actual HUD was very nice to look at and easy to use. 

The Sound:
The soundtrack was distinct and set a nice atmosphere for the work you are about to do. Nothing else really stood out save for some of the menu noises which were neat. 


The Experience:
When getting this game, I thought I would find it mildly entertaining. I was not prepared for how into the game I would end up getting. I was so enthralled with the way the investigation pans out that I got a notepad and started jotting down relevant info and dates to make sure I could solve the case. 

It has a decent amount of replayability since you can choose different options which very satisfyingly changes the context of the rest of the story. The game hit that sweet spot of not being too short nor being too long. Overall I feel Orwell did a good job of putting you in the seat of the Investigator and keeping the game and story fresh.

This game.. Oh man this game. This game is the greatest story, decision making game I have played this year! Let me go over many of the gameplay and story and rate them accordingly.

GAMEPLAY: Gameplay in this game is very, very simple. You just click a statement and drag it too the character it corresponds with. Sometimes you'll get a yellow highlight on text, or AKA a conflicting statement to another statement. This means you have two or more choices too pick from. All choices usually have something different and the game and the advisor will react differently depending on the choice you make. I'll make one up for you if this makes no sense too you; There's one statement "I love this band!" and then there's another statement/post "That lady (talking about the person who said the first statement) hates that band!" Now, you have to decide which is true, or if you want, decide which is false ;) but usually them hating the band or not does not matter as that's not important to the STORY, which I'll get to in a moment. There's also going through text messages, listening to conversations and even going through phones and desktops. For this game, you are a investigator, so you will have to think a bit too determine what you want Orwell to know.  It might sound boring to others, but it's actually not. It can get intense and fun if you put your mind to it. Now, the MAIN thing this game has going for it is it's great STORY!

STORY: A short summary of the game story goes like this: You are a investigator, trying to solve who did a series of consecutive bombings around "The Nation".  That's basically it without spoiling it. The game's story goes indepth, into telling you directly and indirectly. There's websites in the game that have a lot of information about what is happening out in the world. Because of this, I felt so immersed, like there was actual events going on out in the world that you don't see at all. The main story can get a bit twisty too and is great for people who like criminal investigations. I, personally found myself being in love with some of the characters. This was an awesome experience and can't wait to get the sequel!

OVERALL SCORE: 10/10 BOIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIS.

[u] Gameplay [/u]
Orwell allows investigations into the private communications of people of interest, but doesn't allow any one person full access. Instead, Orwell's operation is run by two groups; Investigators, persons outside of the Nation working for the government who search through the communication of target persons and upload items of interest (represented as "datachunks"), and Advisors, people inside of the Nation who use the received datachunks to determine the course of action and to recommend actions to the authorities.

For £7.00-ish at the time of purchase, I'd say that this game is well worth playing. Whilst seeming minimalist in graphics, the UI is slick and easy to follow, and is backed up by an incredibly rich story in which your choices can have lasting repercussions later on. The atmosphere that the game creates, the character development as the story goes on and the like are expertly done; the surveillance that the game encourages you to do shows the targets to simply be real people as well with their own desires and lives, and while humanising them you get the sense of seeing them as something else. To you, a government employee, they are simply another target, creating a conflict as to how you should really view them and how to proceed.

The debate that the game entwines in the narrative, the ideas of mass surveillance, freedom of speech etc. means that the game can really get you thinking back to the real world as well and adds an extra dimension to the game, which again makes the game worth playing. Maybe the medium of a game will allow you to see things differently. Alternatively, you can just go about playing a great game without necessarily thinking about things like that, which is the beauty of it, that within the framework of the game, there is a sandbox element that allows you to play it as you wish.

Overall, I would definitely suggest this as a game to play- it's relatively inexpensive, not all that time consuming, but definitely something that will hook you from start to finish and leave you wanting more!

While the title might imply a heavy-handed narrative (and that's not entirely unfair of a criticism of the game itself), this one impressed me more than I thought a simple concept would. 

The idea is simple. There's been a bombing, and you are entrusted with a spy program that allows you to pry into the personal lives of several suspects, making new connections as you dig up their conversations and posts. You'll be listening in on phone calls, scanning private messages and texts, and figuring out aliases all in hopes of preventing another attack. The morally dubious circumstances are obvious throughout but there's plenty of player choice to determine just how you use a tool of such power.

The way it works is as you read, bits of information flagged as "important" by the program will automatically be highlighted. The twist is that only you can see the context of that information. Once uploaded to your supervisor, it will be taken at strictly face value, no questions asked. This makes no sense at all of course, but just roll with it. So while it would be easy to just upload everything you see, the branching story will turn out much more negatively for everyone involved as a result. 

And you will probably care, too. The characters you're tasked with spying on are all realistically flawed and well-written. You might find yourself getting invested in their lives and relationships as you spend more and more time spying on them, and might even feel motivated to protect them. The classic "will you obey your superiors?" question that comes up in these kinds of games (see also: Papers, Please and etc) is done well and can have serious consequences for how things turn out for each person. Whether it's leaving out something incriminating, or simply ensuring that you don't upload anything out of context, or making a difficult decision between two conflicting bits of information. 

It's a good story, even if it paints its themes of authoritarianism and rebellion in broad, easy strokes, and your personal experience with it will vary depending on a lot of factors. There are some good twists and plenty of believable dialogue. While the concept is far-fetched and sometimes difficult to believe, it's executed well enough that I was sucked into its world for the few hours of entertainment I got out of it. No regrets.

[h1]TL:DR[/h1]

If you expect the real CONSEQUENCES of YOUR actions - do not buy this game.
If you're ok with a tell-tale game with mostly textual narrative and poor amount of player choices - it's actually a good one and you really should try it. I only gave it thumb down because I'm personally not okay with the whole thing.

[h1]Now, the long review[/h1]

At first glance the game looks like a game about consequences. And it really tries to look like one. But in fact, it’s not. In the description they say "the information you supply will have consequences", but most of the game scriptwriters just lead you by the hand. It’s like playing a visual novel with dialogue options, but most of them have only one option (ridiculous, right?). Or two, both leading to the same branch but having different lines as reactions to them.
You see a chunk of info that will certainly make Symes do the wrong thing, because it's out of context, so you decide to omit it. BUT for the further story development it either won't affect a thing, or will be required for the script to go on.
You see the connection between two personages, it’s drawn at the relationships net after you add the corresponding datachunk. But you cannot fill the profile of that new guy, until he’s not a “target”, even tho you have tonns of info right before your eyes. Given there’s often no police records on the suspects, sometimes you’d really have done better with just google, no orwell system needed. So basically in Orwell you just search for the highlighted text in docs or chats and click on it.
And since there were no crucial info in all the unhighlighted text walls (and even if there were, you couldn't do anything about it if it's not highlighted as a data chunk) I've just begun to skip most of the text. The datachunks you see will lead you to the goal, and if there's a script branch, you won't miss it in most cases. But, again, it's hard to tell whether there's a branch (even for the "conflicting chunks") since there's like one real branch per day, and everything else doesn't really affect the day's outcome and seem to differ only in Symes' comments (and sometimes you can even notice mismatches in chains of his comments if you do something not in the order devs predicted ([spoiler]On the third day that Symes guy says "WOW, Harrison and Juliet were together! How interesting", while it's only UPDATE on the notion you make during the second day, Again, from 2nd day's start you get that they were together, but only at the end of the day you finally have a chance to add this to their files, therefore Symes only knows it at the end of the day, because he's out of context, which is FUKKEN STUPID AT THE FIRST PLACE[/spoiler]).

I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.
The best counter argument against anyone who dares to say "I don't need privacy, I've got nothing to hide."

Orwell S1 is an Alternate Reality Game condensed into a single program. Big Brother deals with terrorists, and it tries to turn into a chicken and egg situation. Gameplay consists of filing clips off a mock web into a police social graph, or not. Occasionally you have to read more to resolve contradictions, which is the high point of the experience, along with a midgame sequence I shan't spoil. 

Its UI is pretty but remarkably unrefined. The keyboard shortcuts and wheel scrolling you've come to expect from browsers seem absent. The social graph will let nodes partially overlap and poorly arranges them, but you can't actually manually fix it. The base gameplay loop is spot juicy clipping on the right, open the relevant person's file on the left, then drag clipping into profile. Aliases are occasionally used, but for the vast majority of cases it's obvious who the clip is about, so the rigmarole could have been boiled down to a click. Some views overlap elements in a way the rest of the game doesn't, and dealing with that is awkward.

The finale of Season 1 came remarkably abruptly for me (about 80% too early in fact); this accidental completion meant I didn't get to deal with all as I intended.

Storywise, it works. There's a few polished plot twists and turns, and character color for several members of the cast, and the story arc goes exactly where you expect it to from the get go. It's neither subtle nor [i]Sledge Hammer![/i] in its didactisism, which is good because I expect there's few potential customers who need the lecture. The best addition was the seemingly frivolous choice of player profile picture, which got me to role play a bit an elderly, seen-it-all lady.

I estimate about 4 hours of my playtime was the main arc, and then about one more of reading the weather forecasts and such.

A very clever experience, and with several replayable elements.  (the characters' backstories and motivations remain the same, but it all can play out somewhat differently based on your actions)  The game's not on rails, but most of the major plot points are fixed.

It's likely all you've heard, and more - without spoiling details, you troll through the primary suspect's life, then the people they know, and so on, digging up data points and desperately linking them to try and form a coherent picture of the whole to assist "the greater good".

Oh, and the last day is a real mind-f*ck.  Pay close attention, or you may miss what happens.

TL;DR: 8/10 - good for people who appreciate a good plot, else avoid it.

So I picked this game up on HumbleBundle a good while back and completely forgot to ever install or play it. I just discovered it today and holy crap, this game is a masterpiece. Orwell is a mass surveillance sim in which you investigate a series of bombing incidents by following a string of suspects, reading their emails, recording their phone calls, and of course hacking their computers and cell phones, with of course a generous dose of general media research (papers, web publications) 

The game mechanics, were interesting most of the time, as it was somehow convincing that you were actually doing that kind of work, but at certain points it felt short and disappointing , maybe because of a small budget or maybe because limitations. For example the game lacked voices when recording phone calls (instead of using just text all the time), which would've been more dramatic (especially for certain parts) and made more sense since you are recording voices, also the game lacked more scenes in which you actually can see something happening. 
Even if you are a special agent in a remote location, physically detached from the place and you are watching things from a distance, it’s not so rare these days to have easy access through the web to voices recordings and videos whether be news or surveillance cams so it kind of ends up being short of realism and not that exciting. I suppose these really was a budget limitation more than a creative decision, especially because the story ends up being intricate and interesting.

I would admit that the context of what is happening in the game is something not close to me (luckily I don't have recurring bombings in my country as a way of protest) so I didn't feel attached to the general story, but it was the interaction between the different characters, and their personal stories that got me hooked and made more interested as I was playing and advancing the story until the very end. 

It was also of very special interest to me, to see how reality is perceived through a very tiny lens sometimes, and how one person's judgment could be potentially wrong about something. Understanding of things and self images can be manipulated and changed so drastically if we want to, so in a way I consider Orwell a success in showing me how the public perception can be molded and changed. And of course how appropriate the title name is to the game.

I had my eye on Orwell for quite some time. It looked intriguing; the whole concept of 24 hour constant surveillance isn't that far fetched, if at all, as much as many of us want to believe otherwise. It sat in my wishlist for a while, then it popped up in a Humble Bundle. It sat for a while in my library, then the free episode came up, and reminded me that I owned the game. Might as well give a whirl, yeah?

At first I was enthralled. They built a small universe that was only a hop, skip, and step away from the one I'm familiar with (good ol' US of A), and I was immediately taken in. I went through the first episode dutifully following along, reading everything I could get my hands on in the game. I combed through the info and made sure the data I supplied was tip-top. I finished out the first day (level) and felt good. Then the second day started.

It was the same thing, except I had a couple other targets to watch. I felt like I had already exhausted the gameplay. Find highlighted text, decide whether or not you want it, drag to box. Occasionally switch box from one character to another (which really just become pedantic when you end up only dealing with five or so interconnected characters). There's no real risk unless you just mean to do poorly, if its even possible. You can't really miss anything, so you never have to juggle the lives of all your surveillance targets. Their web-entries, conversation over text and "phone calls" (just more text doesn't read like a real conversation), will patiently wait for you while you sift through all of it. It gets to the point where you're just hunting highlighted words, as if Orwell has already solved the case on its own. Overall, the game is a bit of a dissappointment, which I only finished to see how the story unfolds. You get a few choices, but there is little in the way of making you feel like you had an impact unless you really got into the story.

TL:DR: All in all, the game is repetitive and after playing through the first episode, I really couldn't recommend purchasing the second one unless you really want to continue the story. I can tell the game was a labor of love, but it just doesn't offer any truly unique insights into the surveillance state and the ethical considerations that surround it, let alone the gameplay.

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

While a good concept in reality, and not awfully executed, I find this game has two pretty blatant flaws. The narrative -  at least the little of what I experienced - seems very on the nose. As in, there is no subtly to the story they are trying to tell. Secondly, there is a fatal flaw in the game mechanic. 

The main mechanic is dragging information into a profile of someone to build up a profile of them. Fine and all, but there's two parts to the fatal flaw. Number one: You can't undo dragging in info. New info can overwrite previous info, but you cannot erase something. Secondly, context is not taken into account. During one portion I dragged in a comment from what was effectively facebook which contained a very obvious hyperbolic joke, and the profiler took it as literal and your helper agent freaked out at what the info was. This little thing absolutely killed the game for me. Without context, a way to edit it, or erase this clearly false information, the game is actively working against you when you try to profile people. The obvious counter point is 'Well the game gave you tips not to just drag in information willy nilly', but the fact it BLATANTLY ignores any context that the player sees is ridiculous.

This isn't a bad game, but between a very shallow seeming plot that basically could just be called 'The CIA watches UC Berkeley commits a Riot' and a picky core - no, let me rephrase that - ONLY mechanic, this isn't an experience I wanted to continue playing.

This is the game where you play a bad NSA Agent.

So, this is a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure game, where you are investigating documents, pulling important and not-so important information out to further your investigations, and then making choices between conflicting chunks of information to feed into the system.
The truth you present to the investigation is what drives the story, and otherwise the story is told through newpaper articles, message feeds and other pictures and documents.

The animation in the trailer? That occurs solely within the intro sequence of the game and is not gameplay.
Just FYI.

There is no save system, which is a pity. Putting your fingers between the pages of a CYOA is half the fun, as how else are you meant to see all the endings. This game expects that you will instead play through multiple times for minor differences.

That said, the story is solid, and is to all intents and purposes how these monitoring systems would work in real life.
Namely, an investigation is launched on an individual, you'd search their records off the database based on selected metadata, and then the investigation will spread to related individuals based on a third party's incomplete perspective of the scenario.

This game rather heavily leans on the 'incomplete' perspective however, and more documents only become available to you after you've passed critical choices that may have wanted to rely on this information. It feels like the game is cheating here, as the context is missing on the first playthrough and so the consequence of your actions is not clear. Much like when you turn to page 76 of a CYOA and your gnarly motorcycle jump has your character land in the gaping maw of a space turtle and hideously die.

Not sure if this is still free.
Pick it up if it is; the story is very solid, and all else yields to it.

Otherwise still very good for one playthrough, if short.
Won't be repeating content just to get a different ending.

Without spoiling the plot too much, I'll sum it up this way: You play a person who applied to a super secret government survelliance program called Orwell, which had to launch early (again, in secret) due to a terrorist attack. You job is to monitor persons of interests through their text messages, email, phone calls, bank accounts, and doing your own research about them online. You upload information about them to Orwell, and your 'boss' talks you through the investigation.

The story is great, and it will keep you guessing until the end. It's worth playing for the story alone.

That all said, I felt the game was very much hand-holdy. The information you have to drag-and-drop into Orwell in order to advance the story is highlighted for you. It isn't until you get very late into the game that the information you upload could have a negative effect on your investigation. Until you get to that point, however, you might get a snarky remark about uploaded irrelevant information bits (which there are very few) but that's it. 

I would have preferred if the information wasn't highlighted and I had to dig it up myself and put it into Orwell. I'd really feel like a true investigator if that were the case, but I can understand why a small indie studio isn't able to accomplish that.

It's a short game. I completed it in about 4 hours. I don't see much replayability with this game, unfortunately. I was a little disappointed there wasn't a second story to play through or something like that. (Though I did learn there is a 'second episode' available, which I haven't checked out yet due to other games coming out that I want to purchase)

If you like a game with a really good story, drop the 10 bucks and get this game. Even with the complaints I listed above, I found this game enjoyable and would recommend it.

At first I was expecting Orwell to be about the evils of Big Data, huge data mining operations keeping tabs on everyone and everything, but as you play you realize it's much deeper than that. 

First episode there's a joke between friends and the game lets you [spoiler]update the suspects profile to say that she tortures people [/spoiler]. It seems like a joke at first but then you realize: the system doesn't [i]know[/i] it's a joke. Only your presence and understanding of the situation could prevent someone potentially being incacerated for [spoiler] being a crappy baker [/spoiler]... But surely that would never happen right? So long as there are people to check everything it'll all turn out okay won't it?

Then the conflicts come in. Working or creating an alibi? Patriot or Insergent? People will die if you make the wrong call. But you are human. You are fallable. You make mistakes. That is the point of this game. This for me was the message of Orwell. It's not so much about the evils of Big Data, but the dangers of incomplete information. 

In the ideal world of perfect information (an assumption used for the creation of economic models), Orwell and other Big Data operations could be forces for good. However, we do not have perfect information. Imperfection leads to ambiguity, ambiguity leads to assumptions, assumptions lead to mistakes and mistakes lead to suffering.

So, Orwell is mixture of good stuff and mediocre stuff. I really like the gameplay, structuring and pacing (both of the plot and the gameplay). The central gameplay loop is basically just looking through various documents and conversations to find information potentially relevant to the investigation. I thought it would be boring at first, but it actually never felt tired, and remains engaging throughout. Gameplay wise, it's pretty good, with only a few minor tweaks that could improve efficiency. The story is where it gets less positive. As you progress through the game, you learn more about the characters, who they are, their background, their personality, etc. etc. This is the strongest aspect of the story, because their well written characters, and seeing them react to what's happening after learning so much about them makes you think really carefully about what you do that might affect them. Unfortunately, these characters all seem fixated on the agenda of beating the message of the game over your head repeatedly. The themes and message? That's where we really start to lose traction. First off, the message is obvious. One of the characters at the end practically spells it out. Thanks, if the all the references to the number 1984 didn't make it obvious, nor the chapters being named after phrases from 1984, then I would of still gotten it from the name and premise. Mass surveillance is bad! Like, really unethical! No, really? I thought that was obvious. For the all the 1984 references though, it doesn't seem like the writers really understood 1984. 1984 isn't about surveillance. It's about the manipulation of thought, primarily through language and media. The surveillance is window dressing. In fact, you never even know if the citizens in 1984 are actually being watched, because it doesn't matter. It just matters that they think they are. I digress. The game also comes as thinking it's a bit smarter than it really is. Despite that, it's never boring, and though a little melodramatic, and the tendency to believe that the player hasn't caught on that mass surveillance is kinda screwed up, I did feel desire to continue, and though the end is also a little silly (It forces you to choose between 3 equally culpable people, for no explained reason. Why can't I incriminate them all?), I didn't feel cheated. I didn't pay I got it for free from humble, but I wouldn't have regretted paying for it. Try episode 1, if you like it, it won't overly disappoint from there, and it'll retain its fun.

First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse.
