I got this game for free on Humble Bundle this past week. I'd been wanting to try it out, but didn't really want to spend the money (I'm broke lol). But I am glad I played it. It's not terribly long, but it does have a level of replayability. If I can get over how personally victimized I feel by it, I'll definitely play it again to see if I can get a more ideal ending!

The game isn't perfect. I found typos and small bugs--I would get red star notifications for "urgent" or "important" infochunks to find in areas of the game I could no longer access, for example, and they would not go away. Some of the mechanics also bugged me, although the game did provide a decent excuse for it in the end. One such mechanic being that relevant information simply pops up on your screen, rather than it being similar to Her Story in that you have to activity enter keywords to find this information. But it somewhat makes up for it in providing irrelevant information, like news stories on film or items on target characters like their favorite colors. And the devs gave you no lack of things to explore and read, which really makes the story even more interesting--as an investigator for crime, is it really important for you to delve into someone's dating app messages, or personal photos? Not always... but I found I ended up doing it anyway.

The game has a strong message but leaves the ultimate meaning ambiguous and up for the player to decide, leaving you with several story paths to take (though it's not easy to see when this is happening. I thought the game was totally linear at first!) that effect your experience with Orwell. I like that it leaves the ultimate message morally gray, since the topic of Big Brother and digital monitoring is such a gray area to begin with.

So, having played it, I think it's definitely worth a play. Maybe buy the game on sale, but I probably have another 5 hours of playtime in the game at least, and a buck an hour for my entertainment is pretty worthwhile to me. I'll definitely be buying the sequel, once I dare submit to more emotional rollercoaster.

Ultimately, my review comes down to one question:  "Would I pay for this?"  The answer is, no I don't think I would.  I can certainly see where this game would appeal to some, but it doesn't to me.  Hence, the negative score.  I don't regret playing it for free, but I don't think I would have been missing out had I not played it.

Orwell is a story game, first and foremost.  It has somewhat non-linear story to tell, where your actions will affect the details of the plot, but it'll otherwise run more or less the same, and you'll have a choice of three or four endings depending on how you do the finale.  The game tries to cover the problem of survellience but... IMO, it misses the mark completely when the tools used to spy are... indept.  More on that later.

The game boils down to reading fictional internet pages, spying on emails, calls, and texts, and snooping on people's computers.  Your goal is to find "important" information, that is pre-highlighted for you, and drag and drop what you feel is important.  The game stresses that you try to pick correct and relevant information but, ultimately, there's no failure state.  Being accurate or inaccurate only affects the plot details, nothing else, and kinda underminds the engagement of what little gameplay there is.

There's major problems with this though.  You're an investigator on a case, but your partner and the tools you're using are inept.  You can supply information, but you're often not allowed to include the context too.  Context is stupid important in real investigations, so it really undermines, well, the whole system.  You'll also come across "conflicting data", sometimes before you've even found the info it conflicts with.  A good investigator would record it all and then review it later and dismiss what's incorrect.  In Orwell?  You have to pick one.  And sometimes you have to pick blindly.  Just... why?  You also cannot collect information on individuals related to the main suspects, something I figure would be rather important.

It'll also leave you wondering one major question:  what sort of security and surveillance dystopia doesn't even have basic information, such as dates of birth and known addresses, already on file?  For a government trying to imitate 1984's Big Brother, they're failing hard at it.  Especially when around 75% of the information you're gathering is from public sources...

This here's the whole problem:  the game tries to make you question whether government observation is good or bad and whether things should be more private.  But then it puts you in the role of a guy who spends a lot of the time collecting publicly posted information and digging up stuff slower than a Google search.  Snooping into calls, computers, and bank accounts is certainly fishy, yeah, but nothing that would be legally off-limits to a police officer with a warrant in Real Life™.  And considering the plot... warrants are totally justified for everyone involved.

Orwell tries, and the story is just interesting enough for a 3-4 hour playthrough.  But... the political discussion just falls flat due to its own gameplay.  And there's games that are much better at hunting down and acquiring your information without highlighting it for you, like the parts of Hacknet focused on snooping.  

IMO:  not really worth the buy.  If you're really curious, try the demo and if you still want it, wait for a sale.
WORTH IT

Orwell greeted me with an opening cinematic which brings you straight to the plot to what Orwell is really about: Big Brother. However, there is not much that is animated in this game, as the idea is pretty straightforward. Orwell is what happens when you take the format of Hacknet (same publisher) and turn it into a universe with choices and consequences resonating from games like the Life is Strange series (also, the artsy visuals). Perhaps it is also no surprise this particular series lasts 5 episodes, or "days" in the Orwell world. 

The one thing I felt was missing from the game was the ease of controller support. There is quite a lot of dragging to be done with the "dtachunks" you use, which makes a mouse more useful. Yet, the interface could have been much more friendly and easier with more shortcuts to sift through all the links to explore. I've made do with a workaround, but it is one point which I'd set it down to 9/10 instead of a 10/10. The rest of the game was pleasing. The plotline dynamics were interesting. There's no "blink and you'll miss it". Orwell is straightforward and simple without the overcomplications, which is what I feel should be an example of what gaming should be about.

Overall, I look forward to the future.

A successful interpretation of a glimpse into a reality where "big brother" is watching you, everywhere. Here are some pros and cons for this game.

Pros:
Very good narrative between suspects, especially in interrogations. It feels real.

The player choices: yes it does matter. For the system Orwell to acknowledge a piece of information over another that contradicts it is up to you. This gives you the feeling that you are in charge of the case. However, there are some parts that you cannot change, and that will make you question the system. As I will point out later as much as this distrusting gameplay aspect is an excellent addition to the gameplay, it also is a plot-hole for me.

Cons:
Too short: for such excellent experience, it obviously is better not to squeeze the last breath out of it, however 5 episodes without a DLC is just too short.

You: the Orwell system is essentially the Big Brother from 1984. 

"Is there someone as the Big Brother?"
"Of course. This system is the Big Brother."
"I mean, is the Big Brother alive?"
"Depends. Are you alive?"

The mentality of "the Big Brother" is that it knows, sees, hears EVERYTHING. Not just the stuff that you choose to believe in. This makes your perspective on the game very contradictory to the principals of the Big Brother. One way the solve this could have been being the guy who works for the system, not the guy who makes the system work. Would love to see a DLC like that!

Conclusion:
Even if you missed the Humble Bundle, this game is still very much worth your money.

Orwell is a small indie game that may or may not be good based on what kinds of games the player may enjoy. I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The story is very deep. Imagine watching a murder mystery show, there is alot of plot twists that really makes you wonder things like who really did it since everyone looks guilty. The story is shaped based on the player's decisions on what they consider important or facts. From there the response might be different based on the players decisions.

       Good ambient music. The music is not much but at times it does emphasis the mood that is suppose to be potrayed. In a moment where you discover something shocking the music will change to potray a shocking mood.

        The art is very simplistic. That is not a bad thing by any stretch of the imagination. It is again an indie game but it does remind me of the polygon designs of super hot and that was a decent looking game. The main point is that the visuals do not overly distract the player  from important moments of the game. It allows for a more cleaner visual naritive with it's simplistic design.

Con:
      The game has a few bugs. The main one I faced was moments that the game froze requiring me to ALT+F4 to close the game and continue where I left off. At moments it is possible for the game to have a dialogue box open but on the background there will be an ongoing conversation via texting or calling and it would prevent you from scrolling through the text to properly read it. This is very likely to happen towards the end of the game.

Conclusion:
         The game is pretty good. The stroy did throw me through a few loops. I did not expect a few of these plot twists and playing through the game was exciting to see how the story played out. Unfortunantly replaying is not nearly as great since the story changes are pretty minor at points and lack any worth wild plot twists when going down a different branching path. Ultimatly  I would reccomend this game but mainly to people who enjoy games with a pretty rich story and branching plot decisions like walking dead.

Gameplay, if you don't want to check YouTube, is pretty simple - you drag'n'drop pieces of text between two windows. Window on the right shows you info from web, chats and PC's, and window on the left keeps dossiers on game's characters. By deciding, which info to drop to dossiers, you impact story and it's ending.

This, however, is the biggest flaw of the game. A lot of reviews write about "heavy, morally ambigious choices", but in the end all this morality boils down to "Freedom with a-holes vs Order with a-holes, now choose". I couldn't fullheartedly support any of the outcomes, because throughout the story all of the characters became repulsive and I didn't like any of them. And I also felt discouraged by the "sudden truth" in the end - inconsistent wall of text, which plays for 7 minutes.

Art and overall design, however, is very good. Game looks and plays great.

In the end, game is very cool until chapter 5, which feels rushed and ruins the experience. I got it for free from HumBun, so I am not dissapointed, but I probably would be a little sad if I bought it for fullprice. I will push "Recommend" because most of the game is good, despite it's failed (for me) ending.

If you expect a game to engage more than half a brain cell, this isn't for you. If you want to read a boring, heavy-handed, and pseudo-edgy book while click-and-dragging highlighted text that will interrupt your book reading, this is perfect for you.

There's a lengthy playthrough channel on YouTube. If you think the game gets better or has any sort of progression at all, skip to a later episode, it'll still be the same shallow nonsense.

Orwell. This experience is simply mind blowing.. the ideas and the way this game executes the plausibly realistic scenario of an indiscriminate cyber investigation system being utilised by "investigators" to obtain information on suspects who have been identified to have possible intent to harm "the Nation", legally, or more often then not; illegally.

Not many games have provided me with such a thought exercise and even less have made a lasting impression on me, and this game certainly has done exactly that. This development studio have outdone themselves immensely and I do find myself some regret of obtaining this game freely instead of supporting the developers and obtaining the game myself personally.

Orwell, has an amazing soundtrack, realistic characters (even when they did not have actual voices or anything other than their words and pictures, they felt as real to me as any other) intense story, realistic scenarios and relatable events (such as terrorist attacks, online privacy worries, etc.) I even felt a deep connection with the "advisors" to Orwell in a professional sense, especially the first one who I enjoyed his humour and his concern for things.

When I first started Orwell, I did not expect much seeing as I had jumped right into it without any thought. But after playing through Orwell for the first time, it really does make you think about things and that is the magical effect of Orwell.

"But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." DO not underestimate these words in the description.

Every chunk of information matters, whether it leads to leads to something more, whether it leads to social breakdown or whether it leads to disaster. 

Getting the information wrong, is not tolerable in Orwell.

100% recommend this game. Although it does not have anymore than around 5 hours of content, those 5 hours will be the most intense and enjoyable experience you will discover. Perhaps in the future this scenario will become a reality? Who knows? There is already the familiar CCTV and technology is rapidly advancing.

I wish I could give a middle ground recommendation. Story based game, little gameplay, not a bad thing but parts of the story and the execution are a little wonky. The game revolves around you uploading datachunks as they call them to a system for a detective like person, known as an Adviser, to review, these are highlighted pieces of text that maybe useful information, which is the first big problem. Rarely are these datachunks useless information so 90% of the time is ok to just upload the regular "blue" datachunks and at least half of the 10% remaining are incredibly obviously useless or incorrect, although uploading them allow you to see more "related documents" Conflicting datachunks are yellow, tell you and point to their conflicting datachunk where you generally have to make a choice which is correct, and you'll be able to find the information to make the most informed call almost every time. Quite often when uploading a datachunk it will only provide a bit of a picture from the actual uploaded text or picture but the adviser will add significantly more detail to advance the plot than the piece of information should be providing. I'm going to talk very generally about the end, no character names, examples or spoilers. Another wonky component was the final day, each day is the next episode, entering the final day the rules change and you can only upload 20 datachunks, which is a great mechanic and should've been a mechanic the whole way through the game, the reasoning for this change is really awkward because "something, fairly tame" is going to happen at a certain time during the final day, but this was not a concern elsewhere in the game. The final day brings me to the biggest problem with the game, there is a point after uploading the 20 datachunks which kind of transitions the game into the endgame portion, but during this information was revealed that I didn't know and was prevented as if I had found it, which made me feel like the entire sequence isn't heavily effected by the uploaded datachunks, it made the endgame feel very cheap as you start making what should be the very impactful decisions. You basically just select one of the endgame directions after the transition rather than all or most of your game decisions meaning something. The other problem is the ending seems extremely preachy rather than allowing the player to figure out how they feel about the subject matter.

But whats good about Orwell? The characters in general feel much more realistic rather than when you see someone try to write internet conversations and forum posts. Orwell does a pretty good job of leading and misleading you at different points which does make it more interesting. The pacing in phone calls/text chats feel really good and suspenseful, assuming the player can read fast enough to keep up, same goes for connecting documents, although some can feel way too convenient. The concept and questions it should be asking the player about the extent of security and surveillance is excellent.

Would I buy this game for $10? Probably not, it only took 5 hours to complete, including when I walked away for a few minutes. Sale price? Yah its definitely worth checking out. If its under $3 definitely get it, its an interesting ride.

My only negative point would be that the game has a medium to low replay value, as is the norm with all narrative-driven games. Although it is a bit higher than average.

Outside of that, it really is a great game full of choices, consequences, and most-importantly for me: clarity of choice. You see, the game will explicitly spell the information that is derived from the clue that you have before you. This way, there is no room for a gap between what you thought your choice would convey, and what it actually conveys. (NOTE: This doesn't preclude other characters from seeing the information through their own lens and biaises)

The theme is obviously very interesting, and the game seems to be doing a decent job at letting you form your own real-life opinions on the topic. The investigation mechanics are detailed enough that it doesn't feel like the game is railroading you, but not loose enough that you can get 'suck' or 'lost' for too long, which I really appreciate.

Overall, I'd strongly recommend the game if you are willing to explore themes that make you think about real-life ideas and ethical dillemas, wrapped into a good investigation game.

The Game is best described as an interactive crime novel rather than a full game.

[Pros]
It is well designed and the interaction is very streamlined and has a nice flow to it, combining the feeling of going through files like an actual investigator without the boring drawback of having 500 duds for every lead. IMO the devs nailed the ratio of work/reward in a way that is engaging, story driving and entangling.

The plot is interesting and apparently it has multiple endings with yet again multiple outcomes, it is by no means a "choose your own adventure" but it brings in just enough individuality that a second and even thrid run of the game could be interesting even if you already know the plot.

There are always multiple ways to get them juicy Data chunks you're looking for.

[Cons]

The game does a pretty good job at highlighting important information, be it in form of Data Chunks or in plain text. However oftentimes you find yourself in a spot where you discover information about a person you know has some sort of realationship with one of your POIs. However the game does not let you add said information to their profile which to me came as an enormous break in the flow.  As in: "This person seems to play a pivotal role and I have information about them that might come in handy later, why in the lords name am I not allowed to add this information?" [spoiler] Although this has happened to me a few times I most often encountered this with the lawyer, Joseph if im not mistaken, he is an important character early on yet the game does not let you collect data on him from the get go [/spoiler]
To me it felt like the game does not reward you if you are being extra thorough, which can be very discouraging.

Maybe I have not been thorough enough, but the game has major plotholes, the most annoying to me being the algorythm of Orwell knowing two data chunks are conflictive. How does the programm know that? And if it found such intricate information out without me going over it why am I needed? This could have been solved much more elegantly by having to chose which of the two statements is true; As in "her favourite colour appears to be red but in a previous statement we have assest that it is indeed blue. Do you wish to edit your previous assesment or keep the original?". This could have also gven us more opportunity to bond with our evaluator, whom I have perceived as rather robotic since he basically only shows emotions when you make mistakes. [spoiler] Honestly the big J plottwist was such an anticlimactic ending, although I understand her "motivations" I do not understand how harrison fits in the picture. The life insurance was for his mother ofc. But did he also fake correspondance as Abraham? How does that fit in? Why did we not find any indication of this earlier? It felt like a very cheap reveal alà modern sherlock holmes, where the pieces just happen to fall in a way nobody could have predicted and resolving the story in a very dry and undercut way. How did they manage to find out initiate's number? Why dont we have access to that if they can just, hypothetically, recall? [/spoiler] This way of resolving the main plot does not do their way of engaging storytelling justice in the slightest. 

[Verdict]

A very different approach to the interactive novel, I enjoyed it altough it has some shorcomings. The way the game involves the player and tells it's story is superb and deserves a better plot than what we are given.

I got this from Humble for free, but I finished the game and think I should review it.

[b]WARNING: SPOILERS ARE PRESENT IN THIS REVIEW[/b]

[h1]SUMMARY OF THE STORY[/h1]

You are a interrorgator for the company, Orwell. You have to find out who caused 2-3 bombings depending on the way you played the game. In my playthrough, 2 bombs went off and I helped discover and disarm the 3rd.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

You go through different sites finding information on people and try to find out if they cause the bombing or not. You can also access emails, messages, and calls if you find emails, phone numbers, and usernames. You can even find ways of accessing devices such as computers and phones to find evicence and info. 

[h1]OVERALL REVIEW[/h1]

4/5

Story: 5/5
Gameplay Mechanics: 3/5

Although I think the story is REALLY good for this game, the Gameplay Mechanics are meh. Although the UI isn't confusing like Call of Duty: Black Ops 4's HUD in-game, the way it works is too easy for my taste. They highlight the text for you and tell you who it matches up to. It's a great concept, but it wasn't executed correctly in my opinion. Maybe make the user choose which profile it goes to instead of showing them what profile to add it to instead of trying to guide them into the right direction. Example: There's 2 datachunks that conflict with eachother when trying to find the 3rd bomb. The game babies you by showing you which profile it matches to instead of letting you choose. It's kinda like aim assist in COD: it babies you by helping you kill enemies instead of letting you use skill to kill them. Let the person find out theirself instead of telling them, "Oh by the way, this person was planning this. Put it on their profile."

Besides that, the story is really good. All yellow text effects the story of the game, and I really like it when you have to choose. There are multiple endings, which adds to the replayability. Plus, the concept is really good. You try to find out who planted the bomb at the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd location while learning about other information that people have. Through my playthrough, you learn about other lives. You learn about relationships people have, who people have met, who they are friends with, who are they not friends with, etc. It adds to the story in my opinion because some information you get can show why some people have this problem.

[h1]SUMMARY OF WHOLE REVIEW[/h1]

I think it's a really good game with a good story, but game mechanics that I dislike.
Honestly, I loved it. If it sounds boring to you, it probably will be. If it sounds interesting to you, it probably will be.

Wow, what an immersive experience. Orwell is less of a game and more of an intricate story told in a unique way with VN-like decisions that impact how the game plays out. If you don't like reading or slow gameplay, chances are that Orwell is definitely not the game for you.

But if you skip Orwell, you will be missing out on an incredible story with plenty of character development that actually makes them feel like real people. You play as an investigator who invades the private lives of his/her fellow civilians in order to put an end to the recent terrorist bombings. How far will you go in breaking down the boundaries of privacy in order to potentially save lives? Is the privacy of the few more valuable than the lives of even fewer? In Orwell, no choice is as simple as it initially seems, and it's these philosophical and ethical questions that make the game a blast to play through.

There are plenty of great twists in the story and the soundtrack is ambient, though satisfying. Orwell's primary flaw is actually its greatest strength: the plot has such resonance that it makes the game impossible to replay. Don't let that deter you; Orwell is worth every penny.

Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

The game really takes you through the extremes of an orwellian state in disguise, which makes you more aware in general how realistic the topic might have become.

I really would advise anyone to play, albeit for the conclusion they draw from it themselves.

So I got this game for free on HB, and was eager to try it out. As I am a fan of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia]dystopian[/url] novels and games. Fictions like [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four]1984[/url] or [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brave_New_World]Brave New World[/url] are what I'd love to read.

This game is based off George Orwell's 1984(hence the game's name [i]Orwell[/i]). A government launching a surveillance system in a bid to stop "terrorists" and their "attacks". You are one of the agents that helps submitting [i]correct[/i] information to government intel. Suspects will be arrested or able to escape from arrestments based on what information you provided. Much like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/475550/]Beholder[/url], you can save innocents or those you want to help by not submitting certain data to the Orwell system.

After a few minutes into the game, I decide that this game is quite worth the pennies. It allows you to experience being a "Big Brother" - watching citizens behind, logging every moves they make, and determining their ultimate fate. Although the Big Brother perspective is already popular among dystopian games. I find this one quite interesting. Unlike beholder, you don't need to go around maintaining good terms with residents. Instead you sit right in front of a surveillance system, pretty much like the real world NSA agents would do in their everyday work.

To sum up, I would recommend this game to everyone. Still thinking your privacy is REALLY SAFE online? On the fence of thinking about being spyed on? Play this game.
It's a truly amazing game. You have to experience it for yourself - if they ever make a sequel it could only get even better.

Long over due review for this game. Maybe a few spoilers in it so read if you want. Orwell is a strange game. More like a simulation if you would. It places you as an investigator of a top secret internet detective group. Your primary means of investigation is literally spying on the general populace you are sworn to protect. It's also incredibly immersive with characters that have real life reactions to your actions and events that seem directly inspired by real life. You kind of forget you are playing again. Yes, you know what that spying on these people's personal lives is wrong, you know that taking their online jokes out of context is wrong, but you also know that if you don't do your job people are going to die and it's going to be your fault for not having properly acted on the bits of truth you have. 

It's very crazy. Being forced to piece together elaborate truths based merely shreds of evidence scattered across the web, not knowing if the information you are gathering will be relevant or even lead you to your next clue, trying to minimize the damage of your actions on those you think are innocent while being fully aware you might have to drag them through the mud to get the info you need. They'll live, you know they will which almost justifies the mud you throw at them. Yet the people who're lives are being targeted. Those who are going to be hit the most by the extremists you hunt, unless you're willing to get your hands dirty, they won't live. 

I just finished my first real case to locate the next target of a domestic terrorist and shit I've never been so stressed in a game before. I had to threaten an innocent girl with charges of torture because she was being non-cooperative. It's a trumped charge, won't stick in 100 years and I know it was wrong, but it got her to talk. Got that last piece of evidence we needed to locate the bomb from her and with that my official report was submitted. Most games give you a reply immediately when you do things like this. Not Orwell. It makes you wait. it makes you stew in your methods, in the possibility you might be wrong. After several minutes I get word that the evacuation order was given and that the bomb squad is moving in to investigate. I unknowingly cross my fingers. I have to be right on this. If they find no device that means we were wrong about the location and more people will die. I have to be right. I did too many wrong things to fail. Seconds go by, minutes go by, feels longer. Finally, a report comes in. They found the bomb and disabled it. I sigh in relief as my fingers uncross and my body relaxes. We did it. We saved those people's lives. The girl might be in trouble for a bit, but her cooperation in saving those people's lives will be noted. Charges against her might be dropped. At the worse, probation for her unknowing association with a terrorist group, but she'll live. Everyone will today. 

And that's how my first case in Orwell the game went. Honestly, if you like immersive text based games, buy this. You won't regret it.

Good game - very intense, with an aquired taste in art/aesthetic that I personally enjoyed. It was quite philosophical. Also, unlike many of it's competing "episodic" games (looking at you Telltale), the choices you make genuinely affect the gameplay, as well as the endings (and yes, I did finish the job... like my playthrough of LiS, why wouldn't I continue the very thing I had done the entire game?). The gameplay is detailed and intelligent.

My biggest issue is, as with many episodic games, the short timespan. The game is very short - and this also includes periods of time where you can't do anything, such as during the phone call and text sections. Also, there isn't too much of a progression system - for example, one of the better mechanics called "Insider" is only given to you near the climax of the game's story, and it is only used for about a tenth of the game's span. 

All in all, I do thoroughly recommend the game, especially if you want an intense yet oddly chilled experience (think of it as like a UAV flying simulator, except more personal) as well as ethical thinking as a genuinely thought provoking insight to the current age of omnipresent technology. However, if you want something that you can keep playing (for example, endgame content, replay value etc), then it probably isn't for you.

Excellent little game demonstrating the risks involved in mass surveillance, automated and manual data processing and excessive government oversight without similar levels of accountability. While there are certainly benefits to such things, one has to also consider the costs - and this game does a great job of showing the potential costs vs benefits if you give it a bit of thought.

In terms of gameplay, I found it to be extremely immersive the first time through. There were, however, a few small problems (imo) with the design in that it can occasionally be easy to dead-end yourself if you overlook, or consider irrelevant, the particular piece of information that triggers the "next part" of the game. Then you're in a situation where you're just randomly adding bits of seemingly irrelevant information "until and/or in the hope of something happening". 

Since there can often be very little to indicate which bit of information moves the story along, and which bits are completely unrelated and will get you yelled at for spamming the system, it can be a touch annoying. It also gives some inkling of the extent to which "big data" can be monitoring your life and drawing potentially misleading conclusions about it. So, that's extra scary, I guess?

Unfortunately, the same things that make the game so immersive on the first playthrough (i.e. the semi-occasionally-real-time nature of phone-calls and stuff) also feels to be a detriment on later play throughs. For a conversation where you know exactly what's happening in it, and where there's no "real-time" element, I found no way to speed it up and it got pretty annoying. To the point where I'd just click a button to start the conversation off, then go watch a movie or whatever. Thank goodness for the Steam browser, because if you alt-tab out, you lose your ingame cursor (or at least, I did), so at least I still had something to do during some of the super-long-boring bits.

Overall, though, it's still an excellent game which I think everybody should play - even if just so they know what today's governments are getting up to!

This is not a bad game, but I do think it's overrated. It falls short as a game and as a study of the surveillance state.

The gameplay mechanics are very simple -- you go to different links and and decide whether to upload them to Orwell or not. That's all there is to gameplay. Frustratingly, I ran into a few occasions where to advance the story I had to upload a link that was not obvious as to its value. Additionally, it's silly that you can't correct events later on, even before the information is acted upon -- if you send something over it's set in stone. And I'm not talking about the conflict choices -- those actually were good and created a good choice to have to make in deciding how the fate of certain people would go. 

Some of those negatives really betrayed the gamey-ness of the system. 

But worse was the whole conceit of the game really misses on being a meditation of surveillance gone awry. For one, the investigator is not a member of The Nation, which simply wouldn't happen in the real world, so it undercuts the influence of the government. The pressure that you as the investigator feels is thus negligble (unlike something like Papers, Please). The artificiality of the Orwell setup avoids the influence of government on media or bias of investigators that is very much an issue in the real world. 

Additionally, the game seems to suggest that the mere possibility of some people being investigated without having done wrong is evil. Except, that is how criminal investigations have gone since time immemorial. You start with some clues and investigate from there which will inevitably lead to some innocent people being scrutinized (even sometimes convicted). But that is the outcome of such a human operation and is not really a result of the surveillance state. And remember, we're investigating actual crimes where innocent people died. 

The game would have been much stronger if it showed intentional abuse by the system operators, influence by the government, or the ability to enact control of a population by knowing the way they think and act (think machine learning and how well it can predict certain behaviors/beliefs in people now). Or if the act in question was more dubious in nature, was maybe a false flag, or at least had some element of a frame up instead of an actual terrorist act committed by a true believer.

Another minor gripe is that you can't skip ahead on any chat or phone calls, which are interminably slow. While that might be realistic, it's also a bit boring.

The story also provides choices and branches in the same manner as a Telltale game, so if you like that facade you won't be bothered here. However, I did find it a bit unsatisfying that no matter the choices you made, the next episode would essentialy go the same way. And since everything is told in documents, calls, and chats, it's really lacking the dramatic power that a good Telltale game can have.

It wasn't a bad time but I definitely felt underwhelmed.

[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.

It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me! The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

What an incredible game. I sat down hoping to start and finish a game in one sitting, and I did just that, just over 6 and a half hours later.

The game has you scouring websites and messages to begin with, later involving phone calls and electronic devices too. This action tickles a very specific investigative soft spot, allowing you to accept or reject information as you see fit (with some plot-progression-required points aside). Unfortunately this comes with the caviat that your -intention- is not always understood when making these choices, but the game does the best it can to inform you how the data will be interprited, while staying in-universe.

Now I have to make this very clear: I thought this game was completely different, based on the trailer I watched. I thought I would be monitoring areas using CCTV and pulling up profiles on potential criminals with Watchdogs-style hackery. This couldn't be further from the truth - this is an interactive visual novel through-and-though, much like a previous game I've played, and would highly recommend, Analogue: A Hate Story.

While playing this game I felt genuine emotions, which does not happen often. I felt elation at preventing an attack--something I felt I had complete control over, not just interaction with--and guilt over a death--one I know I caused, but could have potentially stopped with information I realised I had overlooked too late. It's like a more relaxed version of Telltale's The Walking Dead games, where your choices have sincere impact on the world. But don't think it's all just casual browsing either, as there are timed occurances that you need to be quick on your mouse to prevent, should you choose to. Sometimes you have to make uninformed choices, which you will simply have to live with the consequences of, while giving you hindsight for future playthroughs.

All in all, it was a fascinating story and premise that kept my attention for its duration, with the clear possibility of replayability, should you want to see all possible outcomes (and right your wrongs). You couldn't ask for more than that.

I make it a point to go into games blind. Once I picked up the first season of Orwell, not knowing what to expect was definitely the right way to go.

From the get-go, the mere concept of Orwell was enough to get me hooked. Looking into the lives of people in secret, acting like Big Brother, it's a concept that isn't explored that much in fiction. There's obviously 1984 by George Orwell, which this game references alot in its achievements, but other than that I can't think of anything else.

Orwell's story is definitely the best part. It's thrilling and engaging, with twists coming when you least expect them. After playing it blind, this is even more emphasized. The choices you make can also have a huge impact on the outcome of the story, which adds replayability to the game. It can get emotional at times, though not in the "oh my god, I'm going to cry" kind of way. More like "oh my god, what have I done?" The story can also be considered a kind of social commentary on the world, especially concerning surveillance and data and the repurcussions of them (Snowden, anyone?)

Orwell doesn't have much going for it in terms of gameplay, it's really just clicking and dragging. That would normally be a problem if there wasn't an engaging story to back it up, which I think I've already established Orwell has. There were some points that felt a bit slow, such as the dialogue sections that you can't skip through. That might have improved the pacing just a bit, but it didn't detract from the overall experience too much. It's also a bit short, taking me only around 3 hours to complete my first playthrough, but with the different choices affecting the story, again, this adds to the replayability value.

Basically, just go play Orwell.

Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

This game is an unexpected little gem.  In case you didn't figure it out, this game is more than just a title reference to the novel 1984.  In it, you play as a government investigator using monitoring tools to spy on people's conversations, web history and personal data in order to find the culprit of certain terrorist attacks and, if possible, prevent any more.  The game is very text-and-pic heavy, so don't expect a graphic adventure where you get to walk around.  All your spying is done from your computer and save from an intro cutscene you don't get to see anything outside your character's monitor.

Don't let that discourage you, though, this game is quite interesting, and smart.  You play by acquiring data from certain media, trying to find people of interest and then use any data you can find on them to expand your knowledge, extrapolate and be able to find even more data, so you can pursue your goal.  For instance, you might a person of interest mentioning a friend over a conversation.  Following that person's name in social media you might find a picture and a nickname, so you can then read comments made with it that establish a possible motivation, which you can then link to certain dates and articles to establish that friend as another person of interest.  Doing more digging, you might be able to find their phone number, so you can read some chats that will give you clues or even a confession that can lead to an arrest.

Yes, there's a whole debate about weighing the pros and cons of a system like this one, where a government has to violate privacy in order to provide security, and there are many works of fiction that tackle the issue, but this one doesn't take the easy way out.  It allows you to play the investigative side and then it lets you choose what to do.  You are the middle man between the information and the government, and as such you can play the loyal dog and do everything as requested, or you can purposely hide information or feed misinformation in order to either exonerate or condemn a person, whether, in either case, that person is innocent or not.

This means that, effectively, the fate of several people is at your hand.  People can (again, innocent or not) be arrested or be free because of your doing.  Your intervention will be pivotal in deciding if a person lives or dies.  Granted, many parts of the game are still linear, and the story progresses at a certain pace, but the game still does a good job of showing that when you get to make a choice, it matters.

These choices give the game enough replay value, and many of them have achievements tied to them if you're a hunter.  I definitely recommend the game.  If you're not sure, you can play the demo, which does a pretty good job of showcasing the gameplay without revealing all of its tricks.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

[h1]Orwell... or oh well....[/h1]
I love considering our future and wondering how we might become no more than parts of some evolving socially obedient organism, devoid of personal privacy and with it, control of our own lives...  and our truth. For the greater good as it were. It's pure Orwell which probably explains the title.

For mine though, with some retrospect.... this is less about any "Big Brother" surveillance reference that some might have infered by some of the comments I've seen. I think it's much more than that. It's about our inability to recognise a social evolution far more insidious and far more pervasive to society that we're all an unwitting party too. Ourselves. But then... George didn't say what "Big Brother" really was either.

What gets me with this? Hmmm.... The concept is great. It's a scarey thought, possibly not too far removed from what might already be happening. This game attempts to highlight the manipulation of data, of people and of truth to reach a more palatable "truth". A kind of guaranteed "to the victor go the spoils" by first ensuring we're the victor. 

The premise is sound. The execution seems to be not so good - you ultimately click mostly what you're meant to click, read what you're meant to read and do essentially what you're lead, by the nose, towards. 

But I do wonder here. I found I had my own path I wanted to follow, making assumptions from data and threads I had gathered, some quite... spurious although quite compelling. However, either the game forced decisions I would NOT make given same circumstances or would not even allow me to make them at all. Which was annoyingly disconcerting but oddly enough, might actually be very clever and intentional gameplay. I still can't get a fix on it tbh. 

Perhaps the lesson here is that we don't REALLY want disinterested, independent, non affected 3rd parties from doing surveillance or making any kinds of decisions - even controlled ones - on our behalf do we? Nor would we want those disinterested, independent, non affected 3rd party decisions made to appear like objective reasoning and thus proving there is a need to act against people or states... or truth... Are these actions now to be deemed as not only justified but an social imperative... for the owners of the data, oops, sorry, truth?

It'll never happen. Right? RIGHT?

In Orwell, Big Brother has arrived. And it's you. You are his online eyes having complete access to all types of communication and data as long as you know what to look for. Your task as investigator is to research bombings which are supposedly organized by an activist group called Thought. To do this, documents, phone calls, chats or target computers have to be analyzed. To do this, you have to drag relevant facts into profiles of your targets to enable acting on them. Certain key criteria have to be met to set the full power of law enforcement into action to protect the regime.

The game is a visual novel with limited influence. The challenge is to find the information needed to proceed. Sometimes, the data is conflicted and you have to take a choice what you enter in the profile. Some non-conflicted information can be left out of the profile as well to protect a target.

Orwell consists of five levels. Towards the end of a level, it's possible to get stuck for a while when the last information needed to trigger an arrest is missing and you don't find it. But I was able to finish it without having to resort to guides or forum posts. The ending was sudden and a bit disappointing when the game finished immediately after dragging a piece of information into a profile. Thought was disbanded, the members arrested and I as the investigator was subjected to an investigation as well. So I replayed the last chapter to get a 'good' ending. Freedom prevailed and Orwell was mothballed.

I really enjoyed the style of the game. Digging for information isn't too difficult but there's an odd satisfaction to completing a profile. I didn't really felt morally compelled to act 'good' or think about what I was doing. Papers, Please or 1979 Revolution: Black Friday were more stimulating in this concern. But the experience was completely entertaining.

If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.
Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember.
 
[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
 
Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. However, at times the story does slow down, and it is easy to get fatigued with the sheer amount of writing in this game.
I think it’s easiest to sum up Orwell as an interactive, dystopian, detective novel at its best. In a game that hinges on the “choices matter” idea, it does well in treating the player like an intelligent and competent participant. You have the ability to make inferences that might not accomplish what you’re trying to do. Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching.
 
[h1]8/10[/h1]
