A story game where you play as a curator of information to try and help the actual authorities solve a case. Pretty interesting story revelations/twists.

Information you submit determines how the story plays out (so instead of feeding all information and looking at the big picture you're selecting information to make the people act the way you want).

However, there are some unrealisms/restrictions/forced guessing to make the story flow faster. In one example, you're not allowed to determine the destination of a bank transfer and are forced to guess and submit.

Instead of submitting facts as individual data points and looking at the big picture, it extrapolates and takes things as broad facts in a wider scope. You can't submit any context (heated argument, hearsay, depiction of others from one perspective).

Anything you submit to Orwell is taken as fact and representative of the person (instead of one data point in their life). Sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information don't really match what you submit (so be sure to look at the tooltip) and are a bit of a stretch and (sometimes intentionally!) out of context.

Worth a look if you like the idea/concept of being the gatekeeper of information in an investigation.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] Gold/yellow data chunks are important ones ('conflicts') that have a big part in determining what happens.
[*] Reactions to events/information are sometimes extreme.
[*] It would be nice to be able to see (or construct) a visual timeline of events. It can get confusing (if only using memory) when thinking about what happened on which day and what events occurred before/after another event.
[*] I didn't like part of the ending. The argument is that [spoiler]they are forced to prosecute based on what you put into Orwell. But it's not like humans are automated; once the human element is introduced in the process they can ignore/deny/hide the order to prosecute and not actually carry it out. And orders to prosecute (I would think) aren't automatically shown to the public.[/spoiler]
[/list]

[h1] ORWELL REVIEW [/h1]


[b] What is Orwell? [/b] 
Orwell is a story-driven puzzle/mystery game in which you, someone outside 'The Nation', take control of Orwell - the latest security system designed to counteract terrorism, etc. Its a game that focuses more on giving you an experience with its story and plot rather than with engaging gameplay. 

[u] STORY [/u] 
Orwell isn't shy in showing its influences from George Orwells '1984' (clearly), and thats a good thing. '1984' is considered by many to be one of the best pieces of literature ever written, and with very good reason - it predicts a horrible shift in society which results in a dystopian state run with an iron fist and constant survelliance and information control on its populace. George Orwell's novel takes place after this dytopian rule has been established for years, so we do not truly understand how it became so all-powerful to begin with, however, Orwell takes a look at what it may be like at the start of this rule, with a brand new system, called ORWELL, being used to solve a terror attack on 'The Nation'. When Orwell wrote '1984' there was no internet, or social media, etc. and this game takes a look at how '1984' would be had those things been considered, and trying to basically update '1984' for a modern audience and make it culturally relevant today is no small feat, and happily, I can say they have done a superb job of capturing, while updating, George Orwell's original vision.  

Overall Story Score = 9/10 (Masterful) 


[u] GAMEPLAY [/u]
Gameplay in Orwell is probably the games weakest point as there's not much actual 'gameplay' involved. For the most part Orwell's gameplay consists of reading text documents, web pages, phonecall logs, emails, etc. and finding relevant text and info and attaching it to certain peoples files. While this may sound completely mundane it is actually quite a refreshing take on detective gameplay and feels like you are genuinely investigating people. Although, personally, towards the climax of the game I found trying to find that one last clue to tie things together quite frustrating and slowed the pace of the game. 

Overall Gameplay Score = 6/10 (Good)


[u] GRAPHICS [/u] 
Orwell uses a rather unique cell-shaded polygon art style, very similar to something you would find in a visual novel, and it compliments the game well. As someone who isnt a huge fan of completely drawn art styles Ifound myself really liking the approach this game took in its art direction. 

Overall Graphics Score = 7/10 (Great) 


[u] SOUND [/u] 
Orwell has a nice relaxing soundtrack for the most part with occasional moments of high intensity. The soundtrack perfectly fits the game and was particularly noticable during certain parts of the game which greatly increased the impact of those moments. Also, the soundtrack doesn't get annoying or repetative at any point which is impressive considering the length of time you are listening to it. Saying all that though, its by no means a memorable soundtrack or anything special. 

Overall Sound Score = 6/10 (Good) 


[u] LASTING APPEAL [/u] 
It took me roughly 4 hours to play through the story once, and I am plannign at some point to play through it once more, but that will probably be the max I play. I personally wouldn't pay full price just purely due to the price-to-playtime ratio but on sale I would definitely pick it up. Overall though the lasting appeal is quite poor due to it being a story driven game all based on a whodunnit payoff, which makes replayability a bit less appealing. There are multiple endings however so if you want to get all of them you may get more out of it than most.

Overall Lasting Appeal Score = 4/10 (Below Average)


[b] OVERALL SCORE = 7/10 - Great [/b]

Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

A truly fantastic game of detective work and morality. 

You absolutely need to be in the right frame of mind to enjoy it(should you play it like it was any generic game, you'll likely end up disappointed. You have to appraoch it in a cerebral manner to get most out of it). The gameplay is very interesting as it evolves cleverly through the game. The storytelling is executed flawlessly both in quality and flow. 

Perhaps the most interesting part of the game is the subtleness. While the main plotline is told in full, should you play through it "correctly", there are plenty of minor details that are never referred to, but can be deduced logically. 

I was extremely pleased with myself when I deduced the truth behind what was going on by halfway of Episode 4 through simply thinking about it and going through loads of old data. Then, in Episode 5 I got to reach the conclusions I had made, although in an entirely different manner. The way I had analyzed the truth was very different from how the game presented it ultimately. However, all the pieces of information were in the game, just hidden in a slightly different way. A blog post made a day after one certain event happened, a few innocent referrals to seemingly mundane things that put together paint a very interesting picture, and so on. I use this as an example of how expertly crafted the whole experience is. Every single detail has been crafted with painstaking detail, and there are many 'untold secrets' that imply a great deal under the surface. Personal drama for characters that's never made explicit, motivations of characters only left as implications from their personal data, and so on. I can't give it enough praise.

Not only is the writing extremely clever, it's also amazingly coordinated and detailed. It's a true masterpiece of game-storytelling. I never would've guessed I'd like it as much as I did, but in the end it reached a very exclusive spot in my hierarchy of games with very few peers.

Still, it's certainly not a game for everyone. 

PS The ethics and moral problems presented in the game are treated in a very careful manner. While there's an underlying biasedness in the game(as is obvious in the title), it's executed in an incredibly skilled way. Not once did I think it was hamfisted or "obvious" or such. Everything made sense and nothing was purely black-and-white. It's quite the feat, since the inspiration for the game, 1984, is a hamfisted load of nonsense that made me roll my eyes with every page on how unrealistic and stupid it was. This game, however, is pure genius.

I haven't [i]cared[/i] this deeply about a game in a LONG time. This invested. This engrossed. Possessing such a strong sense that this game [b]matters[/b]. If videogames are studied as an art form at some point in the future, and their impact (or potential thereof) upon culture measured, this game will be seen as prophetic.

The premise is very simple: you are sitting at Big Brother's keyboard. There's a terrorist attack, and it's up to you to find the guilty party and bring them to justice. But all the while, you are made acutely aware that your actions have very real, often very immediate consequences. You are digging into people's lives—innocent as often as guilty, possibly even more so—and with every datachunk you choose to upload to the main server, the government has yet more information they have no business knowing, much less acting upon. The results of your choices WILL haunt you: there's no way down the rabbit hole that isn't painful, and there's no way back up. In later episodes, the system itself and the history behind its creation comes into question, and it's up to you to decide the fate of a nation.

The characters in the game are very intelligently written. Many have secrets you may or may not uncover. Some prove to be [i]very[/i] different from what you may first expect once you research them—or they research you. Expect your emotions to be challenged. The scenarios are surprisingly believable, and astoundingly branchable; the game starts to feel very unscripted by the end, which is quite possibly the best compliment I can give the entire game.

If it weren't horrendously ironic for me to say this, given the nature of the game, I'd say that Orwell is as [i]literally[/i] required playing as any game can get. I can't recommend it enough.

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

[h1] Orwell Review[/h1]

The story of Orwell takes place in a fictional country where its citizens are being spied on by a government that basically has access to everything. You play an investigator who starts his or her job right as a terrorist bomb goes off, and it becomes your job to solve the mystery of who is to blame.

What Orwell does well really good, is in building up the mystery. As an investigator, you have access to the game's Namesake Orwell which seems to be a computer, or program that like an octopus has its tentacles in everything. This allows you to listen in on phone calls and read emails, all for the purpose of figuring out who is the bad guy.

But what Orwell does even better is blur the line between what is a good guy and what is a bad guy, and the adventure albeit behind the keyboard, leads you to a realization that maybe things are not as they seem.

What I really enjoyed about the game was its art style, and the way the game is able to take something meant to be very flat and paint a beautiful world as you discover more and more evidence.

It's Pros:

[list]
    [*] + The game is beautiful.
    [*] + The mystery is genuine, by that I mean nothing is easy to figure out.
    [*] + The music is enchanting
[/list]

It's Cons:

[list]
    [*]  - The game is dying for voice actors. 
    [*]  - At times, it feels as though you are being lead.
    [*]  - The game is really designed for a single playthrough.
[/list]

Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

My opinion on the ethical problems presented (Spoilers):
[spoiler]Abraham was an idiot for wanting a human element included in Orwell. Humans are biased and flawed creatures,
 so it should have been obvious from the beginning that an investigator could tailor the information that the advisor receives in order to affect their viewpoint. I am honestly at a loss that the directors behind the project could think that adding another human (the evaluator) into the process would improve the project's capabilities.

Another thing which bothered me: by it's nature, Orwell is reactive instead of proactive. While clearly there weren’t any problems in adding people to be investigated, people were only investigated if they were connected with someone who was a suspect. Which by nature meant that potential domestic terrorists who are radicalized simply through hardship in their life are never investigated (Think Nina, but without involvement in Thought).

I think that some kind of AI / massive neural network could do a much better job and might actually work in preventing terrorism by catching threats before they are realized.

[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading

Orwell is a point-and-click game where you are Big Brother, and it's your job to screw people over! Basically, you are tasked with scouring the internet for information about high-risk individuals who could be terrorists. Choices matter and there is a TON of reading, so be prepared!

The game does an excellent job of showing how manipulating small snippets of information can completely change the story to fit your own narrative. The story is well thought out, and the choices you make throughout the story can definitely creep you out. Many times, I found myself asking, "Does the government REALLY need to know this?" It can be startling to realize just how invasive you have to be in this story, and even if it is for the good of the people, it still feels gross.

My biggest complaints:
- There is no manual saving and loading.
- In order to choose chapters (or basically replay a chapter), you have to complete the entire story first. So on the first playthrough, you're really stuck with whatever choices you made.
- The phone calls and chats take FOREVER. Seriously, there should be a way to adjust speed or skip to the end.
- The conflicting information choices sometimes feel a bit shallow or non-sensical, but some outcomes really hinge on these choices.

The key word about this game is atmosphere. I'm a fan of the game's subject: mass surveillance and privacy. If you read '1984' by Georges Orwell and liked it, you'll probably like the ambience of this game.
This small game is all about story telling through text (you need to read a lot). The writing style is really good, modern and easy to understand.
You play the role of an data analyst who will track some "suspicious" people and you upload any data that may be useful to investigators working with you in the game.

Pros:

- The story is interesting and, depending on how you play, it can also have some suspense moments
- The world is believable. The game encourages you to read everything, even bits that are completely optional
- The writing style is great (I played in English)
- I enjoyed the soundtrack. The music is mainly for ambience and works well with the dynamics of the game
- UI: critical point in this kind of game. It is actually intuitive, well designed
- IRL integration: the game has you creating a profile. If you give your real email address, the game will actually send you email requesting your intervention... Perfect for immersion ;-)
- Replayability: this is a game you need to do multiple times to fully experience everything (HOWEVER, I didn't do it and I explain why in the cons below)


Cons:

- The biggest one for me: sometimes, you will want to submit some data you think are relevant, but the game won't let you do that (even though you are a data analyst, the machine decides what you can upload or can't)
- A lot of characters mentioned in the story are useless. I wish their stories and personalities would be more developed to add more complexity to the game and, ultimately, in your decisions. The main folks are very well developed though, for the most part (some are clichés)
- Replayability: once you finish the game, you will want to replay it. However, once knowing where the key choices you will make would really have an impact, I can't bother redoing the whole story just to see other choices
- Lenght: I finished the game in 4 hours. This is really short and I wish it would be longer (for example, 'This is the police' is doing much better on this point)
- DLCs: extending the game lenght by proposing paid DLC suck. Besides, they are not worth the price (currently the same price as the full game)

I recommend this game and I think 10€ (current price) is a good price for it. I'm happy I played it, but I will probably never play it again.

Orwell is a unique game, I don't even know how to classify it. You could say it is a child of point'n'click and 'choose your own adventure' games, wrapped in a UI and gameplay style most conductive to the topic it tackles. This is nicely complemented by an elegant, simplified graphical style that attempts to give a modern flair to everything and the 'metro' UI. The soundtrack does its job perfectly, mostly just playing in the background but taking the reins when a more dramatic situation comes along.

And those aren't that rare; while Orwell starts pretty slow and almost mundane, it makes sure to ramp up the pacing in the later episodes. The web of connections keeps growing, facts become too numerous to recount and the invasiveness of the system keeps on growing. In the midst of all that, all the benefits and dangers of mass surveillance are shown through actual story even instead of just... you know, reciting them here and there. 

This leads to a few glorious moments when it is easy to be drawn in, slap your knee and declare what just hit the fan. And that is a very valuable part of Orwell, one that bought me; it is easy to immerse yourself in the action. Characters are multi-faceted, decisions will have consequences and being the part of an otherwise soul-less system is a chilling, educating experience.

Hats off.

Orwell is a really impressive and thought provoking game. It puts you in the role of an investigator working for the government of The Nation to investigate suspected criminals by looking through their social media and emails, listening in on their phone calls and texts and even looking through their computers.

What I really liked about this game is how you can influence events in your role as investigator. The choice on what information you upload or don't upload can impact on how your handlers decide to react to certain situations or how to handle suspects. It does make you think twice about what actions you take as sometimes those decisions can have serious reprecussions.

I also found the games story quite gripping. Through your investigation you encounter various suspects and even though you never interact with them directly you still learn a lot about them. Their history, personality and whats going on in their life. It does a great job of showing how much of your life can be pieced together online.

Overall I found this game to be a really pleasant surprise and enjoyed it a lot.  If you like a narrative driven game where your choices matter then Orwell is well worth playing.

Got it on sale for $5, played through it in a single sitting that took about 4 hours. Interesting and definitely worth it, maybe even worth a second playthrough if the choices are as flexable as they appear.

In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

This game truly gets your brain going. It requires you to really think and shows how biased you may or may not be. This is about corruption done by both citizens and government.

This game is not some kind of roleplaying game where you get to speak as your character. This is where you are basically a hidden person behind a computer with a very unique program that allows you to spy on people by gathering what they call "data chunks." Your job is to spy and to carefully figure out who is behind the big guns. Choose wisely.

If you like to exercise your mind, this is a game for you. If you like to be nosy or adore crime thriller, this is also the game for you. Orwell really teases your brain and forces you to keep track of your steps as you're made to retrace them again and again.

If you don't like milling through data and tasks that require you be VERY thorough and thoughtful, this game is not for you. You will find it boring. Although a lot of fun, I can easily see how one might find this boring. This is truly an NSA simulator--you're rifling thorugh data, and tons of it. If you're not one to hunker down and read through information, you'll either get stuck or choose a wrong path. The game is linear in its structure...some choices can send you down different paths but the idea stays the same. I've only finished one playthrough but it's clear when you can take things down a different path.As with true research, you can waste plenty of time collecting incessant things or even collect incorrect information. Your selections DO effect the story and have consequences, similar to the ones you might evoke in real life. You cannot change them, even immediately afterwards. This game has a lot of replay potential as each chapter can deviate significantly as you fill in the holes.

There were two instances where the game requires you to input 'useless' or 'false' information in order to progress, which threw me off as most of the game revolves around you putting down as much 'accurate' info as possible.

I truly enjoy how thought provoking Orwell is...I'm not easily emotionally swayed by games, but I legitimately recieved goosebumps during one chapter, where the realizations of what this game implies about government and observation truly sank in....of how surveillance can provide extremes pulled from both the good and the bad.

Have you ever wanted to have a game with incredible immersion, credible characters, amazing world building, that is entertaining as it is thought-provoking?

If yes, then try Orwell. Right NOW! It is “point-and-click”, and it does that. Better than LOTS of AAA titles can do with millions on the budget. Seriously.

While sometimes the writing seems “too much on the face”, and the decisions the game presents to you seem “bad” or “not properly worded”, like having a character saying “you’re killing me” on the “laughing” sense but the game states that it understands as “murder”, these moments are on purpose. They make you realise how wording changes truth, and how perception is flawed. It does that on so many levels, with decisions that don’t even look like decisions. With things that once may make you go “I must do this thing this way”, and on a second playthrough will get you wondering “...should I really have done this thing this way? What else can I change?”.

The way you act as an investigator seems inane and not powerful at first, but as the game progresses, it becomes so obvious how the information you wield has a significant power. It only gets worse/better as the repercussions of your unthoughtful decisions generate large repercussions that you didn’t asked for, but were still direct result of your way of thinking (or not thinking).

If there is an investigation game that should be looked upon as a reference, it’s Orwell.
Really fun, played through it twice already and looking forward to doing so again.

As the title of the game suggests, Big Brother is here. And it’s you. You play as an investigator for The Nation, a country not altogether unlike some of the nations we have now. Your task is to investigate and stop a terrorist plot, and you’ll be doing this by prying into the lives of the citizens of The Nation.

Sounds simple right? Well this is where the game forces you to confront some very difficult questions. How far are you willing to go in order to keep your country safe? Does a post on twitter constitute the same level of seriousness as a mailed threat? Most importantly, should the government be able to spy on its own people for the greater good?

Inspired by the NSA programs exposed by Edward Snowden, Orwell takes the issues of digital privacy and cybersecurity and brings them into your living room. Though it looks and plays like a simple point-and-click adventure game, this game will test you and force you to question your beliefs in ways you may have never considered before.

In a day and age where truth is an increasingly rare commodity, eyes are everywhere, and even the most innocuous statement can be taken out of context, Orwell is a game that forces us to look in the mirror and ask if we’re really comfortable with what we see.

Orwell happens to be less of a game and more of an experience, and an insight into a Watch_Dogs-esque CTOS system which sees everything you do called by name of the title. Instead of making you an activist however, you're working for the government, the hidden dystopia called "The Nation", where the government knows exactly what you're doing and what you're posting online.

You follow the plot of an activist group, people who had set up a protest. Suddenly, a bomb goes off and you at Orwell are tasked with finding out who planted the bomb. The tone will shift many times in Orwell, pressuring you to think hard and make the right decision, as making the wrong decision could impact the case and result in huge impacts.

Orwell overall is a great storytelling game, and will keep you interested for the time it lasts. My only concern with the game is it's pricing. For the time the game lasts for, the price may be too high for some people. Overall though, it's a great game and one which may leave a lasting effect on you and your opinions on government surveillance going too far.

Additionally, if you've ever seen Tom Scott's, [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIuf1V1FhpY&ab_channel=TomScott] "Oversight" [/url], Orwell is a great demo into what that system would look like in action, and exactly why such a system is such an Oversight.

I recommend Orwell on sale if you enjoy intricate stories and are intrigued by the game's premise & plot.  If you're not sure, then I would hesitate buying it outside of a bundle, because it can take as little as 4-5 hours to playthrough once.  It is largely a text-driven story that unfolds as you reveal more information through reading info from various sources ("Reader"), read call/chat/emails as they happen ("Listener"), and get inside some electronic devices ("Insider"). Your Orwell co-worker/advisor is the only one you audibly hear, but it works well. The story unfolds through 5 chronilogical episodes/days, and to me the info you select tends to affect your & Orwell's perception of the story more than it impacts the story itself. There are clear decision points that appear as conflicting data.  UI made data points reasonable to navigate and track.  I was completely engaged in each episode during my playthrough and was satisfied with my progression & ending. Your own impact or involvement in the story can vary.  
What Orwell is NOT: About hacking like Hacknet, video surveilance (there's only one clip at the very beginning), a totally branching story (your choices affect some actions and the ending, but not enough to drastically change each episode), does not have graphics/text options.
Do I plan to buy season 2 (Ignorance is Strength)?: Season 1 was an engaging story even without the "Big Brother" ethical & political overtones.  S1 did it so well, that I don't know that Season 2 would be different enough or that the new Influencer mechanic would add enough for me to enjoy S2 just as much as S1.  This influences how soon I would buy it, although I hope to buy it eventually.

Remember Spycraft: The Great Game? It was this weird mostly live-action-video adventure game that came on 4 cds back in the 90s, and tasked you to roll up an international conspiracy using your wits and a bunch of cool digital tools.

It played off "real" intelligence work, sifting through documents, collecting tidbits of data.

Orwell is a lot like that, but with just the digital shenanigans, played out in an age when the NSA sees you naked and knows who you're gossipping about.

I like it a lot, although it also kinda makes me miss the bits of Spycraft that felt realistic. Like sifting through a document in search of a password or a connection, having to really notice and remember details, and then piecing it all together yourself. 

It worked your brain and engaged you in a way that Orwell doesn't, but Orwell is so well put together that it makes up the difference. It keeps you hooked on the story and the taboo of looking through these peoples lives, sort of tapping into the "Facebook stalker" experience, thinking "God, what a loser" while you're tracing some two-bit musicians path into terrorism.

There are a couple of minor shortcomings though. There's no voice acting on phonecalls, sometimes you find relevant datapoints and you can't use them simply because they don't have "The Outline", and the conflict system can be a bit obtuse, not unlike the Lie/Doubt thing in LA Noire, which is frustrating, but never enough to bring the game down.

So if you want that experience of losing your soul in the service of a faceless controller-state that gives absolutely no fucks about you, then Orwell is about as good as it gets. Happy hunting, you mindless serfs!

A really well executed visual novel style of game even though it doesn't look like one at all. 

It has some parallels to Uplink, the old hacker game, which is really nice, the stuff you "do" in the game is pretty cool, even if you technically don't "do" anything, you just press the buttons that the game tells you to press. 
Which brings me to the point of it having some really weirdly executed "multiple choice" paths, where if you accidentally select (or purposefully just to see what happens) some "wrong" option, the story can get really weird. It's basically a whodunit and your paranoid coworker/boss usually eggs you on to convict literally everyone, but if you try and pick some obviously false choice (I picked it because it seemed like proof that this person is a liar) he all of the sudden goes "ah it's okay, we got solid proof that this person is innocent" even though it's obvious as hell that the person is lying and five seconds later you find solid evidence of this person being guilty, he just goes "oh that's weird, they just said that they're innocent, oh well just a coincidence then, LOL!". 

It doesn't really detract from the game, it has an amazing feel to it and it really creeped me out at some points, because I've always thought if my identity can be traced from my online profiles and sometimes purposefully provide false info just to screw with my imaginary pursuers. This game made me feel that feeling of paranoia again, in a good, analytical way though. 

It's a shame though that the devs didn't make an Uplink-esque sort of game where you have randomized missions and you try and pick up info about random people, but like a couple of those random people are actually your targets, and it would be really nice if we came to that conclusion ourselves, not with a prompt "CLICK HERE" every few seconds. But one can only dream. It's still a good interactive story kinda game though. 

I think the price is a bit too steep for a VERY straightforward game where you literally just follow the prompt and there's very few in the way of different choices or stuff that you do by yourself, you can only come up with the solution, but surprise, it's the only possible solution. Sometimes it's a "find what I need to click to progress" sorta game, but still, the story is kinda neat and fun, definitely worth a grab when it's on sale.

Is this game a masterpiece? The game itself probably not, but the topics that the game raises are certainly worth of discussion:

Does spying on everyone help make our countries a safer place? Or does it just make everyone a potential terrorist and serve the ones that control the surveillance?

Does achieving your personal goals in which you really believe justify killing innocents???

Those are the main questions that you will have to answer for yourself if you play this little (kind of) interactive movie.

[Spoilers included]

I received the game as a gift and played it almost immediately. Interface was nice a little bit confusing at first, but Symes helped me out for the first part. Story turns very dark very quickly. Over time, a feeling of dread overwhelms me as I submit a vital-looking datachunk to be processed by Orwell. What feels real is how the use of hyperbolic sentences and phrases in the media, usually for comedic effect, can inadvertently be twisted into something that can target you as a threat to the government (case in point, Juliet talking about how Cassi 'tortures' her with muffins/cupcakes, and Symes believing 100% that Cassi indeed tortures Juliet). Scary to think how it would be in the real world.

This game has me reeling. As a fan of Orwell, especially 1984, this feels like a dream. I'm sad it wasn't longer, or that it just follows one track. It reminds me of Papers, Please, with the screening and processing and comparing of vital information. So I was kind of expecting literally screening suspicious targets in the whole country. Then again, the Thought arc was very well-thought out. Again, however, I didn't expect it to end so abruptly on the 5th day. Was hoping for more.

That twist during the conference call was great, but too convenient. The least suspected was the mastermind after all. But why? Were they romantically involved? Were there any signs of fanaticism, obsessive behavior? Don't get me wrong, I love how this played into the story. Just wondering if it's all to convenient for the plot so as to completely throw the investigator off.

Few technical issues, such as the dialogue boxes of the advisors (Delacroix/Symes) sometimes slow down the entire game. During chapter 5, while processing the last 4 datachunks before the call, Delacroix says a reminder and my game just bugs to oblivion. I can't see her message bubble, I can't click on anything. Not to change tabs, heck not even to bring down the main menu of the game. Had to quit the game and open again, thankfully it doesn't restart at the beginning of every day if you quit midway through a chapter, else I'd have never finished it.

If you've watched the trailer and read the game description, you'll quickly understand your role in Orwell. You are an investigator, watching over the lives of a handful of citizens known for being anti-government. Your job is to find incriminating evidence on these individuals by reading through their text messages, emails, and pretty much anything digital that you can get your hands on. This premise alone was enough to interest me, and I was more than impressed by the results.

What you might not understand from the trailer is your ability to sympathize with the people you're supposed to be incriminating. There are consequences for every action and inaction. Orwell gave me power and I was immersed. What I wasn't expecting were the many surprises that were in store for me. I won't spoil any of them, but will say they were all worth spending the extra time exploring to discover.

My only faults with the game were points were it felt like I had hit a dead end. Throughout the game, there are icons indicating information you have not discovered to help guide you. However, there are also many pieces of hidden information which have no indicators that lead to achievements and, in some instances, progress the main storyline. With no indicators telling me there was more to be found, I had to watch playthroughs online to try and find what I had missed. Maybe this won't happen to you, but I will advise you to be very thorough. You do not want to accidentally run into any spoilers while attempting to progress through the game.

This was a hell of a game. It’s one of an emerging genre of… ‘interface’ games, I guess. Like Her Story, you are literally your character in the game - what you see on screen is what your character sees, and you interact in the same way. Because of this, the game is incredibly immersive and therefore, at points, really tense!

Let me stop myself before I get too deep in here. In Orwell, you play as, ostensibly, yourself, hired as an ‘investigator’ in this new program called Orwell situated in a different country. In that country, a bomb has just exploded in a plaza, killing two and wounding a dozen or so people. Moments before the bomb went off, a woman was spotted crossing the plaza and getting on a bus. That woman had been arrested months before for assaulting a police officer in that very same plaza during a protest. Could she be connected to the bomb? Your task is to slowly collect information on her, and the people around her. What information you upload to the system cannot be taken back, and you get to choose what the narrative of what happened becomes. You can take an innocuous joke between friends and upload it, taking it out of a friendly context and giving it a sinister cast. You can shift a bias on a person by only uploading the worst of what they said, but not uploading good things about them. In this story, YOU are the faceless watcher, the cog in the wheel, that would be impeding the heroes of a more traditional story.

Holy shit, does it work.

I blasted through the game’s five chapters in one sitting, about four and a half hours on Saturday night. Nobody in this game is 100% good or bad, and there’s a lot of nuance around protesting for the ‘right’ reason in the ‘right’ way that is especially topical for me, right now, as a young woman living in an America I never really thought I’d be living in. This game doesn’t deliver any hard and fast morals at the end, it doesn’t take a definitive stance, and offers three different endings for the player to eventually pick. The game offers up a scenario and leaves it up to you to decide what you think is right… or at least, what you think is the least wrong.

The game isn’t perfect - it wears a little thin when you’re going back and achievement gathering. Like a Telltale game, once you see the constraints of the ‘world’ of the game, the illusion dissipates pretty quickly. There are a lot of real-time sections (text conversations, phone calls) that, while immersive the first time around, made me really wish I had a fast forward button for the fourth or fifth time I sat through the conversation. These are absolutely small gripes, however, and I would strongly urge anyone to pick up this game - especially while it’s still on sale.

Every choice you make matters. Many games and VNs advertise this, but may be a little more lax in terms of letting you make some "wrong" choices yet still get the outcome you want. Achievements can also be obtained or compromised from being able to be obtained depending on the actions you take.

The game was longer than I expected, which was great, and the conclusions you can obtain feel very much like a solid way to wrap up the story. Getting into the whole plot took a little time as it felt kind of slow in the beginning as you learn the basics of what to do and how to do it as well as feeling more interested in the story and characters themselves. However, it picks up quickly and while the very beginning may feel a little bland, it's still enough to keep you interested and wanting to find out more.

The soundtrack worked well with the game. It was more ambiant background music, which I liked as it wasn't distracting so it didn't take away from the gameplay and more serious atmosphere the story creates. The changes from calm to tension and panic were abrupt as was the change in mood of the game, keeping you alert.

You'll find yourself doing a lot of thinking about what information you want to reveal about someone to Orwell and what you think is okay to leave out, especially at the end of the game as everything draws to a close.

I do wish the live conversations you spy on would go a little faster, particularly the chat ones. I understand that sitting on the screen while the other person has the "..." as their text bubble for a few seconds is to make it feel more realistic, but at times I felt some replies could've been a little quicker.

There's replay value both for collecting all the achievements as it's impossible to get them all in one play through, and both to see how the story changes and what conversations you spy on will pop up, as well as of course seeing how differently the lives of the characters are affected.

I got Orwell while it was on sale for a few dollars less than full price, but I would still say it's worth whatever you invest. There's a lot of reading, so be prepared for that. I remember clearly sitting with my dad looking at games to try, and we tried the demo for Orwell... I was blown away, what a brilliant idea for a game.

The story is amazing, the mechanics are intuative and easy to figure out, I got totally swept away by this game, and the message it has.
A good bit of replay value as you aren't able to get all information in just one run, and it pays off to look for it.
10/10 would recommend.

Although it has its flaws (a few times I was frustrated that some data chunks were "contradictory" although they could both be true, or that some information appeared only after I spent a minute agonizing over which similar data chunk is least incorrect), this is a very finely crafted portrait of surveillance and its moral implications. Even as someone pro-privacy and personal freedom, I found myself thinking "This is justifiable since it's for the good and safety of innocents".
Then the ending cutscene I got was about 30s long, yet somehow I'm still recovering.

Now, when I went into Orwell, I was fairly certain of what I would be getting out of my experience. An interesting little narrative set in an Orwellian-universe where you help figure out who perpetrated a terrorist attack. In a way, that's exactly what I got. But, looking back on my time with the game, I'm struck by how utterly wrong I was. Orwell exceeds all expectations and leaves me itching to either give the game another go, or threaten the developers at knife point to let me play Season 2, which the game helpfully reminded me to add to my wishlist before exiting the program.

I'm sure there's some connection that can be made to the game monitoring me in that last sentence, but I'll let it slide because Orwell deserves all the levity I can grant it.

Addressing the actual game instead of gushing all over my laptop and nearby furniture, it plays out as a sort of Point-and-Click adventure game where websites, conversations, and remote connections act as different areas, and datablocks act as items. The real twist is that, once you collect a new piece of information, there is no undo button. Your supervisor can only see what you let him see, and you can't take any information back if you realize you made a bad call or acted too hastily. And the game makes you live with it. After making a particularly blatant error, I fell back into bad habbits and attempted to quit the game and allow myself another go from whatever autosave the game keeps. 

Unfortunately for my inner gaming sins, Orwell knows exactly where you left off, as the exit screen likes to remind you. If you mess up, you've messed up permanently on that file. Wanna redo? Looks like you're starting over.

This knowledge that everything you do will have intentional and unintentional consequences makes this the most tense and nerve wracking narrative experience i've played in quite some time. This is especially apparent in the final act, which I won't be spoiling because everyone needs to experience the game's final twists and turns for themselves.

As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. And, while I love the eavesdropping system, it can be somewhat tiresome to watch a conversation playout when you're dead set into 'Network Super Sleuth' mode and have to wait for dialogue to end before resuming the hunt. 

But all of those are nitpicks. The game is fantastic, and it makes me long for more games with this style of narrative/gameplay interaction. While I won't be playing through until I thoroughly forget some of the game's twists, rest assured I will be delving back into the world of The Party in the future.

I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

This game is a lot of fun! I played the demo first to get a sense of the game, and believe me, the demo is just the beginning!

You play as an investigator who rakes through people's social media. phones, computers and news articles, taking lots of little snippits of information like their names, associates, attitudes about the government and issues, and report them to your higher ups in the government. It's up to you what to include or leave out (though some facts MUST be included to advance the plot). So you can show the social media post that's vaguely threatening toward the government or the one where the person is calling for reason and rejects hasty or violent behavior. How that person is treated under interrogation or at their arrest is up to you. As the name of the game implies, this is an Orwellian kind of nation, where "the greater good" means giving up some liberties in order for security, to the extreme. Choices matter, like informing the authorities where a person is going to be, whether they're armed. After I got one person killed, I started playing really close to the vest, not revealing information unless the story progression required it.

The story: It's interesting! There's a lot going on, never knowing who is behind the terrorist attack you've been called in to investigate. Some of the characters you end up investigating don't play into the story later (which is a waste), but the conflicting stories and attitudes keeps you guessing. There is a mechanic that lets you decide between two conflicting pieces of information, and it really puts doubt into you.

There's a little bit of replay value in that your choices matter, but a lot of those choices just end up with you just not arresting someone, or affecting the ending. There was one opportunity you have to prevent another terrorist attack, and I was really excited to try and parse through all the information but it turned out you never had enough info to begin with and just came down to a 50/50 guess. I guessed wrong, and people died. It doesn't seem fair, because the answer is obvious after you find out what is going on, but the game didn't allow you to investigate the person actually responsible BEFORE the event, so it really is just an uneducated guess. Missed opportunity for gameplay, in my opinion. You should get rewarded for scouring every document, not punished just because you weren't given the information.

Overall, though, Orwell is a fun experience. It raises a lot of highly topical issues about safety vs. security, about big data and surveillance and all that stuff. This isn't a dystopian future far removed from our reality. I can see this happening right here, right now. And that's why you should play this game.

Orwell is a short but engaging story about an investigator (that's you) being given incredible power to peer into the information of anyone you want. This idea does not seem far-fetched at all. In fact, despite its rather in-your-face name, Orwell presents a world that is quite believable. There really is nothing here that is overly dystopian or fantastic. Rather, the world in Orwell is just our own world, with surveillance taken a few notches up.

The game isn't perfect. The interface sure could use some work. I often found myself having to go through the same emails, chats, etc. until I found the link or "data chunk" it wanted. As such, it was a let down on its initial promise, and felt much more pre-determined than I hoped. There are a few choices here and there, but they don't feel like they matter much. In the end, things will go as they go, and there is little reason not to submit every data chunk.

All that said, Orwell is a good game, and well worth the time to play. It's not long - I did it in a single session. Hoping the sequel adds a bit more choice and complexity. But in a world where these type of games tend to go a bit too far in dystopian future, Orwell is very welcome, because it feels much closer to reality.  It clearly has a point to make, but it is generally not heavy-handed. Its most important trait is that it places you in the role of the investigator. You might find the level of access you have to be unnerving. But you feel like you're the good guy. In that way, it's both humanizing to the agents who pore through our data, and showing how no human should have that power.

Pick Orwell up. It'll be a few hours well spent.

TL;DR at the end.
     "Orwell" is like a choose your own adventure mystery novel mated with web browser of sorts. Unlike the trailer for this game, you do not spend any time viewing cctv footage or identifying and tracking people via facial recognition in the manner made familiar by television's "Person of Interest" or the popular "Watchdogs" game series. Its not like that. Its a look at what the internet, our PCs and social networking devices look like from the perspective of an invasive government investigation. It's got some tense moments that are done well but i've seen done better.
      If you have an interest in the themes of civil rights, criminal investigation and/or government corruption in the age of the internet (information age) you might like the game. The graphics are interesting and add to the personality of the game. The music is not memorable in itself, but musical cues when plot twists are revealed in the game are a nice and unexpected  touch. 
     I enjoyed this game because I like a good mystery. I found the storytelling entertaining and the text based electronic surveillance compelling.  The interface, "Orwell" Itself,  was the low point only because it appeared to be a malleable desktop in the trailer and yet you cannot customize or edit the frames of the interface at all. "Orwell" was cumbersome from the start and towards the end of the story you just have pages of auto-bookmarked docs that you scarcely use. 
     
--TL;DR--
Its ten bucks. Its a good story. I'd play it again if it weren't for the interface. Id recommend it to a friend with a disclaimer: "Don't watch the trailer. It's not like that. "

As reflected by the in-game quote, [i]you never really understands a person until you consider things from his point of view ... until you climb into his skin and walk around in it[/i]. You can make a difference for every piece of information you can get. For every piece of information, you can identify each suspects to narrow down informations and potentially prosecute them. But remember, not all information is essential in giving you the solution to the problems existing.

[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.
