I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

A nice and interesting game. You'll dive into the life of some "potential suspects" of a terrorist attack, looking for datachunks in their online beings (sometimes with the conflict between what we are and what we show to the others in social media) and in their devices.

To that, we have to add a nice developing of some of the characters (others are quite maniquean) but leading the story in a good way.


Recomended, with no doubt!

I rever 1984 as one of the greatest books of the 20th century, and in our turbulent days, examining the topic of state-ordered surveillance, it has never lost its edge. While I wouldn't call this game a spiritual successor of the book, it splendidly represents the ideas of Orwell, and even has a few clever references to him sprinkled here and there.

Without spoiling too much of the story, you are a hired investigator examining the online records and phone calls of certain suspicious subjects. What is surprising that in a game about surveillance and suppression, you are given a surprising amount of choice: Whenever conflicting informations emerge, you have to make a choice which one to forward to your superior, and thus influencing their view on the subjects, making them appear as law-abiding citizens or subversive terrorists. This may decide over their life and death, and those of many innocents.

As you close in on the center of a supposed cell of rebellion, you are even presented with a choice concerning your own fate: Will you persevere your original task and rout the suspects, or will you rise against your superiors and the blatant injustice of the system? It all depends on your ability to copy and paste text snippets.

I played through this game on Origin and recently received the game through steam via a Humble Monthly Bundle; so I felt it was time to put my thoughts on the game out there. I'm someone who is very aware of the constant privacy invasions of our internet connected lives, and how we are losing ground constantly. One of my favorite books is 1984 by George Orwell, so the name of this game was the first thing to pique my interest before I knew what it was about. Without any major spoilers, you play as an employee of a Big Brother-like watch system over the people in your country at the beginning of its implementation. You spend the game looking at a computer OS style UI where you scan through documents, web pages, and other online material to profile people for this "all-seeing" system. 
     
     The most interesting thing about this game is how well it presents all the different types of dangers (as well as pros if you look for them) with surveillance systems like the United States NSA stuff that has come out over the past years. It does such a good job at it because you aren't just looking at leaked documents about the system, but you ARE the system. Which means you make mistakes (or not) which leads to incorrect profiles and taking things out of context, which  endangers everyone. 

     Orwell is by far the best way to have someone that doesn't understand why national surveillance is bad for its citizens, truly understand all the intricacies and nuances of such a complex issue. I highly reccomend everyone play through this game. I honestly wish everyone had to play through this game so that misinformation and ignorance surrounding this issue would be minimized and we could all work together for the benefit of society as a whole. Play this game, and get someone else to play it; you won't be disappointed!

With "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" Osmotic Studios and publisher Daedalic Entertainment deliver a narrative surveillance thriller that quietly turns its own core theme into self parody. The player is asked to watch over the privacy of others, while in the background a telemetry chain made of Steam, Unity and Mailchimp wakes up, of which not a single word can be found on the product page.

[h1]What does the product do?[/h1]On first launch the game already talks to Steam, fetches the SDR config for AppID 491950. In parallel Unity reaches out to Google Cloud, generates a persistent userid and ships a full hardware profile. Only after all of this does the player see a brief in game pointer to an external privacy notice.

[h1]Who operates the product?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH (formerly Fellow Traveller)
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH (current publisher)

[h1]Which service providers are involved?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH
Valve Corporation
Unity Technologies
Google, LLC (infrastructure for Unity)
Intuit Mailchimp (owned by Intuit Inc.)
[noparse]Amazon.com, Inc.[/noparse]

[h1]What data is collected?[/h1]
Unique identifiers have been redacted for the review.
[b]Unity Analytics (no visible notice)[/b]
Unity 6000.3.8f1 fires POST requests to the Unity Analytics config and event endpoints. The endpoints resolve to Google Cloud in the United States.
[list][*] Persistent userid and deviceid, sessionid, session_count
[*] appid and build_guid
[*] Full hardware profile: CPU, RAM, VRAM, GPU vendor, driver, D3D12 feature level
[*] OS version, language, mainboard model, machine hostname
[*] Events appStart, appStop, SubsystemInfo, shaderRuntimeInfo
[/list]No OptIn is shown, tracking cannot be turned off inside the game.

[b]Steam Datagram Relay[/b]
The client fetches the Steam SDR configuration for the game and then opens 34 UDP connections to Frankfurt, Stockholm, London, Paris, Vienna, Warsaw, Amsterdam, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Seattle, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Mumbai, Sydney, Johannesburg and Dubai. For a pure single player thriller this fanout provides no benefit.

[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
The in game newsletter sends first name, email and the tag "Orwell" straight to the Mailchimp REST API. The client uses a fixed HTTP Basic Auth credential baked into the build, "user:[redacted]-us14", which is a full Mailchimp API key visible in any network capture. The server response leaks list metadata, sender, statistics and a contact address (Papenstrasse 27, 22089 Hamburg) that differs from the one in the privacy notice. Headers reveal hosting in AWS us east 2.

[h1]GDPR violations in detail[/h1]
[b]Unity Analytics without consent[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)a Transparency: Transmission starts before the user is informed
[*] Art. 6 Lawfulness: No consent, no documented legitimate interest
[*] Art. 7 Consent: No OptIn dialog, the pointer arrives too late
[*] Art. 13 Information obligation: Unity Analytics and Google Cloud are not named
[*] Art. 25 Privacy by Design: Tracking is default, no in game switch
[*] Art. 44ff Third country transfer: US Google Cloud, no SCC notice in game
[/list]
[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)f Integrity: The API key sits in plain text in the game binary
[*] Art. 13: Hosting in the US is not disclosed in game
[*] Art. 25: No server side email validation
[*] Art. 44ff: Third country transfer to the US, no visible safeguard
[/list]
[b]Steam SDR[/b]
Art. 5(1)c Data minimization: 34 worldwide relays for a solo title are excessive.

[h1]Privacy policy and Opt-in/Opt-out[/h1]
The Steam product page does not show or link any privacy policy or EULA. Inside the game a short pointer appears during profile creation, but only after Steam SDR and Unity have already shipped data abroad. The Steam age rating in Germany is "12 and up" while the Osmotic privacy notice itself requires a minimum age of 18. No age verification takes place.

A second oversight: the in game privacy notice is supposed to exist in English and German. In reality the "German" file is a word for word copy of the English text, only the headline reads "Datenschutzerklärung". A German speaking user has no proper localized notice available in game, which under Art. 12 GDPR is a serious flaw.

The notice itself does not name Unity Analytics, does not mention the Google Cloud infrastructure, does not list the Mailchimp pipeline and says nothing about a hardcoded API key inside the client.

[h1]Can this behavior be blocked?[/h1]
Yes, largely. The Unity Analytics endpoints, the Mailchimp REST API and the Steam SDR config request can all be blocked at the network layer without breaking gameplay. "Orwell" is a pure single player title, neither Unity Analytics nor SDR are required for it to run.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" stages a surveillance state and trains the player to quietly oversee the data of strangers, while at the same time keeping a close eye inside its own engine room.

The Steam product page skips any data protection or EULA information, the in game pointer arrives too late and in a language version that is German only by name. Unity Analytics runs without a visible OptIn through Google Cloud in the United States, the newsletter pipeline goes through Mailchimp with an API key baked into the client, and Steam SDR opens 34 UDP connections worldwide for a solo title.

The thematic punch line lands twice here, once in the script and once in the network log.

Additional details, including a full connection overview for blocking access, involved IPv4 addresses, company information and the German version of the review, are available as usual at [url=https://gameindustry.eu]GameIndustry[/url]. If you're interested, join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/penguindome]Penguin Domination[/url] group to stay informed about new reviews on Steam.

It's hard to say that either Orwell's story or its interface is earth-shattering in any way, but put together they create an experience that's enough to keep you always running after what's around the next corner. As on-the-nose as it may be to call your game on state surveillance "Orwell", the narrative inside is more restrained and explores accurate and disturbing tactics used by state spies. You get the sense that the "choice" in the story is often somewhat an illusion, but maybe that's the point. It's a game that empowers you by letting you crawl inside peoples' PCs and phones while teaching you about privacy invasion and only once it's put you through the preset experiences it thinks are necessary does it let you decide what to do about this spy apparatus.

I don't think anything could have prepared me for Orwell.

Playing the role of a law enforcement agent, researching a potential terrorist cell through the social media and communications of its members, the simple browser-styled interface makes it easy to lose yourself in the characters, their interactions and the over-arching story which often hits close-to-home in 2017.

Overall, a really relaxing play and an interesting look at real-life issues surrounding privacy, social media and free speech.

This game was surprisingly effective. I went in expecting some heavy-handed story based purely on the title, but apart from some suspension of disbelief problems I really enjoyed the game. The UI was a masterpiece, the story interesting enough, but it's the characters where Orwell really shines. Each and every one of them felt believable and real, and I, at least, ended up rather moved by some of the characters and their motivations.

What I thought was especially interesting was how they're written to be very open to interpetation and to your preconception. The user-selectable portraits really help in this regard, as they each seem to represent different facets of the cast's personalities. A novel approach to interactive fiction, and I highly recommend it.

If you read 1984, this is exactly what you'd expect: you're big brother. You're going to need to do some soul-searching after this. And you're going to need to play it more than once.

Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. It highlights what in that page you are supposed to save. It tells you when you have collected all of the information from that page and moves on to the next one. The entire game is just looking at these pages, or conversations, and dragging highlighted text or photos to a folder. That's it.
This game doesn't require thinking, not really. I thought the fact that you could choose what text you send over meant you could omit anything you wanted, but then it won't move on to the next series of pages. You have to send it something, and it pretty much all leads to the same outcomes.
It could have been a lot better. If it wasn't so linear, if you were left to search and find things on your own, if you could pick out which people to build a dossier on, anything like that would have made this awesome.

This game worked perfectly for me and to quickly point out the main reasons why people could like or dislike it, here I go:

- Story is quite brief.
- It doesn't bother with advanced visuals and sophisticated soundtrack.
- You will have to read stuff to play it.
- The premises are absolutely nothing new to the world of conspiracy theories.

Now in a little more detail and opinion:

[h1]Brief story[/h1]

The game doesn't take too much time to complete and although in the end it really doesn't matter what you choose (duh) it still might keep you wondering what could go differently. Because it does offer more than one chance to actually affect the progress.

Still, the game might feel like it's taking a while because at some points you may find yourself struggling to find that one crucial piece that's needed to go forward, at others - you will get overwhelmed by the amount of choice. Not that it's bad, but if you're not really patient you might get actually bored.

[h1]No pretence[/h1]

The game really doesn't bother to give you some superb visuals and sounds. But the fact is it doesn't really need those. I don't even know if the voice-over of some parts of the game would be appropriate or not. But "Orwell" does have a distinct style to it which actually brings some of it's own atmosphere along without a claim to be something very special.

What is special though is an attempt to create an intertwined character development (not for you personally, sorry) that can keep you willing to go on and complete the whole story.

[h1]Reading[/h1]

Well, this game is 90% text. Please read it, please read it carefully and not just because the game plot demands it but because every piece of information in this game can be actually useful later on or right now or maybe a couple of minutes before you made that decision you now regret.

[h1]Conspiracy theories[/h1]

This game is called "Orwell" for an obvious reason. It doesn't even need an explanation. Like the setting? Fancy the idea of total government (or other type of) control? Or maybe you're completely against it? Well, in any case, the game gives some food for thought if you haven't yet though about this topic that much or explores those scenarios you might've already seen somewhere, but this time with you behind the wheel... or rather exactly not behind the wheel (duh).


[h1]Overall opinion[/h1]

This is not the best game of all ages, but I believe its creators brought exactly what they've wanted to bring into it. Which means "Orwell" serves its purpose perfectly.

I would recommend it for anyone who likes smart and level entertainment and doesn't mind spending some time exploring the world of text rather than beautifully rendered landscapes.

Simply put, Orwell condenses all of the moral arguments surrounding a surveilance state to a "let's see you do it."

You are responsible for guiding a PRISM-like system in a quest to unravel violent events surrounding a group opposed to the intrusions upon society.  Somewhat true to life, your superiors act on what information you condense down to them - they don't actually read everything (that's 'your job').  You get to eavesdrop, sift through a computer's hard drive, peruse the private accounts of citizens... all in a quest to 'do the right thing.'

The ethical dilemma is appropriate.  There is a very real threat to the game's citizens.  Yet, you can easily pass along information out of its proper context and paint a picture that doesn't exist from within the ocean-spray of people's activity on the internet.  Even very early into the game, you find yourself ignoring far more text than you are reading as the scope of the investigation expands and you find yourself 'scope locked' to the auto-tag system.

There is some replayability, as well.  Events are influenced by what information you pass along, as well as how you react to some real-time scenarios.

This is where it becomes interesting - your superior isn't entirely sure of everything you are seeing.  You can see that someone is planning a hack in real time... and just ... let it happen.  Or, you can see that a person suspects they are being monitored, and pass along tactical information that could be disinformation.  This is partially where the ethical context of the game comes into play, as the events can unfold in many different ways depending upon how you, as an individual, wish them to.  Don't like a person?  Try to land them in jail.  Like a character?  Try to shield them from the investigation ... or guide the investigation to them in order to justify unleashing the full resources of Orwell on their private life.

Perhaps the forest amid all the trees, however, is that the entire conflict of, at least, the first story arc would not exist were it not for the very system used to defend against it.

In all, it's a great exploration of the ethics of our evolving soviety.  Highly recommended for its philosophical exploration, alone.

It's alright, I wrote a pile of text giving my detailed opinions on the game when steam graciously changed pages to warn me of an update and trashed my entire progress... I don't have the patience to write it again so here goes the short version with the important tidbits:

[list]
    [*] Orwell is a Visual Novel that tries to give a new coat of paint to the genre, kinda like Analogue a Hate Story. You read the plot through logs while doing your "job" of uncovering the truth. Props to the originality. Art style and UI is great and unique.
    [*] For a game that clearly takes upon George Orwell's work, it's not thought-provoking enough. It's very one-sided and not well written enough to make you really care. The only really Orwellian characteristic of this game is that the ending will thoroughly let you angry. It's not a bad thing given that the books 1984 and Animal Farm do just that, the real problem is that this alone can't give you a good experience when the ride there wasn't meaningful enough. The political thriller portion of Orwell is very stereotypical.
    [*] The detective portion of the game is great. If the game were focused solely on that with the political drama in the background, it could've been an amazing experience.
    [*] Decisions are very, [i]very[/i] poorly implemented. They don't change anything in the big picture and the branching path is the laziest type possible of a negative-sum game. You'll always see one side losing because the characters always act as stupidly as possible. To give a couple examples without spoiling anything, you have one witness that has an crucial information to prevent a disaster, and you can only get it out by blackmailing and ruining that person's life, keep in mind that by then you [i]know[/i] that person is innocent. The investigator assigned to help you is probably the most inexperienced and innefective cop ever seen when it can not even get a simple non-invasive information of someone who would cooperate if asked and not threatened. You'd argue that maybe this was the main critique of the game, but it was poorly implemented, it wasn't well written enough to make you believe such an absurd situation could ever happen. The same thing happens later when warning of an armed suspect prompts the investigator to give a "shoot ot kill" order when everything you have on the suspect is still circumstantial. Orders like "shoot to kill" are not so lightly given, especially not to law enforcement. [i]Orwell's[/i] premise is that you, clicking away at your computer, have been employed by a dystopian fragment of the future of western Europe ([i]a la Airstrip One[/i]) to prevent tragedies and [i]illegal crimes[/i], and piece together disparate - but (at least in the eyes of The Party) incriminating - evidence. In this sense, the player engages the narrative as something of a moral agent preceding artificial intelligence; selectively incorporating evidence into a portfolio of 'truth.'

If nothing else, know that I felt compelled while playing to consolidate my thoughts -- it's worth a second look. 

[b]Really neat:[/b] artstyle ([i]everything through the eyes of machines[/i]), 
worldbuilding (there's enough 'fluffing' information that it goes beyond the typical restrictiveness of VNs), 
polish (it's really very sleek, when it wants to be anyway), 
thematic presentation (a lot of the dialogue is very cheesy, but I'm consuming it all quite gleefully).

[b]Suboptimal:[/b] logical consistency (you can see clashes between "datachunks" yet-undiscovered...), 
obtuse gameplay (you can't redact erroneously-entered information, or supplement it with additional factoids... except when you can: on day 3, after deliberately avoiding embracing the alibi of one of the suspects, I dragged an absolving statement into their record without much thought and suddenly undermined my previous carefulness. Annoying, and little else.), 
frequently undue brevity (a supposed debate society with little more than waffling, news articles consisting of two paragraphs...).
achievement structure (story-tied and playthrough-exclusive, mandating inefficient replaying if you desire that category of completion)
Really fun game, eagerly waiting for more content from these guys.

Orwell is a surveillance game (I suppose you could call it). However, there is also a machine/program in the game called Orwell that gameplay centers around. 

The program seems to have two functions. The first is a tracking function: if the player provides a website, a chat handle, a phone number, an e-mail address, or even a computer ID (I suppose this is analogous to an IP address), the program will then "track" it. If a phone call comes in on the number, you can listen in. If a blog has an update, Orwell lets you know, etc. Often, you'll get a chat handle, then in the chat you'll find a phone number or e-mail, which you can then track. From all this data you can create profiles of persons of interest, which is the second function of the program. Through data, you can learn who knows who, and how they know each other.

Law Enforcement uses the information collected to locate and arrest those individuals that you've deemed possible suspects in crimes. The game begins with a bomb exploding in a public square. I won't give any more of the story away, because it's quite an interesting ride.

On the surface, this gameplay sounds straightforward, but there are juicy complications. For instance, if someone denounces the government harshly in a fit of rage after paying taxes, do they represent a danger to the government? If Orwell (the program) didn't have a human operator, could it read between the lines? To further increase the stakes, any data uploaded to Orwell is permanent. So I couldn't designate this hypothetical taxpayer as a threat and then clarify later that he didn't "mean" what he said.

Also, if someone was aware of the program, could they provide false meeting places to divert law enforcment? Do your persons of interest know that you know they know about Orwell? 

It's a very well done and thought-provoking game, especially in the age of big data. Not only does it explore some of the limitations of using data collection for crime prevention, but it makes the player realize just how much information about themselves they've made public online.

For instance, Judith Duportail (a writer for the Guardian) requested the data that the dating site Tinder had collected on her. In September 2017, she published an article detailing the experience. Tinder sent her 800 pages of material.

The game really blew away my expectations, I went in expecting a visual novel type story based around surveillance but instead got a gripping investigative mystery with a unique game style that I hope to see more of in future.

Looking forward to this studios next release, you've gained a fan.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

The gameplay is a bit lacking in this game. It pretends that you have a lot of freedom but this is only an illusion.
You play an agent which needs to collect information from all kinds of sources and put it into a system. This system then might or might not draw some conclusions from the found information. The conclusions are sometimes done by your supervisor who might trigger some action. These actions can be totally unintended by you and you might even think they endanger the investigation.

Sometimes there are pieces of information that you really don’t want to put into the system because wrong conclusions might be taken from them, but as the game seems to be linear (I haven’t been able to find a real alternative storyline yet, only small details that are different but not essential), you sometimes need to enter them to continue. Orwell takes sort of a visual novel framework and bends it until it looks something like a mass surveillance simulator. You're a foreign contractor working within a series of ethical safeguards to perform ethical mass surveillance (if such a thing is possible) for another country's government. And it's an interesting time to be an Orwell contractor, because The Nation is in the grips of a terrorist bombing spree. Your actions and possibly even inaction can bend the arc of the story.

Like most visual novels, your actions don't have major impacts on larger direction of the plot, but they change the details along the way and might make you more sympathetic to ending the game in one way or another. It's neat to go back and see how changes affect things and unlock other achievements, but it does get a little tedious since waiting through real-time chat and phone conversations is a lot less exciting the second time around.

Overall, I had a pretty good time, but most people will probably be one-and-done and put up fewer hours accordingly. Weigh that against how much you're willing to spend.

Orwell:

[h1]Positives:[/h1]

+ The story in this game is great. It covers a goverment project called Orwell, which collects information about citizens. You play as an investigator who is responsible for finding out who committed a series of terrorist attacks. By analysing social media, using phone wire taps and computer hacking, you will pry into the lives of suspects to find the true perpetrator. This is actually really fun and smart. The game does an excellent job of highlighting the problems with mass surveillance too and the plot twists will keep you guessing.

[h1]Negatives:[/h1]

- Because of the low budget, several areas of the game are not as good as they could have been. For example, when "listening" to phone calls via wire-tapping you aren't actually listening to anything - you're reading text which represents each character talking. There's no voice acting in this game at all. A real shame. Furthermore, the digital art sucks. The developers opted for really bizarre suspect photographs in newspapers or social media, which have lots of jagged lines on them. It's hard to explain, but the essence is the pictures in the game look really unrealistic and frankly, silly.

- Most of the game is reading and interacting with the investigator tools given to you. Occasionally you'll receives messages from your government adviser on data chunks you've assembled and their significance. There's literally nothing else in this game. At times it can be a little boring and you just wish there was more creativity, like video footage of potential suspects to review. Something a little different.

- The game is pretty short at about 10 hours. Some limited replayability though.

Overall Score: 7/10

This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

Got this game in Humble Monthy not really knowing all that much about what it was or anything like that, but jesus christ this was one of the most fun and unique gaming experiences I've had in a long time.

You're basically an investigator who has access to certain tools to sift through people's lives and search their phones/computers, monitor their conversations, and search for information on various websites about them. Your goal is to find out who committed a series of terrorist attacks and put them behind bars.

Now the gameplay here is obviously not the strong point. The only gameplay is really clicking and dragging blobs of test to the left every now and again. That being said though, it's not like you're mindlessly dragging things over and not doing/thinking about anything. You have to be cognizant of what you're uploading because you could screw up some stuff and let bad more things happen. Your choices matter, and there are multiple endings and possible situations that can happen in the game based on your choices.

The only thing I can say about the game is that I wish it offered more freedom or at least more thought to what you had to upload. There were instances in the game where it was just a linear click and drag whatever you see because there was nothing else to search. Then you get to episode 5 and you have to be careful of what you upload because you have a limited number of datachunks that you can actually upload before the story starts to unfold. I found that last episode much more interesting because of the fact that it forced you to actually read the documents and search through everything instead of basically just being able to drag the first thing you see. That and there were people by the end of the story that we didn't even get to investigate just because they were viewed as unimportant. Even with them not necessarily being related to the case, I would have liked to investigate those other people as well. This could actually bring more gameplay and they could easily relate some of those people to the suspects and have them tie in when them somehow.

Overall, if you like a game with an intriguing story to follow with serious attention to detail, then you will most likely enjoy this game. I usually don't like games with a deep story, but this game has such a deep and interesting plot that I have to recommend it. I'll definitely be picking up the 2nd one whenever it comes out.

I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

An investigation game with an intriguing premises, [i]Orwell[/i] comes together as a unique experience that keeps you gripped with its narrative, despite fairly limited mechanics. Putting the player in the role of an investigator working with an information-processing system known as Orwell (referencing George Orwell's [i]1984[/i]), the game tasks you to search out information from a fictional set of websites (and later, live conversations and data on individual target personal devices) to investigate the aftermath of a bombing, to determine those responsible and various subsequent events.

The game's core concepts and the way in which the plot develops clearly link to recent contemporary developments, with surveillance becoming increasingly prevalent in many developed countries, and by the end of the game you're very much prompted to take the time to develop your thoughts on the merits of the 'real life' use of surveillance. In-game, this link to modern society serves to heighten the player's engagement with the game's mechanics and plot. Alongside this, there's a clean interface that minimises the friction in the information-gathering mechanics, well-judged use of music to emphasise key developments, and the ability to influence the outcome of certain poignant key events.

Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

Orwell is a game where you step into the shoes of an "Investigator"; an individual specially chosen outside of the dystopian-like nation simply titled "The Nation" to interact with a big-brother type software that allows you to track and keep tabs on every single person in The Nation. You take control of yourself, your name, your info, you. You've been specially chosen for reasons unknown to yourself or anyone else, per the exception of a secretive few, to be hired at Orwell. Your new "Adviser", Symes, is going to show you the ropes of international and domestic espionage, only this time, you aren't taking down super villians or having a martini "shaken, not stirred" as per the classic spy movie or game, Orwell instead hits close to home....a little too close.

Orwell is a Story Rich, Dystopian, "Choices Matter" Indie game made by Osmotic Studios where you "Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terror attacks. Information from the internet, personal communications and private files are all accessible to you. But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences.". When Osmotic says that choices matter, they really do. You feel as if you're truly in this dystopian world, helping, or harming, The Nation's citizens. You get to look through countless web pages, trace and listen to countless phone calls, emails, text message and otherwise, even hack into citizen's computers or mobile phones to gain access to information stored on there, such as browsing history, photos, files, and even deleted files. 

For an example (spoiler free); You will be investigating certain citizens, and obviously need to find certain clues about them, their age, phone number, email address, face id, street info, parents, siblings, workplace, links to them from other sources, and you can even go as far as finding medical info from The Nation's hospitals. 

Now let's say I have a citizen I'm investigating, I can start with their relative name, go from there to their social media pages, find out their DOB, address, friends, maybe even mobile number. let's say I need to (or want to) take it further, I begin to suspect they're somehow a threat to The Nation. I can do a little research, Get in contact with friends, trace their calls and emails,  find out information that was never meant to be seen by hacking their computer by getting their PSI address or their IP address, or find ways into their workplace, or even goof off and research their background, what their favourite colour is, or who they're in a relationship with.

Orwell does an amazing job at immersing the investigator (you) into dystopian earth, into The Nation and it's surrounding countries, the citizens who inhabit them and even smaller things like a simple webpage for a local university or a humanitarian organization. Once I started the game, I honestly did not have high expectations nor did I think it was going to be something i was going to enjoy, since it just didn't look or seem like the type of game or genre that i liked, but once i started investigating and learning more about this country, it's citizens and the lore about this world I simply couldn't put it down. I played all the way through, read tons of webpages, information, emails and texts.

That being said, the game is roughly 3-4 hours long, maybe shorter if you (somehow) speedrun it, but if you really want to get immersed into this game world then it can take a lot longer.

[i] And that's not neccesarily a bad thing. [/i]

This is one of a only video game worlds and lore that I genuinly became interested in and invested in as time went on, it truly made me feel like I was impacting the citizens and world around me, mainly because I actually was.

One of the reasons this game resonated with me so much (and one of the reasons I am recommending it) is because in reality, this is not very dystopian. Things like this very well happen in real life and seem so real it's almost disturbing. The amount of dialogue in this game is astonishing, from everything to simple text messages to elaborate corporate emails, everything seems completely geniune, and feels that way too.

Orwell is a masterpeice at storytelling and really making the player truly become immersed and feel like there are consequences. Season 2 of Orwell is coming out sometime soon, and I WILL DEFINETLY be purchasing this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes immersive game worlds, spy type games, choice matter games, or just mind-f*ck type games. Absolute great game. 10/10

Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

story-telling: best part of the game. it's all told through reading articles, websites, medical records, phone calls, private emails. this game got me feeling equal parts paranoid (about my own online data) and guilty (about how obedient i was in being an oppressive surveillance tool). it just kinda... slowly built up. there were twists and turns galore!

actual story: draws pretty heavily on the 1984 book in terms of central themes, but i feel like it definitely updates it to the present. some parts were pretty hokey and implausible, but eh. but some parts were actually kinda scary and real. idk, there are fears i have when i go about the internet and this game left quite an impression on those fears.

gameplay: it's actually pretty simple yet also kinda inventive. you feed an advisor "datachunks" that help their investigation. they can talk to you, but you can't talk to them. it makes you feel like an alienated observer almost, except you're definitely not because you're basically trying to crush opposition to the government. reminded me of the miller obedience studies a lot, idk. In Orwell, you are the human filter on a state-run mass-surveillance tool called Orwell, hunting the perpetrators of a series of terror attacks. It plays a lot more like a piece of interactive fiction than a game - I've deliberately chosen "interactive fiction" over "choose your own adventure" as I'm not sure there are too many alternate routes to take. That shouldn't be taken as criticism, either - Orwell is really engaging, if a little slow at times.

[b]The good[/b]
[list]
[*]Story - The story is good and is told well as you sort through web pages, phone/text/email conversations and sift through your targets' computers and mobile devices.
[*]Duration - Orwell doesn't outstay it's welcome - it's pretty much the right length. There were a couple of points where I had the feeling things were about to start dragging, but then something happened and picked the pace up again.
[/list]

[b]The bad[/b]
[list]
[*]The tagging process - You have to drag and drop datachunks to the appropriate targets. This makes sense, but Orwell tells you who they'll be tagged to. As your number of targets increases, switching to the right one feels a bit pointless. If the system will only allow the datachunk to be tagged to that target and you’re telling me who it has to be tagged to, just tag it to them - don't make me switch around!
[/list]

This helps Snowden's case as much as John Oliver d*ck pic report. You start with digging through public information, and then quickly slip into the private data of people with the slightest connection to the target. Because, hey, your handler told you that a judge gave you a warrant, right?

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

Orwell is really good. For some reason I had the impression that the gameplay would involve procedurally generated scenarios, in which I'd have to "keep an eye on people" or for all you normal folk "stalk and invade the privacy of civilians". Instead Orwell focuses on a few seemingly connected terrorist attacks and street violence, therein you're tasked with finding the connection between the people involved with said crimes. You can indict people by using uninformed and speculative information. You could alternatively not give away incriminating evidence, which can have immediate and notable impact on the story. 

The driving force behind Orwell (and of course, George Orwell's 1984) is how information can be used and misused, on both a small and large scale. There's a heap of references to 1984 by the way, mostly names and terminology as to be expected. Considering this is Osmotic Studios' first release, I'm very impressed with the quality and depth to Orwell's story. The character interactions can sometimes be a bit unnatural but it's a very minor complaint. The user interface is very clean and simple to use. The plot is quite engrossing and there are a couple questions I was really intrigued to know the answer to. There's also a decent amount of non-pertinent information - either to mislead you down a rabbit hole or merely to let people explore some of the finer, less necessary details of the characters in the story. Either way I tried to read most of it, and found the vast majority of the writing to be solid and interesting. Even some of the joke articles are absurd and enjoyable to read. Also, the music is generally very quiet & subtle, only picking up when a big reveal happens. Was simple, but a very nice touch.

All in all, I think Orwell is a great, unique story presented very well. The gameplay elements help to keep it engaging and involved too. Easy recommendation.

I'm honestly surprised by how deep of an experience Orwell was. 

I felt that I had a pretty strong take on the game I thought I was about to play going into it, and for the most part I did. I thought I would be combing through fake social media and what not looking for clues to help unlock whatever comes next. I figured this would be a slightly different take on "A Normal Lost Phone." 

What I didn't expect at all was a pretty deep story and somewhat relatable characters. It's pretty impressive that this story was able to be told without feeling stiff or crammed down your throat. There were people I hated and those I felt sorry for. No matter what decision I made, it always felt like the wrong one. I felt like a part of the problem which was very much by design. The writers deserve a ton of credit for the impact of Orwell. 

Orwell, as a game, I could best liken to a visual novel. There aren't any real puzzles or keys to unlocking what comes next. For the most part this is just grabbing info and putting it into the right folder to progress the story, which the game makes it impossible to screw up. There is a great deal of decision making which I have to guess can greatly alter the story. It's hard to say without subsequent play-throughs, but I was very satisfied with how my one and only play went. The only thing I'd love to see is the ability to replay a day, especially the last since I feel like there are a lot branching story opportunities that you will miss in a single play. 

Overall this made me feel shady AF and I loved every minute. Can't wait to see what they do with the sequel. RECOMMEND!
