Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

BACKGROUND

Got the game in the October Humble Monthly.

I'm not sure if I've played something like this before. The closest I can think of is Papers Please, but that feels like a slight stretch. 



TOTAL TIME PLAYING

Just over 3 hours. That was enough for me to personally beat the game. the average time on HLTB is 4 hours. 

SPECS FOR PLAY THROUGH 

- AMD FX 8350 @ 4.0 GHz
- GTX 1080
- 8 Gb DDR3 RAM @ 668 MHz
- 7200 RPM HDD
- LG Ultrawide

PERFORMANCE

The graphic style isn't demanding (that isn't to say it's a "bad" looking game). I was able to maintain full 60 FPS the entire time, and I'd be surprised if any modern day machine cannot do the same. 

PROS

+Amazing story. I played through this in two sittings and all I could think about in between the two sessions was going back and playing the rest. 
+ As soon as you start to feel overwhelmed with the massive influx in characters, the game ends. This could be viewed as a con, but I don't think a game like this would benefit from character-over-load. 
+ As I mentioned earlier, the graphics are pretty interesting. Everything has a flat look to it. Really interesting. 

CONS

 - Orwell does a lot right. Unfortunately, I feel like it held my hand far too much. Instead of looking through a wide range of documents, the game was constantly pushing me into specific documents. This would be super hard to work around, but towards the end the choices and clues became very obvious and the game lost it's "detective" feel it built up so well in the first half. 
- As far as I could tell, you can't get anything wrong. Sure some of the "conflicting evidence" could be misdiagnosed, but 
from my play-through adding useless information just got a sarcastic response from your boss. No real consequences. 
CONCLUSION

Alright. So I really liked the game. It was great and a pretty phenomenal gaming experience. At this time I am going to recommend it if found on sale around $5. It's far too short to be worth $10. 

I'm really hoping a sequel or an entire new story comes out. With that new game I really want the choices to be less linear. Hold my hand less, let me mess things up, and let things pivot around my mistakes.

I would recommend this game, but not to everyone. If you enjoy dystopian settings and stories, this game gives you a unique perspective in that this time you are Big Brother's informant. You spy on civilians and you decide what information to pass along.

Getting a handle on the controls is pretty straightforward and easy. It makes you have to decide what kind of person you want to be: one who follows orders and sticks to the rules, one who picks and chooses what rules they want to follow, or one that defies orders and stands for their own beliefs.

My biggest complaint is that the story felt somewhat short. It is designed to feel like the events are happening in "real time" as you play, but I feel like there was a lot of background that could have been brought forward and utilized to extend the story a bit. Overall, though, the story as it stands is still pretty intriguing.

If you're an achievement hunter, they are all easy enough to get in a few playthroughs. One playthrough took me I think around 5-6 hours, and that was taking my time deciding what I wanted to do.

Thought provoking, compelling and very relevent to our modern world.

Basically the book 1984 as a wonderful made game. A wonderful visual novel with some decisions especially towards the end. As a german, with both Nazi, Stasi past and the current Netzdg, one starts thinking which social network is really necessary.

Here's the situation: you have been selected by The Nation (a fictitious country) to test drive this super-secret surveliance program called Orwell. You have the power to snoop up lives of the citizens, be nosy on everything, and read, listen, and access the very personal lives of the people, just for the sake of security. You do trust yourself their data will be in your good hands, but how will you prove your intention?

Orwell depicts that very feeling of handling all the data from the citizens by reading everything on the (fictitious) internet, ranging from news articles, blog posts, to private messages and transcribed phone calls. You are supposed to look for information regarding to crime only, but would you? What information will you extract? Who do you think this person is, by looking behind the screen of Orwell only?

Speaking of reading contents, I can assure you those contents are meticulously written, since the game is based on reading them. They did not just throw in words to make them look like it, but they feel so real as if in real lives. News articles, blog posts, social media posts, even chatlogs look so real. Even typos on chatlogs look so real. I am a nosy person myself, so snooping around the lives of people by reading these "real" stuffs feels like scratching an itch away.

That being said, this game is not that perfect. You should get ready to read everything in order to enjoy the game. If you love reading everything on the internet, especially in English, this game is definitely for you. If not, you will find yourself in the hell full of words and nothing else. You won't see many graphics or anything other than Orwell's clean interface. Every event unveils through the interface only, as if you're sitting in front of your PC (which you are) watching something happening out there through words.

Also, there are some nasty bugs when trying to replay the game for achievements, and I hope the devs will fix them. Please don't let this great game sunk down by nasty bugs!

Orwell begins as a simple story about an investigator following up on a crime, but deviates into a darker story asking the player if what is for the greater good truly is ethical.

There are a few choices that will change the story significantly, and these choices will create different endings, allowing you to play through the story a few times as different investigators before the game truly "ends" so you can get the whole story.

The only con, a large one in my opinion, is that the game babies you and holds your hand. All answers are highlighted to you. Large red (!) signs appear when there is a pertinent piece of information in that story. NON-STORY SPOILER: [spoiler]At the later end of the game, you are limited on how much information you can process, meaning there is literally no skill or real cognitive function required to do your detective work.[/spoiler] For a game that has the feeling of a detective thriller, you are practically on rails to what is already being laid out for you.

Overall, this is a masterpiece of a novel, it emulates the fearmongering that comes from modern technologies, and has the potential to give you goosebumps from the twists and turns you, the lone investigator finds on the trail. While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

Orwell, in a not-so-subtle nod to George Orwell's criticism of totalitarianism (*CoughCommunismCough*) 1984. I've actually read 1984. It's not bad. On a scale of 1-10? Probably a 7. Amusing, but not the best. Slightly better than average.

Anyway, the gameplay of Orwell is unconventional and reminds me greatly of Papers, Please. Which is another game I should write a review on and I do recommend it. In it you scan documents for information and upload this information into a mega-database which contains details on everyone under investigation (at this time). Presumably, Orwell would be expanded to cover all citizens. In the name of peace, surely! Everyone can trust the government to know every detail about them to make sure that they're entirely safe! 

Light Spoiler Warning: Orwell is a narrative, a visual novel of sorts. I'm going to do my best to avoid spoilers.

Throughout the course of Orwell you follow the individuals of an organization called 'Thought' named after some German poem. Thought is an alleged terrorist organization. Your job is to follow the members of this organization to prevent terrorist activity. The first person you investigate is a woman with blue hair and problem glasses because of course she is. Which now presents us with our question. What scale of authoritarianism would be acceptable in the name of protecting people? As the game progresses, it gets to the point where almost the slightest connection to someone (perhaps eating lunch or seeing a movie together) is grounds for investigation. Authoritarianism seems to have a very tough job reigning itself in from being conventionally oppressive. 

You know, I could not help but giggle with glee as I listened to phone calls of people and other people got blamed for things that I did. It was glorious! And it kept happening! I felt no guilt at all for doing my job. Perhaps that's the point of the game. Thinking.jpg

The art style is... quirky. Not bad. Just quirky. The music is pretty okay too. My (small) gripe (I guess) is how long I had to wait for responses when it came to monitoring calls and SMS. I get that it's supposed to be realistic, that's the point. Not really a point against the game, I just felt that it was sometimes a little long. 

Overall, excellent game. Quite a nice length for the price ($10 at the time of posting). Of course, cheaper is always better. I think my first playthrough had a run of about 4 hours and there are multiple endings (all of which, I did not explore). It's a thumbs up from me.

Orwell had me on the edge of my proverbial seat more than once. I played the game from start to (one) end in one sitting. I observed myself become careless, abusing my power as the investigator. I made mistakes, and I felt shame because the game made me care about the characters. I made right choices and figured out secrets, and I felt excitement and pride because the game did not make it easy. 
Sure, some passages were a bit linear and less eventful, just like in a book or a movie. But there are many things to learn and discover, and everything is so perfectly arranged, down to the advertisements on the in-game websites you read. Everything has an explanation, there are virtually no plotholes (at least none that I noticed). Ultimately, I felt like I had real power and my decisions mattered. 
While Orwell is obviously a very story-driven game, the art was also quite appealing to me.

How should we EVALUATE Orwell?

Is it an anti-fascist salute to the famous novel, a revelation toward our digitalized lifestyle, or just simple satire to the authority?

This ultra-realism game is based on actual events that happened in the passed decade. The player acts as an investigator to wiretap multiple POIs in order to investigate and prevent bloodshed. And there is the old question of ethics. You know what this typical pop-cultured question is, and please don't spit that 3 line of words from our beloved author because this game is going to completely obliterate that old-fasioned image of mass-surveillance of yours. 

Because in this game, just like how emergency works in reality, freedom is at stake, and so does lives, integrity , security, and pretty much everything that make the nation stands together instead of falling apart are hanging in the balance. Things were not and will never be that simple. 

Also in the same game, you will make your best decisions based on what you believe in reality. You can be the detective, the judge, or the executioner, but unforturnately you shall never be the big brother, because he's not here and he never existed; because behind the monitor, every investigator and their superior is just common, living and breathing people that has little attitute toward his or her world, like those they observe. Thus mass-surveillance will never be mass-mind controll. So RIP Orwell, prism,electroscreen greatfirewall, KIMorputin.net or anything that attempts to turn security tool into A.I. bigbrother. Your service will be remembered. 

But why do instrument of oppression such as these still exists? This game will give you, your own, answer.

I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

Orwell is a gripping techno-thriller about the consequences of mass surveillance.

In the game, you take on the role of an "Investigator" and soon find yourself tasked with using the mass surveillance system "Orwell" to uncover the perpetrators behind a terrorist attack. However, things soon become a lot more complicated as you creep through the private lives of seemingly innocent citizens, trawling through their social media accounts, phone calls and even private files in an effort to uncover evidence.

From a gameplay perspective, Orwell is very much what I would call an "interactive story". You'll be doing a lot of reading, but the writing is excellent and the feeling of doing detective work will keep you hooked. This is very much the game equivalent of a page-turner.

I don't want to spoil the story, so suffice to say that I found it highly engaging and I was interested all the way through to the end. Not only that, but there are several places in the game where your decisions weigh unusually heavily and will affect the outcome of the story. Finally, the game gives an eerie look into a not-so distant future where we are under the watchful eye of a mass surveillance system. In this day and age of interconnectedness, the plot of Orwell is disturbingly believable.

During my time with Orwell I experienced a few technical issues, including slowdowns and glitches that required ALT+F4:ing out of the game and restarting it. These disruptions did detract a bit from the overall impression of the game, but not much.

All in all, I highly recommend Orwell. If you enjoyed "Papers, Please" I'm sure you will enjoy Orwell.

The second task is technically simple, but morally and ethically difficult -- what you choose to share about a particular target decides their fate -- and it's here that [i]Orwell[/i] shines.

There was a terrorist attack and you, the independent investigator with no bias, need to feed the Orwell system with bits and pieces of information you find on possible suspects and connected people. Digging through public information, going on their social networks and blogs and digging deep, wiretapping calls and reading chats. With the idea being that there a specific data pieces that can objectively help the investigation.

Of course, bits and pieces, torn out of context, are not necessarily simple to use "objectively" and everything can be spun and shaped in very biased directions. Which is shown in, surprisingly, mild and creeping way, for which I can praise the developers. While it doesn't touch upon more extreme examples of both governmental and public misuse of available data, which, I felt, should've been also covered, it gets the point across, not just about more in your face Orwellian government controlled things, but about a lot of things suffering from the same misuse and shaping of out of context materials - sensationalism in media, information wars between and within countries, internet heated discussions gone wrong and just about the faults of human arguments in general. There's a next "season" of the game announced already so there's good potential they can cover more important topics in the future, but I just hope they keep the tightly story-driven element at the core as it really is what keeps it interesting.

And that is fun. For me, the end of the game was largely focused on that. It was too fun to spy on people, too fun to find clues and watch them squirm. It was so fun, in fact, that the peoples whose lives you hurt mean nothing, and not only in a video game way. In the end, they were just images and phrases in a social media site out of thousands, and they all had the same issues and favourite colours and likes and dislikes. The breach of privacy that we feel stems only if we are not the ones making the breaches, and if you think about it, we all do it in a way. Stalking is exactly that. It is the power to follow someone on a social media without them knowing.

I wanted to gather my thoughts a little bit more to write something more focused but I'm not sure I will be able to.

TLDR: This is a game about control and power. It makes you experience it and think about it. It's short but fun in it's own way.

If you like to read, there's a chance you'll like [i]Orwell[/i], even though it's flawed. If you're wanting an advanced narrative with many branching subplots, however, this probably won't be your cup of tea. 

Still, I like [i]Orwell[/i] overall and recommend it. I'm looking forward to season two. There's potential here. I'm just not sure Osmotic have reached it yet. 

In the case of this "season," the story is too small—not in terms of length, but in terms of complexity. There seem to be at least two possible endings, but, no matter the ending you get, [i]Orwell[/i] mostly forces you to be a particular kind of security agent. It does this by requiring you log certain content on suspects to move forward—even, sometimes, if you don't want to log that content. This was mildly annoying, but I also recognize that greater narrative control usually leads to smoother narratives.

So, what really bothered me was Osmotic botched their message. When playing, you're conscious the developers want you to see the dangers of mass surveillance, but the story ironically shows you its possible value. 

By carefully tracking suspects in the game, you don't just follow tragedies; you can prevent them, or at least make sure they only befall guilty parties. This is because you can't really track anyone who isn't believed to be a few degrees separated from a suspected criminal group. There's very little in the way of stereotyping or racial profiling, though a "supervisor" in the game will jump to conclusions on occasion. 

If this was how mass surveillance worked, people wouldn't be nearly as concerned about it. Pretty sure that's not the message Osmotic was going for.

First things first, and quite briefly because there isn’t much to say about the graphics of the game. It is based on a user interface that you interact with, whilst it does emulate the use of an actual browser and its contents, it is very clean and takes the realistic nature away from it with its low poly style photos. This was a nice feature as I could focus more on what the story was offering than what the characters looked like and if the modeling of said characters worked with the rest of the interface. The only time there was animation was in the first cut scene where you were introduced to the game, however, this could be either 2D or 3D with flat colours and a low poly style to keep in with the theme. The only thing I was somewhat disappointed with was the fact that there was very little camera work, the game revolves around being monitored everywhere and it is constantly referenced to that cameras are a big thing, yet we do not experience this even though it was shown that they were capable of doing this. It did not, however, subtract from the story that there weren’t any cameras, it just would have been a pretty cool feature.

The graphics made it easy to navigate around the game, making the mechanics for the game very simple as you just had to click and drag certain pieces of information into a data bank, it was simple and easy to get to grips with, it just meant reading and doing a lot of problem solving. That, however, was the allure of the game, filling in the pieces and finding out just what was going on. Due to the dragging of information, you could affect the outcome of the game depending on what pieces of information you decided to let through, this was the coolest feature, I love multiple endings.

Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

I purchased this, I think, during last year's Christmas sale and it got sidelined to my backlog of games, but recently played through it.  Afterwards, I regret not having played this earlier as it was an incredible experience and has great writing that kept me off guard throughout the game and made me feel responsible for a lot of what was going on in the game.   

At one point in time, while focusing on the reading and tagging data as I went, I accidentally uploaded a tidbit of a joke from two friends where one was joking that she was being tortured by her friend to get her to go somewhere, and this, without the joking context, was added to a person's bio to incriminate them as a violent and dangerous person.   This, as well as other situations in the game - that were intended rather than my mistake - really drove the point home that the developers were trying to make about the ethics, or lack thereof, of a Big Brother police state.

I'd describe this as a very niche game, if you're into point and click, this is perfect for you. The entire game is presented to you through the Orwell system, where you look into people's data and collect things on them. The game rarely leaves you at a point where you don't know what to do, as important information is highlighted for you, whether this is insane hand holding or reasonable is up to you, I think it's a good thing to have some guidance as to do next.

The story revolves around a government called simply "The Nation" controlled by "The Party(real creative, devs.)" creating a system known as "ORWELL" after a bombing. Along with that, The Party had recently passed something known as "The Freedom Bill" which gives police the right to arrest, interrogate, and detain simply on suspicion of a crime. Basically, The Nation is an authortarian government, it is obviously not as authortarian as Oceania is in 1984, as there is still plenty of resistance to the government, but it is pretty powerful. 

You play as an investigator recently hired by The Nation, living outside of it's borders, tasked to collect information on individuals suspected of the bombing to bring them to justice. Throughout the game, there are several points where you can either choose to be defiant of ORWELL and enter embellished or false information into the system, or choose the blunt option. There are five episodes, and they are all very gripping, the game can actually be reletively creepy at some points as well.

There are multiple endings, as well, which is cool. I won't spoil anything though.

Overall, I would certainly recommend the game, as it was very well organized, in depth, and able to capture the attention from any style of player, rule-breaker, rule-follower, and everyone in between.

Orwell depicts a utopian setting where individual privacy is constantly violated thanks to public cyber-surveillance in form of an eponymous system, and justified through an ambiguous "Safety Bill" that sanctions "investigative methods" in order to "protect the freedom of The Nation's citizens."
Just how the knowledge about the individual characters' degree of criminal implication does retroactively affect your choices at the different decisive moments of the game makes the second playthrough the more interesting one: if at first you might have been well-intentioned enough to help the surveillance masterminds spying on your fellow citizens, you might be more inclined to rather try sabotaging the system on second thought, at the risk of course, to become yourself a "target" at the end.
That the game makes you second-guessing your "datachunk" choices is its biggest achievement, but that your superiors leave it entirely to you to distinguish between important and irrelevant information is Orwell's patent weakness since too ingenuous fiction-wise, though you need to contribute pertinent data in order to make the story progress, what can also be taxing at times. 
It might not exactly be a totalitarian setting but it still is shocking to realize that the monitoring of both telephone and Internet communications is something also the citizens of democratic countries are faced with, and the game does a good job in showing the use of this type of top-down espionage. Worse still, it is yourself who is doing that closed-circuit observation with Orwell as your user interface: only once a person becomes a “target” related data can be extracted from the different documents and uploaded to Orwell's servers. 
Orwell's approach might be simplified but it likely is how tracking persons in the Cyber Era does work, even when using a variety of sites, personas, and devices. This way the very conflict between public security issues and private data protection is well laid out, albeit far less preoccupying than in the famous Orwellian dystopia. 
The five different episodes can be replayed separately for the different endings, though repeatedly going through the same dialogues quickly loses its interest during replay. Given the subject's topical interest there might be stuff enough for a sequel, unless your investigations did lead to Orwell being canceled altogether...

I picked up Orwell because I love games that put you in the role of a detective. I previously played "Her Story" and hoped this would be along similar lines (albeit with a different interface), going through data and gaining clues in order to pinpoint suspects.

After playing the game, I was left fairly satisfied and definitely had an enjoyable experience with it, though I did find it lacking in some areas.

The good:
I loved the unique art style, and the whole set up of how you feel like you're logging on to this system as a detective. The music is great and very suitable for the game too, changing in tone dramatically when something in the game changes. I love the overall Orwell theme and how it makes you think about things like government surveillance and whether it's a good or a bad thing. The characters were fairly interesting to me (though mostly unlikable, but that may have been the idea). I enjoyed the way the game is structured and how gathering certain bits of data about a person unlocks more data such as relevant URLs or documents.  I found it intriguing and I wanted to keep on playing after each chapter (there are five chapters in total).

The bad:
The game is pretty short, lasting about five hours, however I do feel like the price point is good for the experience you get. 
I felt like the mechanics of investigation had some excellent ideas but that they could have gone further with it. The game always highlighted where new information was available, and although I suppose that did stop you sifting through all the old documents you had, I kinda wanted to have to do that sifting - as a detective might. It felt a bit too hand-holding as to showing you where to look next, and sometimes that just made it feel like I was just following a path of "look at the new informatiion", "drag it to the person's profile", "look at the new bit of information"... and so on. I think maybe if it wasn't always so obvious which information to go back to, it would have been more fun to find it yourself.

I think in general, I just wanted more of the game, it was definitely a good start, but I would love to see more chapters, or a new story. And maybe an option to not have the right bits of data or documents highlighted, so you had to figure some more stuff out yourself. I think then I would have felt like a more clever detective! 

But all in all, I enjoyed the way the story wrapped up, and a lot of the ideas and mechanics, such as deciding between conflicting information, deciding what to submit and what to ignore to determine what light you put somebody in.. and I enjoyed the end of the game too. 

I think it's a 7/10 for me, an all-round good experience, but lacking in some areas that could have made it more fun/satisfying.

I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

Orwell is one of the most interesting games I've played in a while; it's well thought out, the game experience is smooth and natural and the core elements are solid. It's arguably not a game for everyone but it's a fantastic achievement, that should be beyond doubt.

So who is it for? I guess that's the core question for an indie, niche production such as this so let's get right to it: Orwell is for the player looking for a contemplative, narrative-driven challenge that you can play on your own time. If you like unravelling a mystery carefully, if you like narrative driven games or if you really like surveying people, then this is definitely for you. Who's it not for? It's not for players looking for explosions, fast-paced action or who don't like to read. You read in this game, quite a lot. It's not like reading a novel but expect reading.

In Orwell, you take on the role of an analyst who's trying to unravel a terrorist plot using the governments newest super-surveillance tool, Orwell. The system highlights 'datachunks' in POIs internet activity, chat activity, phone activity, anything really, and it's your job to decide what information is pertinent and what isn't. You build files on suspects while you slowly expand the network of POIs and what you choose to include is what decides the 'system's' attitude towards groups and individuals. Of course, the question soon beckons; should you be doing any of this?

As the story moves forward, the player is confronted with many choices and they have real consequences for the story, not merely symbolic ones. Furthermore, while the system highlights important information, some decisions can only be made accurately through the players own memory and deductions from text pieces that at the time perhaps seemed inconsequential. It's a game that rewards the player for keeping up and thinking for themselves.

Review:

Orwell is a love letter to Orwellian fiction. It is a plot filled with mystery and intrigue that evolves fast enough so you will never think about getting bored. I especially enjoyed how the game doesn’t paint the organization you work for as inherently bad/evil. Flawed, but in a way that makes it real, not malicious. This gives each individual person the chance to come to their own conclusions about this potential future.

There are a few issues with this game such as certain data chunks having potentially vague outcomes (much like a Bioware dialog wheel). Also the slow writing in personal messages, while realistic, did get a bit tiresome where you can read the text 3 times faster than they can type. And sadly you cannot walk away, wait for the convo to finish, and then come back, as certain data chunks are time sensitive (I learned this lesson the hard way). All those issues are trivial however and I did not feel that they ever interfere with my ability to play and enjoy the game; a minor annoyance. The ending however, did rub me the wrong way. 

Without spoiling anything, I will just say that the ending is multiple choice depending on how you act. Initially I enjoyed this reveal, yet ended up accidentally choosing an ending I did not want, after not being bale to figure out how to select the one that would make the most sense with my character/play style. Then once I realized what I had done I tried to go back, however once you beat the game that save file is forever stuck at the epilogue after the choice. This requires you to complete an additional play through.

With all that said I would definitively recommend this game!

Summary: A pretty good game that makes you think about how people see things from different perspectives. From the Government's point of view: you're doing a good thing. From the citizen's point of view: invasive and controlling. As you play this game you will constantly think about this as you go through your work. As far as I'm aware, there are 3 endings to the game, and make for roughly 3-5 hours playthrough depending on how quickly you work through it.

Positives: 
-A game that makes you think. If you're like me and you try and solve the game before it's over, it will have you guessing yourself over and over, because the ending is not quite who you suspect. (Even if you do guess correctly - it's not likely through the means that you're thinking.)
-The style of the game is very pretty and modern, with the futuristic features being clean and eye catching. Personally, I loved the layout and setting of the game.
- Time IS important! Like in real life, if you find critical information that might affect something in your life and don't immediately act to stop it, you may face consequences. (I learned the hard way when I Alt + Tabbed out of the game for a minute.)

Negatives:
-Not many, honestly. The story was great and consistent and always had you going back to double-check your infirmation. (Great thing imo, but I guess people can see this as tedious.)
- There are occassionally blips where it says there is more possible information for you to look at, but there isn't.
- It's too short in my opinion. You only really play 'one' story, and I feel like you should be able to play a couple more than that, and the ending you get should influence it too.

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's [i]1984[/i] will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.

[i]Orwell[/i] is an episodic thriller involving the vulnerabilities of social media and easy access to critical digital information. You play as an employee of an NSA-like private government cyber-security agency called "Orwell", of course, named after George Orwell, and peep into your suspects' lives as you dig around for information that could tell if they are involved in anything that could put the lives of innocents in peril. The game is completely story-oriented, and at times, even choice-driven. 

[h1]Story:[/h1]

It's a thriller that follows the episode template like the [i]Telltale Games[/i], played as if you're a guy who's logged into his computer. Everything you do, see, or read is like as if you're logged into a computer. The story has a few interesting characters to read about, to peep into their lives and see just how much information you can dig up on them, and see how connected they are altogether. At times, you'll come across plot twists, and other kinds of ways the story could put you off with how you applied your actions by considering what you just saw right then first-hand, i.e., there may be more than meets the eye here. As the story progresses, the story gets deeper and darker, and your decisions will have to be considered more carefully. Sometimes, even the terms or choices given to you are there just to put you off. 

To me, I felt it drained down a bit when the whole plot unfolded, but it was pretty good overall. I haven't played the game extensively yet to see how many endings I could get, but there are indeed multiple endings. I don't dislike the endings that happen to you based on your choices. But the part of the story that you cannot change - the [b]huge[/b] plot twist - well, I didn't like it much. 

But more importantly, this game shows us just how exposed we are to everyone, and just how oblivious people are these days about this fact. It's pretty sci-fi, but who's to know that this could be our reality in a few years, give or take? We're slowly stumbling our way to a more surveilled future in which, you could say, we are going to live in an almost-communist digital world, where every singly word we type in the webs is taken for granted, and smeared on us as if we have anything troublesome to show for it. Hell, we go "Sorry, NSA" at times. So, in a way, we're just enjoying a false form of freedom. I could go into detail with how this is both good and bad, but this is only a game review, so... moving on. 

[h1]Visuals:[/h1]

The game looks like the people in it gave their own photos, and then they just used a heavily modified version of that Prisma app to convert it all to make it look like as it is. It's not bad. But, it kinda takes away the realism of it. I dunno if I could say it sits well with the tone of the game. I don't think it does. But, it's visually appealing. 

[h1]Mechanics & Gameplay:[/h1]

There's very little to no mechanics. Having the whole investigative thing in the game, it surely  calls for implementing the use of the keyboard. The devs could've considered adding search terms and stuff, but sadly, this mechanic wasn't added to the game, and that, too, takes away the realism from the game. Something like, if you can't find something in the game that you're looking for, that's related to a certain character, search the appropriate term up, and find it (like [i]Her Story[/i]). That's what would make it more engaging, because there's no knowing what you could possibly find. Clicking and dragging can get stale. Hopefully, if they make a follow-up to [i]Orwell[/i], they could implement this.

In the sense of gameplay, it's pretty interesting. As you play, you come across multiple choices to make. You're basically making choices constantly. When you have an info that you have the choice of either using it or not, you will probably think of the following:

"Do I drag this information to the profile?"
"[i]Should[/i] I drag this information to the profile?"
"How does this information have an effect?"
"Is this info even worth putting into the files?"

A simple statement that has to do something with the character - you will think it about in a much deeper manner. Because when you do enter something, it gets reflected on the reports, and that could have a cause-and-effect thing going on. The "choices matter" tag on this game is appropriate. And that's the whole point of the game. You, as an investigator, must see to it that everything you do in this works out perfectly in the end, for the people in Orwell, as well as the public.

[h1]Music:[/h1]

The music fits well with the theme of the game, it's sci-fi-y, it gives off the mysterious vibe, and if you see a plot twist, the music suddenly changes to a very tense, "oh damn" type of tone. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

If all you do in a game is walk, then you call it a "walking simulator". This game is that. All you mostly do is click and drag stuff. Which makes it a "clicking simulator". But, it's appropriate, because you can't really do much with a computer other than click and drag and type, can you? 

Funny (lol, not) jokes aside, the premise of the game is solid, and how they elaborate on it, with you as the very thing that gets to use what's given to you against those [b]like[/b] us. Just imagine if this happened ([b][i]*cough*ishappening*cough*[/i][/b]) in real life. The primary focus of the game was definitely the story, and the story only. The replayability of the game relies on the achievements, and the multiple endings present in the game (for most, even trading cards).

I recommend this game to story lovers, I don't recommend this game to those who get bored of simple mechanics, and I recommend you get this game during the sales. I enjoyed the story a lot, but, I wanted more to do than just clicking and dragging. There's a [i]f-i-i-i-ne[/i] grey area between those two, and I'm right smack in the middle of it. But, being a game that focuses entirely on the story, and the kind of message it's trying to interpret to us, I give it a thumbs up.

Orwell is a fitting name for this game; the inspiration from 1984 is extremely prominent, but the plotline will still feel fresh to anyone who's a fan of George Orwell's iconic novella. Imagine 1984 from O'Brien's point of view, with the technology we have in today's society, and that's Orwell.

Let me begin by saying that the thing that sets this game apart from others is its unique gameplay. It's incredibly immersive; you could easily really be an investigator with this fictional government, spying on a terrorist organization and accessing all their personal files. Through the "Orwell" interface, you can click between relevant websites that contain information on those you are investigating; phone, chat, and email correspondance (both archived and happening currently) of your suspects; and PC and phone desktops that contain files, photos, and contacts vital to your mission. Anyone who's fond of "Facebook stalking" to see how much information they can gain just by browsing the web will be 
thrilled with this game.

The story progresses by uploading "data chunks," snippets of relative information found through your resources, to the Orwell server, where it is analyzed by your advisor. While you have access to all the information in front of you, the advisor only has access to that which you upload, meaning that the information you give will have a vital impact on the story; contradictory information can be found all over the place. As such, this isn't just a scavenger hunt where you look for information relating to your mission, this is a game of judgment where your gut feeling and deductive skills will impact the outcome of the game. 

There is no voice acting, no action sequences, no cutscenes; only emails. texts, and phone calls you read through to see what's happening in the world of the game. This lack of animation makes it all the more impressive when you're left on the edge of your seat at the end of an episode and must immediately move to the next to find out what happens. The story is extremely well-told.

The story has an interesting message to give to its players. While we all read 1984 and sympathized with Winston as he was persecuted and brainwashed by a totalitarian government that claims that privacy is only an obstacle in the way of public safety, the game challenges this by putting the player in the shoes of an agent of the equivalent Ministry of Love. As you spy your way through these suspected terrorists' files, emails, and personal pages, one can begin to think that, with good intentions, an agency like this could stop attacks before they happen and save lives. It's a valid question in our current social climate, and is posed elegantly through Orwell's gameplay and story.

To give you an idea of how long the game is, the game has 5 "episodes" to it, and I finished the game in a total of 4.5 hours. However, I will be going back to replay it; as I want to see what happens in the game if I make different choices and upload different data chunks. The game definitely has a replay factor that will increase the amount of time played.

All in all, if you're a fan of dystopian/reverse utopian stories, games with unique interfaces, branching storylines that you have control over, and games you can crank out in a day but definitely will want to replay, I'd recommend Orwell to you.

Orwell is a great gem of a game which involves you taking on the role of an 'investigator', hired to snoop on people and submit information you deem important to the security of the ficitonal country known as 'The Nation'. You are given tasks via a handler who is part of the Orwell system and progresses the story as you pass on details. It's not heavy on politics as such but rather is a 'real time' system and more about understanding people.

Its visual style combines blocky/colourful art with the smoothness of an OS which only has one use. You follow leads and drag info onto appropriate files and whatever you choose to submit will further the story. 

This first run took me 4.6 hours but I think there's more to it than how I played. I chose the hard working straight laced investigator who didn't care about personal issues and basically had no qualms putting innocent people behind bars. I get the impression you can play it differently but perhaps only to a certain extent.

I have to get the cons out of the way: 

- In game the 'relationship viewer' (a part of your display) is rather clunky and you can only clumsily navigate it as your list of suspects grow. I think being able to control movement via arrows oer WASD instead of the mouse would help here. Heck even zooming out!

-Conversations appear to lag and so you can see a reply before the previous message is loaded.

- Finding a 'hot tip' or key piece of information prompts your handler to talk to you (text only, there is no audio, which is a shame) and grey out the text you're reading, forcing you to skip or skim their advice. You very often snoop on phone calls or chat conversations and so this is annoying. Thankfully time is not important in this game but it's still immersion breaking.

What I enjoyed was detaching yourself and being something close to a spy but in reality, you're breaking down the walls of cyber security and seeing how easy it is to investigate something for more or less no reason at all. It questions your conscience constantly and that kind of information can be interesting to process.

I really enjoyed this game, despite being so short, for it's immersive role playing aspects and the questions it raises about our technological future. It so wonderfully sucks you in and weaves a story with characters the are finely tuned. So much intrigue and many times you will consider a decision before acting on it. Thats some damn fine game making.

Lots of reading, so bear that in mind.

Definitely deserves some DLC or a big upgrade including voice work.

[h1] Orwell [/h1] is a very interesting game to say the least. While gameplay wise you just have to pull and drag some text into a box, the story is captivating as well as how you influence it.

[b] Gameplay [/b]: So Orwell is a game where you embody Big Brother or more like a part of it, an essential yet very subjective part. You goal will be to choose and extract informations on people from their websites, social medias and other public informations but also the data inside their cellphone, personal computer, private phone calls and message, crossing the border of privacy. You interfere with the story by choosing what information are revelante or not, making you think about which information you want to upload or not to Orwell (the Big Brother server). Futhermore choosing to upload one information can make others being not uploadable because it has some conflict with it (2 piece of information can say opposite thing, it's up to you to choose which one is legit or not). this will makes you even more careful about it, and that's good because even if I just had to pull and drag some text, I really got tense during some phase of the game. Felt very immersive

[b] Art [/b] : The art for the pictures is a tad special, but I liked it a lot. The interface is well done and very comfortable to browse. 

[b] Musics and sounds [/b] : The music really got me in this game, I first expected not bad but plane music for this game but it's really not the case. I think that the music is a big factor of why I got this tense (in a good way) in that not so tense pull and drag gameplay. When something bad happens (or will happen) I felt like I had to do things faster even if this game never had timer or whatsoever like it and that you have all your time.

[b] Story [/b] : The characters that you will dig in their privacy are fairly good, they all have interesting personality and felt really human. Story wise it's a little predictable but, well you ARE the big brother so you had every pieces to know what will happen but what I want to focus on is how you influense the story. In the gameplay part I said that what you want to focus on is wheter a piece of information is revelant or not, but that's not quite true if you don't want to be controlled by big brother, you are a small part of it but an essential one, and indirectly you are the one who control the police and the media in this game, so instead of contribute to big brother you can do the opposite, to give you some ideas. (This game have multiple endings and variations depending of which pieces of information you upload or not)

[b] Summary [/b] :

Pros : 
- The story and mostly how you influence it
- The music
- Fairly good characters 

Cons :
- Maybe a tad short even with the multiple endings but it is a wonderful game so I can't really blame it

Orwell is the tale of an idealistic german teacher and privacy crusader, who once thought that Privacy and Security could go hand on hand, linked and managed by the use of a Glorified Ethics Manual.

Like all nice things, of course that was doomed to fail. Not an oversight, a bug, or any kind of mistake on the system. It was humanity itself that doomed the man's dream to fail...or succed. 

In Orwell, you are that "humanity", a virtual avatar of yourself, selected by the Goverment of "The Nation" to operate this impressive machine, and act as judge and jury (but not executioner, mind you), all in the name of Security and Stability. A game where choices matter, and even the most petty things you decide to inform (or ignore) have consequences to people out there, decides their fate, their lives. I have to say that at first I couldn't grasp this concept. My first play was very pro-Goverment, and by the end of it, I felt good: I improved the Nation, I helped people. 

But if you are going to play, play more than once. Try to change your choices, ignore things and highlight others. With repetition, the characters started growing on me. People I saw as assholes at first were suddenly adquiring new traits I never saw or thought before. And with repetition, I saw how Orwell was fucking the lifes of these people, I saw the tragedy of these little self-contained stories. 

+Interesting plot
+Simple and clean visuals add to the overall theme of the game
+It's good to play a Big Brother Simulator

-Some...concepts about how Orwell works in Ep.5 are a bit silly. "Abe's" plan doesn't make much sense, while there are plenty of reasons for following Initiate's plan, or even for following Delacroix's orders. 

Score: 8/10. Would play again.

Orwell is excellent- it treats a serious ethical issue with the maturity and magnatude it deserves while still delivering an enjoyable and compelling experience. This is a narrative driven experience with an overall linear story but one in which choices do matter- the information you choose to provide can save lives, but it can also cause harm and even death to innocent people. The story does fall into heavy cliches at times, but it also manages to deliver meaningful moments.

If you don't like reading and visual novel style stories this is not for you- most of the game involves combing through conversations and webpages looking for pieces of information that the game helpfully highlights. The main story is also quite linear- you proceed through the main story datachunks in a fairly strict order, but you do have some control over the events of the main story based on what side information you provide, as well as the opportunity to open up diffrent side stories affecting the lives of the different characters. It's fairly short, though it's clearly intended to be played several times, approaching various problems differently each time. 

I did encounter a couple of bugs, but nothing game breaking- at one point a vital datachunk didn't get marked properly and in another the game glitched out during a dialogue and got stuck, but restarts fixed the issue each time.

Overall, an excellent game and highly recommended.

If you have read 1984, if you are interested in where cyber security is headed, if you want a great, immersive story, you should get this game. It is quite linear but there are significant choices you must make (that you won't necessarily know the outcome of) which will stay with you for the rest of the game. You truly feel like you are apart of the system in this game and it is extremely powerful. Please get this game for a deep experience and to support these great developers.

More of an immersive novel than a game, Orwell begins as a smart and thoroughly engaging experience that accurately captures the dilemma of state surveillance: The violation of privacy is bad and comes with risk, but there are still real threats that motivated the imposition of surveillance in the first place. Within this context, the events of Orwell are situated within "The Nation" - a hypothetical highly developed country saddled with all of the assets and burdens of the U.S., France, the U.K. or any similar nation. Osmotic deserves praise here - they tightly and intelligently create a nuanced setting without overburdening the player.

But the success doesn't last.

As the game progresses, Orwell begins to exhibit a grasping take on modern security that feels naive. The moderated presentation that offered a balanced dialectic fades, and the political messaging of the developers becomes increasingly heavy handed and blunt. None of this occurs in a way that is surprising or unique within the context of the public surveillance debate, it is only disappointing that they couldn't have done better.

In terms of technical game mechanics, while Orwell's gameplay is a slick, engrossing and well-crafted experience - the buyer should not expect any replay value outside of a 3-5 hour playthrough.

Leaving a negative review feels somewhat harsh, although within the context of a 91% positive title, it feels appropriate for balance. It is by no means a bad game - only one that fell frustratingly short of its potential.

This turned out to be a far more captivating game than I anticipated. The concept is definitely interesting right from the get-go, you as an investigator in control of a highly-sophisticated surveillance framework, invading privacies left and right. I'll confess and point out right now though, that there are no NSFW stuff to spy on... Which.. Well. [strike]Might be a downer.[/strike]

BUT NEVERTHELESS.

Great game; thought provoking. I thought myself jaded by this genre, to be honest - what with the lengthy texts and the amount of reading to be done. However, the game mechanics was interesting enough to keep me engaged. I began to feel like I needed to continue just to see what would happen next. The best part about this is definitely the multiple branching paths.

It's nice to feel like your decisions actually make a difference this time. Due to the nature of how the surveillance framework operates, you have to be aware of what you flag and upload, as it might determine how your target is perceived. Of course, how they are perceived translates into how they are treated, resulting in radically different outcomes depending on how you decide to treat them. Would you thus be the empathetic guardian angel, the impartial deliverer of justice or the callous manipulator?

Oooh, [b]lovin' it[/b]. Also loved that many of the names of Achievements were references to George Orwell's 1984. Small little aside, sure, but hey, I'm a sucker.

Musically, there're really only like, three tracks. One plays over more or less the entirety of the game, the other's a rather appropriate ominous musical cue... and the last's a punk rock song. Yep. Not much to comment on, not their biggest selling point, that's for certain.

What is their biggest selling point, and one I want to emphasize here: the story.

This is where it gets very subjective, so read this with a gigantic pinch of salt - your mileage may vary.

Also, mild spoilers (no plot information, just overall themes)

[spoiler]To me, the story was especially relevant because I read George Orwell's 1984 before prior to playing this game (it was the reason why I bought the game, admittedly). Not only that, it also showcases how this might be in our modern world today... Making it, to me, in some ways, an updated version of 1984. The story conveys the impact of such surveillance tools, particularly on privacy, and highlights how... removed it can be from the most important element (to me) in any given situation: CONTEXT.

Whether or not this can be reflected in our reality remains debatable - after all, the framework described is sophisticated enough to transcribe voice conversations (going by how YouTube's auto-captions work... I'll say we're not quite there yet). But I think this is a highly relevant game for our time. It might also be even more pertinent today what with the way we readily provide information online (be it voluntary or not).[/spoiler]

All in all, I feel safe to recommend this game at full price. I had incentive to replay it, coming up to a good length of play-time that I feel justifies the price (more so since I bought it at the Summer Sale). If not the full price, then a discount - always the smarter choice as a consumer.

Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. In this it's again similar to Papers, Please because the endings are either "Stay loyal to the government," "betray the government," or "do something else."

The problem is that none of these endings really... 'satisfy'.

With Papers, Please, all the endings were satisfying. If you stayed loyal to the government, you were congratulated for being a loyal citizen. You were able to keep your job. You were assured your life would continue and it would be good for your character. This is a very satisfying ending.

If you betrayed the government, you were also congratulated for doing so. You were given a vision of a new, better society you were helping to build and that you had genuinely done the right thing in helping the revolution. This is *also* a very satisfying ending. They both manage to be positive, even when the player does the exact opposite things. Perhaps it's not entirely rational, but a player who goes either path will enjoy their ending.

In Orwell though... none of the endings feel completely positive.

If you stay loyal to the government, if you prove the surveillance can work and bring down the terrorists and get the "ultra-loyal" ending, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth because you still don't feel like justice was done.

If you completely disobey the government, that doesn't feel right either. It doesn't feel like the people in opposing the government are right, or even doing things out of 'necessity'.

When I complete a video game, I want to feel some accomplishment. I'm fine with middling 'you did some bad things and good things, so you get a middling ending where both bad and good things happen,' but if I really put the time and effort to try to do everything 100% right by people, I want to feel congratulated with a positive feel-good "You did a good thing" ending. I want the game to acknowledge I tried. In that case, I didn't feel like there was enough celebration, so to speak. There's no 'ultra-happy ending'. Not necessarily a non-confrontational ending where no one is hurt, but at least one in which the guilty are punished and the innocent are spared.

The options that are presented for you to choose for your 'ending' are valid choices that I liked, but I think it could've used just a little bit more development to make it feel like a 'reward'. That is my only criticism, but even then, I replayed it through to see all the different variations, so it's not a game-ruiner by any means.

Again, it's recommended if you like story-oriented games with unique gameplay ideas.

No game is perfect, of course, but Orwell holds a special place in my heart. It's an interesting and unique take on Orwellian dystopias, and incorporates surveillance technology that is kind of already a thing. Fans of the cyberpunk genre can also definitely see similarities in Orwell.

The biggest problem is that the game relates itself with 1984. It creates expectations which the game does not meet. George Orwell described a sovereignty whose aim is to maintain its power. Surveillance is only a means for the ends. In 1984, war is a tool to maintain power. Who cares about a little bomb and civilian casualties? In such a world, you don't catch terrorists but political enemies (then called them terrorists in news report). 

Half way through the game when I was going after real bomb terrorists, I thought I am in the prologue and wondering why the tutorial took so long. Also, because of 1984 I expected the "twist". Turn out there is none. And the game finished. It is quite disappointing. These wrong expectations have made my gaming experience weird.  I think I would vote for "yes" if it does not relates itself with 1984.

ps. The government in the game is really decent and ideal. It arrest and prosecute according to evidence.

[h1]Orwell is, overall, a doubleplusgood game[/h1]

To begin with when I first looked at this game I was vaguely concerned - this was a game based on George Orwell's 1984, and could anything live up to the theme of that novel without butchering it? To put things bluntly, Orwell avoids all butchering and is a fantastic game. 

The plotline is incredibly immersive and your work as the role of big brother is fascinating, and I feel as if the game also has a significant relevence to modern day society. The concept of surveillance and over-surveillance is a theme often debated in our society and this game plays upon that perfectly. 

The artwork and soundtrack for Orwell have a structured theme that make the game seem almost robotic, which makes the setting of using the Orwell system so much more immersive.

I would definitely reccommend this to any fan of George Orwell's works, or even just to someone who likes playing the part of the investigator - albeit as an investigator in a controlling society.
