So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

I played this game through once, and am surprised to read so many positive reviews, especially about the witing and characterisation which was weak, cliched and overall, spoilt my sense of immersion. 


I felt railroaded by this game- especially by your "advisor" who is constantly interrupting with inane nonsense. I rarely felt as though my choices seemed to matter. More so at the end, but by then I'd already resigned myself to the fact that this was an experience, not a game. 


The story itself was fine, and I like the general idea and premise of the game- putting you in the role of the investigator, making decisions which would cause the lives or deaths of the people you were investigating in, what must be seen as, a morally dubious way. 

The problem is, I never really did feel as though I was investigating, because for at least the first two days the game completely spoon feeds you, and feels as though nothing you do matters- the course of the story is inevitable. I don't mind being railroaded, but the game should at least have the illusion of choice. Every "data chunk" you upload causes something else to beep, leading you to the next. There is very little true decision making till the last day. 

Another problem is the extremely weak cast of characters who are all based on familiar and unimaginative stereotypes: the rebellious rich girl, the arrogant rockboy agintant, the foriegn professor with a mysterious past. The stereotypes might have been passable if it were not for the atociously written dialogue, which felt more like a high school drama conducted entiely by people with sub-par IQs. I found myself disliking all the characters and being irritated by the dialogue which so clearly served an agenda to ilucidate parts of the plot, instead of giving any sense of them being real people with real motivations. 

I also found the constant interruptions, the slow type speed of the conversations to be obnoxiously aggravating. The "assistant" rarely says anything of actual worth, and when taking data chunks in mid-conversation I really wish I could have switched him off, or the developers had limited his appearence. I also found the way that all new or unread data pinged up and highlighted in red meant that I almost never needed to think. I am sure that you could complete this game in a foriegn language just by clicking where the game told you, without understanding a single word of what's written. 

Now, having said all of this, I bought the game on sale and it's cheap. 5 hours of play time for £3.50- I guess there is a limit to what you can expect a studio to produce for that sort of budget. I'm pleased I didn't pay £7 for it though. 


Overall I think it's a poor handling of a great concept, and thus a wasted opportunity.

[h1]Highly recommended for fans of point-and-click detective games, with fast reflexes where needed.[/h1]

[b]The good[/b]
[list]
[*] Well crafted, detailed story. A strong grasp of the English language and a cup of some soothing drink of your choice is recommended to appreciate the breadth of the written text found within.
[*] Choices truly matter, what you do may have long-lasting consequences. [spoiler]Tread carefully, lest you YOURSELF end up hung out to dry for your insubordination.[/spoiler]
[*] Thematic design has been executed properly, with the visual elements and soundscape fitting the ambience.
[*] Game encourages you to think about it in scope of Orwell's 1984. Consider Orwell as a possible future scenario.. and ask yourself, is it a desirable one?
[/list]
[b]The bad[/b]
[list]
[*] The story is fairly short, and [spoiler]the most meaningful actions are concentrated on the end of the storyline, meaning they are fast discovered with the replay functionality[/spoiler].
[*] The game is not always entirely precise on what things are still unread; one may have to look several times until one finds the information Orwell indicates you still have not found. This may slow gameplay unnecessarily, as that missing clue may unlock the next steps in the storyline.
[*] Actions are often not revisable even in the face of new information; while this may be necessary for technical reasons, it is still an issue (although a fairly minor one). 
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

I regret not playing this earlier, as once you get in the story, it is amazingly captivating - you will want to know more as more and more elements unfold in front of your eyes. Ambience in this game is brilliant, as punctuated by the variety of events that occur while you progress onward in the story.

[b]If you have the spare money for it, go for it.[/b]

A word of warning: [spoiler]you are not outside of the system. No-one is.[/spoiler]. Keep that in mind with your actions.

It is an excellent primer on the dangers of exposing too much over social media and online in general in a post-Snowden post-Vault7 world. The politics presented are often heavy handed, in my opinion, but with this sort of topic it's basically impossible to not be a bit heavy handed. I'd say if you watched Captain America: Winter Soldier(aka "Marvel Thinks Edward Snowden is an Okay Guy: The Movie") and enjoyed yourself the politics here shouldn't be too heavy.

I started playing and couldn't stop; it was so intriguing! I was a bit worried at first whether it was going to get repetitive, but the story completely gets rid of any doubts, and the choice element is neccessary, yet fantastic. It definitely kept me on my toes; very highly reccomend.

A surprisingly immersive psuedo-visual novel that plays on the tropes of governmental surveillance in a way that makes you question every action that you make in the game. You really begin to feel that you are an investigator, prying into the personal life of these people, and for a game so simple to do that is absolutely fantastic imo.

The mechanics are simple point, click, drag. The gameplay itself requires deducing events and character motivation through the combination of various news sources, emails, and hacked text messages. It requires a lot of reading and more thinking than I anticipated, leaving me stumped a few more times than I care to admit, but it doesn't feel boring in the slightest.

Characterisation is superbly done, with regular shifts in opinion of characters based on what they may or may not have done, new information comes to light constantly and you as the PC having to delicately manage your personal opinion against what is 'right' and meting out data that will in turn mete out justice.

To some of the other critics here, when looking at the gameplay elements:

There is often frustratingly insufficient evidence to go one way or the other on conflicting information - [i]That's the point[/i]. There's an allegory here for judicial systems of all stripes, that none have perfect information, even here in the information age.
And yes, sometimes you feel the need to submit certain pieces of evidence that aren't in line with the narrative you'd like to create order to progress - [i]That's the point[/i]. I felt conflicted and frustrated as a player of this [i]game[/i]. Imagine the confliction you would have in reality if you knew facts you provide would be wilfully misinterpreted by others to serve their own agenda? To be able to balance such a fine line of generating frustration in a player against the desire to see the story through to conclusion was masterful in my opinion.

A beautiful exploration of this very deep, philosophical point - that is matched by the aesthetic and depth of information to wade through in the game.

Bravo Surprise Attack Games - Orwell sets the bar in this 'cyperpunk storyteller' that will be difficult to surpass; and I'll definitely look forward to the 'datachunk' that you provide.

This game is fantastic. This game has great potential, but I wish it offered a greater variety of paths, endings, and choices. Another issue is that there is no way to tell what information you have to process and what information is unnecessary. For this reason, you can find yourself stuck at parts, unsure of what information you're missing to trigger the next scene. At full price, I do not recommend this game. However, if you can grab it at a discounted rate, I'd say go for it. It is an enjoyable little game that is definitely worth one playthrough, but it can be slow paced at times and there's little to no point in replaying it.

Extended Review:

First off, I HIGHLY recommend this game for people who want a story. With the gripes that I have (written below), this game still stands extremely well- which should speak to just how good this game is. This is a story driven game with deductive/mystery reasoning being the engine.

I phrase it this way intentionally, as the major issue I have with the game is in determining what information is ESSENTIAL to progress through the story. There can be times where you feel that you have to determine to send between three or four pieces of information, end up sending them all, only to find out that you didn't notice that one page linked to another.

This situation of needing to progress, sending in numerous pieces of information, and finally getting the right one or realizing another page you missed, can heavily hinder the feeling of deduction and mystery solving. One possible solution would be to provide different color for the text that is aboslutely required to continue. Alternatively, provide us with MULTIPLE SAVES. 


Some last quality of life suggestions that I would have:

-Clicking on someone's image to bring up their profile would be a nice QOL change
-A clear indication/confirmation of what the final decision in the game is and what you're trying to accomplish with it (Could just be me though)

Orwell is an awesome game and here is why I think so (no spoilers and I won't say much about the story and storytelling, because without spoilers I can say only: I really liked it):
[list]
  [*]Like the description is saying, the first chapter explains you how to use your tools, but this is only the technical "how to use". You will have to learn a lot more and you will learn.
  [*]You, your imagination, your thoughts and your conclusions are the most important part of the game. It's feeling more like the game does what you want and not the other way arount and I really appreciate this.
  [*]You have many options to handle things right until the end. And some decisions you made earlier may have an impact on later events.
  [*]It's very immersive if you are willing to let it happen (maybe even if you're not).
  [*]There are some more intense and some calmer phases in the game but it really never felt boring. There was never a point where I was like "yeah, and now?".
  [*]If you want to take a break, you can do it every time you want to or take the offered breaks after every day. Or finish the game in one playthrough like I did ;)
  [*]The music and artstyle fit the game perfectly and the gameplay itself is simple, but that is how it should be. You will find a reason why it is how it is in the story.
[/list]
So, I really reccomend this game if you're into games which let you make decisions, have a storytelling which lets you rethink your conclusions again and again and again, get you involved if you want it or not and handle current subjects and events (in a fictional way of course).

I will definitely play it again to see what changes my decisions make.

Outstanding story driven game. The core game mechanics are very simple, mostly pouring through e-mails, texts, websites, all in the search of clues regarding a terrorist network. The information more or less is highlighted for you, so simply gathering the required information is easy. However, the player's decision to share certain pieces of information with the government can have profound impacts on the story and the characters involved. The decisions are far from black and white, often with undesired consequences. The interface is intuitive and immersive, creating a genuine impression of spying on suspected terrorists and political activists. It would be easy to assume the entire game is a critique of authoritarian government adapting "orwellian" tactics. However, theres is substantially more depth to the story. From a benevolent perspective (the player) it's easy to see how such powerful tools saves lives. Conversely, and predictably perhaps, the consequences and implications of such a system are made very apparent. The story is genuinely well written, the characters being surveilled are well fleshed out, and the mystery at the center of the plot is incredibly intriguing. There isn't much depth to the gameplay, or length for that matter (roughly 4 hrs), but it's worth playing for the story itself. This is one of those "story driven, choices matter, indie" games that genuienly earns those taglines and is well worth a playthrough. The only game I can relate it to is the similarly fantastic "papers, please". In much the same regard, this game engrosses the player in the mechanics of beurocracy, of distilling peoples lives, relationships, motivations, into government business. You'll find yourself so engrossed with the mechanics of discovering as much as possible about these people, the hidden agendas, the breadcrumbs left across blog posts and webpages, that you'll forget about their actual humanity. It would be boringly simple for the developers to phone the plot in with a simple anti-orwellian plot. They go so much deeper than that, using the player's perspective itself within the message. A truly well written game, with a genuinely innovative and engaging core mechanic.

There's social commentary that makes you think, and then there's social commentary that makes you nod. I regret to inform you that Orwell falls into the latter category. It's still worth checking out, especially if you've been living under a rock for the last 150 years.

Orwell has you play as the operator of a new surveillance system in the wake of a terror attack to catch the perpetrator(s). Starting off with a single suspect, Cassandra Watergate, you must sift through texts, emails, phone calls and websites to unravel the truth behind the attack. [b]This game is best played going in blind[/b] so I'd recommend just purchasing it now as I will spoil minor plot details. The game is very good, but not quite as good as I'd expected.

[h1][b]SPOILERS START HERE[/b][/h1]

To begin with, I read all of the information I could. The interface of Orwell is designed to pressure you into reading everything, seeming almost 'unclean' if you don't. However, the main mechanic of the game is the relevant text which is highlighted, regardless of whether or not you've read the whole page. Overall, this was a good move, but it did mean that I soon started scrolling through webpages, reading only what was highlighted.

Another game mechanic is the conflicting information system. If a piece of information conflicts something else that [i]can[/i] be read, it is highlighted in yellow and only of these pieces can be uploaded to Orwell. These are the points where the game branches, but it does not do so to a large extent and the development of characters is nothing like larger games with branching stories. Some of these pieces of conflicting information are pure guesswork, a poor choice made worse by the fact that [spoiler]a third terror attack[/spoiler] will occur if the player does not guess correctly.

The game has four endings. Because the player is not seen as much of an actual character, these endings didn't stir any emotion inside me, something that I believe could have been remidied by making the game longer. In all likelyhood, you will only see one ending because the game has a low replayability factor.

On a positive note, the music is amazing and, when you discover critical information, there is a sudden dramatic noise which I can only describe as feeling like my heart shat its pants.

I have focused on negatives in this review. Overall, the game is great fun, sends a good message and is certainly worth its price tag.

Orwell is an narrative game with unique gameplay. The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator whose job it is to keep the Nation safe. You work with the titular program 'Orwell' which is an advanced search engine that lets you browse the in game internet in search of terrorists. You will start of by reading through public blogs, forums and social media. But as the stakes rise and the public information dries up you will find yourself spending more and more time eavesdropping on phone calls and hacking into personal files.

The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Deus Ex. I personally loved hacking computers and reading emails in those games, and Orwell turns this side activity into a full game. This means that you will do a lot of reading, although the useable pieces of information are always highlighted. You can upload these 'data chunks' to your superior, who will act on the information you feed him. Your superior cannot read anything except for the parts you upload, which gives you the freedom to interpret the data and even 'spin' it. Do you focus on the information that marks someone as potentially dangerous or do you focus on their peaceful side? This will ofcourse have consequences down the road.

Speaking of consequences, these are actually real in this game. Although your actions will not change the core structure of the narrative, they will have a very clear impact. All suspects can be arrested, one can be killed, or you can let them all go free. What makes this game unique is that most consequences are not directly tied to a single choice, but to a whole set of smaller decisions. There is no 'do you let this person live?' moment. Instead the choices you made in what data you upload and what information you ignore will determine the fate of the characters. The ending may appear to be a 'choose your own ending' affair at first, but a replay made it clear to me that your earlier choices will still impact the ending you get.

The theme of the game is privacy vs safety. But unlike other games or media on this subject, there is no clear black or white. The game shows that your work can save lives, but that it also has the potential to ruin them. The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves.

Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second.

There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day.

Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

While the game mechanics may not be appealing to people—you are essentially combing through web pages and social media like profiles of different "target" characters as a cyber detective trying to gain information about them, which ultimately amounts to the same experience you would have actually surfing the web or social media sites—the storyline and scenario are EXTREMELY engaging and thought-provoking. The topics of surveillance is more relevant than ever these days, and one has to wonder if the Orwell system of hacking into other people's digital lives is not already in use in more or less the same form by the NSA and so forth.

If you are someone like me who is skeptical about the benefits of surveillance technology and who supports people like Edward Snowden's efforts of exposing the secrecy of our government, then this game will be particularly fascinating to you. The characters are interesting and feel well developed, and the developers did an amazing job packing tons of content to read and sift through, so the "world" feels fairly believable. There are tough decisions to be made and deep issues at hand here, not just about surveillance but freedom of speech, terrorism, and there are many gray areas to delve into. Nothing is ever as it appears, quite like life. Some great twists in the story as well. 


If you are looking for a thoughtful, provocative experience that gets right into the hard questions we should be thinking about these days, then I highly recommend you check out Orwell.

The story is definitely intriguing and it unfolds very nicely given the pacing. There is quite a bit of freedom as a result (ironic, huh) and while there is somewhat limited replayability, it's definitely really good at keeping the tension and suspense, some of which you may be able to find out depending on what you do or don't flag.

Ok Honestly this game is a treat. Incredibly interesting themes showing a modern interpretation of the prologue to 1984 in a sense. The mechanics work really well, making your decisions hold weight and using your own progress play into the games narrative hands (you'll see what I mean near the end). The music is well done too, a lovely little score playing in the background that never became annoying and felt at ease with the visuals and what I was doing, with some incredibly well timed swells in music and emotion as twists were revealed, something rather hard for a game which is mostly reading.
To explain what made me love the game is to describe a singular moment. Orwell floods you with information that seems useful and useless at the same time, using a highlighting system where certain phrases, words, numbers are made available to you to drag over to the left and thus profile your target. This occurs while reading throught the information, so it will pop up and if you are lazy, make you reliant on it, you may rush through the first couple hours just relying on this system, easy enough. But there was a point where I had to choose between two pieces of information to submit, and none of the lists of highlights I had collected seemed to help. Thankfully I like to take my time with my games and so had been reading everything carefully for intentions of characters and the like. Which made it all the more satisfying and magical when it clicked. When I realised that I had vague recollections of a small part of a post that I had read 30 minutes ago (I did say I like to take my time). This post had no highlights. The mechanics had not made me look at it. There was no cue on screen saying, "looking at this bit may help you decide on your answer". It was just me and my memory, rewarding me for actually paying attention to the game, I felt intelligent and attentive, even more so when it helped me make the correct choice without relying on luck.
I'm even going to replay it, something I've never done with an intensely story driven game like this, where I know how it unfolds. This will easily stay in my top ten for a long time I think.
There are only a couple of niggles I have on this game, one is that I kind of wish we had multiple cases to go through  instead of the large overarching one to see different uses and consequences to the use of Orwell, and the other is a technical one. At some point the game froze oddly and I had to quit out of the application, but thankfully the autosave is pretty damn sold and I never lost more than a few seconds of gameplay, I assume every action is autosaved and is the reason fo that.

The most intriguing part of the game is that the player as a person, not a a character, becomes part of the surveillance-machine with his actions and decisions. The Information you collect molds the picture of the person you investigate. You decide, which information get into the file and, if there are conflicting chunks (articles from different times, statements from different persons, rumors), which one will get into the system. Every chunk you pass is treated as a fact by the system and nactions on these are mandatory, so beware of consequences. It's terrifying how easy it is to put those people you check in categories and how the investigations progress while you play.

Regarding the presentation, the player sees what the character sees (i.e, the orwell-UI, apart from the intro), there's no speech and the art-style of the photos may not be everyone's taste and sometimes look strange. Nevertheless, the game still manages to evolve an intense atmosphere after the 1st episode with almost text only, only by viewing live-chat and call protocols.

All usable data-chunks are marked by orwell and only (more or less) relevant information for the current day are available. Even if you could add information for a person's file which WILL become relevant later, orwell wouldn't let you create a file on that person until the game tell you to. The player may encount "useful" information which is not a chunk and can not be added to the file. Although this is counter-intuitive sometimes, this mechanism keeps the game on track and the player only focuses on relevant events and persons. Just think: If you can not add it, it's not relevant to the plot or you can get the same information from elsewhere.


All in all, a good expierence and i was surprise on how the narrative and the mechanics both worked out.

What a fantastic experience. Orwell is a text-based game with a fairly linear progression. You play an investigator who uses an all-encompassing crowdsources surveillance system called Orwell. You are tasked with uncovering and identifying members of an alleged domestic terrorism group called "Thought" in the fictional country called "The Nation." You work your way through this task by investigating the phone calls, texts, emails, social media, dating profiles, bank information, and relationships of the various "suspects." You take snippets of highlighted information and upload them to Orwell (an irreversable process). It's up to you to decide, at times, which data is relevant. Choose poorly, and you can cause the deaths of certain suspects.

 If you hadn't guessed, this game is like an interactive modern version of the book "1984" by George Orwell (my favorite book of all time, by the way.) It offers a striking glimpse into what a complete surviallance state would look like in the modern world, and what the benfits and pitfuls to such a system may be. The game is pretty short at around 4 hours, but that's really all it needed to be. It definitely lacks replayability, but I don't think the story would have the impact of the first playthrough if I were to play it again. If you're interested in the subect matter or in story-based games in general, play Orwell. If you're looking for action or exploration, seek elsewhere. Just be mindful, because you never know who is watching.

The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.

[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.
However, Orwell is far better experienced (in my opinion) to just "do" and let the events unfold.

But as I said, if you are anxious about making the wrong call, you might not enjoy this game.
If you are neither scared by that nor by "this-isn't-a-game"-sayers, then you might really enjoy this game. I picked it up at a sale and enjoyed my time with it - hopefully you will too.

If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

[h1] A very enjoyable game with hidden depth, despite the very simple game mechanics. [/h1]

You investigate persons of interest in a bombing (i.e read a whole bunch and invade peoples' privacy) through their online information and electronic devices via Orwell, The Nations new secret surveilence system. The people and ways you can investigate are not all immediately available, you unlock more options and imformation based on the data you upload and where you are in the story. The gameplay ultimately boils down to drag-and-droping the datachunks (that the game hightlights) that you think are relevent, into Orwell.

While on the surface the game may seem not very challenging or lacking in replayability as some claim, there are subtleties that make Orwell really great.

Such as the fact that you, as the investigator, are the only person who will see the [b] context [/b] of the data you're uploading. Mild episode 1 spoiler: [spoiler] See a woman joking with her boyfriend that she stole his credit card (which she uses to buy a bottle of wine), which he seems mildly annoyed by but seemingly fine with? Upload that into Orwell and all your superiors know is that she "stole a credit card". [/spoiler] Whether or not you think reporting that is morally right or not, it does have an effect on how things turn out for her.
There are several times such as this when the information you can upload is damning, incomplete or inaccurate simply because the datachunk lacks context. There are times when you can use this to your advantage, if say you want to frame someone winkwink.

There are also times where you will encounter "conflicting data chunks", where you have the choice of which one (sometimes if any) you wish to upload. These choices often lead to a person or circumstance being viewed in an entirely different manner. Sometimes it is the drastic difference between someone being seen as a terrorist or an innocent.
This is why it's very important to look very carefully at what a datachunk is really uploading to Orwell and remember you needn't and perhaps shouldn't upload everything.

Overall this game puts you into a position where you have to make a lot of moral decisions around privacy, relevancy, and generally be the judge of everyone you investigate. Your choices/ethics directly and indirectly influence the fate of all the characters you meet.

A brief note on replayability: I found there to be plenty of reasons to replay the game; be it for achievement hunting, because you messed up a lot the first time around (like me ^-^'), or just to see how everything pans out if you'd played differently. As of writing I have 11.3 hours on record and I still intend to play it further as I don't feel remotely done yet.
How much time you'll get out of it depends a lot on your playstyle and whether you're a completionist or someone who blitzes through games and doesn't bother with a replay.
The average time to finish your first run through seems to be around 4 or 5 hours for most people.

tldr: Tbh as long as you like detective and/or story-driven games, I whole-heartedly recommend Orwell. While I got it on sale, since playing I would totally pay full price.

Having followed this game for a while, waiting for the episodes to release, and meeting the devs at PAX, I can say that this was probably one of the most unique "point and click" experiences I've ever had. I can't even go into much detail, because I truly want you to experience this game for yourself, but there are a few things I will say:

+The game really does a good job of making the in-game world feel "real". From a terse, yet thorough, well-thought explanation to "The Nation's" geopolitcal standing, to the online advertisements and clickbait filler that often pepper the relevant articles

+All of the characters have very distinct, memorable lives, and you'll have a chance to explore each and every one of them. There are no characters which get passed over, and this really drives home the point that what you're doing is very 1984. You're not just seeing information relevant to your case, you're seeing ALL of the information.

+The audio. There is, quite frankly, very little music or ambient noise in the game, but this is actually a positive point for this title. Whenever you come across a particularly shocking datachunk, this intense riff plays, and maintains itself until you move on. I often found myself hearing the music before I realized what I was actually looking at, and it made me super excited to keep reading.

-The episodes did feel rather short, despite there being a lot of content in each. This is offset by the fact that you're not paying per episode. When you buy the game, you get the whole game, not just episode one.

-There was a mechanic near the end (not a spoiler), where you are given a limit on how many data chunks you could upload, given the explanation that "as you know, datachunks cost time". This was never really well illustrated in earlier episodes, and, while you were scolded for uploading silly or irrelevant information (such as Cassandra's location being "over the rainbow and into wonderland" in the first episode), you were never really penalized at all unless you uploaded the incorrect answer for a conflicting (yellow) datachunk. I think the entire "limited datachunk" mechanic could have been implemented a bit better, since the player was previously unprepared to deal with that. I think that perhaps an actual time limit (via countdown timer) would have made the whole thing seem a bit more frenzied, instead of the player idly dawdling, and having time to carefully consider their decisions.


All in all, this was a great game, and I seriously look forward to seeing more great ideas come out of this developer!

There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

In Orwell's [i] 1984, [/i] we follow Winston Smith, an ordinary member of the Outer Party, who is fighting against the Party's ideas in his own way. [spoiler] However, we find out that the Party has been watching him the whole time, as well as watching his partner Julia. 'Orwell' is a fascinating first-person adventure game that explores the implications of online surveillance -- by having the player act as Big Brother! You play an investigator tasked with capturing perpetrators responsible for a lethal bombing. With the help of an investigative advisor, you collect Datachunks to build profiles of suspects.

However, profile building is not a rote task because you'll need to pore through online documents, phone and chat transcripts, resolve conflicting information, and be judicious and definitive about which Datachunk to add to the profiles. Given that, your decisions in building a suspect's profile will have both short-term and long-term consequences, affecting how the story unfolds. 

'Orwell' makes players reflect on, or perhaps even reconsider the value of and impact of surveillance on public safety. It's both entertaining and thought-provoking, and I was compelled to replay it twice more so that I can see how different decisions will yield different outcomes. With such high value in entertainment, intellectual stimulation and replayability for its price, 'Orwell' gets my enthusiastic recommendation.
If you ever wanted to find out what it's like working for the NSA but you want to keep your dignity, this game is for you.

[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

[h1] THE GAME THAT WILL LEAVE YOU EMOTIONALLY CRIPPLED [/h1]

TL;DR Worth the price of $10 USD, incredible story. You're gonna like the way you get hooked. I guarantee it.

*sigh* This game is gonna leave me scarred for a little bit.

So. Orwell is a short interactive narrative game where you take the seat behind a new, high tech computer system called "Orwell." This system is meant to be a means to an end, a platform for an investigative war or terrorism.

The story is deep and rich. And there's a lot of different events going on, all of which tie into the decisions you make and how the characters feel about everything going on.

It all starts off with a single bombing and a letter. At first, all seems simple. You watch a little CCTV footie, you think "OH THAT'S THE PERSON. RIGHT THERE. THIS GAME'S GONNA BE EASY AF." No. Because soon, you don't know what to think. You'll find yourself conflicted as the information provided to you begins to conflict. You begin to feel lost, like you're not really sure what or who you are looking for.

At the end. It'll take you for a loop. And you're given a huge decision. A decision that impacts who you are.

[b] Do you go through with it? Make it all finally end? [i] Or do you sympathize? Bring everyting to a fitting end? [/i] [/b]

It all comes down to what you feel justice is for you. In fact, this game will have you questioning that the entire time.


Now, I'd like to bring up something I felt was... ehhhhhh, displeasing. We'll go with displeasing.

[h1] THIS GAME IS RATHER SHORT [/h1]

Or so it seems. 

There are a lot of things to consider. If you just focus on the main issues, the main information, yes. It can seem a little short lived. But if you take the time to read everything, get to know the characters for who they are, their interests, their emotions, their... [i]thoughts[/i]... It's really not that short at all. And all of this information can affect your ability to make decisions in this game. At times, you'll feel something is unjust, or unfounded. You'll struggle at times to think about what information is relevant.

I've said it before. I'll say it again. [b] The way you play this game is heavily reliant on your own sense of justice. [/b]

So think about it. And think about it again.

What decisions will you make?

This game had me on the edge of my seat through the whole experience.

I started out thinking this was gonna be a decent experience, finding out info on people using Orwellian tactics, and that's about it. I was kinda wrong. You don't have access to everything from the get-go. People start to cover their traces when they're up to no good.

You are a contractor for Orwell, a government surveillance agency as an outside contractor. Yoor focus is to find evidence against a terrorist group and make sure they can no longer bomb people and places. You extract data from a variety of sources, articles, private messages between users (You need to find out their phone numbers/emails yourself) and access thier personal devices (You'll need a device ID for that though, which may or may not be hard to find). You tap phone calls and messages to learn about each character and their role in the story, and you can decide their fates.

Here's the catch: your superiors can only see what you upload to them. You decide what they can and can't see.

The first episode is more of a tutorial than anything, then episode 2 serves as an intro, and 3, 4, and 5 is where the story really takes off. The finale left me blown away, and I am definitely looking foward to the next game by these developers.

If you want a great short story for a lazy day (or lazy days), check this out.

Well, it was everuthing I expected. Ever read 1984? Watched the series Person of interest? Ever wondered how privacy and safety are balancing in this world? Ever wondered how powerfull information can be? Not easily creeped out by knowledge yourself? Then, this is a game for you.

You play an investigator working for a government "Big Brother" agency, named Orwell. As an objective observer you review evidence that your advisor sends your way, and respond to it by uploading what you consider to be relevant details regarding potential suspects in a crime - a crime that ends up only being an element of the overall story. 

The story itself feels well thought out, although some of the literal interpretations of your data by your advisor are jarring - context really is everything and some information is easily misunderstood by those you work under. I found some of these limitations to be irksome - if I was doing this sort of job in real life I would certainly have included some of the information your superiors reject because it provides a more rounded view of the suspects.

The most negative thing I would say about my experience with Orwell overall is that some of the consequences to choices felt contrived, forcing you off-track in a way that was obviously a narrative techinique. 

Entertaining, could have been longer but for the price it worked out to be reasonable. Shame it's a single story really, the setting had a lot of scope for expansion. The game does offer some replay value though. 

Essentially a choice-and-consequence game with an element of mystery.

What I like about the game was that I went into the game trying my best to do right within the constraints of a flawed system, and...well, let's just say the road to hell is paved with good intentions. So, yes, the gameplay can be annoyingly restrictive - you won't get to make choices that you want to make sometimes - but it makes sense, given the premise.

Very smart point and click game with a great narative. If you enjoy a slower paced game that you can sink yourself into with a rediculous time burden, this is a game for you. i tend to prefer survival games and action rpg's, but this is definitely keeping me glued to my screen.

I'm speechless as in what to say for this game, since the entire story totally got me so hard that I'm quite sad it's >only< 5 hours long.

I had quite high expectations, considering the price of the game and the game's length, and I'm very happy to say that Orwell didn't disappoint, not even a little. Episode 1, which is also included in the demo is very short and serves more like a "tutorial" than actual gameplay, and after completing it I was afraid that the rest would look similar - nothing like that, all other 4 episodes were so intense and well-written that I immediately went back to my previous happy state and enjoyed my fun.

And believe me - I hate all sort of VNs and games with huge amount of text, they're usually boring for me and I quickly lose my interest, that's why I was a bit sceptical at first whether I'm going to enjoy Orwell, but I decided to go with it due to a nice -43% (bundle) discount, and I can say that the experience is well worth the money, even at full price.

You should DEFINITELY grab the game if you're interested in all sort of government spying on people, but apart from that it'd be also interesting position for people interested in "working" for government in general, doing detective work, connecting various pieces together and enjoying awesome story. In fact, the story is the most polished thing in the entire game, and it's alone worth the time and money spent on the title, that's why I'd recommend this title even for people that expect more gameplay than reading, such as myself.

From the bad things, the game can seem a bit too "casual", especially for more oldschool gamers like myself - I'd appreciate difficulty setting that would turn off highlighting relevant facts, and definitely allow to jump onto conclusions with only half-available data. Don't get me wrong - the game is awesome and those are not any crucial things that would heavily affect the gameplay, but I kinda miss the option of actually "losing", by jumping onto false assumption and getting fired. Losing should definitely be an option here.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time, this is at least a 9/10 from me - missing point only for being too casual, although that didn't stop me from enjoying the awesome story that the devs coded for me, since I had a lot of fun. I can definitely recommend the title to everyone!

Now this is a thriller. I love how this game manages to walk the knife's edge between tense mystery and ethical conundrums.

It's a very detective-y, snooping sort of game. You're ferreting out clues in blog posts and text chats and more, trying to stop terrible crimes from happening. That means there's a lot of reading, of course, and it's to Orwell's credit that most of it still feels fascinating through several hours of play. I was committed to solving the mystery, but as I delved deeper into the story, I felt increasingly ambivalent about my role in the narrative: I HAD to snoop to save lives, but each piece of information I deemed relevant might result in an endangered or wrongly imprisoned suspect. You're voiceless, unable to shout "STOP I'm not SURE this seems more nuanced than that." Your only power lies in the information you pass along, 

All in all, I really enjoyed this game, and I'll definitely replay it. While I found several of Orwell's mysteries, I know there's more to uncover.

Orwell can best be described as a chilling depiction of just how intrusive surveillance can be on ordinary people's lives. You play as an outsourced investigator working for "The Nation" with the goal of finding out the truth behind a terrorist attack. This is done by recording the actions of people via the surveillance tool 'Orwell, which can monitor phone conversations, internet usage and other methods of communication, all of which we take for granted in our society. 

While the game is relatively short (it only took me about 4 hours to complete a run of the story), the plot is both entertaining and unnerving, acting as a commentary of what we know various governments throughout the Western world are doing. According to Orwell, everyone is guilty until proven innocent, and even then the innocent can be caught in the crossfire.

Fantastic game. Immersive, intriguing, great idea from the origin. I've always love playing a game like these and it's such a niche thing to find: to play as someone using a computer to investigate and analyze. The closest I've come to is Her Story (another story rich game, really great if you've got the time and your into that sort of thing). 

I think one of Orwell's best features is the how your decisions can effect the outcome of the game. It also tests your morality and your own ethics. It may start a conversation in you about the far reaching power technology has to achieve absolute security measures. Is it right in order to save people from getting killed? Or should privacy be preserved in order to prevent non-criminals from being lumped as potential suspects? Overall, it will make you think afterwards about what you think is wrong or right.

A fun and interesting concept, perhaps under-realized.

Orwell is less of a game and more of a scenario; you are given the role of an NSA data analyst (by another name) who, in the aftermath of a terrorist incident, is given the investigative assignment and jurisdiction to peer into the lives of several suspects with various ties to the event and each other - with a set of invasive and controversial tools.

What I liked:
- The ambience. The music was, for the most part, ethereal and relaxing, and the graphics minimalistic yet evocative. 
- The theme, overall. If you can suspend your disbelief you can effectively see how this scenario would play out in real life, and it exposes you to the very necessary dialogue about personal freedom in this day and age, though I have some issue with how it’s expressed (see below).

What I thought could be better:
- Linearity. The game itself is mostly a tunnel. That’s fine if it’s the developer’s desire to tell a story, but investigations in real life are rarely so straightforward - it was a frustrating inconsistency for me.
- Datachunks, and their purpose. Datachunks are the game’s terminology for data points that you gather from various places; this is *the* gameplay here and I have to admit I was a bit underwhelmed. They aren’t explained very well to begin with. The role of conflicting datachunks isn’t well understood even as you’re finishing the game and there seems to be little to no penalty for assimilating bad information. Add to that the fact that the chunks themselves are pretty limited and spelled out for you (in blue and yellow highlighting against the page), and it makes for a pretty pedestrian mechanic. I was still able to suspend my disbelief enough to finish the story, but I couldn’t help think that a little more complexity and freedom and a little more trust in the player would reap a more satisfying conclusion.
- The story itself has zero sympathetic characters and several predictable plot points. The overall theme of ‘limitless government overreach’ comes at you with all the nuance of a sledgehammer. I guess that’s to be expected when the name of the game is literally ‘Orwell,’ and sometimes sledgehammers can even be fun; but if you’re looking for a multifaceted and deep exploration of this topic in a game format, I think we’re still waiting.

The point: 6.5/10.
Is it the most complete and satisfying gameplay possible? Probably not. But like most story-centric indie titles I think the concept is what is most important; it is fertile subject matter and I’d love to see it further explored, perhaps even in an episodic format. It took me about 4.5 hours to finish and apparently that is dead average, so use that for your own personal evaluation of whether the price you pay is worth it. Recommended, with qualifications.

[i]Orwell[/i] is a text-based game that puts you in the shoes of a crowdsourced cybersurveillance data clerk.

So, in the late 2000s The Nation has been suffering from a spiralling crime rate and unstable neighbours. This propelled the notoriously authoritarian Party to power, who then passed the vague-named Safety Bill. Basically, The Nation is an Americanish country that is careening towards a police state: the Safety Bill allows the government unlimited remote access to any electronic device they can identify, and extended detentions without charge for even slightly unfortunate turns of phrase. They have bots that can sift through that data for those unfortunate phrases. However, knowing the kind of jinn they are letting out the bottle, they created the solution: ORWELL, and you. As the anonymous Investigator, a foreign citizen, you are to evaluate the “datachunks” the automated system highlights among the information on designated target persons. The police only see the datachunks you feed into the system, and will generally take them literally; they can send you texts, but that’s it. It’s up to you to balance nuance, ethics and expedience, and to choose what to submit and what not to submit.

This gives you quite a bit of liberty. You can be the zealous [i]chekist[/i], using your omnipotent tools to not crush bones but crush souls, helping the police ravage through people’s lives. You can be the manipulator, minimizing the collateral damage and keeping the often trigger-happy police from harming their own cause. Or you can go full rebel and do your best to sabotage the investigation.

Now, as a bombing kills several people, and an apparently radicalized anti-surveillance group seems to be behind it in a massive bout of irony, you are to put your Internet detective hat on, and validate the system in a trial by fire, and a race against the clock.

Beyond the sometimes counterintuitive plot twists, I’ve found no issues with the game.

You’ll probably like it if you liked [i]Papers, Please[/i].

[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

It's the first time I give a revew on Steam but I feel I had to do it for this game. I bought it this week and started playing yesterday. I stopped at 3 am to go to bed, then continued playing today as I was completely hooked. I did a complete playthrough in 9.5 hours, which is really great for the price. It could take less time, but I really got invested in the story and actually took time to make every decision carefully. 

TL;DR : This game is a masterpiece. Buy it.
I'll try to break down my impressions :

PROS
-AMAZING storyline! It was intricate, well written, complex... I enjoy puzzles & solving enigmas, I'm not new to it... but this game got me wandering in the dark, completely distabilized. And the side stories just adds to it.
-Well written characters! The game is litterally about digging into targetted people's life, going as deep as possible. It could have been so bad, it could have been superficial data made up just for the story. But it was interesting. You have to make choices, decide what information you give up to Orwell and what other info you keep to yourself, and it impacts the story and these people's life. I developped sympathy for some and aversion for others. The characters felt real.
-The ending was great. At that point, I was expecting it, but it was still so satisfying.
-Very intuitive and easy gameplay. Just a tip : don't go too fast. Wait a bit before sending a piece of information, try to make up your own opinion with other infos first.
-Nice art style. It's simple yet beautiful, I really enjoyed it. 
-Nice soundtrack. The music was always appropriate and guided me through the story. 

CONS
-Only one story. I wish there was more enigmas, I wish it wasn't over! Even if I could change the playthrough slightly, it's still the same. I'm eager to play more of this game!
-Some bugs. Was never really detrimental to my gaming experience, but still slightly annoying. I sometimes had trouble dragging the infos to the dropping box, and somtimes there was the alert symbol like I sill had unseen data chunks, which wasn't true, so I would search for missed info that weren't there. 

CONCLUSION
If you're the kind of player to aggressively click your mouse at every dialogue box to skip it as fast as possible, this game is not for you. It's a game for the critical thinkers, for people who like to pause to think and come up with theories. This is my personal opinion on the game and I am going to talk about a few reasons that I would recommend this game.

A few things that make this game great:
[*] A quasi-realistic and relatable world for most people, the artstyle is pleasing. I personally find the "transparent" feel as representing how Orwell oversees everything. Characters might start off as stereotypical but are psychogically developed during the course of the story.

[*] Your choices do affect the ending to a certain degree 

[*] The fact that you play as an outsider to the system is thought-provoking and you can oversee the outcomes of your choices and question the ethics and utility of your actions

[*] The plot-twists were attractive and made me more eager to keep on reading




Here are a few points that displeased me: 

[*] You might not like this if you are not ready to examine and read long text chunks, there are some information that seem boring some will not even bother to read (but still relevant to the world building in the game)

[*] Some choices leading to certain outcomes may not seem logical and unpredictable, making the gamer confused and maybe frustrated to a certain level. [spoiler]For instance, Nina being killed or not in the game due to signaling that she has a weapon didn't make much sense to me.[spoiler] 

[*]There is a time in the story that can feel stagnating and boring since you might have to review information already seen previously in order to get new ones. 


Conclusion: I would recommend this game for people who have some time to spend, and like investigative games who isn't afraid of going into details. Also, if you are a fan of dystopian stories and interested in problems related to surveillance.

Orwell is part-hacking, part-detective sim which satisfies both those unrealised career desires for me, but which does get repetitive. The concept is great. You're essentially an NSA agent for some generic authoritarian state, trying to prevent terrorist attacks. You scour documents, social media pages, snoop through emails and listen in on phone calls, putting all the pieces together to build a profile of the terrorist organisation. The moral choices come in when you can decide what information to provide to your colleagues and what, if any, to conceal. The UI is basic but feels smooth. The gameplay consists of reading through these sources until the game highlights information of importance for you, and you decide whether or not to put it on record. After the initial novelty wears off this can get tedious because it's too easy. I was longing for real detective work, but found myself mindlessly clicking through sources until the game showed me something, because the need for you to really think about where and what you're looking for most of the time just isn't there. Sound design is...OK. Suitable ambient background tones until you hit a breakthrough and send out the troops. Voice acting would have been a great addition to the wiretapping segments, because...

Despite all this I didn't get bored. Why? Because the characterisation in this game is spot on. I was amazed at how much I found myself invested in some of the people I was investigating. Characters formed only from pieces of text on a screen and an impressionistic picture. You get to read into these people's lives, into their social media personas, their private correspondence, and the depth here was delightful. I found myself laughing at the detail written into the Not-Facebook profiles and the musician's website. The game might not be fully realised; it has mechanics limitations and content gets explored fully early on, leaving it stale fairly quickly, but if you like playing detective there is definitely enough material to keep you amused for a few hours.

I just finshed playing Orwell for the first time and personally, I already want to dive back in, but maybe that's just me. If you are going to enjoy this game, it helps if you have read 1984 by George Orwell (all the quotes in the game are from the book and the subject of the game deals heavily with subject of state surviellance and control.)

Orwell is essentially a similator that allows you to use a version of the kind of Big Data surviellence tools that the NSA uses, such as PRISM. You can look at web pages, snoop on chats and phone calls and hack into phones and machines if you can get the IP.

The way the game is actually played is you sift through the various sources you have at your disposal and upload chunks of information to Orwell. Because the intelligence agency can only see the data that you point to as relevant, what data you upload will have a big effect on the outcome of the game.

Fortunately though, Orwell highlights the bits of intelligence (chunks) as you go through the page, which makes it a it easier.

Essentially then, Orwell is a game about being employed as an intelligence analyst. What data you feed to the government will determine who gets arrrested and who lives and dies if you don't get to the bomber.

Having only played through once, I am not sure how much replay value Orwell has. Given the large amount of text, I suspect that if you waited a few weeks and went back to it, you would find new things. I certainly did not get the optimal ending the first time.

Personally, I cannot reccomend this game highly enough. The platform that it is built on could be used to make so many other stories and scenarios, so I really hope they have Stem workshop access.

However, keep in mind that Orwell is a highly cerebral game that involves alot of reading. If you are not really into Intelligence as a subject, you might not get it.

On the other hand, if you are an Intel nerd, then you will love Orwell, which imho, is kind of like the new Uplink.

[h1]General[/h1]

This is [b]not really a game.[/b] Most of the time you would only be pointing out "data chunks" to relevant character, and the said data chunks has been conveniently pointed out to you by the highlight, so you can't miss it. The only time you get a little pressure is on the final episode, when there are "data upload" limit imposed on you.

[h1]There is minimal gameplay[/h1]
There is minimal gameplay, as it is mostly just drag and drop something. The clues are too easily pointed out to you. Sometimes there are some conflicting data, but it is easy to resolve this kind of things. It is also bad that you don't know how the data chunks you are given is processed. A wrong data chunk could suddenly net a very violent response although previous data chunks you have given it is not the way. 


[h1]Story-Rich Gameplay[/h1]
However, the story in the game is excellent. It is not overly long and complicated, but it is quite complicated enough to keep you guessing on who is who and what is the truth beneath all of these things. All of the characters are alive, and the way they are chatting with each other, with you snooping in, at times make you guilty for snooping on someone's conversation. You will also see another person's life, and at times you will feel guilty that you are the one that send them into prison, sometimes by bending the truth so they can be arrested. And seeing their hobbies and their life, but watching their conversation, their blogs, or their social medias, sometimes makes you really hopeful that this guy/girl is not guilty so you could release them, and make you guilty if you have to arrest them.

[h1]Politics and Mass Surveillance[/h1]
Of course, this game is quite a political game, on the issue of mass surveillance. It subtly asks the player on how far the government could go in the name of security, and how is privacy should be treated if you have connection with a terror group. The game beautifully does not refer to any country or any political party (though a subtle jab at "Freedom" and "Peacekeeping" is done). 

Overall a beautiful game.
