Good for people who don't mind reading a bit. Not dissimilar to games like Papers, Please. Interesting narrative with multiple outcomes; although it's short, it's easy to play again to make different choices.

A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.

Play as an investigator in a new secret gov. program named 'Orwell' that -- unsurprisingly -- spies on its own citizens' e-mails, phone conversations, laptops, etc., and selectively hunts for evidence of unlawful activity. The focus in this 5-part story is anti-governmental terrorism.

The name Orwell is on the nose, of course, and the writing is mostly along those lines. (This game is all text, all writing, so this is very important!) It, however, begins unraveling near the end, reaching for genuine philosophical depth. A favorite moment that's a bit too prescient is at the end while digging through the (optional) files that led to Orwell's creation. One of the creators calls the program Orwellian in its sinister direction. It's meant as a pejorative. The other creators have no idea who Orwell is -- one of the most famous English writers of the 20th century, and most influential on pop culture for over 50 years. They just think Orwell is a cool name, and so they use it unironically to name their entire Orwellian program. 

Do you see what's neat here?

I went in thinking Orwell didn't exist in this game's universe. But he does. And he's still a huge influence. The fictional government is so ignorant, run by idiots hell-bent on imaginary terrorism and protecting themselves and their interests, though, that the messages of Orwell's books are lost on them -- and they just don't care. 

This should sound familiar. This game felt like a fluffy beach-read dystopia in 2016, but it quickly turned accurate once January 20th rolled around in 2017. Awesome.

However, the gameplay is very simple and not that interesting. Just some point and click actions on a PC screen, with lots of help from the game, so it doesn't really present a challenge. Orwell isn’t the most engaging of games in terms gameplay. Sometimes you have to choose between conflicting bits of information, but other than that, there’s generally little reason to not put information in the system as you come across it, except maybe to avoid your handler’s smart-arse remarks.

Orwell is a far more engaging game in terms of the ideas it presents and the world it builds. As I am sure you have guessed, Orwell derives heavily from the ideas put forward 1984 by George Orwell. Similarly to 1984, Orwell is set in a fictional country where media and many other outlets are controlled by the government. That being said, the Nation in which the game is set is more of an authoritarian society as opposed to full totalitarian.

By the time the ending rolled around, I was surprised by its direction. I mostly expected a “twist” where you are betrayed and would have to fight the government you were working for. But there was nothing quite that overt or direct, as you were presented with several opportunities with how to proceed. It was an interesting enough story built inside a world into which a lot of effort had been poured into its construction.

Orwell is not a thriller or a game that will keep you in suspense. Instead, it is a quiet and simple exploration of an old idea through a different lens, done tastefully and staying far enough away from the usual tropes to retain some uniqueness.

You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.

When you find something incriminating, you upload it. The system then opens up other related sources for you to look through, and highlights the relevant data. It's up to you to upload it for further analysis or not.

Basically, you have to drag and drop the right highlighted text to Orwell in order to advance the story. It's not hard to do, and it keeps the story flowing nicely. It works, even if the ending is a bit rushed, and out of the blue.

This is a difficult one! The premise and the story are both quite complicated and intelligently woven. However, the execution is less so. This game suffers from the very same type of problems that LA Noire did: how to make a detective/analysis game without too little or too much handholding.

The idea of the investigative software is quite well-written; and depending on your ending, has a lot of payoffs. But the fact that the software pinpoints what it thinks is important and relevant kinda breaks the realism and limits a lot of your options. A lot of times, decisions that you make won't have the intended consequences and not because "life is complicated" or "shit happens" but because that's now how you linguistically interpreted the data. And that is the limitation of every game that has attempted to use language as a mechanic. There are still too many unknowns and interpretations to be able to identify and script every possible `effect` after you've set a `cause`.


Of course, there's no undo or rollback so you have to keep going with what you've done so far. The concept of `conflicting info` is also weird and unrealistic. Sometimes, it warns you that this info conflicts with some other info that you haven't even loaded or read. How does the software know that?! I realize that this aspect of analysis needs to be "gamefied" but that's where this game shows its greatest weakness. It's as if the software is already run by an AI and you just need to answer a few multiple choice questions here and there.

There's also a number of annoying UI issues like notifications. I kept gettings notifications for new or unread articles when I had accessed them and read them numerous times. Same with the datachunk notification. And when you're hunting for something specific towards the end of the game, and you have a ton of data, those icons can get downright annoying and misleading forcing you to skim and scroll through heaps of useless articles.

Still, the game and the story have a lot to say about our current society and it's definitely worth a replay for things you might have missed the first time. Not to mention that it has multiple endings.

The music's quite good too!

As many others have mentioned, an interesting concept. Don't purchase this game looking for a good gameplay experience. This is certainly a visual novel with a little more interaction than usual, closing in on Point & Click Adventure territory.

It certainly has its own contemporary agenda, which they do a fairly good job at conveying. Its execution isn't always the best, some moments fall flat but are remedied by the pacing and -for me, personally- the desire to see what is going to happen next. While short, it offers enough of interest to be worth a purchase (perhaps at a 40-50% discount, depending on your tastes). 

The 'choices' you will encounter in this game usually boil down to 'jump to conclusion' and 'don't jump to conclusion', which can admittedly work out well in some cases. However, there are times where you will encounter unforseen consequences. These can definitely have an impact on how the game progresses, in increments. For the most part you are playing through a story on rails, with only a few forks in the road that eventually lead to the same place, anyways. The biggest choice you will get takes place at the end of the game, where you will most likely arrive after about 4 hours. 

I would say the game is worth playing for its subject matter alone, it stands on its own as an experience. Some food for thought is to be found, as well.

Few games manage to solve the equation to be interesting, involving, and fun. Orwell is such a game. While it provides a biased view on the topic of surveillance (a view I wholeheartedly approve of, incidentally), it manages to stay informative. The possibles misuses made by the "Orwell" tool you are in control of clearly address the old myth that yes, contrary to what your grandparents say, everybody does have something to hide.

The game portrays a situation where nothing is ever white or black. Even the all-spying government you work for seem to have good intents. Orwell does not try to tell you that you live in a secret dictatorship, instead, it describes perfectly the mechanic of how a tool, a system can be used, abused by a soulless entity to draw wrong conclusions and to make void of the old concept of "private life".

As a game, and that means I will address gameplay here, Orwell partially fails. The game seems to imply that the things you decide to add to the Orwell database have all to be relevant else there is going to be some serious consequences : during my one and only playthrough, however, it felt like I was on rail and that I could not fail anything. Only in the final episode of the game choices I made during that episode seemed to matter, and I am not even sure to which extent (besides the choice of endings). If you are looking for a game of strategy, this is not your game.

If, however, you are looking for either a compelling story, an education on how your Internet activity can tell all about you, proof that the concept of serious games is not a futility, or an interesting twist on the old detectove point&click adventure genre, Orwell is definitely your game. It's a Snowden's Paper Please.

This game f*cked with my mind. Oh heavenly gods of nerddom, did it ever. Gather round, boys and girls, as I tell you why:

Orwell takes place in a country called "The Nation" (obviously not to be confused with anything casually tyrannical like "The Empire"). The political ruling party, The Party (much imaginative), has come into power and, thanks to the newly created office of the Secretary of Security, has in the last few years passed a Safety Bill meant to protect The Nation from any and every individual(s) who pose a threat to national security (think of the Patriot Act as a IRL equivalent). And just like NSA wiretapping, the Safety Bill gives the government dubious leeway to monitor suspected individuals through various channels (i.e., social media, email, phone calls, text messages, etc). The computer program the government employs to collect and complie such information is ironically named "Orwell" and you are hired as an Orwell investigator to track down a group of suspected individuals believed to be responsible for a series of bombings that have occurred in The Nation's capitol city of Bonton (ridiculous name I have to say, I couldn't stop thinking of bonbons). As an investigator you are paired with an adviser through whom you pass information on to higher channels who take the appropriate action. Although you are given objectives whose completion is information-dependent, it becomes ultimately clear that you, the investigator, your judgement, your discerning eye, your evaluation of possible repercussions of all the information at your fingertips, is what drives the game. The endgame of Orwell depends on you and your choices. Will you do the right thing, whatever you believe is the right thing? 

Aesthetics-wise, this game is just pretty damn near pleasing. It's a simple point-and-click with elegant yet simple graphics. The attention to detail is great, from the texts to the functionality of Orwell itself. The whole feel of the game, especially at certain moments (I'm not going to be a no-good, spoiley spoilsport), makes one forget that this is JUST A SIMULATION, NOT REAL LIFE CALM THE F*CK DOWN. I will say it's easy to get overwhelmed by the sheer density of information and how to appropriately navigate, in terms of the expected outcome. But hey, maybe it's a personal thing. I am more used to FPS than this sort of genre of game. 

In conclusion: PLAY THE GAME, FAM. DO IT. JUST DO IT!

Compelling. Immersive. Intense. Orwell is all of these things as it shows us the future of online privacy (increasingly an oxymoron in this age) and how easy it is/will be to curtail our civil liberties, even with only the best of intentions.

Much like Papers, Please, this game gives you an unpopular (to say the least) but reasonably straightforward job. Soon, however, you discover just how crucial your decisions are - and how dire the consequences can be. Of course, you are simply doing your job; you're not a [i]villain[/i]... but, looking at your actions, are you distinguishable from one?

Orwell is a game that touches on many important topics, including but not limited to...

- privacy, both as a basic societal concept and as a political issue
- the importance of context (and the dangers of losing/removing it)
- whether the ends justify the means (openness to truth versus confirmation bias/cherrypicking)
- the importance of critical reading (instead of passive credulity)
- identity, which can be variously represented as one's experiences and/or past actions and/or speech (and the pitfalls of giving any one instance too much weight)
- idealism and its potential for corruption
- law as a power unto itself

I enjoyed and [b]recommend[/b] this game for its well-paced character-driven story, effective mood-setting music, and overall attractive presentation.

[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

Still, this is an excellent game with excellent graphics and a pretty deep storyline too. 10/10

On the internet, no one knows you're a grandma.

Jokes aside, Orwell captures what I love most about indie games: a simple idea that invokes thoughts and feelings.

Orwell provides a nice overview of the current state of our privacy: constantly surveillanced, seldom noticed.
I backed two other similar games on Kickstarter (Top Secret and Need To Know) wishing for the same thing I can feel playing this game: the responsibility (or the lack thereof) of spying on other's privacy, and deciding how they should be looked at or dealt with: a small oversight on a character's relationship status could make me think about it till the end of the game. Even though such details may not be important to the story, it still bothered me: because it is the identity that I altered, and there was no turning back. It fits well with doublethink, and made me Winston: I might be the only one who knows the truth that he is divorced, but to everyone else, he is still married (this circumstance did not sound familiar until I wrote that line down, makes me curious if the given decision is put in delibrately). And this thought is freightening; because "he might be alone in holding that belief, and if alone, then a lunatic... the horror was that he might also be wrong." This thought of people not caring about this as it serves no function, and the possibility that I might be actually wrong and it really does not matter, troubles me greatly.

The mechanics are similar to what workers do at Recdep, but of course not entirely, as the purpose of Recdep does not fit the current state of politics nor the theme of this game. Instead of altering history, we are 'phrasing' history, finding quotes which can be used for our advantage and possibly against our target, the quotes may not need to be said seriously or truthfully, nor are they meant to be always perceived literally, but we use them all the same: perhap an alternate form of "the indifference of reality". Although not altering history in any way, you are still creating history, and that is very doublethink.

Choices. Whether this is not Ingsoc is debatable, as there are preferable choices and crimethink for Ingsoc. However, choices in Orwell definitely allow the player to be as Orwellian as they wish to be, in terms of accusations. You can charge a person with crime from a single sentence and thought, some may not even be said seriously. Of course, Orwell needs to allow you the freedom of choice, because our current state of freedom allows it, or as we think. Nevertheless, the ultimate choice is still yours. In my first playthrough I decided to unbellyfeel my superior. Perhaps I will do something else next time.

Overall, this game at least is able to capture the Orwellian idea of possible surveillance and control, while attempts to inform the players that we may still have the ultimate power of choice. Whether of not this game will still ring true 4 years later is uncertain for me at the moment, but as a person who loves Nineteen Eighty-Four, I am happy to see that people can make an effort to prove that oldthinkers unbellyfeel Ingsoc.

(4 years later: fortunately not)

Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

As a newly appointed investigator, you are tasked with bringing the far-reaching powers of the Orwell spying system to try and find the perpetrator of a bombing. It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

Pros:

- I love 1984 and obviously this game is heavily inspired by it.
- Relaxing gameplay.
- Thought-provoking story, especially as we seem to be moving towards a world of 'alternative facts' and other Orwellian concepts in real life.
- Game is long enough that I felt like I got my money's worth, but not so long that it started to get boring and overstay its welcome.
- Seems to have enough replay value for at least two playthroughs.
- Is not too heavy-handed with the anti-surveillance message. Clearly that is the point of the game, but they don't treat you like an idiot with it.
- Some of the choices do require actual thought and planning to make the right choice.
- Consequences for making the wrong choices.
 
Cons:

- In my opinion, the artsyle is a bit too 'whimsical' for the plot of the game. They seemed at odds with one another most of the time.
- It would have been nice if there had been some voice acting. I didn't mind that most of the game was just text, but when listening on phonecalls it would have been nice for them to have been voiced with subtitles.
- The story is extremely linear where one piece of located text triggers the next event and nothing will happen until you find it. Once you realize this it does take some of the urgency out of the game. It would be nice if things like IM chats and phone calls happened whether you were ready or not, so that there could be some threat of you missing information or getting swamped.
- The game holds your hand the entire way. When I first booted it up I thought that I was in a tutorial segment and that a while the highlighting around relevant text and the constant prodding from your supervisor would slow down, but they don't. Every bit of important information is highlighted for you already, so you really don't have to read anything if you don't want to. In a way the game will play itself in a way. There are times when you can choose the wrong info and get scolded, but I found that 95% of the time you just upload whatever data Orwell has already highlighted for you. It eliminates the biggest part of the gameplay, in my opinion. I think the game would have benefitted a lot from taking a Papers, Please approach where you have to scour the data and decide what you think is important and your supervisor chimes in every now and then to punish or praise you, depending.

This game is a pretty neat take on the "actual computer as game interface" genre made famous by (the much better) Her Story, and it is a provocative take on government spying as well. The gameplay itself is fun and interesting, but not nearly as deep as it could be. Unlike in Her Story, I rarely felt like I was truly investigating; between the red highlights, the prompts from your handler, and the linear structure of the investigation itself, I more often than not felt like the game was just leading me along by the nose. Indeed, the prompts from the handler almost ruin the whole experience - in addition to giving you several totally unnecessary hints, he often comments on the investigation itself in ways that are very disruptive and eye-rolly (i.e. "wow, what a strange development!"). I'd rather just be allowed to form opinions on the narrative myself, thank you very much, but unfortunately he cannot be turned off. 

Still, it is definitely worth checking out, especially for its price point. I particularly enjoyed the social network mapping mechanic, the way that you gradually see the connections build between all the people you are investigating. Overall, the game could have been much better, but still a decent game.

This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

This was a very enjoyable little game, and pretty fairly priced at just £7. I found it in an article in PC Gamer magazine and decided to give it a go, being a big fan of George Orwell's strong writings myself. This game is surprisingly tense and fast paced at times, while at other times the story can be kind of slow. The thing is, this game shows the player the whole "Big Brother State" issue from the other side, you get to see reports of terrible events you could have stopped and it really hit me very hard.

This is a game that has obviously taken real events into consideration as much as Orwell. The undertones in The Nation and the leadership by The Party feels like it would work well as a prequel to one of Orwell's most famous works, Nineteen Eighty-Four, which was so influential it even got a big screen adaptation and starred a great cast for the time including a very young John Hurt. But I digress. The storyline is based around a crowd-surveilance computer interface called Orwell and is brought about in secret after The Party passes the Secrecy Bill. I won't spoil anything about the investigation, but the Bill is very reminiscent of British PM Theresa May's highly controversial Snooper's Charter.

The fact is, the game has this utopian near-future look while having tense feelings of underlying political risk to every act. The five chapters work pretty well to split them up, and the way the interface works is really nice. Every part of the investigation manages to have a consequence, but it leads to the same kind of point in the end. So, in Conclusion:

Pros:

1) Excellent storyline with strong characters and some really tense chapters, such as Nina's storyark (that was both intense and really threw me off, again one you'll have to see for yourself) and the antics of Initiate.

2) An interface that really makes you feel like the investigator.

3) Attention to detail - the game doesn't hold back with its attempts at realism.

4) A real feeling of influence and a concern that this game may be showing the future.

Cons

1) The lack of potential for follow-on sequels - The game ends on a sort-of final note, as you'll find out if you play it.

2) CCTV or Camera Footage actually plays very little part in the game, with text being very dominant. Would be nice have to access event footage, more access to records in the hands of actual authorities and the like to even out the fact it is a government project, not a bedroom-hacker.

3) The length of the game could be greater, If a longer sequel appeared I would certainly want to buy it!

4) Finally, the route taken is too narrow. This game is meant to show the full potential and range of issues a Big Brother style investigation would have, so more routes for different events would create greater depth and realism, as well as adding replayablity.

So, I thoroughly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good who-done-it with a political/ sci-fi twist. 100% a decent little game!

I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

About the game:
- You're an operator of a massive surveillance system named Orwell. 
- You spy on people's private life to investigate a bombing scene and prevent another disasters.
- Orwell is just a tool to find correlation between data fed on it. You're responsible for feeding it with correct and relevant data. GARBAGE IN GARBAGE OUT!
- You will often find many contradictive/conflicting data. That's your call to decide which one to fed on Orwell.
- Once it's in Orwell, you can't take it back.
- Orwell will only starts collecting more data source when there's enough evidence data provided by you.


Personal thoughts:
- The game is pretty short, but can be longer if you read everything. Mine was around 4hrs of gameplay, with a lot of skimming.
- The real thrill starts around chapter 3. [spoiler]When people start realizing they're being spied[/spoiler]
- It's basically a highly interactive visual novel. The deciding/branching factor is on the conflicting data. You decide which one is true.

Though this game is (like some bad voices say) a drag and drop simulator, it is amazing. It is fascinating how everything branches out just by searching evidence in texts, conversations, phone calls, things they do on their PC etc..

Orwell... What can I say... 
I went into Orwell knowing that information quickly becomes a rabbit hole... but I did not think it would become as deep as it became. Every choice, Every action became a thing that you regret. I would liken Orwell to any big name company out there, collecting information, creating a profile then using it for advertisements but this shows what that concept could become.

In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

Long story:

This can be an exciting game if you're not one who likes nitpicking. However, if you do (which is maybe why you're drawn to it in the first place), you will pull some hairs out in rage and discontent.

The game focuses on monitoring an increasing set of data (news, websites, chat logs, phone calls etc) to look for leads in a specific case on which the game is built up. Whatever the game means is relevant will be highlighted, and you'll have the choice to either submit it to the investigators or ignore it. The info will also be rewritten, i.e. concentrated to what the game thinks it means.

This poses two problems - 1) the data YOU might think is highly relevant or more relevant isn't highlighted. And 2) the data you find may not be the data that will be submitted. For example, someone SUGGESTS to someone else that they do something. If you submit it, it's altered to say that the person PLANNED it. When talking about a crime that may or may not have occurred, this is a very important difference. Casually suggesting something and planning it is not the same. Everything you submit will be used by the police to decide which actions to take, so you might want to ignore that piece of info then.. if you can (explained further down).

Sometimes you find "contradicting info", and you can only pick one of the contradicting pieces (or ignore them altogether, of course). Sometimes these pieces of information don't contradict each other, but you still have to pick only one.

The game follows a story, and some key facts are needed in order to move it along. Once in a while you experience that the game doesn't progress, apparently because it won't continue until you've provided a key "fact" in the story. So you'll have to go through the stuff you ignored and guess which one the game wants you to submit before moving on. And yes, sometimes that includes incorrect information. Which causes rage quitting on my part, because the whole point of you making sure facts are provided is taken away.

The developers should have points for making a complex story and managing to implement this as a game - the way they have made it both simple, complex and engaging should be praised, as well as the psychological profiles of the suspects, showing how easily having inner access to their thoughts without having the proper context can lead to false conclusions. But the lack of preciseness and logical snafus in the interface makes what could have been an interesting take at the pros and cons of the surveillance society into a silly, semi-intellectual murder mystery for the masses.

A story-based game, played through a browser-like interface with the mouse. You play an investigator, picking through emails, web histories, phone calls and the like, investigating a group of potential terrorists. 

The storyline was engaging. The stylised interface was easy to use and the core mechanic of reading articles and picking the interesting points out of them was more fun than it sounds. The graphical style seemed fresh and exciting. I enjoyed the "1984" references.

The downsides are that the game is quite short, with low replayability due to its story-based nature. The story itself, while largely good, was missing a decent twist at the end. Unfortunately the characters were completely unlikeable, which meant I had little empathy with any of them.

The game itself seems designed to make you think about surveillance. It probably does, but the game itself is probably too opinionated to be objective.

Having said that, I enjoyed playing it and found it three hours well spent. It's worth the budget price, and the fact there's few similar games makes it worth playing.

If you all haven't heard of Orwell I recommend checking out the trailer and then playing the demo. Its sorta like Papers, Please if it was set in modern times and instead of letting people into a country you are looking for a terrorist. There parts of the game that make you think about how much can people really get to know you online without ever having to meet you. The game is so beautiful and I highly recommend it.

Orwell is a fun, engaging, clever, brilliant, unique game that I would say is a mix of L.A. Noire, Her Story, Papers Please, and a touch of Telltale Games thrown in.

You go about solving a main crime which, along the way, you will discover a group of characters--all suspects. You do this by examining, accessing, reading through, and hacking into many different kinds of online resources (this would be the 'Her Story' aspect of it: A game where you get bits of the story unlocked, piece by piece and out of order, over time). As you go on, you will learn more and more about the suspects and characters and you need to try to figure out what information is relevant and what is not. What points of info is truth and what is false. What bits of knowledge and writings and conjectures are sarcasm or jokes and what is being said with true belief.... (the LA Noire side of it). Can you read between the lines and use logic and intuition to decide what will help you with the case and what may NOT be so smart to share with the database? 
You see, what you share with the database is totally up to you. This is the TellTale Game and Papers, Please side of it... in Papers, Please, you had the option, sometimes, to break the rules or turn your head to things based on what you believed to be morally right or true..or even just due to personal hunches or gut feelings.  What you choose to forever put into the database will affect the story, characters, and outcomes in a big way...there are multiple ways things could play out depending on if characters are free, in jail, or even killed. Sometimes you even have choices to make in the spur of the moment. Events that will happen in a few minutes (in game time) that you can either stop or allow to happen to see how things play out.


...but once you choose to document something into the database, the die is cast and you must live with your choices and  then all you can do is sit back and watch things play out and hopefully not live to regret how it all turned out.

Would strongly recommend.
An amazing game, go in blind for the best possible results.

Orwell shows the incredible power and usefulness of mass surveillance while also challenging the player to think about the negative repercussions on personal privacy and freedom of thought. It must have been difficult to create such an excellent game-ified depiction of the abilities that mass surveillance grants nation states. I couldn't stop playing and ended up spending 5 hours plowing right through my first playthrough. There is enough detail to make the characters believable, and there is enough information that actually conflicts to make you question the motives of the characters as if they were real people who potentially know that they're being spied on.

The story is well-written and can play out many ways - I only got 50% of the achievements from a single playthrough. I really enjoyed the Thought blog posts and would love to see them posted outside of the game as promotional material, because the ideas contained within them are quite profound!

I highly recommend this game to everyone, whether you have some technical background or none at all. The ideas contained within this game should be shared with all.

Cons:

[h1]Short, simple and yet so very much worth it.[/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] places the player in a role of an investigator for a mass surveillance system of the same name. After being assigned a case, the investigator's job is to gather information related to it using means provided by the system - relevant websites, private chats and so on. Information gathered is passed along to an 'adviser' who provides feedback and proceeds with other actions if necessary.

[u]The gameplay itself is rather simplistic.[/u] Shortly put, it consists of a lot of reading and putting highlighted information into the system (with a mere hold'n'drag method), though some of the data may conflict with each other and it will be up to the player to decide which information is correct. I do agree with those who say that [u]the mechanics could be improved[/u], as there is only a small amount of any form of detective work for the player to perform and some may feel like their hand is being held way too often. I should definitely mention though that [u]your choices do matter and influence the story.[/u]

Since I have mentioned it, it would be unforgivable not to say that [u]I found the story incredibly engaging[/u]. The [u]high-level of character development[/u] kept on working me over and over, changing how I feel about specific characters, making me alternate between love and hate for them, leading me on thinking I might have figured out the bad guy only to be presented an even more attractive suspect. 
One bad thing about it? [u]I completed the game in about four hours[/u], which is a liiittle bit short..

[u]The art style itself is very appealing, something which can also be said about the soundtrack[/u] (though do keep in mind it's meant to serve as background music - don't expect high energy or colourfulness!)

I don't think I would be too far off if I called [i]Orwell[/i] a novel which slowly unfolds itself before the player. In my opinion [u]it is a really great experience[/u] and [b]the developers released a demo version[/b] - make sure to play it to see if the game is for you! If you still have your doubts, which are very much understandable due to the simplistic gameplay, consider getting it on sale. It's worth it.

The game is overhyped - all those fanboys are probably carried away by the topic of mass surveilance.
Although the game looks good on screenshots, the gameplay is clumsy, you basically click, drag and drop, click, drag and drop and so on. Sometimes you can influence what's going on by choosing what not to drag and drop, but it is about 5% of the cases - too little.
About half of the characters in the story are not written well.
So stay away from this one, or wait for 50% discount if you are like me - you enjoyed Papers Please and can't believe that something that looks so good can be so unsatisfactory.

Ugh. So this is one of those games I wish Steam had a 'meh' review button for.

It started off strong. I really was hooked on my first playthrough. The concept is neat - you really feel like you're in charge of what information gets through and what doesn't. It took me about 3 hours (with reading everything) to get to the end my first time around. I was very disappointed it was so short - primarily because I honestly thought that there was going to be more than one case to investigate. Yeah - not the case.

Since I'm an achievement whore, I started another run through. This is where the game completely fails. It has, in my opinion, very little replay value. You start to learn that your choices don't actually do much to effect the outcome of the game. You can sort of control what happens to each person based on the information you submit, and occasionally certain things only unlock with certain choices....but other than that the dialogue is very very similar throughout. There is no fastforward button (that I could find) and no back button in case you screw up, which means you would have to completely start over if you mess up a chain of events to get a specific achievement.

It took two more playthroughs (three total) of two and a half hours each (aqain, can't skip ANY dialogue) to finish all achievements (gameplay time is a little higher because I would leave it running while doing other things). I was literally not at all invested in the game at this point because the changes in dialogue/direction are so small that they reduce replay value to nill.

I'm glad I got the game on sale because it's not worth $10, considering how short it is and how little replay value there is due to limitation of choice.

I dunno - the concept is unique and it was fun to play the first time around, so I do recommend it if you're looking for something intriguing to play on a rainy day. But I recommend getting it on sale.

This game is great. It's one of a kind and I love the concept of this game. Great story and very interesting to play. I'd recommend it to anyone.

An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

Named after George Orwell, the author of the famous dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, comes a game about internet surveillance on potential 'terrorists'. You play the controller of a system called Orwell, sending information you feel is valid to your supervisor. This being a game about omnipresent government surveillance, you will see all manner of personal conversations, photos, bank statements etc. Is it all valid? Is all fair when the person you are investigating is the top suspect in a terrorist attack? What about if they are friends with the suspect? What about if they are a relative?

Much in the vein of Papers Please. this game will take your moral compass for a spin. I come from the UK, the soon-to-be Internet surveillance capital of the world. Orwell was a startling and interesting look into the world of surveillance. Can it be misused? Or can the use of it be justified? Yes and yes. This game did a miraculous job of showing you both sides of the argument with an interesting story to boot.

Orwell has the bones of a great game but falls short in a few areas.  The game handholds you by highlighting the information you need throughout the game.  This would be fine if there were negative consequences for uploading irrelevant information.  But, you end up with a game comprised of clicking and dragging highlighted information to the correct profile.  This makes the game into more of a guided story.  One other complaint I have is how you cannot replay episodes on the same profile.  If you want to replay an episode, instead of giving you the option of loading a save file, you are forced to start a new game.  I guess this enforces the idea that your actions have impactful and lasting consquences, but it really comes off as more of an annoyance.

Having said all that, I did enjoy the game.  Fans of this genre or fans of "police state"-themed games will also find Orwell to be an enjoyable experience.  But, I cannot recommend the game to a broader audience unless either more content is added or a replay/save option is implemented.

EDIT: The developers have subsequently added a rewind feature.  Therefore, with my biggest complaint being rectified, I must change my recommendation from No to Yes.

Your mission is to "pilot" the test version of Orwell, a program that can monitor EVERYTHING on the internet - may it be mail, chat conversations, phone conversations, what files you've got on your computer, forums, medical records and ... yeah, a whole lot more. There has been a terrorist attack, a monument has been blown to smithereens and some people has been injured during the attack. The CCTV notices a woman prior known to the police and the first assignment is to find information about her, pinning her to the attack.

Gameplay wise, you're placed within a glorified web browser, more or less. To the left you have a profile and a map for all the known persons and their connections. To the right, you can read articles on the internet, chat conversations and all that good stuff. Then you drag the valuable information to the left panel and the story goes along.

If you like games such as Papers, Please, you may like this. There's a lot of story but it's also very dystopian. You could almost say it's a detective/mystery game, but then again, not. It's somewhat short, but it's one hell of a interesting ride, to put it that way. There's also some replayability, which makes it so I'll play it at least once more in the future, to get all the achivements and then see what'll happen when I choose to gather different information.
