Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

Orwell is a difficult game to review.  You work as a member of a surveillance system and your task is to identify who is responsible for a bombing that happened on the city and why. I don't normally write reviews, but felt I had to give a thumbs up to this one!

While it is undoubtedly largely linear, and it's more of an experience rather than a game, I was surprised how much - all logic aside - that I felt swept into the narrative and felt like I was having influence over things. There were a couple of times I even closed the game and went away to reflect. This game really is immersive.

To that end I'd recommend playing it in one or two sittings, and really investing into the experience. Put your earphones in and submerge yourself. Because by the end even though I know it's linear I feel like I've created the outcome. And I forget all the individual points I did, it just adds up in my mind that I had lots of control over the outcome.

What I also like is that for a game that could be heavy handed - and the name Orwell is hardly subtle - it was very nuanced. Not all the time, but the most part it had very good restraint. I also like that no one comes across as very good - it's all shades of grey and right up until the end it's muddy decisions and muddy outcomes. I don't feel I've won, I just feel I've made a decision and now I will live with it.

Grumbles are minor... your 'colleague' is often annoying, and spoon feeds you a bit too much. Information that is relevant in one context is dismissed out of hand another, which does at times snap you back to its linear nature. Chat sessions also keep moving when you're trying to read them at a different point in the thread - a small fix there would be welcome.

But great production values and style add to the polish to the game, and I highly recommend it.

Anyone with a Facebook page should play this. Great commentary on the age of the internet where privacy may very well be just an illusion we feed ourselves. It's also an interesting twist on the idea of a power fantasy. You don't have big guns or magic powers, you have personal information of everyone at your finger tips. And information is power no?

Be prepared tho for a somewhat guided experience. To keep the story in line, there are only chosen lines of text that you can pick out, but you still have the power to pick whether or not you include some of them. Main issue I have with this otherwise smart game is that it's a little difficult to keep track find data you chose to not pick out because you previously thought it wasn't relevant. And it's kinda hard to tell what data will move the story forward vs what is data that you can leave out to change the outcome.

Cons:

-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

What to say about this game....

You play as a loyal outsourced investigator for "The Nation", and their new security program called Orwell.  The Orwell program is essentially surveillance designed to "keep the people of the Nation safe."  You investigate a group of individuals in an attempt to determine the culprit of a series of terrorist attacks.  Armed with the most invasive software at your disposal, you use every tool to spy on, and hopefully locate, all of the responsible parties.

Personally, it took me some time to get past the eerie feeling that what I was doing to spy on the lives of these virtual people wasn't too far off from what's probably been taking place in the world for a number of years.  This aspect of the game alone can make you feel almost uncomfortable with what you are doing.  However, your contact within Orwell does well, reminding you that what you are doing is for the safety of all.

The game itself, while it is a reading game at heart, does a really good job of pulling you in.  There are plot twists galore, and the game leaves you wanting to see the next piece of information you can dig up.

TL;DR - If you enjoy a dystopian setting, and enjoy reading-intensive games/mysteries, then I think you'll enjoy this game.  It is a short game; only a few hours, but it is definitely worth a few bucks.  I personally hope that they can use this to make a sequel of some kind.

To those who know the references and like the source material this game is based off of, this is perhaps the best Big Brother/Orwellian Surveillance system simulator I've seen so far, and is well worth the price its asking for. 

Fans of Papers, Please will probably enjoy this game just as much. Except instead of being the Border Crossing Guard, think of yourself as the Investigator for their Surveillance Corps.

Its a short game, sure, you can beat it once probably within 4 hours, but it does have some replayability (plus the fact that there is no hard save points, the game constantly saves after everything you do with no way of going back outside of making a new profile, so it forces you to choose wisely). To me, the shortness is forgiveable for how much this game costs (which isn't much).

The writing is amazing for it being a game with only written dialogue, the characters feel real and individual and you're the spider trying to weave out the web of how they fit into the plot that's going on. It also does a great job of getting you into the role of being an Investigator of a secret service public spying agency, you feel as if you're in the game just as much as any of them at times.

The art style is consistent and works for the game that this is, but IMO they could have had clear photos and models and you would have had the same game, this style merely gives it a more individual feel rather than it being like any other game like this.

The gameplay is simple, but great if you're into investigative puzzle-solving.

The music is very good for eliciting responses and making you feel certain emotions at particular times, as its supposed to, though IMO it moves a little too fast at times in transitions. You're often left with an abrupt music cue and wondering "What the hell, what did I just find?" before you can properly read what found. But otherwise its good.

Only encountered one bug at the very end of the game where it froze and looped the last second or two of the music track I was listening to, and I had to exit out with alt-tab, but I had beaten the playthrough by that point so it wasn't a huge deal.

All and all, a great game for the price its asking for, and if you're a fan of the type of genre this is.

A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

I absolutely recommend this game wholeheartedly; it's been over a year since I've been this immersed and emotionally invested into a game.  The game makes a point, but it's never heavy-handed about it; I really appreciate that, since too many stories of this nature is ruined by the author's soapbox.  The short pool of characters, and the fact that you are digging into aspects of their lives, learning information that they wouldn't tell anyone else, results in a special level of investment in the world.

It's nice to see a game where your choices do actually matter; the story branches out depending on what you do.  And while it does follow the same parallels, and generally tie back into itself at the end, it's not in such a way that negates the choices you've made up until that point.  The link between your choices and the results is usually sensical, and generally tied to how diligent you are in the game as opposed to needing a guide or crystal ball.  Usually, anyways; there is one situation where doing an objectively better job leads to an objectively worse result and (to me) felt like it should have been avoidable if I had just done better, but nope.  It's a fly in the ointment, but it's not bad enough to spoil the obvious care that's gone into this game.

There are a couple more minor niggles here and there; for example, I wish the game made it more clear that the information above a submittable piece of information is exactly what gets added, as opposed to a summary.  Relatedly, make it clear that they act on the information given without outside context.  This being unclear at the beginning tripped me up a couple times.

It's amazing how internally consistent the game is; nothing happens out of the blue, and if you look back (or on a second playthrough), you can see the events in retrospect.  The in-game rules aren't broken, either.  It's actually rather impressive.

The only major downside I can think of to the game is the general lack of replay value.  The first time through, you'll probably take about five hours or so.  The second time would be to go back and see everything as it occurs with the benefit on knowing the truth, plus more achievements.  Another playthrough or two after that to mop up achievements, if you really want to.  The game has no way of restarting the current day, or from a previous day, and only has one save file that overwrites itself automatically after every choice you make, so most of your time in subsequent playthroughs will be watching conversations that can't be skipped or sped up.

On balance with the replay value, and the skill and care that went into the game, I'd definitely say it's worth the ten dollar price point.  As I said at the start, it's a game that's had me more enthralled than any game I've played in the last year.  If you like this sort of thing, definitely give it a shot.

Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

Creepy and well-written, Orwell tells the tale of what happens when the state gets unfettered access to your communication data, whether that be from the telephone or the internet. It's very topical, but it should be added that the scope of the access you have makes the recent "Snooper's Charter" in the UK look like lightweight. Nevertheless, your ability to screw with people's lives really hits home, especially when the twist at the end is revealed and all the consequences of your actions - and how misinterpreted data can be overblown - is laid bare.


That said, the game stays rather neutral in its moralising. It's clear the developers are anti-surveillance, as those *for* it would find the moral ambiguity of this game inconvenient, but they are not trying to whack you over the head with ideology. If you decide to come to the conclusion that, despite being messy at times, surveillance is a necessary evil then this game allows you to come to that conclusion. But it's going to push the extremes of what all-encompassing surveillance can do before it lets you come to that conclusion.

And while the politics of this game are clearly unavoidable, Orwell is also a pretty neat detective story, if not very typical. Instead of being in the front line looking for evidence, your sleuthing is invisible, but otherwise it has all the hallmarks of a good whodunnit, including red herrings, characters with strong motivations, and a twist at the end.

I'm not sure what else to say, really. It's pretty good and I happily recommend it.

The game puts you in control of a system that is essenically the worlds largest surveillance system, and not a whole lot of rules of what you can and cannot do. 

The gameplay itself is simple: Find what you need, attach it to the right person. The game mostly holds your hand by highlighting more or less EVERYTHING you can use, and even has a "star" next to a page that still has information you missed. The real trick are the "conflicting" databanks: you can only choose one, and whichever one you choose will determine how the end of the chapter plays out (and certain achievements).

If anything Orwell reminds me of a much more "personal" Papers Please. You are a security person who must go through several people to find out if they are legit or not. Except instead of person after person, its file after file..... and on a much more private scale.

Some people have called this game Orwellian (hell, it's in the name), and likened it to Nineteen Eighty-Four or Papers, Please. Personally, I'd argue its value is far greater than that; Nineteen Eighty-Four was written nearly 70 years ago and Arstotzka is an almost comically totalitarian state, but Orwell is set in what could very easily be any present-day democracy... and feels like it's set in one, too. In Orwell you are not working for glorious Arstotzka or in service to Big Brother, blithely stamping out potential traitors left, right and centre; you and all the other characters you interact with are genuinely trying to protect the people of The Nation from an evidently real terrorist threat. You spend the game trying to do good, trying to protect people, you and the supporting characters agonising over whether this data-gathering is really necessary...

...and then the game makes sure you realise what you've done. Superb.

Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.

I will start off by saying, I am not traditionally a text-based gamer. In fact, I am sure many players of text-games are reading this right now and turning red with giddy, trollish excitement over the prospect of correcting me in that this probably qualifies as another genre.

The game does do something like this at one point - minor spoiler – [spoiler] the amount of datachunks you can upload becomes limited. That means you spend more time agonising over what kind of data you should or shouldn’t upload. Which is great! You can only explore certain paths. It felt way too on rails before this point.[/spoiler]

Putting other constraints like time, far more bad data (maybe having to input data yourself rather than just highlighting and dragging it?) – in essence, raising the interactivity could drastically improve it. What spoils it for me is realising that I was never going to massively fail, I could just scroll through each highlighted source and pick everything out. Her Story had none of the same problems, you were free to explore each narrative in any order you wanted.

Anyway – enjoyed it a lot. Felt more could be done with the format, but a great exploration of how detective narratives can be done, and loved the themes (I felt myself uploading less info to Orwell as I grew more uncomfortable with how invasive it was getting). I look forward to a detective game or something that picks up on the same style.

Orwell is a game developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Surpise Attack Games. Orwell is a compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned. It has an intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode..."

It does have some interesting characters who are easy to become attached to but not for long due to its short story and the game is intellectually satisfying. The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation, basically meaning, it doesn't treat you like an idiot

However, Orwell is a fairly short game, finishing just one story with one ending in 2-3 hours is pretty damn short and currently there are no revising chapters and changing decisions. You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices, however the developers have stated that they will change this in the near future with a patch

Orwell plays similar to a detective visual novel. If you are looking for flashy cutscenes and first/third person character control, then this is not the game for you. You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world. In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story!

Orwell pays homage to one of the greatest writers of all time; George Orwell himself who has created some classic literary works such as Animal Farm and 1984 which this is inspired from!

Orwell is a game that has motivated me to take the time to write a review again, something I have not done in a while.  I'll admit, the title using the name of the author of a favorite book of mine grabbed my attention, and the description of the gameplay was enough to get me to take the plunge during the winter sale.  What followed was several hours spent parsing through the personal data of a group of fictional persons to solve the mystery of a terror attack and to consider the tradeoffs between privacy and security.

Let me start by saying that Orwell is at no point pedantic.  On the very rare occassion a character has been preachy, it was entirley in character for an activist.  This game has you violating privacy in order to achieve a verifiable and practical good; if you are a successful investigator you can literally save lives.  I'd do a diservice to potential players though to say any more than the very vague and cliche question of "At what cost?"

The gameplay is surprisingly interesting and reminded me is a lot of ways of the surprise hit "Papers, Please."  In the not-to-distant future The Party has enacted a new security measure that gathers every scrap of digital information a person could leave.  However, to address internal privacy concerns no one person sees everything and makes decisions.  You play an "Investigator" who has been hired to comb through relevant data as determined by the search algorythims of the Orwell system.  As you read people's emails, chatlogs, and visit their blogs and social media sites you decide what information to pass onto your Advisor.  His role is to determine who merits investigation and draw conclusions from the data you send.  That is to say, the only information the insider in law enforcement is allowed to see is what you deem relevant.  To do your job well you must avoid not only missing relevant data, but oversharing data that could be taken out of context or is irrelevant.  Of course, since it is completley up to you to decide what is relevant, this opens the door to different investigation outcomes I fully intend to explore in future playthroughs, even if I do know the answer to the mystery.

The mystery is also quite enthralling.  I write this review at 3AM, having completed the game in a single sitting of several hours, sucked in by the need to uncover "just one more" piece of the puzzle until suddenly I was furiously not only trying to solve the whole riddle, but making ethical considerations over what I should share or if I should continue to do my job "properly."  If you enjoy a good mystery or if you like very interactive VN-style games like Analogue: A Hate Story (which I also reccomend), then I can't tell you to buy this quickly enough, even if it isn't on sale.  This was a unique and wonderful gaming experience that I am glad I had.

Long story short: I would recommend this game. That being said, I had a lot of criticisms--so forgive me if the rest of this seems self-contradictory. There are plenty of other reviews that thoroughly cover what the game does well. 

After the intriguing trailer, I found the first two episodes dissappointing. The art style was clean and pleasant as expected, but I found the characters to be boring and slightly unlikable, which prevented much investment in the story. 

However, the game does shift as you progress through later episodes--interesting developments, twists, overturned expectations. It wasn't phenomenal, but I did get invested, and found the whole experience ultimately worth purchasing.

My biggest problem with the game--some of it felt like a trudge through data files, rather than the investigative puzzle I hoped for. The few times I was prompted with a high stakes question, where my answer actually mattered, I felt like I had to find the answer through mindless clicking, rather than any logic or puzzle solving. It felt a little pointless, honestly.

In sum, I felt like the game didn't quite live up to its potential--although there were definitely moments where I felt for the characters, and was confronted with the discomfort and ethical ambiguity of violating their privacy. I was put in tense situations, was surprised, and had some control over the course of events. Despite my disappointment in the beginning, I really enjoyed the final episodes. So that's why I would recommend this game--Orwell has a novel premise that was executed fairly well, and it's defintiely an experience worth having.

Theories aside, let me move on to my pros and cons before I bore all of you scrollers:

I shall have to come back and edit this review after more playing/when I'm not sleep deprived but right now I just felt the need to post my first ever Steam review because this game has really grabbed me like nothing else.

Downloaded Orwell on a whim about 4 hours ago, opened it and thought I'd have a look whilst I readied myself for bed. Four hours later, I'm lying here in the same position clutching my laptop, heart racing from endless twists and turns and from surprisingly genuine moments of fear. 

Story and characters are well done - I found myself having biases towards/against certain characters and so was very shocked when things didn't work out as I'd expected. The way the player is brought into the game towards the end is also excellent - you feel like your choices matter and as if you are actually under threat. Details of characters' lives were interesting to explore, and I thought the conversation felt pretty real (unlike in many other games where transcripts of conversation are robotic and plainly fake). The game may be based around looking for bits of evidence in conversation/documents a la 'Papers, Please' but this is infinitely more gripping with none of the drab routine that I sometimes find a little tiring in PP. 

Of course, as a bit of a George Orwell fan, I was probably predisposed to enjoy this - and there are many 1984 references scattered throughout which will be provide amusement for fans of his work. The design/interface is very pleasant - very modern but not overly so in a way that makes it sci-fi; one of the scary things about 'Orwell' is how realistic this dystopia really is. If you care to let it be, this game is a very interesting and thought-provoking way to consider the ethics of state surveillance. I happen to have gone into playing with a very strong opinion on the issue but I think the game is well balanced in the way it allows you to hold any perspective/develop your own opinion (the narrative in the game is such that you could argue both for and against the government-snooper employment of the player). 

Concerns/negatives: I worry that the game is very short - I reached an end after my four hours of feverish play. There would appear to be other endings I can explore so I eagerly look forward to doing that after some sleep, but I don't know how much more there is for me to discover and I guess I'll have to edit this after a bit more exploring. I've achieved a half of the achievementh so there's evidently more to do, but this still is definitely not a game which goes on and on forever (shame - I really didn't want it to end). 



* All of this is written at 5am when I'm rather sleep-deprived after racing through the game so apologies for lack of clarity/usefulness. Tl;dr I really enjoyed this so much. Even if after further exploration I realise there isn't much more to the game, I'm still definitely not sad I parted with ~£7 for this. Would definitely recommend

This game serves as a curious, yet chilling, simulation of what may happen to society as our technology, and deep desire for safety, continue to evolve.  

It starts off simple enough: there's basically been a terrorist attack, and you are the son-of-a-gun assigned to sort through tons of data from all kinds of digital sources, including the internet, emails, and even phone calls, to profile and ultimately make decisions on, people and situations that have far-reaching effects on darn near everything.

This game is not for everyone, as it requires attention to detail, and a keen yet curious mind. Naturally, many will get bored or disappointed quickly, as the game isn't about action but rather the intellectual journey. The sound effects at key moments were a nice touch too.

The theme of the game is very interesting, particulary if you enjoyed 1984 book or like conspiracy theories. Beside that I cannot recomend the game mostly because I find it very simplish for it`s price... it`s just a point and click on web pages, some kind of modern read tale where you  can make choices by selecting bunch of data from websites.

In [i]Orwell[/i], you are an investigator, employed by a nondescript democratic nation to dig through news, intercepted communications, websites, and personal computers in order to unravel a mystery.

It's not a simulation so much as an interactive story, with several routes to the end, and several possible fates for many of the characters.

Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terrorist attacks. Your job is solely to go through a heap of modern-day data, everything from standard phone numbers, police files and bank account details, through to more dubious emails, blogs and social media posts. Collecting information, looking for clues, flagging any possible suspects and chasing them down.

You can decide how much of the information you want to sift through as the data chunks are highlighted in blue and easily stand out. There are five episodes in total with each one structured as a ‘day’ and the gameplay will be on average one hour per episode.

A lot of effort went into creating the content for [i]Orwell[/i] and it is really impressive. It’s simple but fun with unexpected twists along the way. Orwell is an excellent experience.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Fascinating Story
- Convincing characters and plot
- Impactful choices and discoveries
- Complex and Innovative
- Fitting soundtrack

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Text logs of phone conversations feel unnatural

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

AN ACHIEVEMENTS REVIEW

-------------------------------------------------

Here's a review of the my experience while earning the achievements that you might find useful:

[b]It took me 3 full playthroughs to unlock 100% of the 27 achievements.[/b] At the moment, [spoiler]with some chapter(s) having 3 different endings - but most having 2[/spoiler], it is impossible to earn them all in any less than 3 playthroughs and you are guaranteed about 7 to 9 or so just by playing the 5 episodes in full once. [b]It took me 6 hours to complete the entire game[/b], genuinely following along and reading the content as a normal person would. The next playthrough was significantly less time at 4 hours, and even less on my last run: 2.5. Even if you aren't mindful of the achievements as you progress - say, you ended up missing a lot of optional things - you can still achieve 100% within 3 playthroughs in total; no worries.

My only gripe with this game is that after playing it once, your interest in the story drops considerably, and starting a new game can feel like "[i]going through the motions.[/i]" [spoiler]Even despite the changes in the story that occurs at the end of each episode due to your decisions, you can expect most of it will be the same across your 3 playthroughs, with the exception being a couple of episodes. I won't specify which, because that would spoil the experience...[/spoiler] Nonetheless, if you're patient in your first gameplay and take the time to remember a lot of things, you can easily speed through the last 2 runs. Alternatively, you may even choose to start 3 games simultaneously and finish them together (by completing an episode each, saving/quitting, and loading the next).

It did not push me at all not to cooperate with the government, it just let a few hints slip - like "We had to change the facts a bit to prevent panic" - sure, that's not a big deal, it's just the beginning, the first little white lie that ends in a dogma.

The best job Orwell does is making you feel helpless and powerfull all at once - only you know the whole story, you choose what Orwell knows and what it does not, you can set someone up or you can set them free but ultimately, you never know what the Agent is going to do...will he misinterpret the data and send someone to prison? Will he understand the reason you upload certain information? He never sees the "bigger picture", or the part of it that you have access to.
Are the people getting hurt really not on your conscience; did you JUST do your job? Are you really as impartial as you fancy yourself to be? What if it was your life being dissected?

Pros:
- The achievements are super clever in execution. They help to illuminate where the stories diverge, making your second playthrough a charming foray through a new line of consequences.
- You can literally choose between being a benevolent buddy and a snitching tyrant. You decide the fates of these characters. It's a pretty heady power trip.
- The music cues, while a little hokey, are still a nice touch.
- This game doesn't use typical time restraints. It's not a rush to the finish line. You choose when to end the day. Together with the music, it's a more laid-back atmosphere.

Cons:
- The interface is a little unweildy. Trying to sift through the character web gets super annoying when swapping back and forth between individual storylines.
- The experience is super streamlined, so there's really very little point in another playthrough after you unlock all of the achievements.
- This game likes to hold your hand. It literally tells you which pages are important to progressing the story. It has a predefined arc that refuses to progress until you upload the right piece of information. Really takes away any illusion of organic play.
- The act 5 reveal literally comes out of nowhere.

Conclusions: it's a deeply flawed game and it's not for everybody. But for the right person, it's well worth the price of admission, especially if it's on sale.

8/10 - A compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned
+ Intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode, sleep is not THAT important..."
+ Interesting characters who are easy to become attached to
+ Intellectually satisfying.  The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation.  It doesn't treat you like an idiot (which I can appreciate)

- Fairly short game play (Start to finish is roughly 5-7 hours)
- Currently (Dec 5, 2016), no revising chapters and changing decisions.  You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices (developers have stated that they will change this in the near future).

Note that this game plays similar to a detective visual novel.  If you are looking for flashy cut-scenes and first/third person character control, this is not the game for you.  You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world.  In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story.

After vaguely remembering this from a crowdfunding site whose name escapes me, I went into this game feeling like it would be a copy of the hacker simulators of the early 2000s, but I was pleasantly surprised.

I love this game. Not because of "social commentary" (Which is eerily close to what might be going on) Not because of the art style, or anything like that. But because that this is a game that, in a long while, made me feel like my choices really mattered. That a simple click and drag could mean either saving countless lives, or ending them. It made me feel like I was THAT guy behind that desk in a government building, torn between two choices, either ruining a life, or completely ignoring one. And when I realized that I had been chasing the wrong person the entire time, I felt like a failed detective, who chased that big case his entire life, only to be let down. 

No other game I have ever played, has made me feel like this. It really made me think about the choices I made, and also gave me 20/20 hindsight. And for $6, you can't go wrong with this captivating story. I never thought that I would be dragged into a game like this again after playing other mind-fuck games, but in all honesty, this game doesn't quite do that. It takes you to dinner first, then when you least expect it, you start to get drowsy, and you wake up in a daze at the end of this story, wondering what happened, and what went wrong. And oddly... you want to do it again.

I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

[h1]Review:[/h1]
The most terrifying part of Orwell is just how easily its events could come to pass in our own world. George Orwell himself could not have predicted the level of surveillance we all voluntarily subject ourselves to by keeping always-listening, always-tracking smart devices on our persons, in our cars, and in our homes. It doesn’t take a lot of imagination to see a system such as the one portrayed in the game being used by a real nation, especially since we know the United States already conducts mass surveillance in a multitude of ways.


Orwell (the game) did an excellent job keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout its entire duration. Even though you only interact with them (or rather, their information) through a screen, it was hard not to feel connected to the characters. Whether that connection is based on sympathy or a desire to lock them up is up to you.


The game lends itself well to multiple playthroughs in order to achieve different endings, and there are tons of different ways to get to those endings. However, by the second or third time the first few chapters begin to feel very repetitive. I often found myself checking my phone while waiting for in-game conversations to finish so I could decide which chunks of data to grab. There is tons of interesting stuff to read in Orwell, but it would be nice to skip past some dialogue when I’ve already read it three times.


The length of the game really surprised me. For $11 I didn’t expect as much story and detail as I got. While it only took me about 6 hours my first time through, and I can definitely go through quicker now if I wanted, looking over all of the great little details that have been thrown in definitely takes time. That’s not a bad thing, as Orwell’s realism is only helped by how believable its characters (and their social media profiles, emails, and phone calls) are.


This is definitely a great game, and it was an awesome surprise when I discovered it while browsing the web one day. Be warned, though - after you play you’ll often find yourself thinking about your online conversations, and if something you said years ago (or even yesterday) could somehow be used to incriminate you.

Orwell is absolutely Orwellian, but for any literature nerds like me out there, this isn't like an adaptation of 1984 or Animal Farm or even Homage to Catalonia. But The Nation, the central society that the game takes place in, is an Orwellian state. Someone's always watching. In this case, it's you. An act of terror has been committed, and it's up to you to sift through blogs, emails, telephone calls, texts, photos, even remote-accessing citizen's computers in order to find out whodunnit. Esentially, you ARE Big Brother. Similarly to Papers, Please, you work for the system. But that's where the similarities stop because Orwell is visually stunning, with an intuitive interface and in-your-face consequences for your actions.

I've played every dystopian, utopian, cyberpunk, post-cyberpunk, pre-cyberpunk, and anything that even sounds like cyberpunk game I could get my hands on, and this is easily in the top five percent. Orwell allows you the freedom to choose what kind of observer/reporter you'll be. Will you try your best to do what's right by the Nation? Will you use your position on the inside to help the resistance? The choices can be subtle - I found myself making honest mistakes, people going to prison who didn't deserve it or worse. And what's equally intriguing as what's in Orwell is what is implied - the type of society you're observing, her inhabitants. There's a lot of reading, but it establishes a base for a complex and interesting world. If I had to fault it, it would be on replayability. You're allowed to explore so much and the resolution is so memorable that I can't imagine being as surprised again. Even so, I immensely enjoyed my playthrough.

Orwell is a fun and unique game. You play as a government agent tasked with investigating a terrorist attack, it is your job to act as a gatekeeper between the personal information of those under investigation, and the agency that will act on your information. Through this role you can filter out incorrect information (or pass it on), color your employer's perceptions of those under investigation, and ultimately, play a hand in their fate. The game has you make multiple choices that affect the outcome of future episodes, and decide what endings will be available to you. Don't let the demo fool you, it doesn't stay linear for long. One playthrough is fairly short(~4-5 hours for me), but it has some good replay value if you make different choices the second, third, or fourth time around.

Orwell is a story-based experience, along the same vein as Papers, Please. You play as a citizen, recruited by a country called The Nation, to help spy on their citizens for possible criminal activities. You use a program, called Orwell, to spy on people's emails, phone calls, computers, or anything else that may help you in your investigation.

You submit information to Orwell, called Datachunks, which can help or hinder your investigation - some are useless and others are very useful bits of info. The gameplay consists of you scouring though social media feeds and other information to try and find suspects involved in a bombing - then submitting those datachunks to Orwell where a 3rd person, named Symes, interprets your findings. Because of this nature, it's possible many things you submit will be out of context and Symes may think the information more dangerous or important than it appears.

In short, Orwell is an intruging experience where the player is constantly questioning the validity of such a spying system and as a player you have to make some important choices indeed. Do you withhold information because these people are not dangerous at all? Perhaps you submit faulty information to get Orwell off the trail? Or do you be a good citizen and help The Nation find these terrorists?

I'd recommend Orwell for those looking for a rich story experience. If you liked Papers, Please or Telltale games, this should definitely be up your alley.

Orwell has you performing surveillance on citizens of The Nation to ameliorate and defend against terrorist threats. 
The plot is compelling and is currently made up of five episodes, which altogether will take the average player around 2 hours to complete.
Unusual in it's gameplay mechanic, Orwell asks you to collate data about subjects (or targets) from the internet; using sites similar to Twitter, Facebook and blogs, you submit information to The Nation which allows it's security service to act. 
Information found and submitted is dependant on you, the human factor - decide to omit a vital piece of information, or include a misleading fact and you will influence what happens next.

Okay first off, I just finished the game for the first time through, so I can only speak to the progression of the game through my single experience. 

What an entangled, involved, deep ride it was! All the minor and major bits of plot and character development... left me speechless. When I first got into this game, I was hopeful that it wouldn't be a flimsy investigative journalism style that left gaping holes in character development in favor of quick story progression. So with endless red herrings, conflicting information, tiny bites (bytes?) of data that all weave together, I very quickly became engrossed in finding out everything I could, and frequently found myself at odds with my own judgments and thoughts based on what the information was telling me. 

The atmosphere of the game is sober, at times haunting, and at times pulse quickening depending on what's going on. And I think that this is very much appropriate for the moral of the story. This is invasive, what the player is forced to do... to get this job done. It spends time and effort bringing the player from one side of the spectrum to the other in terms of how helpful or hurtful a surveillance system like Orwell can be. 

In the end, or at least the end of the story I found... I was left with a feeling of completion... ... and thoughtfullness. Yes it's a game, but it has a very real moral message in it, that when the end credits roll make you really consider the implications of our REAL digital lives, and how easy it is to comb through and assemble these very damning dossiers. And how dangerous that could be if the 'powers' that be decided to use it as a means of control and 'protection'. I haven't reacted to a game in this way in a long time... so it bears a review.

Orwell is a very unique experience. It puts you in the role of a beta tester for a new peice of software that allows for total monitoring of the populus. You work with an employee of the company that developed the software and look into clues via many different methods of investigation (web browser, hacking into PCs, monitoring text chats & phone calls, etc.). You get to choose which peices of information go into the report taht is sent to the company - which then makes decisions on how to react to that information - so it adds an element of choice that is intersting and most scenarios are not morally clear. Without going into too much detail on the story, the representation of your "big brother" monitoring techniques is very well done and makes you feel like you are blending the line between helping keep the country safe and violating their right to privacy. It has some pretty emotional outcomes and definately does a great job making you care about the choices / really feel the outcomes. Again, nothing quite like it. A great game to experience. In Orwell, you are the operator of the super software that can trace every citizen digital information, and you are after  a terrorism activist group called Thought who plans to disrupt society safety through violent manifests. Then reason behind it is fear for government peeping your personal life a la NSA/Edward Snowden case. 

My thoughts

The Detective Hacking game mode made me to instant purchase Orwell game, as it combines two of my favorites genres. However it turned out to be VERY frustrating to me.

Slow pacing: I did not expect this game to be in pace with some freaky japanese action game, however what I felt is that they tried to compensate this short game with a slow pace of events combined with tons of wall texts for you to read, search, and try to link pieces with terrorisms acts. You will spend a lot of minutes reading dialogues, text messages, emails, even facebook posts lol, and others stuff, to figure out who is who, and where to go next.

Story: It has only one mainplot, no additional stages or cases, which made me judge the worthness of this purchase. The plot is short, and again, what made it last 9 hours are a bunch of useless information that visually polluted the game, and contributed barely nothing to the storyline. You spend most of your time digging useless information that sometimes take you to nowhere and suprisingly to the next part. One example, how the US gov do not even know a US citizen full name, dob, place of work? Any normal citizen could just Google them to figure out, however you find yourself stuck into finding this information no matter what! (lol) In the beginning there was some air of suspense about some terrorism acts suspects, however at the end... it was pretty lame the way it turned out. And what is even sadder is that in the end you are not in control of how the game ends, so choices don't really matter. After finishing Orwell, you can only describe this game as a Visual Novel game, and not a Detective Hacking game.

The first moment I saw a gameplay of Orwell on YouTube, I was intrigued. I played first episode myself and instantly bought full game. I regret nothing.

The closest genre, Orwell could belong to, is adventure games. Keep in mind it is not a typical Point and Click or Telltale-style adventure game. In Orwell you are a user of the application called Orwell. Your job is to find all information on the internet connected to a suspect - Facebook, blogs and MySpace included. All of Orwell the game is a simple interface of the Orwell the application. That's it - no HP bars, EXP or equipment. You - the player - feel deeply connected to the plot. [b]Immersion[/b] is very strong with this game and is used very, very smart.

Most of the gameplay is reading TONS of text to find crucial piece of information, so you can find your target guilty. Or not. Not all information should be added to the files. You can MAKE someone look guilty, taking their words out of context. You have the ultimate power to judge people based on what you read or heard in conversations.

Game knows what it's doing and does it well. Every episode is well written, plot sticks and hard decisions are not getting any easier. You would be surprised how well Orwell can play on your emotions using only text, highlights and music. I can't say much about story without spoilers but there are several endings based on your decisions.

Tl;dr 
Orwell is a great game following original concept. It stays true to it's goals throughout 5 episodes getting better with each episode. Immersion, choices, dillemas, privacy over security are main aspects of the game. If you like conspiracies, questions about ethics and invigilation, and you like to read a ton of english: you MUST try Orwell.

You don't even really have to read it, unless it's highlighted yellow, and then, generally, only to figure out which of the conflicting statements are most likely to be accurate.

You won't have to expend any brain-power trying to figure out who-dunnit, as your dragging of highlighted text from one box to another will largely do this for you. I never really got the feeling that I was investigating anything. Just dragging sentences from one window to another.

It's very reminiscent of Spycraft: The Great Game, from 1996... though with a much more engaging art style, and far less full motion video. Also, there don't appear to be any failure conditions... so far the plot/investigation largely takes care of itself. At least in Spycraft you could mess up if you didn't investigate the problem properly.

As an interactive story, however, it's engaging and so far pretty cool. This does, however, mean that it's likely to be very linear. I doubt it's going to have much replay potential.

I'd have to say that I'm enjoying it, but I could see it potentially getting old pretty quickly. 

Worth getting, but I'd suggest waiting until it's on sale.

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

After playing Orwell through all five acts, I definitely have to say that this is one fantastic game and I highly recommend it, especially if you enjoy thought-provoking storylines, investigation simulation (like Her Story), and Orwellian dystopian themes.  The best quality about this game is how immersive it is - you're not just a player, you're a major component of the plot and your decisions affect it.  I can't remember the last time a game made me step back and think about how I felt about the situations presented to me, or even reconsider what I thought was the right choice.  

PROS:
- Amazing thought-provoking storyline influenced by dystopian genres such as Brave New World by Aldous Huxley and 1984 by George Orwell.  This game allows you to decide for yourself how you perceive the situations presented to you as well as what decisions you decide to make about them.  
- Unique innovative gameplay that involves surveillance and data mining
- Choices DEFINITELY matter, and not just on an episodic basis, but for the overall plot as well
- Multiple endings, with alternative plot elements that increase replay value
- Fourth wall breakage: you're not just playing the game, you're IN it
- Great soundtrack
- Character development is on point - not only was there development in the people I investigated, but I also felt myself developing as well.  There were multiple points that had me thinking about certain issues presented in the game, reconsidering my decisions, and experiencing many bouts of emotional conflict.  It was awesome.

CONS:
- Lots and lots of reading: if you don't like to read, this game is NOT for you
- There's a few bugs that need to be fixed here and there
- To get alternate endings, you have to make an entirely new profile and start all over.  You can't just "see what happens with other choices" with the same profile you've used to play through the game.  

Overall, for the price, it's a pretty amazing game.  Not only was it thought-provoking, but it was certainly addictive.  The gameplay length is pretty substantial and there's plenty of replay value.  So, yes, I definitely recommend this game.  I have to say this definitely ranks as one of my favorite indie games of all time.

Welcome to Orwellian Big Brother where every action by every citizen of "The Nation" is captured and recorded, and where citizens can be arrested for even the slightest transgression or declaration of anti-Orwell thoughts against The Nation.  You have been recruited by the government as one of its anonymous investigators who must dissect pertinent data and upload this to the government affiliate working with you to prevent a series of terrorist attacks that have been taking place.  Your affiliate can only act on the information you provide (they have no access to the information you have) so your choices matter!

The interface is a joy: very simple and clean, everything very obvious, and the game leads in with a simple tutorial to introduce you to your three tools of Orwell.  On one side of the screen you can open a person's profile to see what information you've gathered on them, and on the other will be their calls messages and mail, with potentially-relevant text highlighted in blue for you to choose whether to add to a person's profile (it cannot be undone if you make a mistake).  You will have to discern who's telling the truth or not, and sometimes you don't have enough information to be 100% sure.  Drag information to a person's profile to attach it to them, and hope you've made the right decision because there is no way to undo this action.

The game would best be described as a combination of simulation, visual novel and point-and-click, but it carries none of the downsides of these games.  Any reading to be done is short, brief and well written, it's really simple to play, and what you can click on is limited to small nuggets of information that the Orwell system deems potentially relevant (and you must decide whether this will help or hinder the government in thwarting the terrorism).  It's not a difficult game, but it's gripping and all too easy to implicate the wrong individual.  At the end I saw the mistakes I'd made.  The best of it is that I somehow suspected that some information was not right as I was playing, but felt compelled to upload it anyway!  My bad!  Replayability is there because there are different outcomes along the way.  The ending is huge but I cannot tell you a thing about it without spoiling the game, but it is worth reaching.

And the soundtrack is amazing.  It's the first time I've ever bought a soundtrack for a game!

If you're unsure, there is a separate playable demo (that's what convinced me to buy the game) and I'm so glad I did.  Yet another great hit for an Indie team who also made the marvellous Hacknet game.  I can't wait to see what Osmotic Studios produce next.

My intention was to write this review after completing the fifth and final chapter after its release. Now that I've completed the game, I feel that I can give this game the review that it deserves. 

I was very, very surprised with how well this game was executed. I've never come across a game quite like this. Orwell is a game where you play as an investigator who is trying to discover the person behind a crime by ruffling through relevant internet posts as well as phone calls, emails, etc. You then send information you deem as relevant to your advisor, who then decides what to do with said information. As I was playing this game, I really felt the pressure on what kind of narrative I was showing to the government and the policeforce regarding the people I was investigating, which is why I believe this game is so brilliant. You really feel the need to think carefully about what things you send out because there is no taking back what you submit once it's out there, which I believe is one of the underlying messages of the game's story. 

I would liken this game to an interactive choose-your-own adventure. Regarding the gameplay, it does not involve much other than reading through files and articles, and clicking to drag data of your choice into the government's database. Certain pieces of information will unlock more articles and files for you to read through. That being said, while I was playing the game these simple mechanics actually helped me stay more immersed in the story. They were uncomplicated and helped my attention stay focused on my "job" and the impact I was having. If your idea of a good game involves more gameplay elements than this, I would not recommend it to you, but if you really enjoy a good story, then please consider giving this game a try. 

Where this game really thrives, I believe, is its attention to detail. The writing in this game is fantastic, as well as the music. The music is mainly ambient, but when you come across important information the music changes dramatically to match the feeling of what you have discovered. The writing paired with the music really kept me at the edge of my seat throughout each episode. I really enjoyed how versatile the writing was as well. The writers managed to create incredibly in-depth characters that each felt very real with their own motives and personalities. At times I felt obligated to protect these people or felt awful about info I might have uploaded about them if it turned out I was incorrect. Without spoiling anything, the writing really makes you think about how people generally show many different aspects of themselves to different people, and as the investigator you have to decipher which "mask" is the way that person really feels or thinks. 

Unfortunately for people who buy the game at this point, you will not be getting the weekly emails to report back to duty  because all five episodes have already been released. These emails really helped me stay immersed in the universe of the game and I really felt like I was reporting back to duty for a job, and I commend the developers for these small touches that added to my immersion in the game. Even though players who buy the game now have access to all episodes at once, I would really recommend taking a break of a day between each episode if you can. I really think it will help you stay immersed in the world. 

Honestly, if you enjoy dystopian stories like 1984 and want to experience an innovative way of playing, you will really enjoy this game. I hope that many people give this game a chance because it will really make you question government security and the things that you post publicly online. I'm going to keep an eye out for more games by these developers because I feel that they are really creating a new, innovative market and I am really excited to see what else they can bring to the gaming industry.

Orwell is a strange game to assess; having conducted several complete playthroughs I would cautiously reccommend the experience and certainly state that it is a well put together game, however, it is not without fault.

Before starting it is worth noting that your role in the game is very restricted, and meant to be, but this leads to frustrating situations wherein important information pertaining to context or inference is only privy to you, and you aren't allowed to present such information to Orwell, it's not your role. This creates a couple of game situations where you the player may be sensibly concluding one thing, but forced to provide information against your better judgement. This however seems intentional and part of the narrative so I don't judge the game poorly for it.

The game itself is politically minded without being pushy, allows for multiple playstyles at crucial moments, and certainly understands the value of consequence. Every choice made in the game is done relatively blindly, and all are irreversable, indeed it's the first thing you are warned of at the start. However with proper foresight and judgement, it is still possible to make correct and sensible decisions that result in an outcome that you desire.

The characters featured feel fleshed out, with rich characteristics and histories that add to a full feeling of an interwoven narrative, and with a plot that utilises these characters well, with innovative twists and character revelations that on a first playthrough are very satisfying.

Overall I would highly recommend this game to the fans of the genre, and to players in general, but I would state that subsequent playthroughs lose a lot of the initial spark, as a great deal of the game is built on tension and a well written narrative.

I just finished the last chapter of this game, and this is what I have to say:
Orwell is a very, very, very, VERY good game. An amazing game! Worth every penny I spent on it! It's nominated for The Game awards 2016, and toatally deserves it.
If you like invastigations, mysteries or investigating mysteries, if you like story-driven games or if yoy simply enjoy stalking people online, I HIGHLY recommend you give this game a try. You will not be disappointed!
The gameplay may feel to simple and the plot too linear at first (I know some people got that first impression), but please hear me out: This first impression is almost as far from the truth as it can get.

Now that you understand how good this game is, let's talk about what this game is ACTUALLY ABOUT :
So, in this game you are playing an investigator for the secret goverment program called "Orwell". Your job as an investigator is, well, to investigate.
How? Well, you have Orwell at your disposal! This program allows you to snoop around in other people's data that can be found online: public data and private data. data that was posted online willingly and data that noone knew even existed on the web. True, useful data and lots of half-truthes, misinterpreted information and straight-out lies. You need to find and gather this data, decide what's right and what's not, and report it.
Watch out, though, once a data chunk has been reported there's no going back - you must commit to whatever you belive the truth and face the consequences.
And believe me - THERE WILL BE CONSEQUENCES. Your decisions can and will affect the lives of tens if not hundreads of people. Maybe even the entire nation.
The story starts right after a bomb was set off in the middle of the city of "Bonton" in the nation called "The nation", (I know, such a good name for a country. Wanna guess what's the name of the prime minister's party? Yup - "The party".) killing many (can't remember the number) civilians and generally making everyone feel a bit worse about everything (What can you expect? A bomb just exploded in the middle of their city...) You start with barely any information - your only clue is that one person - a blue-haired woman - who's known to the police was spotted near the site of the attack just before the explosion.
Now you and your trusty advisor "Symes" must get to the bottom of this attack and try to prevent any future ones from occuring. On your way you will start to uncover many secrets - about your suspect (and the others that may or may not appear later on), about the mysterious group "Thought", and even about the entire nation, it's leaders, and Orwell itself.

Good luck ;)
